questions.stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of low back pain for 3 months and increasing thirst and constipation for 2 weeks. He takes no medications. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL. Serum calcium is 12.8 mg/dL, creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL, and total protein is 9.4 g/dL with a normal albumin. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a narrow spike in the gamma region. A blood smear shows red cells stacked like coins. X-rays of the skull show several round, punched-out lytic lesions.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his increased serum calcium?

options.text: Reduced renal calcium excretion from a thiazide

questions.explanation: Answer: osteoclast activation by cytokines from the tumor cells (multiple myeloma). Why: an older adult with bone pain, anemia, high calcium, kidney injury, a high protein level with an M-spike, rouleaux (red cells stacked like coins), and punched-out skull lesions has multiple myeloma. Clonal plasma cells in the marrow release substances that switch on osteoclasts, which dissolve bone and release calcium into the blood. The same process makes the lytic lesions and bone pain. Light chains clog the distal tubules and injure the kidney. Diagnosis needs at least 10% clonal plasma cells in the marrow, and IgG is the most common M protein (50 to 55%). Newer treatment options include anti-CD38 antibodies, CAR-T cells, and bispecific antibodies.

whyWrong.b: A parathyroid adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism. It would not explain the M-spike, rouleaux, or anemia.
whyWrong.c: PTH-related peptide causes high calcium in solid cancers such as squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. In myeloma, the calcium comes from bone destroyed locally by the tumor.
whyWrong.d: Granulomas in sarcoidosis and other diseases can make calcitriol, which raises calcium. Nothing here suggests granulomas.
whyWrong.e: Thiazides can raise calcium slightly, but he takes no medications.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Multiple Myeloma
MSD Manual Professional: Hypercalcemia

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician because of headaches, blurred vision, and nosebleeds for 3 weeks. He has mild enlargement of lymph nodes and spleen. Funduscopic examination shows widened, sausage-like retinal veins with scattered hemorrhages. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a large monoclonal spike that is identified as IgM. A bone marrow biopsy shows small lymphocytes and plasma-like cells. There are no lytic bone lesions.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his headaches and vision changes?

options.text: Plasma cell tumors pressing on the brain

questions.explanation: Answer: thick (hyperviscous) blood from a large circulating protein (Waldenström macroglobulinemia). Why: an older adult with a monoclonal IgM spike, lymph node and spleen enlargement, marrow full of lymphoplasmacytic cells, and no bone lesions has Waldenström macroglobulinemia. IgM is a large pentamer, so high levels make the blood thick. Slow, sludging flow causes headaches, blurred vision, bleeding from the nose and gums, and swollen retinal veins. MSD Manual calls a MYD88 mutation the hallmark of the disease. Hyperviscosity is treated first with plasma exchange, which removes the IgM quickly, and the tumor is then treated, for example with a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

whyWrong.b: Plasma cell tumors fit multiple myeloma, which causes lytic bone lesions. A mass would not explain swollen retinal veins and nosebleeds.
whyWrong.c: Amyloid deposits can come from light chains, but they do not explain swollen, sausage-like retinal veins and nosebleeds, which come from thick blood.
whyWrong.d: Hypercalcemia from bone destruction is typical of multiple myeloma. This patient has no lytic lesions.
whyWrong.e: Some IgM proteins act as cryoglobulins, but the swollen, sludging retinal veins here are the classic sign of hyperviscosity.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Macroglobulinemia
MSD Manual Professional: Multiple Myeloma

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of headaches and itching all over his body after hot showers for 4 months. He has also had episodes of burning pain and redness in his fingers. He does not smoke and has no lung or heart disease. His face is ruddy. The spleen tip is palpable. Hemoglobin is 19.5 g/dL, hematocrit is 58%, leukocyte count is 13,500/mm3, and platelet count is 610,000/mm3. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: low serum erythropoietin (polycythemia vera). Why: a high hemoglobin with high white cells and platelets, a large spleen, itching after hot water (aquagenic pruritus), a ruddy face, and burning, red fingers (erythromelalgia) in someone with normal oxygen levels is polycythemia vera. The marrow makes red cells on its own because of a JAK2 mutation (V617F in about 90%, exon 12 in about 5%), not because of an erythropoietin signal. The extra red cells shut off the kidney's erythropoietin output, so the level is low or low-normal. Treatment aims for hematocrit below 45% in men and 42% in women by phlebotomy, plus low-dose aspirin. Peginterferon or ruxolitinib is now often preferred when cell-lowering drugs are needed, because hydroxyurea may raise the risk of leukemia.

whyWrong.b: High erythropoietin is the body's normal response to low oxygen, as in lung disease or high altitude, or comes from an erythropoietin-making tumor. In polycythemia vera it is low.
whyWrong.c: Low arterial oxygen would cause a secondary polycythemia. His oxygen saturation is normal.
whyWrong.d: Carbon monoxide exposure, as in heavy smoking, causes a secondary polycythemia without high white cells, high platelets, or a large spleen.
whyWrong.e: Red cell mass is increased in polycythemia vera. A normal red cell mass with high hematocrit would suggest low plasma volume instead.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Polycythemia Vera

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he has been drinking large amounts of water and wetting the bed for 2 months. He also has a scaly, red rash on his scalp. His right eye bulges forward. X-rays show several punched-out lesions in the skull. A biopsy of a skull lesion shows sheets of cells that stain positive for CD1a, CD207 (langerin), and S-100.
questions.leadIn: His excessive thirst and urination are most likely due to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: lack of antidiuretic hormone, that is central diabetes insipidus (Langerhans cell histiocytosis). Why: a young child with lytic skull lesions, a bulging eye, a scaly scalp rash, and excess urination has Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Lytic skull lesions, exophthalmos, and diabetes insipidus form the classic triad. The abnormal Langerhans cells express CD1a, CD207 (langerin), and S-100, and about two-thirds carry BRAF V600E. Diabetes insipidus occurs in 5 to 50% of patients because the cells infiltrate the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk and stop antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release. The disease most often appears between ages 2 and 5.

whyWrong.b: Kidney resistance to ADH (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) comes from kidney or drug causes such as lithium. Here the problem is in the brain.
whyWrong.c: Type 1 diabetes causes thirst and urination from high glucose, but it would not explain skull lesions or a bulging eye.
whyWrong.d: High calcium can cause thirst and urination, but the classic link between this disease and excess urination is loss of ADH.
whyWrong.e: Primary polydipsia is drinking too much from a behavioral cause. The skull and eye findings point to infiltration of the pituitary area.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A has had three bleeds into his knee this year despite factor VIII infusions three times a week. His factor VIII activity is less than 1%. He now has an antibody (inhibitor) against infused factor VIII. His physician starts weekly subcutaneous injections of emicizumab to prevent bleeding.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?

options.text: Bridges activated factor IX and factor X
Releases stored factor VIII from endothelium

questions.explanation: Answer: bridges activated factor IX and factor X (emicizumab). Why: in the intrinsic pathway, factor VIII normally holds activated factor IX next to factor X so that factor X is activated. Emicizumab is an antibody with two arms, one binding activated factor IX and one binding factor X, so it does factor VIII's job. Because it is not factor VIII, inhibitor antibodies against factor VIII do not block it, and it is given under the skin. Hemophilia A is X-linked, accounts for about 80% of hemophilia, and prolongs the PTT with a normal PT and platelet count. Severe disease means factor activity below 1%, and about 30% of patients with severe hemophilia A develop inhibitors. Recent change: other non-factor drugs now act on natural anticoagulants instead, as in options B and C.

whyWrong.b: Lowering antithrombin is how fitusiran works, a different non-factor treatment that removes a natural anticoagulant.
whyWrong.c: Blocking tissue factor pathway inhibitor is how concizumab works, another non-factor treatment that removes a natural brake on clotting.
whyWrong.d: Desmopressin releases stored factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, but it helps only mild hemophilia A, not severe disease with factor below 1%.
whyWrong.e: Blocking complement C5 treats paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and has no role in hemophilia.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hemophilia
MSD Manual Professional: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of heavy menstrual periods since menarche, frequent nosebleeds, and bleeding for a day after a tooth extraction. Her mother has similar symptoms. Platelet count is 260,000/mm3. Prothrombin time is normal, and partial thromboplastin time is slightly prolonged.
questions.leadIn: Further testing is most likely to show a low level of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: von Willebrand factor antigen (von Willebrand disease). Why: lifelong mucosal bleeding (heavy periods, nosebleeds, bleeding after dental work) in a girl whose mother is affected, with a normal platelet count, points to von Willebrand disease. Type 1 is the most common and is autosomal dominant, with a low amount of normal von Willebrand factor. Von Willebrand factor helps platelets stick to injured vessels and carries factor VIII in the blood, so factor VIII falls too and the PTT can be mildly long. Testing measures von Willebrand factor antigen, its activity, and factor VIII. Desmopressin releases stored factor and helps type 1, but it does not work in types 2 and 3 and can worsen type 2B. Other source: your Heme-Onc notes (El-Husseiny, p. 23) list an increased bleeding time for von Willebrand disease. MSD Manual says bleeding time testing is unreliable and no longer done, so expect von Willebrand factor tests instead.

whyWrong.b: Low factor IX is hemophilia B, which is X-linked and mostly affects males with joint and muscle bleeding.
whyWrong.c: Her platelet count is normal, and the bleeding pattern with an affected mother points to a problem with platelet adhesion, not platelet number.
whyWrong.d: Low fibrinogen would prolong both the PT and the PTT, and it is rare as an inherited cause of heavy periods.
whyWrong.e: Low factor VII would prolong the PT, which is normal here.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Von Willebrand Disease
MSD Manual Professional: Hemophilia

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of tiny red spots on her legs and bruises on her arms for 2 days. She had a cold 3 weeks ago and now feels well. She is afebrile. There are scattered petechiae and ecchymoses. There is no lymph node, liver, or spleen enlargement. Hemoglobin is 12.5 g/dL, leukocyte count is 7,800/mm3 with a normal differential, and platelet count is 9,000/mm3. A blood smear shows a few large platelets and no other abnormal cells.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains her low platelet count?

options.text: Pooling of platelets in an enlarged spleen

questions.explanation: Answer: removal of antibody-coated platelets in the spleen (immune thrombocytopenia, ITP). Why: a well child with sudden bruising and petechiae a few weeks after a viral illness, a very low platelet count, and an otherwise normal blood count and smear has ITP. Autoantibodies coat the platelets, and macrophages in the spleen remove them early. The marrow responds by making more, so the platelets on the smear are often large. In children it often follows a viral infection and usually resolves on its own. Treatment, when needed, includes glucocorticoids or IV immune globulin. Recent change: for ITP that persists, options now include thrombopoietin receptor agonists, rituximab, fostamatinib, and rilzabrutinib, and splenectomy is often not necessary.

whyWrong.b: Leukemia would usually also lower the hemoglobin or white cells and might show blasts on the smear. Her other counts are normal.
whyWrong.c: Platelet clumping in small clots is the mechanism of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which also causes hemolytic anemia with fragmented red cells.
whyWrong.d: Consumption from widespread clotting is disseminated intravascular coagulation, which happens in very sick patients and prolongs clotting times.
whyWrong.e: Pooling in a large spleen requires splenomegaly, and her spleen is not enlarged.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
MSD Manual Professional: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)
MSD Manual Professional: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of confusion and slurred speech for 1 day. She has had fatigue and easy bruising for a week. Her temperature is 37.1°C. There are scattered petechiae. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, platelet count is 14,000/mm3, LDH is markedly increased, and haptoglobin is undetectable. A blood smear shows many fragmented red cells (schistocytes). Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are normal. Serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?

options.text: Autoantibody against red cell surface antigens
Consumption of clotting factors in DIC
Loss of complement-regulating proteins on red cells

questions.explanation: Answer: autoantibody against ADAMTS13 (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, TTP). Why: anemia with schistocytes, a very low platelet count, brain symptoms, and normal clotting times is TTP. Most adult cases are caused by an autoantibody that blocks ADAMTS13, the enzyme that cuts very large von Willebrand factor strands. Without it, the long strands catch platelets and form clots in small vessels, which shear red cells and injure the brain. ADAMTS13 activity below 10% supports the diagnosis. The direct antiglobulin test is negative because the red cells are broken mechanically, not by antibody. Severe kidney failure is rare, unlike in hemolytic-uremic syndrome. Treatment is urgent plasma exchange with glucocorticoids and rituximab; caplacizumab is used only rarely. Other source: your Heme-Onc notes (El-Husseiny, p. 16) list fever among the findings, following the classic teaching. MSD Manual says fever does not usually occur, so do not wait for fever to make the diagnosis.

whyWrong.b: Shiga toxin causes hemolytic-uremic syndrome, usually after bloody diarrhea, with prominent kidney failure.
whyWrong.c: Autoantibodies against red cells cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which gives a positive direct antiglobulin test and spherocytes rather than schistocytes.
whyWrong.d: Disseminated intravascular coagulation uses up clotting factors and prolongs the PT and PTT. Hers are normal.
whyWrong.e: Loss of complement-regulating proteins is paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, which does not cause schistocytes with this pattern.

MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Hemolytic Anemia
MSD Manual Professional: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)
MSD Manual Professional: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department because of sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. The uterus is firm and tender. Shortly afterward, she begins oozing blood from her IV sites and gums. Platelet count is 48,000/mm3. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are prolonged, fibrinogen is low, and D-dimer is markedly increased. A blood smear shows a few fragmented red cells.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains her bleeding?

options.text: Consumption of platelets and clotting factors
Antibody destruction of platelets in the spleen
Inherited lack of von Willebrand factor
An inhibitor antibody against factor VIII

questions.explanation: Answer: consumption of platelets and clotting factors (disseminated intravascular coagulation, DIC). Why: placental abruption releases tissue factor into the mother's blood. Tissue factor sets off clotting throughout the small vessels, which uses up platelets and clotting factors faster than the body can replace them. The result is bleeding from many sites at once, with a low platelet count, long PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, and high D-dimer from broken-down clots. Fragmented red cells come from the small clots. Treatment is to fix the cause, here delivery, and to replace what was used up. Factor VIII helps tell DIC from liver disease: it is low in DIC but normal or even high in liver disease.

whyWrong.b: Antibody destruction in the spleen is immune thrombocytopenia, which lowers platelets but leaves PT, PTT, and fibrinogen normal.
whyWrong.c: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT and PTT, but platelets and fibrinogen stay normal and D-dimer is not raised.
whyWrong.d: Inherited von Willebrand disease causes lifelong mucosal bleeding, not sudden bleeding from every site with low fibrinogen.
whyWrong.e: A factor VIII inhibitor prolongs the PTT alone. It would not lower platelets or fibrinogen.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
MSD Manual Professional: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)
MSD Manual Professional: Von Willebrand Disease
MSD Manual Professional: Hemophilia

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of pain and swelling in her left calf for 3 days. She started a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive 4 months ago. Her father had a pulmonary embolism at age 40. Duplex ultrasonography shows a deep vein thrombosis in the left popliteal vein. Later testing shows that adding activated protein C to her plasma does not prolong its clotting time as it should.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of her clotting tendency?

options.text: Factor V resists inactivation by protein C

questions.explanation: Answer: factor V resists inactivation by activated protein C (factor V Leiden). Why: a young woman with a deep vein thrombosis after starting estrogen, with a family history of clots, most likely has an inherited thrombophilia. Factor V Leiden is the most common one. A single change in factor V stops activated protein C from cutting and switching it off, so clotting keeps going. That is why adding activated protein C fails to prolong her plasma clotting time (activated protein C resistance). About 5% of White Americans carry the mutation. It raises the risk of venous clots, especially with estrogen, but it is not a risk factor for arterial clots. A clotting-based resistance assay screens for it, and a DNA test confirms it.

whyWrong.b: Antithrombin deficiency is another inherited thrombophilia, but it would not cause resistance to activated protein C.
whyWrong.c: Prothrombin gene mutation raises the prothrombin level and the risk of venous clots, but the plasma still responds to activated protein C.
whyWrong.d: Lack of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (Glanzmann thrombasthenia) makes platelets unable to clump, causing bleeding rather than clots.
whyWrong.e: Antiphospholipid antibodies cause clots and pregnancy loss, but they do not cause the specific failure of activated protein C to work on factor V.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Factor V Resistance to Activated Protein C (APC)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old African American man is brought to the physician because of fatigue and dark urine for 2 days. Five days ago, he started dapsone to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia. He has mild jaundice. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, reticulocyte count is 7%, LDH and indirect bilirubin are increased, and haptoglobin is low. A blood smear shows red cells that look as if a bite has been taken out of them, and a special stain shows small round inclusions inside red cells.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following pathways is most likely responsible for this patient's anemia?

options.text: Glycolysis at the pyruvate kinase step
GPI anchor synthesis in marrow stem cells

questions.explanation: Answer: the hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) shunt, that is G6PD deficiency. Why: sudden hemolysis a few days after starting an oxidant drug, with bite cells and inclusions of clumped hemoglobin (Heinz bodies), is G6PD deficiency. G6PD is the first enzyme of the hexose monophosphate shunt and makes NADPH. Red cells need NADPH to keep glutathione in its active form, which protects hemoglobin and the membrane from oxidant damage. Without it, oxidized hemoglobin clumps into Heinz bodies, which spleen macrophages bite out of the cells. G6PD deficiency is X-linked and affects more than 10% of African American males. Triggers include dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, and methylene blue, as well as infection. G6PD levels can look falsely normal during an episode, because the oldest, most deficient cells have already been destroyed, so testing is repeated weeks later.

whyWrong.b: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a glycolysis defect that causes ongoing hemolysis from birth, not sudden hemolysis after an oxidant drug.
whyWrong.c: Heme synthesis defects cause sideroblastic anemia or porphyrias, not drug-triggered hemolysis with bite cells.
whyWrong.d: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis, which shows spherocytes rather than bite cells and Heinz bodies.
whyWrong.e: Loss of GPI anchors causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, in which complement attacks red cells. It is not triggered by oxidant drugs.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency
MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Hemolytic Anemia
MSD Manual Professional: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and episodes of dark urine, most noticeable in the morning, for 6 months. Last month he was treated for a clot in his hepatic veins. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL, leukocyte count is 3,600/mm3, platelet count is 105,000/mm3, LDH is markedly increased, and haptoglobin is undetectable. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Flow cytometry shows that many of his red cells and granulocytes lack CD55 and CD59.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his hemolysis?

options.text: Warm IgG autoantibodies against red cell antigens
Oxidant damage from a lack of NADPH
Loss of spectrin from the red cell membrane

questions.explanation: Answer: complement attack on cells that lack GPI-anchored complement regulators (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, PNH). Why: hemolysis with a negative direct antiglobulin test, a clot in an unusual site such as the hepatic veins, low counts of other cell lines, and cells missing CD55 and CD59 is PNH. An acquired mutation in PIGA in a blood stem cell blocks the making of the GPI anchor that holds CD55 and CD59 on the cell surface. These proteins normally stop complement, so without them complement destroys red cells inside the vessels. Only about 30% of patients notice dark urine. Flow cytometry, including the FLAER test, confirms it. PNH is linked to aplastic anemia. Recent change: besides the C5 blockers eculizumab and ravulizumab, newer drugs block C3 (pegcetacoplan), factor B (iptacopan), and factor D (danicopan). Patients need meningococcal vaccination at least 2 weeks before complement-blocking therapy.

whyWrong.b: Warm IgG autoantibodies cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which gives a positive direct antiglobulin test. His test is negative.
whyWrong.c: Lack of NADPH from G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis after oxidant drugs or infection, with bite cells and Heinz bodies.
whyWrong.d: Shearing on small clots causes schistocytes in conditions such as TTP and DIC, which would not explain missing CD55 and CD59.
whyWrong.e: Spectrin loss is hereditary spherocytosis, an inherited red cell disorder that does not lower white cells or platelets.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)
MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Hemolytic Anemia
MSD Manual Professional: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of irritability, poor appetite, and stomach pain for 1 month. He plays less than before. His family lives in a house built in 1955 that is being renovated, and he has been seen putting paint chips in his mouth. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 72 fL. A blood smear shows red cells with fine blue dots spread through the cytoplasm. A fingerstick (capillary) lead screen is high.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: measure a venous blood lead level. Why: a toddler in an older house that is being remodeled who eats paint chips, with irritability, belly pain, less play, microcytic anemia, and basophilic stippling (fine blue dots in red cells), most likely has lead poisoning. Houses painted before 1978 carry the greatest risk, especially during remodeling. A capillary (fingerstick) test is good for screening, but every positive result should be confirmed with a blood lead level, and CDC recommends a venous draw for that confirmation. The diagnosis is definite at 3.5 mcg/dL or higher. Weeks of irritability and less play can come before lead encephalopathy, which is an emergency. Children with very high levels receive chelation, such as succimer by mouth.

whyWrong.b: Hemoglobin electrophoresis looks for thalassemia or sickle cell disease. It would not confirm lead exposure.
whyWrong.c: Serum ferritin checks iron stores. Iron deficiency often coexists with lead exposure, but ferritin does not confirm lead poisoning.
whyWrong.d: Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and not needed when a blood test can confirm the diagnosis.
whyWrong.e: Knee x-rays can show lead lines at the ends of long bones, but they are supportive. The blood lead level confirms the diagnosis.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Lead Poisoning
CDC: Recommended Actions Based on Blood Lead Level

questions.topic: Hemolytic anemia: spherocytes and the direct antiglobulin test
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and yellow eyes for 2 weeks. She has had no prior anemia, and no one in her family has had anemia, gallstones, or splenectomy. She has not had a transfusion. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, reticulocyte count is 9%, LDH and indirect bilirubin are increased, and haptoglobin is low. A blood smear shows many small, round red cells without central pallor.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following tests best distinguishes between the two most likely causes of these red cell changes?
questions.explanation: Answer: the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test. Why: anemia with high reticulocytes, high LDH and indirect bilirubin, and low haptoglobin means hemolysis. Many spherocytes on the smear point to either hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm antibody type). The direct antiglobulin test tells them apart: it is positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, where IgG coats the red cells, and negative in hereditary spherocytosis, where the defect is in the red cell membrane proteins. Her new symptoms in adulthood and empty family history favor the autoimmune cause. If she had been transfused in the last 3 months, a positive result could instead reflect antibodies against donor cells. Warm autoimmune hemolysis is treated first with glucocorticoids.

whyWrong.b: Osmotic fragility is abnormal in both hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia, because both have spherocytes. It does not separate them.
whyWrong.c: Hemoglobin electrophoresis detects abnormal hemoglobins such as sickle hemoglobin. It does not explain spherocytes.
whyWrong.d: G6PD deficiency causes bite cells and Heinz bodies after an oxidant trigger, not a smear full of spherocytes.
whyWrong.e: Iron studies evaluate microcytic anemia from low iron. They do not distinguish causes of hemolysis.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Hemolytic Anemia

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of left lower abdominal pain and light vaginal bleeding for 1 day. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She was treated for a chlamydial infection 3 years ago. Her pulse is 96/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. There is tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Serum beta-hCG concentration is 4,200 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows no gestational sac in the uterus and a small mass next to the left ovary.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: ectopic tubal pregnancy. Why: a woman with a positive pregnancy test, pelvic pain, and bleeding, whose hCG is high enough that a pregnancy in the uterus should be visible but is not, most likely has an ectopic pregnancy. Most ectopic pregnancies are in the fallopian tube. A past chlamydial infection or pelvic inflammatory disease raises the risk, as do a prior ectopic pregnancy and tubal surgery. Most patients have pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, or both, and rupture can cause sudden severe pain and shock. Small unruptured ectopic pregnancies can be treated with methotrexate if there are no contraindications, and surgery is done if rupture is suspected. Recent change: your Obstetrics notes (pp. 14 and 43) use 1,500 mIU/mL as the hCG level above which a uterine sac should be seen on transvaginal ultrasound. MSD Manual says the recommended threshold has been raised to 3,500 mIU/mL, so that a wanted early pregnancy is not mistaken for an ectopic one and treated. Her hCG is above both cutoffs.

whyWrong.b: Above the hCG threshold of 3,500 mIU/mL, a normal pregnancy inside the uterus should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound. None is seen here.
whyWrong.c: A complete mole usually makes the uterus larger than expected, with very high hCG and a uterine mass full of cysts. Her uterus is empty.
whyWrong.d: Threatened abortion means bleeding with a pregnancy inside the uterus. No pregnancy is seen in her uterus.
whyWrong.e: An endometrioma (chocolate cyst) is an ovarian cyst caused by endometriosis. It does not explain a positive pregnancy test with an empty uterus.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Ectopic Pregnancy
MSD Manual Professional: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
MSD Manual Professional: Endometriosis

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 34 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a headache for 2 days. Her blood pressure was normal at all earlier visits. Today her blood pressure is 154/102 mm Hg, and it is 156/100 mm Hg 4 hours later. Platelet count is 86,000/mm3, and AST and ALT are each about 3 times the upper limit of normal. A urine dipstick is negative for protein, and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is thought to contribute to the development of her condition?

options.text: Aldosterone made by an adrenal adenoma
Ascending infection of the fetal membranes

questions.explanation: Answer: poorly developed placental spiral arteries (preeclampsia). Why: new high blood pressure after 20 weeks with a low platelet count and raised liver enzymes is preeclampsia, even without protein in the urine. The exact cause is unknown, but poorly developed spiral arterioles in the uterus and placenta, along with genetic and immune factors, lead to poor placental blood flow. Widespread spasm of blood vessels then injures the mother's brain, kidneys, and liver. Her platelets below 100,000 and liver enzymes over twice normal are severe features. Delivery is the only definitive treatment. Low-dose aspirin started between 12 and 28 weeks is recommended for women at high risk. Recent change: your Obstetrics notes (p. 75) require proteinuria for the diagnosis. MSD Manual says preeclampsia can also be diagnosed without proteinuria when new high blood pressure comes with signs of organ damage, such as low platelets, raised liver enzymes, kidney impairment, pulmonary edema, headache, or visual symptoms.

whyWrong.b: Autoantibodies against platelets cause immune thrombocytopenia, which lowers platelets but does not cause high blood pressure or raised liver enzymes.
whyWrong.c: An aldosterone-making adrenal adenoma causes high blood pressure with low potassium. It does not start after 20 weeks of pregnancy with low platelets and liver injury.
whyWrong.d: Trophoblast with only paternal genes is a complete mole. A mole can cause preeclampsia early, in the first or second trimester, but this is a normal pregnancy at 34 weeks.
whyWrong.e: Infection of the fetal membranes causes fever and uterine tenderness, not this pattern of high blood pressure and organ damage.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Preeclampsia and Eclampsia
MSD Manual Professional: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation is admitted with preeclampsia with severe features. She receives magnesium sulfate, 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes, followed by an infusion of 2 g/h. Ten hours later she is very drowsy. Her respirations are 8/min and shallow. Patellar and biceps reflexes cannot be elicited. Her serum magnesium concentration is markedly elevated.
questions.leadIn: In addition to stopping the infusion, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Answer: intravenous calcium gluconate. Why: magnesium sulfate prevents seizures in preeclampsia with severe features. It is given as a 4-g IV load over 20 minutes, then 2 g per hour, and continued for 12 to 24 hours after delivery. Signs of too much magnesium include a sudden decrease in reflexes, heart problems, and slow, shallow breathing (hypoventilation). MSD Manual recommends calcium gluconate 1 g IV for very high levels with significant symptoms, because calcium counteracts magnesium's effects. Checking reflexes during the infusion catches toxicity early.

whyWrong.b: Naloxone reverses opioids. She has not received an opioid, and her absent reflexes point to magnesium.
whyWrong.c: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, is given only IV, and can cause seizures. It has no effect on magnesium toxicity.
whyWrong.d: Labetalol lowers blood pressure in preeclampsia, but it does not reverse magnesium toxicity.
whyWrong.e: Potassium does not counteract magnesium. Calcium is the antidote.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Preeclampsia and Eclampsia

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes for her first prenatal visit at 9 weeks' gestation. Her blood type is O, Rh-negative. Her first child was born at home 2 years ago and was Rh-positive. She did not receive Rh(D) immune globulin during or after that pregnancy. The physician wants to know whether she has made antibodies that could cross the placenta and harm this fetus.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following tests on the mother's blood best answers this question?
questions.explanation: Answer: the indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) test, which is the maternal antibody screen. Why: an Rh-negative mother can be sensitized when Rh-positive fetal red cells enter her blood. The first pregnancy is not affected, but in later pregnancies her anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal red cells, causing anemia and possibly heart failure or death. All women are screened at the first visit for blood type, Rh type, and antibodies. The indirect antiglobulin test detects free antibodies in the serum, which is what this question asks. If antibody titers pass a critical value (usually 1:8 to 1:32), the fetus is followed with middle cerebral artery Doppler to look for anemia. Rh(D) immune globulin is given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive baby to prevent sensitization. Correction: your Obstetrics notes (p. 24) say blood type and Rh are determined with the direct Coombs test. The maternal antibody screen is the indirect test, as your own p. 30 says. The direct test detects antibodies already attached to red cells, such as the baby's cells in hemolytic disease of the newborn.

whyWrong.b: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibodies already attached to red cells. It is used on the newborn's cells, not to find free antibodies in the mother's serum.
whyWrong.c: The Kleihauer-Betke test measures how much fetal blood has entered the mother's circulation, for example after delivery, to dose immune globulin. It does not detect antibodies.
whyWrong.d: Hemoglobin electrophoresis looks for abnormal hemoglobins such as sickle hemoglobin. It does not detect Rh antibodies.
whyWrong.e: The rosette test is a first screen for fetal blood in the mother's circulation. It does not show whether she has already made antibodies.

StatPearls: Coombs Test

questions.topic: Diabetes in pregnancy: infant of a diabetic mother
questions.stem: A boy is born at 39 weeks' gestation to a 33-year-old woman whose diabetes was poorly controlled throughout pregnancy. He weighs 4,600 g. Delivery was complicated by shoulder dystocia. Two hours after birth he is jittery and feeding poorly. His blood glucose concentration is 28 mg/dL.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his low blood glucose?
questions.explanation: Answer: neonatal hyperinsulinemia. Why: high maternal glucose reaches the fetus, whose pancreas responds by making extra insulin. After birth the supply of maternal glucose stops suddenly, but the baby's insulin stays high for a time, so the blood glucose falls. Hypoglycemia from fetal hyperinsulinemia is reported in infants of diabetic mothers. Other newborn problems include low calcium, jaundice, polycythemia, and breathing trouble. A large baby (macrosomia, birth weight over 4,000 to 4,500 g) raises the risk of shoulder dystocia. Poor control around conception and early pregnancy also raises the risk of major birth defects (MSD), and StatPearls lists heart defects such as ventricular septal defects and transposition of the great arteries, and caudal regression syndrome. Gestational diabetes is screened for at 24 to 28 weeks with a 50-g glucose load.

whyWrong.b: Insulin cannot cross the placenta, so the mother's insulin does not lower the baby's glucose.
whyWrong.c: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes low glucose between feeds, but the clue here is the mother's poorly controlled diabetes and a very large baby.
whyWrong.d: Adrenal insufficiency can cause low glucose, but nothing here points to it, and the mother's diabetes explains the findings.
whyWrong.e: Congenital hypothyroidism causes poor feeding and jaundice later, but it does not explain low glucose in a large baby of a diabetic mother.

sources.title: StatPearls: Diabetic Embryopathy
MSD Manual Professional: Diabetes Mellitus in Pregnancy

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, has a quadruple serum screen at 16 weeks' gestation. Gestational age was confirmed by ultrasound in the first trimester. Her levels of alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG, unconjugated estriol, and inhibin A are all low for gestational age.
questions.leadIn: This pattern is most consistent with which of the following fetal conditions?
questions.explanation: Answer: trisomy 18. Why: MSD Manual describes the trisomy 18 pattern as low levels of all 4 serum markers. Confirmed dating matters because these results depend on gestational age. Screening results are never diagnostic. Abnormal results are confirmed by karyotyping of fetal cells from chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. Other source: your Obstetrics notes (p. 27) offer cell-free DNA testing after an abnormal quad screen. MSD Manual says ACOG now recommends offering cell-free DNA screening to all pregnant women. Its sensitivity is about 99% for trisomy 21, 98% for trisomy 18, and 91% for trisomy 13.

whyWrong.b: In trisomy 21, AFP and estriol are low, but hCG and inhibin A are high (standard teaching). In the first trimester, high hCG, low PAPP-A, and thick nuchal translucency suggest trisomy 21.
whyWrong.c: An open neural tube defect raises AFP, which is low here.
whyWrong.d: Abdominal wall defects raise AFP, which is low here.
whyWrong.e: A molar pregnancy causes an unexpectedly high hCG, not a low one.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Noninvasive Prenatal Fetal Screening Tests
MSD Manual Professional: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 6, para 5, delivers twins vaginally after 20 hours of labor that required an oxytocin infusion. The placentas are delivered intact. Over the next 30 minutes she loses about 1,300 mL of blood. Her pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg. The uterus is soft and boggy and is felt above the umbilicus. Inspection of the vagina and cervix shows no tears.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
questions.explanation: Answer: uterine atony. Why: after delivery, the uterine muscle must contract to squeeze the blood vessels at the placental site shut. A soft, boggy, enlarged uterus that does not contract is uterine atony, the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Her risk factors include an overstretched uterus from twins, a long labor, and grand multiparity (5 or more previous deliveries). Treatment starts with uterine massage and IV oxytocin, which should not be given as a fast IV push because it can cause severe low blood pressure. Methylergonovine is avoided in women with high blood pressure, and prostaglandin F2-alpha drugs are avoided in women with asthma. Tranexamic acid can be added if the first drugs fail. Recent change: your Obstetrics notes (p. 132) define postpartum hemorrhage as 500 mL or more after vaginal delivery or 1,000 mL after cesarean. MSD Manual now defines it as more than 1,000 mL, or blood loss with signs of low blood volume, within 24 hours of birth.

whyWrong.b: Retained placental tissue is another cause, but both placentas came out intact, and the soft uterus points to poor contraction.
whyWrong.c: Lacerations bleed even when the uterus is firm. Her uterus is soft, and no tears were found.
whyWrong.d: Uterine inversion means the uterus turns inside out, so the top of the uterus would not be felt above the umbilicus.
whyWrong.e: A bleeding disorder is possible, but she has no history of one, and the boggy uterus explains the bleeding.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Postpartum Hemorrhage

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding that soaked a pad. Both previous children were delivered by cesarean. She smokes half a pack of cigarettes daily. Her pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. The uterus is soft and not tender. The fetal heart rate tracing is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: placenta previa. Why: placenta previa means the placenta is implanted over or near the internal opening of the cervix. It typically causes painless vaginal bleeding after 20 weeks. Risk factors include prior cesarean delivery, multiparity, and smoking. Transvaginal ultrasonography is an accurate and safe way to make the diagnosis. A digital pelvic examination is contraindicated until ultrasound has ruled out previa, because it can cause heavy bleeding. In women with previa, each prior cesarean raises the risk that the placenta also grows too deeply into the uterine wall (placenta accreta spectrum), from about 3% after one cesarean to 67% after five or more.

whyWrong.b: Placental abruption is usually painful, with a tender uterus. Her bleeding is painless and her uterus is soft.
whyWrong.c: Uterine rupture is more likely after prior cesareans but usually causes sudden pain, an abnormal fetal heart tracing, and maternal shock, especially during labor.
whyWrong.d: Cervical cancer usually causes irregular or postcoital bleeding, not sudden heavy painless bleeding at 32 weeks.
whyWrong.e: Ectopic pregnancy happens in early pregnancy. She is at 32 weeks with a normal fetal heart rate.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Placenta Previa
MSD Manual Professional: Cervical Cancer
MSD Manual Professional: Ectopic Pregnancy

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of vaginal bleeding and severe nausea and vomiting for 1 week. The uterus is the size expected at 16 weeks. Serum beta-hCG concentration is much higher than expected for her dates. Ultrasonography shows a uterine mass with many small cysts and no fetus or amniotic fluid.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the chromosomes in this tissue?

options.text: Triploid, with an extra paternal set
Diploid, with maternal and paternal sets
Monosomic, with a single X chromosome

questions.explanation: Answer: diploid, with only paternal chromosomes (complete hydatidiform mole). Why: bleeding, severe vomiting, a uterus larger than dates, very high hCG, and a cystic uterine mass with no fetus is a complete mole. Complete moles are diploid, most often 46,XX. The egg's own nucleus is missing or inactive, so all the chromosomes come from the sperm. Partial moles are triploid, from fertilization by two sperm or by one diploid sperm, and may contain some fetal tissue. Moles can also cause hyperthyroidism, ovarian theca lutein cysts, and preeclampsia in the first or second trimester. Treatment is suction curettage, followed by serial hCG levels. Choriocarcinoma develops after 2 to 3% of moles, more often after a complete mole.

whyWrong.b: Triploid tissue with an extra paternal set is a partial mole, which may contain fetal parts. Here no fetus is seen.
whyWrong.c: A diploid set with one maternal and one paternal half is a normal pregnancy, not a cystic mass with no fetus.
whyWrong.d: Trisomy 18 is a chromosome disorder of a fetus. It does not cause a cystic uterine mass with very high hCG.
whyWrong.e: Monosomy X (Turner syndrome) is a fetal chromosome disorder, not a trophoblastic tumor.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician 8 weeks after delivering her second child because she has been unable to breastfeed and feels very tired. The delivery was complicated by severe postpartum hemorrhage requiring transfusion of 6 units of blood for shock. Since then her milk has never come in. She has noticed thinning of her pubic and axillary hair.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

options.text: Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary
Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex
Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland
Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor

questions.explanation: Answer: ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary (Sheehan syndrome). Why: the pituitary enlarges during pregnancy, which makes it especially sensitive to infarction when blood pressure falls. After a hemorrhage with shock, the gland can die. Lactation then does not start because prolactin is lost, and patients may report tiredness and loss of pubic and axillary hair. In hypopituitarism, growth hormone is usually lost first, then the gonadotropins, and finally TSH and ACTH. ACTH deficiency causes fatigue, low blood pressure, and poor tolerance of stress, and TSH deficiency causes hypothyroidism.

whyWrong.b: Autoimmune adrenal failure (Addison disease) causes fatigue, but it does not stop milk production after delivery.
whyWrong.c: A prolactin-secreting adenoma raises prolactin, so it would cause milk production (galactorrhea), not a failure to lactate.
whyWrong.d: Autoimmune thyroid disease can cause tiredness, but it does not explain a complete failure to lactate after a hemorrhage with shock.
whyWrong.e: TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies cause Graves disease, with hyperthyroidism. They would not stop lactation or cause hair loss of this pattern.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Generalized Hypopituitarism

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menstrual periods since menarche, with only 4 periods in the past year. She has acne and coarse hair on her chin and lower abdomen. Her BMI is 33 kg/m2. There are areas of dark, velvety, thickened skin on the back of her neck and in her axillae. Serum testosterone is mildly elevated. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows enlarged ovaries with many small follicles.
questions.leadIn: Without treatment, this patient is at increased risk for which of the following?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix

questions.explanation: Answer: endometrial carcinoma. Why: irregular periods from infrequent ovulation, signs of excess androgen (acne, hirsutism), and polycystic ovaries meet the Rotterdam criteria for polycystic ovary syndrome, which need any 2 of these 3. Insulin resistance with high insulin levels is central, and high insulin may increase ovarian androgen production. The dark, velvety skin is acanthosis nigricans, caused by high insulin. Because she ovulates rarely, her estrogen is not regularly opposed by progesterone, which raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Estrogen-progestin contraceptives are often first-line to regulate periods and protect the endometrium. Metformin can improve insulin sensitivity, and clomiphene or letrozole can induce ovulation when she wants to conceive. Recent change: in May 2026 a global consensus published in The Lancet renamed the condition polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), with a 3-year transition, and MSD Manual now uses that name. Both names may appear.

whyWrong.b: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma is linked to HPV infection, smoking, and immune deficiency, not to polycystic ovary syndrome.
whyWrong.c: Women with polycystic ovary syndrome are not estrogen deficient. Their estrogen is unopposed by progesterone.
whyWrong.d: Dysgerminoma is an ovarian germ cell tumor. It is not a known complication of polycystic ovary syndrome.
whyWrong.e: A hydatidiform mole is an abnormal pregnancy, not a complication of polycystic ovary syndrome.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)
MSD Manual Professional: Cervical Cancer
Contemporary OB/GYN (12 May 2026): Global consensus renames PCOS to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of severe pain with menstrual periods for 3 years, pain during intercourse, and pain with bowel movements during her periods. She and her partner have been unable to conceive for 18 months. Pelvic examination shows tenderness and nodularity behind the uterus. Laparoscopy shows dark implants on the uterosacral ligaments and peritoneum and a cyst in the left ovary filled with thick, dark brown fluid.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most widely accepted explanation of how this condition arises?

options.text: HPV infection of the transformation zone

questions.explanation: Answer: retrograde menstruation through the fallopian tubes (endometriosis). Why: painful periods, painful intercourse, and infertility form the classic triad of endometriosis, in which functioning endometrial tissue is implanted outside the uterus. Common sites are the ovaries, posterior cul-de-sac, uterosacral ligaments, broad ligaments, and peritoneum. An ovarian cyst filled with old blood is an endometrioma, or chocolate cyst. The most accepted theory is that endometrial cells travel backward through the fallopian tubes during menstruation and implant in the pelvis, and such retrograde flow is common. Laparoscopy with biopsy can confirm it but is not required. Treatment includes NSAIDs, hormonal therapy that suppresses the ovaries, and surgical removal of implants.

whyWrong.b: Chlamydial infection causes pelvic inflammatory disease, which can scar the tubes and cause infertility, but it does not create endometrial implants or chocolate cysts.
whyWrong.c: Unopposed estrogen from infrequent ovulation, as in polycystic ovary syndrome, thickens the endometrium inside the uterus. It does not place tissue outside it.
whyWrong.d: Abnormal trophoblast growth causes gestational trophoblastic disease, such as a molar pregnancy.
whyWrong.e: HPV infection of the transformation zone causes cervical cancer and its precursors.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Endometriosis
MSD Manual Professional: Ectopic Pregnancy
MSD Manual Professional: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
MSD Manual Professional: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease
MSD Manual Professional: Cervical Cancer

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man comes to the physician because of a painless swelling of his right testis for 2 months. He had surgery as a child for an undescended right testis. A firm mass is palpable in the right testis. Serum alpha-fetoprotein concentration is normal, and beta-hCG concentration is slightly elevated. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is done. Microscopic examination shows sheets of large cells with clear cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli, divided by fibrous septa that contain many lymphocytes.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: seminoma. Why: testicular cancer is the most common solid cancer in males aged 15 to 35, and an undescended testis raises the risk. Seminomas make up about 40% of germ cell tumors. They show sheets of pale or clear cells divided by fibrous septa with lymphocytes, and a lymphocytic infiltrate is present in almost every case. AFP is not raised in pure seminoma, while beta-hCG is mildly raised in 5 to 10% of patients. If AFP is high, the tumor contains nonseminomatous elements and is treated as a nonseminoma. The testis is removed through an inguinal incision, with the spermatic cord clamped before the testis is handled. Survival is over 95% when found early.

whyWrong.b: Yolk sac tumor is a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. A high AFP would point toward nonseminomatous elements, and his AFP is normal.
whyWrong.c: Embryonal carcinoma is a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. The sheets of clear cells with lymphocyte-filled septa here are the seminoma pattern.
whyWrong.d: Choriocarcinoma is a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. A slightly raised hCG can occur in seminoma, and the histology here is seminoma.
whyWrong.e: Teratoma is a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor made of tissues from different germ layers, not sheets of uniform clear cells.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Testicular Cancer
StatPearls: Seminoma

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of breast enlargement. He is 191 cm tall with long legs. He has had difficulty in school. Both testes are small (about 3 mL) and firm. Semen analysis shows no sperm. Karyotype analysis shows 47,XXY.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following sets of serum hormone levels is most likely?

options.text: High FSH and LH, low testosterone
Low FSH and LH, low testosterone
Normal FSH and LH, high prolactin
Low FSH and LH, high testosterone

questions.explanation: Answer: high FSH and LH, low testosterone (Klinefelter syndrome). Why: tall stature, small firm testes, gynecomastia, and no sperm with a 47,XXY karyotype is Klinefelter syndrome. It affects 1 in 500 to 1,000 males and usually results from nondisjunction. The seminiferous tubules become scarred (hyalinized), so the testes cannot make sperm or inhibin B, and testosterone is low or low-normal. Without negative feedback, the pituitary raises FSH and LH, with FSH usually higher. This is primary hypogonadism. Testosterone replacement is the core treatment, and sperm can sometimes be retrieved surgically for assisted reproduction. Affected men have a higher risk of male breast cancer.

whyWrong.b: Low FSH and LH with low testosterone is secondary (pituitary or hypothalamic) hypogonadism. In Klinefelter syndrome the testes fail, so FSH and LH rise.
whyWrong.c: High LH with high testosterone fits androgen insensitivity (standard teaching), where the body cannot respond to testosterone. He is virilized and has a 47,XXY karyotype.
whyWrong.d: High prolactin causes low gonadotropins and can cause breast changes, but it does not explain small testes with a 47,XXY karyotype.
whyWrong.e: Low FSH and LH with high testosterone suggests an outside source of androgen, such as anabolic steroid use, which suppresses the pituitary.

sources.title: StatPearls: Klinefelter Syndrome
StatPearls: Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome

questions.topic: Disorders of sex development: androgen insensitivity
questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period. She has normal breast development and a normal growth spurt. She had surgery for bilateral inguinal hernias as a child, and small masses were found in the inguinal canals. Pelvic ultrasonography shows no uterus. Serum testosterone is at the upper end of the normal male range, and LH is increased. Karyotype analysis shows 46,XY.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: androgen receptor (complete androgen insensitivity syndrome). Why: a 46,XY person with testes that make testosterone, but a female body and no uterus, has androgen insensitivity. Mutations in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome leave the body unable to respond to testosterone. Puberty brings normal breast development, but menarche never happens because there is no uterus. In standard teaching, the breasts develop because testosterone is converted to estrogen. The testes are often found during hernia repair or when primary amenorrhea is evaluated. In standard teaching, testosterone after puberty is normal to high with a high LH, because the pituitary cannot sense androgen either. Gonadectomy is advised because of a tumor risk that rises in adulthood.

whyWrong.b: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT. These 46,XY individuals often have atypical genitalia at birth and frequently virilize at puberty.
whyWrong.c: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which virilizes 46,XX girls. It does not cause this picture.
whyWrong.d: Aromatase converts testosterone to estrogen. In standard teaching, her breast development shows aromatase is working.
whyWrong.e: Without SRY, testes would not form. She has testes that make testosterone.

sources.title: StatPearls: Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome
StatPearls: 5α-Reductase Deficiency

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular vaginal bleeding, often after intercourse, for 3 months. She smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily and has not had cervical screening for 12 years. Speculum examination shows a friable mass on the cervix. Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma arising at the transformation zone. Testing of the tumor finds HPV type 16 DNA.
questions.leadIn: The main oncoproteins of this virus inactivate which of the following pairs of host proteins?
questions.explanation: Answer: p53 and retinoblastoma protein (Rb). Why: about 70% of cervical precancers and cancers are caused by HPV types 16 or 18, and nearly all arise in the transformation zone around the external os. Most (80 to 85%) are squamous cell carcinomas. High-risk HPV makes 2 key oncoproteins. E6 binds the host ubiquitin ligase E6AP and causes p53 to be degraded. E7 causes Rb to be degraded, which releases E2F transcription factors and pushes the cell into division. Losing these 2 brakes lets damaged cells keep dividing. Smoking and immune deficiency are added risk factors. The first symptom is usually irregular, often postcoital, bleeding. HPV vaccination before the first sexual activity prevents most cases, and screening uses cytology and HPV testing.

whyWrong.b: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations are inherited causes of breast and ovarian cancer, not the targets of HPV proteins.
whyWrong.c: APC and beta-catenin are part of the WNT pathway disrupted in colon cancer, not targets of HPV.
whyWrong.d: MYC and BCL2 are oncogenes activated by translocations in lymphomas, not targets of HPV.
whyWrong.e: RET and NF1 are linked to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 and neurofibromatosis, not to HPV.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Cervical Cancer
Pal A, Kundu R. High-Risk Human Papillomaviral Oncogenes E6 and E7 Target Key Cellular Pathways to Achieve Oncogenesis. Int J Mol Sci. 2018

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump in the front of her neck for 3 months. She received radiation therapy to the head and neck for a childhood cancer. A firm 2-cm thyroid nodule and an enlarged lymph node on the same side of the neck are palpable. Thyroid function tests are normal. Fine-needle aspiration shows cells with pale, clear-looking nuclei, nuclear grooves, and nuclear inclusions, along with small round laminated calcifications.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: papillary thyroid carcinoma. Why: papillary carcinoma causes 80 to 85% of thyroid cancers, and radiation to the head and neck in childhood is a known risk factor. Its diagnosis rests on nuclear features: clear chromatin ("Orphan Annie eye" nuclei), grooves, and pseudo-inclusions, often with psammoma bodies (laminated calcifications). It tends to spread through lymphatics to neck nodes. BRAF V600E mutations and RET rearrangements occur. The prognosis is generally excellent. Treatment is lobectomy or total thyroidectomy, sometimes followed by radioactive iodine and TSH-suppressing doses of levothyroxine.

whyWrong.b: Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed only by capsular or vascular invasion on the removed tumor. Fine-needle aspiration cannot show this, and it lacks these nuclear features.
whyWrong.c: Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, makes calcitonin, and shows amyloid. RET mutations occur in inherited forms.
whyWrong.d: Anaplastic carcinoma presents as a rapidly enlarging neck mass, with mortality near 100%.
whyWrong.e: Follicular adenoma is benign and is separated from follicular carcinoma by the lack of invasion. It does not show these nuclear features.

sources.title: StatPearls: Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
StatPearls: Thyroid Cancer

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man comes to the physician because of episodes of severe headache, sweating, and a pounding heartbeat for 4 months. During one episode his blood pressure was 220/124 mm Hg. Plasma free metanephrines are markedly elevated. CT scan shows a 4-cm mass in the right adrenal gland. Surgery is planned.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drugs should be started first to prepare him for surgery?
questions.explanation: Answer: phenoxybenzamine. Why: episodes of headache, sweating, and palpitations with very high blood pressure, high plasma metanephrines, and an adrenal mass is a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of chromaffin cells. Before surgery, alpha-blockade comes first, usually with phenoxybenzamine. Beta-blockers are not given until alpha-blockade is adequate, because unopposed beta-2 blockade removes beta-mediated vasodilation and can raise blood pressure further. Plasma free metanephrines are up to 99% sensitive. About 10% of these tumors are bilateral and about 10% are malignant. Pheochromocytoma can be part of MEN types 2A and 2B, von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis, and succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations.

whyWrong.b: Propranolol given before alpha-blockade can paradoxically raise blood pressure, because blocking beta-2 receptors removes beta-mediated vasodilation.
whyWrong.c: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and treats primary aldosteronism, not catecholamine excess.
whyWrong.d: Hydrochlorothiazide is a diuretic for routine high blood pressure. It does not block the effects of catecholamines.
whyWrong.e: Metyrapone blocks cortisol synthesis and is used in Cushing syndrome, not pheochromocytoma.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Pheochromocytoma
MSD Manual Professional: Cushing Syndrome

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician 2 weeks after passing a kidney stone. She has had mild constipation and fatigue. She takes no medications. Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL, phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL (low), and intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) is elevated. Twenty-four-hour urinary calcium is high. Serum protein electrophoresis is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypercalcemia?

options.text: PTH-related peptide from a lung carcinoma

questions.explanation: Answer: parathyroid adenoma (primary hyperparathyroidism). Why: high calcium with a high PTH, low phosphate, and a kidney stone is primary hyperparathyroidism. It is probably the most common cause of high calcium in people who are not in the hospital, and it is more common in postmenopausal women. About 85% of cases are caused by a single adenoma, and about 15% by hyperplasia of 2 or more glands. PTH increases osteoclast activity, which can thin the bone, and long-standing high urinary calcium leads to stones. High calcium also causes constipation and, at higher levels, confusion. Surgery to remove the abnormal gland is indicated when the disease is symptomatic or progressing.

whyWrong.b: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia causes mild high calcium with low urinary calcium. Her urinary calcium is high.
whyWrong.c: Multiple myeloma raises calcium by destroying bone, which suppresses PTH. It also causes an M-spike, and her electrophoresis is normal.
whyWrong.d: PTH-related peptide from a tumor raises calcium, but the patient's own PTH would be suppressed, not high.
whyWrong.e: Granulomas in sarcoidosis make calcitriol, which raises calcium and suppresses PTH.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hypercalcemia
MSD Manual Professional: Multiple Myeloma

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history comes to the physician because of weakness, swelling of his legs, and weight loss for 2 months. His blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. Twenty-four-hour urinary free cortisol is markedly elevated and does not fall after low-dose or high-dose dexamethasone. Plasma ACTH is very high. A chest x-ray shows a mass near the right hilum.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his excess cortisol?

options.text: Ectopic ACTH from a lung tumor

questions.explanation: Answer: ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer. Why: high cortisol that is not suppressed by dexamethasone, with a very high ACTH, means the cortisol is ACTH-dependent and the ACTH comes from a source that does not respond to feedback. In a heavy smoker with a hilar lung mass, small cell carcinoma of the lung is the classic source. Low potassium is a classic clue to ectopic ACTH (standard teaching), and MSD notes that adrenal enzyme inhibitors can control severe metabolic problems such as hypokalemia. A pituitary source (Cushing disease) usually suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone, while an adrenal tumor or ectopic ACTH does not. Many centers no longer use the high-dose test, and petrosal sinus sampling may be needed to separate a pituitary source from an ectopic one. A low or undetectable ACTH would instead point to the adrenal gland.

whyWrong.b: A pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) usually suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone, and nothing points to the pituitary here.
whyWrong.c: A cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma makes cortisol on its own, so ACTH would be low or undetectable, not very high.
whyWrong.d: Taking glucocorticoids suppresses the patient's own ACTH and cortisol production, so ACTH would be low.
whyWrong.e: An aldosterone-secreting adenoma causes high blood pressure and low potassium, but not high cortisol.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Cushing Syndrome

questions.topic: Rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman who moved from rural Central America 2 years ago comes to the physician because of shortness of breath with exertion for 6 months. As a child she had several weeks of fever with painful, swollen joints that moved from one joint to another after a sore throat. Auscultation shows an opening snap followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Echocardiography shows thickened, fused mitral valve leaflets with a narrowed opening.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the damage to her mitral valve?

options.text: Direct bacterial infection of the valve

questions.explanation: Answer: an immune cross-reaction after group A streptococcal throat infection (rheumatic heart disease). Why: acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by about 2 to 3 weeks, most often in children aged 5 to 15. Skin infections do not cause it. Antigens of rheumatogenic strains, including M proteins, share features with proteins in joints, heart muscle, and heart valves, so the immune response attacks them too (molecular mimicry). Migratory polyarthritis and carditis are major Jones criteria. Granulomatous collections called Aschoff bodies are typical. Years later, chronic rheumatic heart disease most often involves the mitral and aortic valves, and mitral stenosis is its most common lasting result. Injections of penicillin G benzathine every 3 to 4 weeks prevent recurrences. Your Osmosis notes (PDF pp. 95 to 97) also cover molecular mimicry, Aschoff bodies, and long-term penicillin prophylaxis.

whyWrong.b: Direct infection of a valve is infective endocarditis, which causes fever and vegetations, not a slowly narrowing valve after childhood rheumatic fever.
whyWrong.c: Calcific valve disease is a disease of older adults and usually affects the aortic valve. Her childhood illness points to rheumatic disease.
whyWrong.d: Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse with a click and regurgitation, not fused leaflets with stenosis.
whyWrong.e: Amyloid infiltrates the heart muscle and causes a restrictive cardiomyopathy, not fused mitral leaflets.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who injects heroin comes to the emergency department because of fever, chills, and cough for 5 days. He has had sharp chest pain when he breathes in and coughed up streaks of blood. His temperature is 39.4°C. There are needle tracks on both arms. A holosystolic murmur is heard at the lower left sternal border. A chest CT scan shows several round lesions in both lungs, some with cavities. Two of 3 blood culture sets grow gram-positive cocci in clusters.
questions.leadIn: Where is the infection most likely located?
questions.explanation: Answer: the tricuspid valve (right-sided infective endocarditis). Why: people who inject drugs have a much higher rate of right-sided endocarditis, which makes up about 5 to 10% of all cases. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 90) list IV drug use as a risk, especially for the tricuspid valve. A vegetation on the tricuspid valve causes a tricuspid regurgitation murmur and sheds infected clots into the lungs (septic pulmonary emboli), which cause cough, pleuritic chest pain, and coughing up blood. Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus cause 80 to 90% of endocarditis cases, and gram-positive cocci in clusters point to staphylococci. At least 2, ideally 3, sets of blood cultures are drawn before antibiotics. Transthoracic echocardiography is done first. Acute endocarditis develops over days, while subacute endocarditis develops over weeks to months.

whyWrong.b: Mitral valve endocarditis sends emboli to the body, such as the brain, kidneys, or skin, not to the lungs.
whyWrong.c: Aortic valve endocarditis also sends emboli to the body rather than the lungs, and it causes a diastolic murmur when the valve leaks.
whyWrong.d: The pulmonic valve can be infected, but right-sided infection in people who inject drugs usually involves the tricuspid valve.
whyWrong.e: An infected ventricular septal defect can also cause a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, but MSD Manual says such sites are infected only occasionally, and he has no known defect.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Infective Endocarditis

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of sudden, severe chest pain that he describes as ripping and that moves to his back. He is 196 cm tall with long arms and fingers. He had surgery for a dislocated lens in one eye as a teenager. Blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg in the right arm and 116/70 mm Hg in the left arm. A chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. CT angiography shows a tear in the ascending aorta with a second channel of blood in the aortic wall.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following findings in the aortic wall most likely predisposed him to this condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: cystic medial degeneration (also called cystic medial necrosis), in a man with features of Marfan syndrome. Why: sudden tearing chest pain that travels to the back, a blood pressure difference between the arms, and a widened mediastinum point to aortic dissection. An intimal tear lets blood flow into the media, creating a false channel. Hypertension contributes in more than two-thirds of patients, but in a young man with tall stature, long limbs, and lens dislocation, the weak medial layer of Marfan syndrome is the likely cause. Bicuspid aortic valve and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are other predisposing conditions. CT angiography is usually the first imaging test. A beta-blocker is the first drug, to lower heart rate and blood pressure. A dissection of the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) almost always needs surgery, while an uncomplicated descending (type B) dissection can often be treated with medicine alone. Your Osmosis notes (PDF pp. 18 and 22) cover aortic dissection, including cystic medial necrosis.

whyWrong.b: Atherosclerosis and hypertension are the usual setting for dissection in older adults, not in a 26-year-old with Marfan features.
whyWrong.c: Granulomatous inflammation of the aorta occurs in large-vessel vasculitis such as giant cell arteritis, which affects people over 50.
whyWrong.d: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affects small arteries and arterioles in diabetes and hypertension, not the aortic media.
whyWrong.e: Medial calcific sclerosis (Mönckeberg) makes medium arteries rigid without narrowing them (standard teaching). It does not cause aortic dissection.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Aortic Dissection
MSD Manual Professional: Nonatheromatous Arteriosclerosis
MSD Manual Professional: Giant Cell Arteritis

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man comes for a routine examination. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years and quit 5 years ago. His brother had surgery for an aortic aneurysm. A pulsatile mass is felt above the umbilicus. Ultrasonography shows a 5.8-cm dilation of the abdominal aorta that begins below the renal arteries.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: cigarette smoking. Why: an abdominal aortic diameter of 3 cm or more is an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and most begin below the renal arteries. MSD Manual lists smoking as the strongest risk factor. Male sex, older age (peak at 70 to 80 years), and a family history (in 15 to 25%) also add risk, and atherosclerosis often weakens the wall. Screening men over 65 who have ever smoked with abdominal ultrasound lowers death from these aneurysms. Elective repair is recommended for aneurysms over 5.5 cm in men and over 5 cm in women. Rupture causes abdominal or back pain, low blood pressure, and a fast pulse. Your Osmosis notes (PDF pp. 18 to 19) also list smoking, high blood pressure, and family history as risks.

whyWrong.b: A family history is a real risk factor, found in 15 to 25% of patients, but smoking is the strongest.
whyWrong.c: Risk rises with age, but MSD Manual names smoking as the strongest risk factor.
whyWrong.d: Male sex is a risk factor, but smoking is the strongest.
whyWrong.e: Diabetes is not listed among the main risk factors for this aneurysm.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA)

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy collapses during a basketball game and recovers after a few seconds. His uncle died suddenly at age 30. A harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. The murmur becomes louder when he strains against a closed glottis (Valsalva maneuver) and softer when he squeezes a ball tightly (handgrip). Echocardiography shows a markedly thickened upper interventricular septum.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of his septum is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Thin walls with widely dilated chambers

questions.explanation: Answer: disordered, hypertrophied myocytes with fibrosis (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). Why: fainting during exercise, a family history of sudden death, a thick septum, and a systolic murmur that gets louder with less filling (Valsalva, standing from a squat) and softer with handgrip is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. It is usually caused by a mutation in a sarcomere gene, most often MYBPC3 or MYH7. The septum thickens unevenly, and the septum and forward motion of the mitral valve can block blood leaving the left ventricle. Histology shows myocyte hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, interstitial fibrosis, and thick-walled small coronary arteries. It is a relatively common cause of sudden death in young athletes. Beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are first-line, dehydration and vasodilators are avoided, and an ICD protects patients at high risk. Recent change: cardiac myosin inhibitors such as mavacamten are now an option when symptoms persist. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 39) give the same murmur changes.

whyWrong.b: Thin walls with dilated chambers describe dilated cardiomyopathy, which causes weak pumping rather than a thick septum.
whyWrong.c: Amyloid deposits cause a restrictive cardiomyopathy with thick walls but low ECG voltage, usually in older adults.
whyWrong.d: Granulomas with giant cells suggest sarcoidosis or giant cell myocarditis, not a familial thick septum.
whyWrong.e: Lymphocytes with myocyte necrosis describe myocarditis, which usually follows a viral illness.
