MSD Manual Professional: Amyloidosis

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman comes to the physician because of shortness of breath with exertion and swelling of her ankles for 2 months. Two years ago she was treated for breast cancer with surgery and several cycles of doxorubicin. She does not drink alcohol. An S3 gallop and a soft holosystolic murmur at the apex are heard. Echocardiography shows dilation of both ventricles with globally reduced contraction and an ejection fraction of 25%. Coronary angiography is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her heart failure?
questions.explanation: Answer: anthracycline toxicity causing dilated cardiomyopathy. Why: dilated cardiomyopathy means enlarged ventricles with weak contraction (systolic dysfunction). The walls thicken in a way that matches the dilation (eccentric hypertrophy), and stretching of the valve rings causes mitral or tricuspid regurgitation. An S3 or S4 gallop may be heard. Causes include anthracyclines such as doxorubicin, trastuzumab, alcohol, viral myocarditis (such as coxsackievirus B), pregnancy (peripartum), Chagas disease, and inherited forms, which account for 30 to 40% of cases. Her normal coronary arteries rule out ischemic damage.

whyWrong.b: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes thick walls with strong or even excessive contraction, not dilated, weak ventricles.
whyWrong.c: Amyloidosis causes stiff, thick walls with mainly diastolic dysfunction (restrictive cardiomyopathy), not dilated chambers.
whyWrong.d: Constrictive pericarditis limits filling with a rigid pericardium. The ventricles are not dilated and weak.
whyWrong.e: Mitral stenosis causes a diastolic rumble with left atrial enlargement, not dilated, poorly contracting ventricles.

MSD Manual Professional: Pericarditis

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of sharp chest pain for 2 days. The pain is worse when he lies down or takes a deep breath and better when he sits up and leans forward. He had a cold 10 days ago. His temperature is 37.9°C. A scratchy sound with systolic and diastolic parts is heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows ST elevation in most leads with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression. Troponin is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Answer: an NSAID (or aspirin) plus colchicine. Why: sharp chest pain that eases when sitting up and leaning forward, a friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression after a viral illness is acute pericarditis. In North America and Western Europe, infectious pericarditis is most often viral or idiopathic. Unlike myocardial infarction, pericarditis does not cause reciprocal ST depression, except in aVR and V1. First-line treatment is aspirin or an NSAID, usually with colchicine. Colchicine for 3 months significantly lowers the chance that pericarditis comes back. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 102) also pair an NSAID with colchicine.

whyWrong.b: Coronary angiography is for myocardial infarction. Diffuse ST elevation without reciprocal changes, PR depression, and a normal troponin point to pericarditis.
whyWrong.c: Heparin is not a treatment for pericarditis and could cause bleeding into the pericardium.
whyWrong.d: Glucocorticoids alone are not first-line for viral or idiopathic pericarditis.
whyWrong.e: Viral or idiopathic pericarditis does not need antibiotics.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Pericarditis

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer comes to the emergency department because of worsening shortness of breath for 3 days. His pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 84/62 mm Hg. His systolic blood pressure falls by 18 mm Hg when he breathes in. The neck veins are distended, and the heart sounds are faint. The lungs are clear. An ECG shows low voltage, with QRS complexes that alternate in height from beat to beat.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his low blood pressure?

options.text: Impaired diastolic filling of the heart
Acute volume overload from valve rupture

questions.explanation: Answer: impaired diastolic filling of the heart (cardiac tamponade). Why: fluid in the pericardial sac under pressure squeezes the heart so it cannot fill. Less filling means a smaller stroke volume and low blood pressure. Low blood pressure, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds form Beck's triad, though MSD Manual notes that the triad is not reliable on its own. A drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mm Hg during inspiration is pulsus paradoxus. Low voltage and electrical alternans on the ECG suggest tamponade but are neither sensitive nor specific. Echocardiography shows the effusion with collapse of the right heart chambers, but tamponade is mainly a clinical diagnosis. Pericardiocentesis removes the fluid. Cancer is one of the causes of pericardial effusion. Your Osmosis notes cover pericardial disease and Beck's triad on PDF pp. 103 to 107.

whyWrong.b: Loss of heart muscle after a large myocardial infarction causes cardiogenic shock with wet lungs, not pulsus paradoxus with electrical alternans.
whyWrong.c: Outflow obstruction, as in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or aortic stenosis, causes a loud systolic murmur, not faint heart sounds.
whyWrong.d: Sudden valve rupture causes a loud new murmur and pulmonary edema. His lungs are clear.
whyWrong.e: Sepsis causes low blood pressure with flat, not distended, neck veins.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a new, severe headache over her right temple for 2 weeks. Her scalp hurts when she brushes her hair, and her jaw aches when she chews meat. For 2 months she has had stiffness of her shoulders and hips in the morning. The right temporal artery is tender. Visual acuity is normal. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 96 mm/h, and C-reactive protein is elevated.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Answer: start glucocorticoids now (giant cell arteritis). Why: a new headache after age 50 with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a tender temporal artery, and very high inflammatory markers is giant cell arteritis. The average age at onset is about 70, and 40 to 60% of patients also have polymyalgia rheumatica (morning stiffness of the shoulders and hips). Vision loss from arteritis of the ophthalmic artery branches is the feared complication, and jaw claudication raises that risk. Treatment should not be delayed to do the biopsy. A temporal artery biopsy can still be useful up to 2 weeks after glucocorticoids start. It shows granulomas of T cells and macrophages, sometimes with giant cells near the elastic lamina, in segments that alternate with normal artery. Recent change: tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor blocker, should be considered when glucocorticoids are started so they can be tapered faster. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 171) also describe the temporal artery biopsy findings.

whyWrong.b: Waiting for the biopsy delays treatment and risks blindness. The biopsy stays useful for up to 2 weeks after glucocorticoids start.
whyWrong.c: Brain imaging does not show giant cell arteritis, and it would delay treatment.
whyWrong.d: A lumbar puncture is for meningitis or bleeding, which do not cause jaw claudication and scalp tenderness.
whyWrong.e: Sumatriptan treats migraine and constricts arteries. It does not treat vasculitis.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Giant Cell Arteritis

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever for 6 days. He has red eyes without discharge, red cracked lips, a red tongue, a rash on his trunk, and red, swollen hands and feet. A 2-cm lymph node is palpable on one side of his neck.
questions.leadIn: Without treatment, this child is at greatest risk for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: coronary artery aneurysm (Kawasaki disease). Why: fever for at least 5 days with 4 of 5 findings (eye redness without discharge, lip and mouth changes, hand and foot changes, a rash, and a neck lymph node of at least 1.5 cm) is Kawasaki disease. Eighty percent of patients are younger than 5. The coronary arteries are involved in about 25% of untreated children. Echocardiography is done as soon as the disease is suspected. IV immune globulin plus aspirin, ideally within the first 10 days, lowers the rate of coronary aneurysms from 20% to less than 5%.

whyWrong.b: Mitral stenosis follows rheumatic fever years later. It is not the main risk in Kawasaki disease.
whyWrong.c: Glomerulonephritis is not the feared complication of Kawasaki disease. The coronary arteries are.
whyWrong.d: Splenic rupture is not a feature of Kawasaki disease. The coronary arteries are the main risk.
whyWrong.e: Aortic root dissection is linked to connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome, not to Kawasaki disease.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Kawasaki Disease
MSD Manual Professional: Rheumatic Fever

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of shortness of breath, low-grade fevers, and a 4-kg weight loss over 3 months. Last month she had a sudden episode of weakness in her right arm that resolved within a day. An early diastolic sound followed by a low rumble is heard at the apex. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is elevated. Blood cultures are negative. Echocardiography shows a mobile mass on a stalk attached to the atrial septum in the left atrium.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: atrial myxoma. Why: myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor and is benign, and most occur in the left atrium. A myxoma can cause a triad of heart failure-type symptoms from blocked flow, emboli (such as her transient arm weakness), and constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss, possibly from IL-6 release. About 15% of pedunculated left atrial myxomas make an audible "tumor plop." Diagnosis is by echocardiography, often with cardiac MRI, and surgical removal is usually curative. Carney complex is an autosomal dominant syndrome of recurrent myxomas. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 33) also place myxoma most often in the left atrium.

whyWrong.b: Rhabdomyomas are cardiac tumors of children, and up to 90% of children with them have tuberous sclerosis.
whyWrong.c: Most cardiac tumors overall are metastases, but a stalked mass on the atrial septum with fever and emboli is classic for myxoma.
whyWrong.d: A left atrial thrombus usually forms with atrial fibrillation or mitral stenosis and does not cause fevers and weight loss.
whyWrong.e: Endocarditis forms vegetations on valves with positive blood cultures. Her cultures are negative and the mass is on the septum.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Cardiac Tumors
MSD Manual Professional: Infective Endocarditis

questions.topic: Congenital heart disease: tetralogy of Fallot
questions.stem: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he has episodes of turning blue and breathing fast when he cries. During an episode, his mother pulls his knees to his chest, and his color improves. A harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. A chest x-ray shows an upturned cardiac apex with a concave pulmonary artery segment, giving a boot-shaped heart.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his episodes of cyanosis?

options.text: Mixing in a single arterial trunk
Reversal of flow through a PDA

questions.explanation: Answer: right-to-left flow across a ventricular septal defect (tetralogy of Fallot). Why: tetralogy of Fallot combines a large, malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, obstruction below the pulmonary valve, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The more severe the right ventricular outflow obstruction, the more blood shunts from the right ventricle into the aorta, bypassing the lungs. During "tet spells," right-to-left flow increases and oxygen saturation falls. Knee-chest positioning raises systemic vascular resistance, which pushes more blood through the lungs. The chest x-ray shows a boot-shaped heart. About 20 to 25% of cases have a genetic syndrome, including 22q11.2 deletion. Your Osmosis notes (PDF pp. 51 to 52) also describe the boot-shaped heart.

whyWrong.b: An atrial septal defect shunts left to right and does not cause cyanotic spells in infancy.
whyWrong.c: Two parallel circulations describe transposition of the great arteries, which causes severe cyanosis from birth.
whyWrong.d: A single arterial trunk is truncus arteriosus. It does not cause a boot-shaped heart with spells relieved by the knee-chest position.
whyWrong.e: Reversal of a patent ductus arteriosus shunt occurs late, after pulmonary hypertension develops, not as spells in a 5-month-old.

sources.title: StatPearls: Tetralogy of Fallot
MSD Manual Professional: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)

questions.topic: Congenital heart disease: coarctation of the aorta
questions.stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the physician because of headaches and aching in his calves when he runs. Blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg in the right arm and 108/70 mm Hg in the leg. The femoral pulses are weak and arrive later than the radial pulses. A systolic murmur is heard over his back between the shoulder blades. A chest x-ray shows notching of the lower edges of several ribs.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the rib notching?
questions.explanation: Answer: enlarged intercostal collateral arteries (coarctation of the aorta). Why: coarctation is a narrowing of the aorta. Blood pressure is high in the arms and lower in the legs, usually by more than 20 mm Hg, and the femoral pulses are weak and delayed. Older children and adults can have headaches, nosebleeds, or leg discomfort during exercise, and a murmur is often heard over the back between the shoulder blades. Blood bypasses the narrowing through the intercostal arteries, which enlarge and erode the undersides of the ribs. The chest x-ray can also show a "figure 3 sign." A bicuspid aortic valve often comes with it, and coarctation is frequently seen in Turner syndrome. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 12) describe two types: postductal coarctation, past the ligamentum arteriosum, which presents in adulthood like this patient; and preductal coarctation, which is linked to Turner syndrome and a patent ductus arteriosus. Other source: StatPearls does not use these two types. It says the narrowing typically sits just past the left subclavian artery at the site of the ductus arteriosus. In newborns, closure of the ductus can cause sudden shock.

whyWrong.b: Lytic metastases destroy bone in irregular patches. They do not cause smooth notches under several ribs in a young man with high arm blood pressure.
whyWrong.c: Rickets causes bowed legs and widened growth plates, not rib notching with a blood pressure gap.
whyWrong.d: Hyperparathyroidism causes bone loss and high calcium, not notching under the ribs.
whyWrong.e: Marrow expansion from chronic hemolysis widens bones such as the skull. It does not explain his arm-leg blood pressure difference.

sources.title: StatPearls: Coarctation of the Aorta

questions.topic: Congenital heart disease: ventricular septal defect
questions.stem: A 6-week-old girl is brought to the physician because she tires and sweats during feeds and has gained little weight. Her respirations are 60/min. A loud, harsh holosystolic murmur is heard at the lower left sternal border. The liver edge is 3 cm below the right costal margin. She is pink, and her oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: ventricular septal defect (VSD). Why: a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border is typical of a VSD. Blood shunts from the left ventricle to the right, and larger defects cause heart failure by 4 to 6 weeks of age, with poor feeding, sweating, fast breathing, and an enlarged liver. Small muscular defects often close on their own in the first few years. Without repair, a large defect can lead to pulmonary vascular disease, and the rising pulmonary resistance eventually reverses the shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome). Other source: your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 16) call VSD the most common congenital heart disease. MSD Manual calls it the second most common congenital heart anomaly, after bicuspid aortic valve.

whyWrong.b: An atrial septal defect usually causes a soft murmur and a fixed split second heart sound and rarely causes heart failure in early infancy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A patent ductus arteriosus classically causes a continuous "machine-like" murmur below the left clavicle (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanosis and spells. She is pink with normal oxygen saturation.
whyWrong.e: Coarctation causes weak femoral pulses and an arm-leg blood pressure difference, not a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
StatPearls: Tetralogy of Fallot
StatPearls: Coarctation of the Aorta

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is admitted with crushing chest pain and ST elevation in leads V1 to V4. Despite treatment, he dies 2 days after the pain began. At autopsy, the anterior wall of the left ventricle is soft, pale, and slightly yellow.
questions.leadIn: Microscopic examination of the affected area is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Dense collagen scar with few cells

questions.explanation: Answer: neutrophils among necrotic myocytes. Why: after a myocardial infarction, the dead muscle goes through a set series of changes. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 5) give this timeline: in the first 24 hours, early coagulation necrosis, edema, and wavy fibers; at 1 to 3 days, extensive necrosis with acute inflammation by neutrophils; at 3 to 14 days, macrophages and granulation tissue at the margins; and after 14 days, a contracted scar. At 2 days, this patient is in the neutrophil phase. Other source: StatPearls splits the timeline more finely: wavy fibers at 0.5 to 4 hours, neutrophils predominating by about 12 to 24 hours, macrophages clearing dead cells at 3 to 7 days, granulation tissue at 7 to 10 days, and a scar by about 2 months. Troponin peaks at about 12 hours and stays raised for about 7 days.

whyWrong.b: Wavy fibers without inflammation are seen in the first hours, before neutrophils arrive (within the first 24 hours in your notes).
whyWrong.c: Macrophages clearing dead cells come after the neutrophil phase: at 3 to 14 days in your notes, or 3 to 7 days in StatPearls.
whyWrong.d: Granulation tissue appears at 3 to 14 days in your notes, or 7 to 10 days in StatPearls.
whyWrong.e: A contracted scar forms after 14 days in your notes, and by about 2 months in StatPearls.

sources.title: StatPearls: Acute Myocardial Infarction

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing high LDL cholesterol dies in a car crash. At autopsy, the intima of his coronary arteries contains early plaques. Microscopic examination shows many large cells with foamy, lipid-filled cytoplasm beneath the endothelium.
questions.leadIn: These foam cells are mostly derived from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: monocyte-derived macrophages. Why: in atherosclerosis, LDL builds up in the intima and is oxidized and otherwise modified. Activated endothelial cells express adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 that recruit monocytes. Inside the intima, monocytes become macrophages with scavenger receptors that take up the modified lipoprotein, turning them into foam cells, a hallmark of the early plaque. Smooth muscle cells from the media then migrate into the intima, and smooth muscle cells and collagen form a fibrous cap over the lipid core. Plaques with a large lipid core and a thin cap are prone to rupture, the most common cause of the clot in acute myocardial infarction. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 111) describe the same steps, from foam cell formation to plaque.

whyWrong.b: Endothelial cells recruit monocytes by expressing adhesion molecules, but they are not the main source of foam cells.
whyWrong.c: Neutrophils are short-lived cells of acute inflammation and do not become foam cells.
whyWrong.d: Plasma cells make antibodies and are not the lipid-filled cells of early plaques.
whyWrong.e: Fibroblasts of the adventitia are not the source of foam cells. Smooth muscle cells from the media migrate into the plaque.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Atherosclerosis

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe headache and blurred vision. His blood pressure is 238/142 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows swelling of both optic discs with retinal hemorrhages. Serum creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.2 mg/dL. A kidney biopsy shows arterioles with concentric, layered thickening of the wall that narrows the lumen, with areas of fibrinoid necrosis.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of these arteriolar changes?
questions.explanation: Answer: malignant hypertension, causing hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis. Why: extremely high blood pressure with optic disc swelling and acute kidney injury is a hypertensive emergency. Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis shows laminated, concentric thickening with a narrowed lumen, sometimes with fibrinoid deposits and necrosis of the vessel wall (necrotizing arteriolitis). Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 110) link this "onion-skin" smooth muscle proliferation to malignant hypertension. By contrast, hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a glassy thickening of small arteries and arterioles in diabetes and chronic hypertension that narrows the lumen and causes slow ischemia, mainly in the kidneys.

whyWrong.b: Long-standing diabetes causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis, a glassy pink thickening, not concentric layered thickening with fibrinoid necrosis.
whyWrong.c: Polyarteritis nodosa inflames medium-sized muscular arteries, with lesions at different stages, rather than causing onion-skin arterioles with very high blood pressure.
whyWrong.d: Medial calcific sclerosis calcifies the media of arteries without narrowing the lumen.
whyWrong.e: Atheroembolic disease blocks small arteries with cholesterol crystals, usually after an arterial procedure, not layered arteriolar thickening.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Nonatheromatous Arteriosclerosis
MSD Manual Professional: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of weight loss, abdominal pain after meals, and weakness of his left foot for 2 months. He has chronic hepatitis B. His blood pressure is 172/104 mm Hg. He has a lacy, purple, net-like rash on his legs and cannot lift his left foot. His lungs are clear. Serum creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL. Angiography shows multiple small aneurysms in the kidney and mesenteric arteries.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: polyarteritis nodosa. Why: polyarteritis nodosa causes segmental, transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium-sized (and sometimes small) muscular arteries, most often at branch points, with lesions at all stages of development and healing. About 20% of patients have hepatitis B or C. Nerve involvement causes mononeuritis multiplex, such as his foot drop. Gut involvement causes abdominal pain, kidney involvement causes high blood pressure and kidney injury, and the skin can show livedo reticularis, ulcers, or tender nodules. The lungs are usually spared. Diagnosis is by biopsy of affected tissue or by angiography showing aneurysms in medium-sized arteries. It does not cause granulomas. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 176) link it to hepatitis B and C.

whyWrong.b: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis causes granulomas and usually involves the lungs and upper airway (standard teaching). His lungs are clear, and MSD notes that polyarteritis nodosa does not form granulomas.
whyWrong.c: Giant cell arteritis affects large arteries in people over 50, causing headache and jaw claudication.
whyWrong.d: Kawasaki disease affects young children, with fever and coronary aneurysms.
whyWrong.e: Takayasu arteritis affects the aorta and its main branches, usually in young women, with weak arm pulses (standard teaching).

questions.stem: An 81-year-old man comes to the physician because of shortness of breath and leg swelling for 6 months. He had surgery for carpal tunnel syndrome in both wrists 8 years ago. An ECG shows low QRS voltage. Echocardiography shows thick ventricular walls with impaired filling and a normal ejection fraction. Serum and urine tests show no monoclonal protein. A technetium pyrophosphate nuclear scan shows strong uptake in the heart.
questions.leadIn: Deposits of which of the following proteins are most likely causing his heart failure?
questions.explanation: Answer: transthyretin (wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis, ATTRwt). Why: thick heart walls with a low-voltage ECG suggest infiltration of the myocardium, which causes a restrictive cardiomyopathy with diastolic dysfunction. Wild-type ATTR is increasingly recognized as a cause of infiltrative cardiomyopathy in older men, and carpal tunnel syndrome can appear years before heart symptoms. A technetium pyrophosphate scan detects ATTR heart disease and can avoid a heart biopsy once blood and urine tests rule out light-chain (AL) amyloidosis. Amyloid of any type shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light. A hereditary variant, V122I, is present in about 4% of Black Americans and Caribbeans. Recent change: transthyretin stabilizers (tafamidis, acoramidis) reduce death and hospitalization in ATTR cardiomyopathy, and gene-silencing drugs such as vutrisiran have trial evidence in cardiomyopathy. Your Osmosis notes (PDF p. 41) describe wild-type TTR deposits in the hearts of older people as "senile cardiac amyloidosis."

whyWrong.b: Light-chain (AL) amyloidosis comes from a plasma cell clone that makes a monoclonal protein, which was not found. Cardiac AL amyloidosis has the worst prognosis.
whyWrong.c: Serum amyloid A deposits in chronic inflammatory diseases and usually affects the kidneys rather than the heart.
whyWrong.d: Beta-2 microglobulin amyloid occurs in long-term dialysis patients and mainly affects joints and bones (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Amyloid beta deposits in the brain in Alzheimer disease, not in the heart.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Amyloidosis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral valve disease comes to the physician because of low-grade fevers, tiredness, and a 3-kg weight loss over 5 weeks. Six weeks ago she had two teeth extracted. Her temperature is 38.1°C. There are small linear hemorrhages under several fingernails and painless red macules on her palms. A new apical holosystolic murmur is heard. Three sets of blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci in chains.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Answer: viridans streptococci (subacute infective endocarditis). Why: a damaged valve, dental work, and fevers with weight loss developing over weeks is subacute endocarditis, which progresses slowly over weeks to months. Bacteremia from the mouth, even from toothbrushing or chewing in people with gingivitis, is usually caused by viridans streptococci, which are alpha-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci in chains. Splinter hemorrhages and painless macules on the palms (Janeway lesions) are typical signs. Painful nodules on the fingertips are Osler nodes, and retinal hemorrhages with pale centers are Roth spots. Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is recommended only for high-risk patients, such as those with prosthetic valves or previous endocarditis.

whyWrong.b: Staphylococcus aureus grows in clusters and usually causes acute endocarditis that progresses over days.
whyWrong.c: Enterococci cause endocarditis, often after urinary or bowel procedures (standard teaching), rather than after dental work.
whyWrong.d: Staphylococcus epidermidis grows in clusters and is a classic cause of prosthetic valve infection (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Candida is a yeast, not a gram-positive coccus in chains.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Infective Endocarditis

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of joint pain in her hands and wrists, tiredness, and a rash on her cheeks for 3 months. The rash gets worse after time in the sun and spares the folds beside her nose. She has two painless sores on the roof of her mouth. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and red blood cell casts. Antinuclear antibody is positive at 1:640, and serum C3 and C4 are low.
questions.leadIn: A rising titer of which antibody would most likely accompany a flare of her kidney disease?
questions.explanation: Answer: anti-double-stranded DNA (systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus nephritis). Why: SLE is about 10 times more common in women, usually of child-bearing age, and is more common and severe in Black and Asian patients. ANA is positive in more than 95% of patients, so it is very sensitive but not specific. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE, and its titer can be followed when it has tracked disease activity before, although it may not rise with flares outside the kidney. C3 and C4 are often low in active disease and lowest in active nephritis. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 149) describe the same pattern: anti-DNA immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli, anti-dsDNA signals renal disease and a worse prognosis, and renal disease is the most common cause of death. Hydroxychloroquine is given to every patient with SLE because it reduces flares and mortality.

whyWrong.b: Anti-Smith is highly specific for SLE but, like anti-dsDNA, not sensitive. your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 149) call it specific but not prognostic, so it does not track kidney disease.
whyWrong.c: Antihistone antibodies are typical of drug-induced lupus, which seldom causes nephritis (StatPearls).
whyWrong.d: Anticentromere antibodies occur in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST), not SLE (MSD).
whyWrong.e: Anti-Jo-1 is a myositis antibody linked to lung fibrosis, arthritis, and Raynaud syndrome (MSD).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
StatPearls: Drug-Induced Lupus Erythematosus
MSD Manual Professional: Systemic Sclerosis
MSD Manual Professional: Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, aching joints, and sharp chest pain when he breathes in for 3 weeks. He has heart failure treated with hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate for the past 14 months. There is no rash, and a pleural friction rub is heard. Urinalysis is normal. Antinuclear antibody is positive.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be present?
questions.explanation: Answer: antihistone antibodies (drug-induced lupus from hydralazine). Why: StatPearls estimates that 5 to 10% of patients on long-term hydralazine and up to 20% on long-term procainamide develop lupus-like symptoms. Antihistone antibodies are present in more than 95% of hydralazine- and procainamide-induced cases, but they also appear in up to 80% of idiopathic SLE, so they are not specific. Joint pain, fever, and serositis (pleuritis more often than pericarditis) are typical, while nephritis and brain involvement are seldom drug-induced. Slow acetylators build up more of the parent drug and are at higher risk. Symptoms usually improve within weeks to months after the drug is stopped, though ANA can stay positive for years. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 150) list hydralazine, isoniazid, and procainamide, slow acetylation, and antihistone antibodies in more than 95% of patients.

whyWrong.b: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are generally absent in classic drug-induced lupus from hydralazine or procainamide (StatPearls). TNF inhibitors and interferon-alpha are the exceptions.
whyWrong.c: Anti-Smith antibodies are specific for idiopathic SLE (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 149), not drug-induced lupus.
whyWrong.d: Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) is more likely in diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (MSD).
whyWrong.e: Antimitochondrial antibodies point to primary biliary cholangitis (standard teaching), not a drug-induced lupus syndrome.

sources.title: StatPearls: Drug-Induced Lupus Erythematosus
MSD Manual Professional: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
MSD Manual Professional: Systemic Sclerosis

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless swelling in front of her right ear that has grown over 4 months. For 3 years she has had gritty, dry eyes and a dry mouth that makes it hard to swallow crackers without water. She has had many new dental cavities. Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies and rheumatoid factor are positive. The right parotid gland is firm and enlarged; the left is normal.
questions.leadIn: This patient is at greatest increased risk for which of the following?

options.text: Warthin tumor of the parotid gland

questions.explanation: Answer: B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (Sjögren syndrome). Why: Sjögren syndrome occurs most often in middle-aged women. CD4 T cells and B cells infiltrate the exocrine glands, causing dry eyes and dry mouth. Only anti-Ro (SSA) is part of the classification criteria, and rheumatoid factor is present in more than 70% of patients. The parotid glands enlarge in about one-third of patients, but persistent enlargement of one gland should be evaluated for a tumor. The risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is about 16 times that of the general population, including MALT lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 148) list dental caries, corneal ulcers, and MALT lymphoma presenting as one-sided parotid enlargement late in the disease.

whyWrong.b: MSD describes an increased risk of non-Hodgkin, not Hodgkin, lymphoma in Sjögren syndrome.
whyWrong.c: Sjögren syndrome involves chronic B-cell stimulation (standard teaching), so the excess risk is B-cell lymphoma, not myeloid leukemia.
whyWrong.d: Warthin tumor is a benign parotid tumor linked to smoking (standard teaching), not to Sjögren syndrome.
whyWrong.e: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell cancer that is not the lymphoma risk MSD describes in Sjögren syndrome.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Sjögren Syndrome

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis comes to the emergency department because of a severe headache for 2 days. Her skin has been thickening over her fingers, forearms, upper arms, and chest for a year. Two weeks ago she was started on high-dose prednisone for muscle pain. Her blood pressure is 214/122 mm Hg, up from 118/74 mm Hg a month ago. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 2.9 mg/dL. A blood smear shows schistocytes, and the platelet count is low. Anti-Scl-70 antibodies are positive.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Answer: captopril, an ACE inhibitor (scleroderma renal crisis). Why: scleroderma renal crisis is often heralded by sudden, severe hypertension with thrombotic microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, low platelets) and rising creatinine. Prompt treatment with an ACE inhibitor can dramatically prolong survival, and the crisis is often reversible if treated quickly. Renal crisis and interstitial lung disease are major complications of diffuse cutaneous disease, where skin thickening extends above the elbows and knees, and anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) is more likely in this form. Corticosteroids are a risk factor for renal crisis and should be avoided. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 162) also say to treat renal crisis with ACE inhibitors.

whyWrong.b: Labetalol lowers blood pressure but does not block the renin-angiotensin system that drives the crisis (standard teaching). MSD names ACE inhibitors as the treatment that prolongs survival.
whyWrong.c: Corticosteroids are a risk factor for scleroderma renal crisis (MSD), so more steroids would make it worse.
whyWrong.d: Calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine are used for Raynaud phenomenon (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 163), but ACE inhibitors are the treatment for renal crisis (MSD).
whyWrong.e: A diuretic does not treat the renin-driven hypertension of renal crisis (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Systemic Sclerosis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of trouble climbing stairs and combing her hair for 2 months. Her upper eyelids are swollen and purplish, and there are scaly red papules over the knuckles of both hands. Strength is 4/5 in the shoulders and hips and normal in the hands and feet. Reflexes and sensation are normal. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated.
questions.leadIn: Along with starting treatment, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies of the legs

questions.explanation: Answer: screen for an occult cancer (dermatomyositis). Why: proximal muscle weakness with a high CK, a purplish swelling of the upper eyelids (heliotrope rash), and scaly papules over the finger joints (Gottron papules) is dermatomyositis. Both rashes are relatively specific. The evidence for an increased cancer risk is fairly consistent in dermatomyositis, and MSD advises considering cancer screening when it starts at age 40 or older. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (pp. 152-153) also describe dermatomyositis as possibly paraneoplastic (ovary, lung, pancreas) and recommend evaluating for an underlying cancer. Corticosteroids are the first drugs, usually combined with a second immunosuppressant so prednisone can be tapered. Anti-Jo-1 is linked to lung fibrosis, arthritis, and Raynaud syndrome. Other source: your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 153) describe perimysial CD4 T-cell inflammation with perifascicular atrophy on biopsy. MSD describes perifascicular, B cell-predominant infiltrates with inflammation around vessels. Both contrast with polymyositis, which shows endomysial CD8 T cells.

whyWrong.b: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies test for myasthenia gravis (standard teaching), which causes fatigable weakness without a rash or a high CK.
whyWrong.c: Dystrophin testing is for Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy (standard teaching), which starts in childhood, not with a new rash at age 58.
whyWrong.d: Her sensation and reflexes are normal, and the weakness is proximal. This points to a muscle disease, not a neuropathy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Oligoclonal bands support multiple sclerosis (standard teaching), which does not cause these rashes or a high CK.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has a bone density scan after breaking her wrist in a fall from standing height. The T-score at the femoral neck is -2.8. She is started on weekly oral alendronate and told to take it on an empty stomach with a full glass of water and to stay upright for at least 30 minutes afterward.
questions.leadIn: This drug lowers her fracture risk mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Binding bone mineral and inhibiting osteoclasts
Blocking RANKL to stop osteoclast formation
Inhibiting sclerostin to stimulate bone formation
Activating PTH receptors to build new bone

questions.explanation: Answer: alendronate binds bone mineral and inhibits osteoclasts. Why: a T-score of -2.5 or lower defines osteoporosis. Bisphosphonates preserve bone mass by inhibiting bone resorption (MSD). Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 214) describe them as pyrophosphate analogs that bind hydroxyapatite and inhibit osteoclast activity. They are also used for Paget disease, hypercalcemia, and bone metastases. Oral bisphosphonates can irritate the esophagus, which is why they are taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of water while the patient stays upright for at least 30 minutes. Osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical fractures of the femoral shaft are rare. Because they are excreted unchanged in the urine, they need care in kidney failure (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 214).

whyWrong.b: Blocking RANKL is how denosumab works. Stopping denosumab can cause rapid bone loss, so a bisphosphonate should follow (MSD).
whyWrong.c: Inhibiting sclerostin is how romosozumab works, with both anabolic and antiresorptive effects (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Teriparatide is a PTH fragment given by daily injection to stimulate new bone formation (MSD).
whyWrong.e: Activating estrogen receptors in bone is how raloxifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, works (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Osteoporosis

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because his hats no longer fit and he has trouble hearing with his right ear. He also has a dull ache in his left shin. The left tibia is bowed forward and warm. Serum alkaline phosphatase is 420 U/L (normal 30-120). Serum calcium, phosphate, and liver enzymes are normal. A skull x-ray shows a thickened skull with mixed areas of increased density and lucency.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of the affected bone would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Mosaic lamellar bone with cement lines
Sheets of small round blue cells

questions.explanation: Answer: a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone with prominent cement lines (Paget disease of bone). Why: Paget disease is a localized disorder of bone remodeling. Overactive osteoclasts, often large with many nuclei, are followed by overactive osteoblasts that lay down coarse, disorganized bone. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (pp. 122-123) say the late sclerotic stage gives a dense mosaic of lamellar bone separated by prominent cement lines, and that Paget disease is the most common cause of an isolated high alkaline phosphatase after age 40, with normal calcium, phosphate, and PTH. Skull involvement causes skull enlargement and frontal bossing, and hearing loss can be sensorineural, conductive, or mixed. Rare complications include high-output heart failure and transformation to osteosarcoma in less than 1% of patients. Zoledronic acid is first-line therapy.

whyWrong.b: Thin trabeculae with normal mineralization describe osteoporosis (standard teaching), which does not raise alkaline phosphatase or enlarge bones.
whyWrong.c: Unmineralized osteoid is osteomalacia, which causes low calcium, high PTH, and low phosphate (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 122).
whyWrong.d: Woven bone in fibrous tissue describes fibrous dysplasia (standard teaching), which usually starts in younger people.
whyWrong.e: Small round blue cells are seen in Ewing sarcoma, a tumor of children (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 132).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Paget Disease of Bone

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy comes to the physician because of pain and swelling above his right knee for 2 months. The pain wakes him at night. He had both eyes treated for retinoblastoma as an infant. There is a firm, tender mass over the distal femur. An x-ray shows a destructive lesion in the metaphysis of the distal femur, with the periosteum lifted into a triangle at the edge of the lesion.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of the mass would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Sheets of small round blue cells
Giant cells scattered among spindle cells

questions.explanation: Answer: malignant cells producing osteoid (osteosarcoma). Why: osteosarcoma is most common in children and teenagers, with a second peak at age 60 or older. It usually arises around the knee, in the distal femur more often than the proximal tibia. The lifted periosteum forms Codman's triangle. Hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53), Paget disease, bone infarcts, and past high-dose radiation all raise the risk. It may spread, usually to the lungs or other bones, and is treated with chemotherapy and surgery. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 131) describe a malignant proliferation of osteoblasts with pleomorphic cells that make osteoid, in the metaphysis of long bones near the knee.

whyWrong.b: Small round blue cells are Ewing sarcoma, which usually arises in the diaphysis (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 132; MSD).
whyWrong.c: Multinucleated giant cells among spindle cells describe giant cell tumor of bone (standard teaching), usually in young adults at the end of a long bone.
whyWrong.d: Malignant cartilage is chondrosarcoma, which arises in the pelvis, proximal femur, and humerus (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 132).
whyWrong.e: Atypical plasma cells are multiple myeloma, a cancer of older adults (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Primary Malignant Bone Tumors

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy comes to the physician because of pain and swelling in the middle of his left thigh for 6 weeks. There is a tender mass over the shaft of the femur. An x-ray shows a lytic lesion in the diaphysis of the femur with several layers of new bone around it. A biopsy shows sheets of small, round blue cells.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following genetic changes is most likely in the tumor cells?

options.text: Loss of both copies of the RB1 gene

questions.explanation: Answer: a t(11;22) translocation creating the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion (Ewing sarcoma). Why: your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 132) describe Ewing sarcoma as a very aggressive tumor, usually of boys under 15, that spreads early but responds to chemotherapy. It most often involves the diaphysis of long bones, with some extension into the metaphysis. On x-ray it destroys bone, and layers of new periosteal bone can give an onion-skin appearance. Histology shows a small round blue cell tumor. The 11;22 translocation produces the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion in about 85% of cases. Treatment is chemotherapy and surgery, with or without radiation. Other source: MSD gives a peak age of 10 to 20 years rather than under 15.

whyWrong.b: The t(X;18) SS18-SSX fusion is characteristic of synovial sarcoma (standard teaching), a soft-tissue tumor.
whyWrong.c: The t(8;14) MYC-IGH translocation is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Loss of both RB1 copies is linked to retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma (MSD), not Ewing sarcoma.
whyWrong.e: MYCN amplification is a marker of aggressive neuroblastoma (standard teaching), another small round blue cell tumor that usually arises in the adrenal gland.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Primary Malignant Bone Tumors

questions.topic: Pediatric orthopedics: slipped capital femoral epiphysis
questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of pain in his left knee and a limp for 3 weeks. He has no fever and recalls no injury. His BMI is 34 kg/m2. Examination of the knee is normal. When the left hip is flexed, it rotates outward, and internal rotation of the left hip is limited and painful. He holds the left leg turned outward when he walks.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Septic arthritis of the hip joint

questions.explanation: Answer: slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). Why: SCFE usually occurs in early adolescence, more often in boys, and obesity is a major risk factor. The femoral neck moves upward and forward on the epiphysis. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 111) describe the same slip from the other side, as the femoral head slipping backward and inward off the neck, like ice cream sliding off a cone. Pain from the hip often radiates to the thigh or knee, and about 26% of patients present with knee pain, so the hip must be examined. Hip flexion, abduction, and internal rotation are limited, and the leg is held turned outward. AP and frog-leg lateral x-rays of both hips are taken, and the patient should not bear weight until SCFE is excluded or treated. Treatment is screw fixation across the growth plate. It is bilateral in one-fifth of patients, and loss of blood supply can cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

whyWrong.b: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head, peaking at ages 5 to 7 (your El-Husseiny MSK notes, p. 111), not in an obese teenager.
whyWrong.c: Transient synovitis usually follows a viral illness in younger children and settles within days (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Septic arthritis causes fever and a very painful, hot joint (standard teaching). He has no fever.
whyWrong.e: Osgood-Schlatter disease causes pain and swelling at the tibial tubercle (standard teaching). His knee examination is normal.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because of painful sores in her mouth for 2 months and blisters on her chest and back for 2 weeks. The blisters are thin-walled and break easily, leaving raw, painful erosions. Rubbing normal-looking skin next to a blister makes the top layer slide off. A biopsy shows a split within the lower epidermis with loss of adhesion between keratinocytes.
questions.leadIn: Autoantibodies against which of the following are most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Answer: desmoglein 3 (pemphigus vulgaris). Why: in pemphigus vulgaris, IgG autoantibodies bind desmoglein 3, and sometimes desmoglein 1, on the keratinocyte surface. Keratinocytes lose their attachment to each other (acantholysis), creating intraepidermal blisters that form in the lower epidermis. The blisters are fragile, and the upper epidermis slides sideways with light rubbing (Nikolsky sign). Oral lesions often come before skin lesions, and the disease usually occurs in middle age. Without treatment it is often fatal, usually within 5 years. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (pp. 176-177) describe the same disease: blisters just above the basal layer, basal cells left stuck to the basement membrane like a row of tombstones, a positive Nikolsky sign, and IgG around each keratinocyte in a fishnet pattern on immunofluorescence. For treatment, MSD (Feb 2024) gives rituximab or prednisone for mild disease and rituximab with higher-dose prednisone for moderate or severe disease.

whyWrong.b: BP180 is a target in bullous pemphigoid, which causes tense blisters below the epidermis in older adults (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Type VII collagen anchors the epidermis below the lamina densa and is affected in dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (standard teaching), not in a split within the epidermis.
whyWrong.d: Epidermal transglutaminase is the target in dermatitis herpetiformis, which causes itchy grouped vesicles with celiac disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Keratin 5 and 14 mutations cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex (standard teaching). That is an inherited gene defect, not an autoantibody disease.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Pemphigus Vulgaris

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry is brought to the emergency department because of fever, sore red eyes, and painful mouth sores for 2 days. Two weeks ago he started carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia. There are crusted erosions on his lips and dusky red patches with blisters on his chest, where the skin peels away over about 8% of his body surface area.
questions.leadIn: Testing for which of the following before starting the drug could have identified his risk?
questions.explanation: Answer: HLA-B*15:02 (carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome). Why: SJS involves less than 10% of the body surface, SJS/TEN overlap 10 to 30%, and TEN more than 30%. It starts 1 to 3 weeks after the drug, often with a fever prodrome, and causes painful oral erosions, eye inflammation, and genital lesions. Antiseizure drugs, sulfonamides, allopurinol, and NSAIDs are common causes. HLA-B*15:02 and HLA-A*31:01 are linked to carbamazepine reactions, and MSD says testing may be considered, particularly in certain Asian and Northern European populations. Cytotoxic CD8 T cells kill keratinocytes. The drug must be stopped immediately, and all but mild cases are treated in a burn unit. Mortality can reach 25 to 35% in adults. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 181) also describe SJS as usually a drug reaction, typically involving two mucous membranes, and call the form covering more than 30% of the body TEN.

whyWrong.b: HLA-B*58:01 is the variant linked to SJS/TEN from allopurinol (MSD), not carbamazepine.
whyWrong.c: HLA-B*57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: HLA-B27 is linked to the spondyloarthritides (standard teaching), not to drug reactions.
whyWrong.e: HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis (standard teaching), not to drug reactions.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a rash on her hands and arms for 3 days. She had a cold sore on her lip 10 days ago and gets them several times a year. She takes no medications. There are round lesions on her palms, the backs of her hands, and her forearms, each with a dusky center, a pale ring, and a red outer halo. There are two small erosions inside her lower lip. No skin is peeling.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this rash?
questions.explanation: Answer: herpes simplex virus (erythema multiforme). Why: the classic lesion of erythema multiforme is round, with a violet center and a pink halo separated by a pale ring (a target or iris lesion), on the distal limbs, often the palms and soles, and the face. Herpes simplex infection is the most common cause. Mycoplasma and other infections and drugs such as allopurinol, anticonvulsants, and sulfonamides are less common causes. Mouth lesions can be painful and make eating hard. For frequent recurrences, 6 months of continuous acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir may be tried. Recent change: your Osmosis Dermatology notes (p. 17) describe "erythema multiforme major" as often drug-related, with skin detachment and a Nikolsky sign. MSD now considers erythema multiforme a different entity from Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, so drug exposure with mucosal erosions and peeling skin should make you think of SJS/TEN instead. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 180) also name HSV as the most common association, with Mycoplasma, drugs such as penicillins and sulfonamides, SLE, and cancer as others.

whyWrong.b: Mycoplasma can trigger erythema multiforme, but MSD lists it among the less common causes. Her repeated cold sores point to HSV.
whyWrong.c: Borrelia burgdorferi causes erythema migrans, a single expanding ring at a tick bite (standard teaching), not many target lesions on the hands.
whyWrong.d: Coxsackievirus A16 causes hand-foot-and-mouth disease, with small vesicles rather than target lesions (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Secondary syphilis causes a scaly rash on the palms and soles (standard teaching), not target lesions after cold sores.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Erythema Multiforme

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever, irritability, and a painful red rash for 1 day. It began around his mouth and in his neck and armpit folds, and the skin is now wrinkling and forming large, thin blisters. Gentle pressure makes the top layer of skin slide off. His lips, mouth, and eyes have no lesions. A crusted sore was present below his nose last week.
questions.leadIn: The toxin responsible for this condition cleaves which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: desmoglein 1 (staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome). Why: some Staphylococcus aureus strains release exfoliative toxins A and B, which cleave desmoglein 1, an adhesion protein of the epidermis. The split lies high in the epidermis, just beneath the granular cell layer, so the blisters are superficial and the Nikolsky sign is positive. SSSS mainly affects children under 6, especially infants, and rarely adults with kidney failure or immunosuppression. The mucous membranes are spared, unlike toxic epidermal necrolysis, which follows a drug and splits at or below the basal layer. Cultures come from sites such as the nose, conjunctiva, or a primary infection, not from the bullae, which are sterile. Treatment is IV antistaphylococcal antibiotics such as nafcillin or oxacillin, and glucocorticoids are contraindicated. Your NBME Top Concepts (p. 461) and El-Husseiny MSK notes (pp. 191-192) agree: exfoliative toxin binds desmoglein 1 and the skin splits at the stratum granulosum, while TEN splits at the dermal-epidermal junction. Correction: your El-Husseiny Micro notes (p. 44) say the bullae form under the epidermis. The split is inside the epidermis, at the granular layer (MSD; NBME Top Concepts p. 461; MSK notes p. 191).

whyWrong.b: Desmoglein 3 is the main target of autoantibodies in pemphigus vulgaris (MSD), which usually affects middle-aged adults and often involves the mouth.
whyWrong.c: Inactivating elongation factor 2 is how diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A stop protein synthesis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Shiga toxin acts on the 60S ribosomal subunit (standard teaching). It causes bloody diarrhea, not peeling skin.
whyWrong.e: Tetanus and botulinum toxins cleave SNARE proteins (standard teaching), causing muscle spasm or paralysis rather than blisters.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
MSD Manual Professional: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old Black man comes to the physician because of a dark spot on the sole of his right foot that has grown over the past year. It is a 14-mm brown-black patch with irregular borders and several shades of color. An excisional biopsy confirms melanoma.
questions.leadIn: Which feature of the excised tumor best predicts his risk of metastasis?

options.text: Number of different colors in the lesion
How long the lesion was present

questions.explanation: Answer: depth of invasion, the Breslow thickness. Why: MSD states that metastasis correlates with the depth of dermal invasion, and staging is based on tumor thickness and ulceration. Prognosis depends heavily on the stage at diagnosis. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is recommended for melanomas 1.0 to 4.0 mm thick without palpable nodes and for those thicker than 4.0 mm. This patient has acral lentiginous melanoma, which is only 1% of melanomas overall but the most common type in people with darker skin. Superficial spreading melanoma accounts for 70%, lentigo maligna for 15%, and nodular melanoma for about 5%. The ABCDE warning signs are Asymmetry, irregular Borders, uneven Color, Diameter over 6 mm, and Evolution. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 187) also call Breslow thickness the most important prognostic factor for metastasis, and note that acral lentiginous melanoma is found on the soles and palms, is seen more often in people with darker skin, and is not linked to sun exposure.

whyWrong.b: A diameter over 6 mm is one of the ABCDE warning signs for spotting melanoma (MSD), but metastasis risk follows depth of invasion, not width.
whyWrong.c: Uneven color is an ABCDE warning sign used to suspect melanoma (MSD), not a measure of metastatic risk.
whyWrong.d: Irregular borders help raise suspicion for melanoma (MSD), but they do not predict spread.
whyWrong.e: Change over time (Evolution) raises suspicion for melanoma (MSD), but staging and prognosis are based on depth and ulceration.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Melanoma

questions.topic: Basal cell carcinoma: hedgehog pathway inhibitors
questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has had more than 20 basal cell carcinomas removed since he was 18 years old. His father and sister have had the same problem. He now has a large basal cell carcinoma next to his left eye that has grown into nearby tissue. Surgery and radiation therapy are not options, and treatment with vismodegib is started.
questions.leadIn: This drug blocks which of the following signaling pathways?
questions.explanation: Answer: the Hedgehog pathway. Why: many basal cell carcinomas starting at a young age with an affected parent and sibling suggest basal cell nevus syndrome (Gorlin syndrome). This autosomal dominant disorder causes multiple basal cell carcinomas, mostly through loss-of-function mutations in PTCH1, which leave Hedgehog signaling switched on. Vismodegib and sonidegib inhibit the Hedgehog pathway and may be given for metastatic or locally advanced basal cell carcinoma when surgery and radiation are not options. Cemiplimab, a PD-1 inhibitor, is an option for patients who cannot tolerate them. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer and appears on the head and neck in 80% of cases. It rarely metastasizes, but local growth can be very destructive. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 204) also call it the most common skin cancer, locally invasive but rarely metastatic, with nests of basal cells whose outer layer lines up in a palisade.

whyWrong.b: BRAF and MEK inhibitors are used for BRAF-mutated melanoma (MSD), not for Hedgehog-driven basal cell carcinoma.
whyWrong.c: Cemiplimab blocks PD-1 and is used when patients cannot tolerate Hedgehog inhibitors (MSD). Vismodegib does not act on PD-1.
whyWrong.d: EGFR inhibitors are used for some lung, colorectal, and head and neck cancers (standard teaching), not basal cell carcinoma syndromes.
whyWrong.e: mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus and everolimus are used in transplant immunosuppression and some cancers (standard teaching), not in Gorlin syndrome.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Basal Cell Carcinoma

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because her skin burns after only a few minutes in the sun. She has had white hair and very pale skin since birth. Her eyes move back and forth involuntarily, she squints in bright light, and her vision is poor. Her parents are normally pigmented. A skin biopsy shows a normal number of melanocytes.
questions.leadIn: Reduced activity of which enzyme is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: tyrosinase (oculocutaneous albinism type 1). Why: in oculocutaneous albinism, melanocytes are present in normal numbers but make little or no melanin. Mutations in the TYR gene cause absent (OCA1A) or reduced (OCA1B) tyrosinase activity. Most cases are autosomal recessive, which fits her normally pigmented parents. Eye involvement causes photophobia, strabismus, nystagmus, and poor vision. Patients burn easily and have a high risk of skin cancer. MSD stresses squamous cell carcinoma, and your El-Husseiny MSK notes (p. 183) add melanoma and basal cell carcinoma to squamous cell carcinoma. The only treatment for the skin is protection from sunlight. Albinism-like features also occur in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (with platelet problems) and Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (with immunodeficiency). Your notes (pp. 182-183) contrast albinism, with normal melanocytes that cannot make melanin, with vitiligo, where autoimmunity destroys the melanocytes.

whyWrong.b: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is phenylketonuria (standard teaching), which can lighten skin and hair but mainly causes intellectual disability if untreated.
whyWrong.c: Homogentisate oxidase deficiency is alkaptonuria (standard teaching), which darkens cartilage and urine rather than removing pigment.
whyWrong.d: Tyrosine hydroxylase makes L-dopa for dopamine and other catecholamines in nerve tissue (standard teaching). It is not the melanin enzyme in melanocytes.
whyWrong.e: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts dopamine to norepinephrine (standard teaching). It plays no role in melanin.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Albinism

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of a rash that has been spreading for 2 years despite topical treatment. There are sharply bordered red plaques with silvery scale on his elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back. New plaques have appeared along a recent scratch on his forearm. Treatment with secukinumab is started.
questions.leadIn: The cytokine this drug blocks is made mainly by which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: Answer: Th17 cells. Why: psoriasis is keratinocyte overgrowth driven by innate and adaptive immunity. Activated dendritic cells secrete IL-12 and IL-23, which expand T helper cells, and the most commonly implicated pathway is Th17-mediated, producing IL-17 and IL-22. Secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab, and brodalumab are IL-17 inhibitors. Tildrakizumab, risankizumab, and guselkumab are IL-23 inhibitors, and ustekinumab targets both IL-12 and IL-23. Classic lesions are sharply bordered red plaques with silvery scale on the elbows and knees, and injury can trigger new plaques (Koebner phenomenon). Psoriatic arthritis develops in 5 to 30% of patients (MSD key points). Systemic glucocorticoids should not be used, because they can cause flares or pustular psoriasis. Your El-Husseiny MSK notes (pp. 173-175) add the histology: a thickened epidermis (acanthosis), nuclei kept in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis), neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum (Munro microabscesses), and pinpoint bleeding when scale is lifted (Auspitz sign). Recent change: your notes list topical steroids, vitamin D analogs, PUVA, methotrexate, and cyclosporine. MSD now also lists IL-17, IL-23, and IL-12/23 biologics.

whyWrong.b: Th2 cells make IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and drive allergic disease such as atopic dermatitis (standard teaching), not IL-17.
whyWrong.c: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses with IL-10 and TGF-beta (standard teaching). They do not make IL-17.
whyWrong.d: Plasma cells make antibodies (standard teaching), not IL-17.
whyWrong.e: Mast cells release histamine in allergic reactions (standard teaching). MSD describes psoriasis as driven by the Th17 pathway.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Psoriasis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department because of severe pain in his right leg for 12 hours. Yesterday he cut his shin on rocks while wading in warm seawater on the Gulf Coast. His temperature is 39.2°C, and his blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg. The leg is swollen with dusky skin and blood-filled blisters. His pain is far worse than the skin findings suggest.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Answer: Vibrio vulnificus (necrotizing soft-tissue infection). Why: a subgroup of monomicrobial necrotizing soft-tissue infection follows wounds from water in warm coastal areas, especially in people with chronic liver disease such as cirrhosis, diabetes, or weakened immunity, and Vibrio vulnificus is the usual pathogen. Pain out of proportion to the skin findings is a key warning sign, and crepitus from gas in the tissues may develop. Most other necrotizing infections are either polymicrobial or caused by group A streptococci, with S. aureus second. Treatment is mainly urgent surgical debridement, repeated as needed, plus antibiotics started at once. Clindamycin or linezolid is often added to inhibit toxin production. Even with treatment, mortality is about 20 to 30%. Your El-Husseiny Micro notes (p. 124) add that infection can also come from eating raw oysters, and that people with liver disease or iron overload (hemochromatosis) are at high risk of rapidly spreading necrotizing fasciitis with bloody blisters and septic shock.

whyWrong.b: Aeromonas causes wound infections after freshwater exposure (standard teaching). His wound came from warm seawater, and he has cirrhosis.
whyWrong.c: Pasteurella multocida infects cat and dog bites (standard teaching), not wounds from seawater.
whyWrong.d: Pseudomonas causes infections in burns and hot tub folliculitis (standard teaching). It is not the classic seawater pathogen in cirrhosis.
whyWrong.e: Clostridial gas gangrene can follow deep traumatic injury (MSD), but seawater exposure with cirrhosis points to Vibrio vulnificus.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of swelling of her lips and face that began a few hours after a tooth extraction. She has had episodes of swollen hands and feet lasting 2 to 3 days since her early teens, and some episodes of crampy abdominal pain with vomiting. The swellings do not itch, and she has never had hives. Her mother has similar episodes. Serum C4 was low when she was well last month.
questions.leadIn: Which mediator is mainly responsible for her swelling?
questions.explanation: Answer: bradykinin (hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency). Why: hereditary C1 inhibitor deficiency is autosomal dominant, and the swelling is bradykinin-mediated rather than histamine-mediated. Itching, hives, and bronchospasm do not occur. C4 is low even between episodes, and diagnosis requires a low C1 inhibitor level or reduced function. C1q is normal in the hereditary forms but low in acquired deficiency. Mild trauma such as dental work, and estrogen-containing drugs, can trigger attacks. The gut is often involved, with pain that can mimic bowel obstruction, and laryngeal edema can cause stridor and sometimes death. Glucocorticoids, epinephrine, and antihistamines usually do not work. Acute attacks are treated with C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (a bradykinin B2 receptor blocker), or the kallikrein inhibitors ecallantide and sebetralstat. Lanadelumab and berotralstat, which also inhibit kallikrein, prevent attacks. Your El-Husseiny Micro notes (p. 433) describe the same mechanism: without C1 inhibitor, kallikrein is uncontrolled and bradykinin rises, C4 is low, and ACE inhibitors are contraindicated because they also raise bradykinin.

whyWrong.b: Histamine causes allergic angioedema with hives and itching (standard teaching). MSD notes that hives and itching do not occur in C1 inhibitor deficiency.
whyWrong.c: Leukotrienes cause bronchospasm and mucus in asthma (standard teaching), and bronchospasm does not occur in C1 inhibitor deficiency (MSD).
whyWrong.d: C5a is a complement fragment that attracts neutrophils (standard teaching). It does not explain itch-free swelling with low C4.
whyWrong.e: Prostaglandin D2 is a mast cell product of allergic reactions (standard teaching), not the cause of this swelling.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hereditary and Acquired C1 Inhibitor Deficiency or Dysfunction

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with Down syndrome comes to the clinic with his mother for a planned removal of part of a painful ingrown toenail under local anesthesia. He lives in a group home, works at a grocery store, and has no court-appointed guardian. The physician explains the procedure, its risks, and the choice of warm soaks and waiting instead. In his own words, he says that the side of the nail will be cut out, that his toe will be numbed first, and that the toe could get infected afterward. He says he wants it done because his toe hurts every time he walks to work. His mother says she does not want him to have it because he "doesn't really understand."
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed with the procedure based on his consent
Obtain written consent from his mother instead
Request a court ruling on his competence
Postpone until a psychiatrist formally assesses him
Ask the group home manager to decide for him

questions.explanation: Answer: proceed with his consent. Why: For this decision he shows decision-making capacity. He understands the information, weighs it against his own goal (walking without pain), and states a clear choice. Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 266) say that intellectual disability alone, such as Down syndrome, does not exclude a person from informed decision-making. They also say that a physician decides capacity for a specific decision, while competency is a legal ruling made by a judge. StatPearls agrees that capacity is a clinical judgment about one decision at one point in time and that competence is decided by a judge, never by medical providers. He is an adult without a guardian, so his choice stands even though his mother disagrees.

whyWrong.b: His mother is not his legal decision-maker. A surrogate is used only when the patient lacks capacity (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 266), and he has it for this decision.
whyWrong.c: Competence is a court ruling about broad decision-making (StatPearls). It is not needed when the physician finds capacity for this one decision.
whyWrong.d: Any physician can assess capacity (StatPearls). A psychiatry consult can help in unclear cases, but here capacity is clear.
whyWrong.e: A group home manager has no authority to decide for an adult who has capacity (standard teaching).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Ethics (decision-making capacity), p. 266
StatPearls: Competency and Capacity

questions.stem: A 78-year-old widowed man is in the intensive care unit after a large hemorrhagic stroke. He does not respond to voice or pain and cannot make decisions. He has no advance directive and never named a health care proxy, and no court has appointed a guardian. His 50-year-old daughter visits every week. She says that last year he told her he would not want a feeding tube if he could no longer recognize his family. His younger sister, who has lived with him for 5 years, insists that a feeding tube be placed and everything be done.
questions.leadIn: Whose decision should guide the plan about a feeding tube?

options.text: His daughter, based on what he would have wanted
His sister, because she lives with the patient
The attending physician, based on medical judgment
The hospital ethics committee, by majority vote
Whichever relative is willing to sign the form

questions.explanation: Answer: his daughter. Why: When a patient has lost capacity and left no advance directive, a surrogate who knows the patient decides what the patient would have chosen. Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 266) give the usual order: spouse, then adult children, then parents, then siblings, then other relatives. He is widowed, so his adult daughter comes before his sister, and she is reporting his own stated wishes. StatPearls calls this substituted judgment: the surrogate chooses what the patient would have wanted. Other source: StatPearls notes that state law sets who may act as surrogate, and the details differ between states.

whyWrong.b: Living with the patient does not move a sibling ahead of an adult child in the usual order (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 266).
whyWrong.c: The physician gives medical facts and a recommendation but does not make value choices for a patient who has a valid surrogate (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: An ethics committee can help settle a conflict, but it does not replace the surrogate (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Being willing to sign does not make someone the surrogate. Priority is set by law and by the patient's relationships (StatPearls).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Ethics (surrogate decision-maker), p. 266
StatPearls: Advance Directives

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man comes to the physician because of a painless sore on his penis for 10 days. Examination shows a clean-based ulcer with firm edges and painless swelling of the lymph nodes in both groins. Both a nontreponemal test and a treponemal test are positive. He is diagnosed with primary syphilis and treated in the office. He then asks the physician not to put his name "on any government list" because he is afraid his employer will find out.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Explain that the case must be reported to the health department
Agree not to report because he has already been treated
Report it only if he refuses to tell his sexual partners himself
Inform his employer so the workplace can be screened
Report the case only with his written permission

questions.explanation: Answer: report the case to public health. Why: Reporting certain infections is an accepted exception to confidentiality. Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 267) list reportable diseases, such as sexually transmitted infections, hepatitis, and food poisoning, among these exceptions; public health officials then notify people who are at risk. CDC confirms that syphilis has been a nationally notifiable disease since 1944 and that state and local health departments collect the case reports. The physician can reassure him that public health reports are kept confidential and are not shared with employers, and encourage him to tell his partners so they can be tested and treated (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Treatment does not remove the duty to report. The report lets public health reach partners who may be infected (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 267).
whyWrong.c: The case is reported whether or not he tells his partners himself (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 267).
whyWrong.d: Telling his employer would break confidentiality and serves no public health purpose (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Reportable diseases are an exception to confidentiality, so his permission is not required (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 267).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Ethics (confidentiality), p. 267
CDC National Center for Health Statistics: Sexually Transmitted Disease (STD) Surveillance

questions.topic: Patient safety: disclosure of medical errors
questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman is in the hospital for pneumonia. A nurse realizes that 2 hours earlier she gave the patient a 25-mg dose of metoprolol that was meant for the patient in the next bed. Over the next 4 hours, the woman's blood pressure and heart rate stay normal, and she has no symptoms. She is alert and has decision-making capacity. The nurse asks the resident whether the patient really needs to be told, since "nothing happened."
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Tell the patient what happened and what is being done
Do not tell her because she was not harmed
Tell her only if a complication develops in the next day
Tell her family but not the patient
Document it only in the incident report

questions.explanation: Answer: tell the patient. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 274) say that medical errors should be disclosed to patients whether or not they cause harm. The AMA Code of Medical Ethics (Opinion 8.6) says physicians should disclose the error, explain the possible harm, and give the patient the information needed to make decisions about future care, even when the new information will not change treatment. It adds that worry about legal liability should not affect a physician's honesty. The event should also go into the hospital's reporting system so the process can be fixed (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 273, safety culture and event reporting).

whyWrong.b: Errors are disclosed whether or not they cause harm (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 274).
