whyWrong.c: Waiting for a complication delays disclosure. The AMA says to disclose even when the information will not change treatment.
whyWrong.d: She has capacity, so she is told first. Sharing her information with family needs her permission (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: An incident report helps fix the system, but it does not replace telling the patient (AMA Opinion 8.6).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Quality and safety (medical errors), pp. 273-274
AMA Code of Medical Ethics, Opinion 8.6: Promoting Patient Safety

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man returns to the clinic to hear the results of a liver biopsy. In a quiet room, the physician asks what he already knows, and he says he is worried it might be cancer. After he agrees that he wants the full results, the physician tells him the biopsy shows pancreatic cancer that has spread to the liver. He looks down, is silent for a moment, and starts to cry.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next response by the physician?

options.text: Pause, then acknowledge that this is very hard news
Start describing chemotherapy options to give him hope
Tell him that many patients do well with treatment
Ask whether he wants to hear the survival numbers now
Leave the room to give him some time alone

questions.explanation: Answer: respond to his emotion with empathy. Why: SPIKES (Baile and colleagues, The Oncologist, 2000) is a six-step plan for giving bad news: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, and Strategy and summary. The physician has already done the first four steps. The E step is an empathic response: notice the emotion, name it to yourself, identify its cause (usually the news itself), and, after giving the patient a short time to express his feelings, make a statement that connects the feeling to its cause. The authors call responding to emotions one of the hardest parts of breaking bad news. Treatment plans come later, in the Strategy step.

whyWrong.b: Moving to treatment while he is crying skips the Emotions step; plans belong to the later Strategy step (Baile 2000).
whyWrong.c: Quick reassurance is not empathy and may not be true for cancer that has already spread (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Offering more information now skips over his emotion, which SPIKES says to address first (Baile 2000).
whyWrong.e: Leaving him alone withdraws support at the moment he most needs it (standard teaching).

sources.title: Baile WF et al. SPIKES: a six-step protocol for delivering bad news. The Oncologist 2000;5:302-311

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman who speaks only Vietnamese comes to the clinic to discuss an abnormal Pap test result and a planned colposcopy. Her husband, who speaks English well, offers to interpret. It is not an emergency. The clinic has interpreter services available by phone and video. She has not asked for her husband to interpret.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate with her?

options.text: Use a qualified medical interpreter by phone or video
Have her husband interpret since he is fluent
Speak slowly in simple English and use gestures
Have a bilingual receptionist with no training interpret
Use an online translation app on the phone

questions.explanation: Answer: use a qualified medical interpreter. Why: The federal rule for health programs that receive federal money (45 CFR 92.201) says language help must come from a qualified interpreter. An adult who comes with the patient may interpret only in an emergency that threatens someone's safety when no qualified interpreter is available, or when the patient asks for it privately, with a qualified interpreter present, and it is appropriate. A minor child may interpret only as a temporary measure in an emergency. StatPearls (Informed Consent) also says medical interpreter services must be used for patients with limited English proficiency. Family members may leave out or change information, and a sensitive topic such as a gynecologic result can be hard to discuss through a spouse (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: A companion may interpret only in an emergency or when the patient asks for it in private (45 CFR 92.201). Neither applies here.
whyWrong.c: Simple English and gestures will not let her understand her result and give informed consent (StatPearls).
whyWrong.d: Speaking two languages does not make someone a trained medical interpreter who can render medical terms accurately (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Translation apps can make errors with medical terms and are not a qualified interpreter (standard teaching).

sources.title: 45 CFR 92.201: Meaningful access for individuals with limited English proficiency (eCFR)
StatPearls: Informed Consent

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man comes for follow-up of hypertension. Six months ago he was prescribed amlodipine, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide. Today his blood pressure is 164/98 mm Hg, the same as before treatment. Pharmacy records show that he filled the prescriptions only once. When the physician mentions this, he looks at the floor and says nothing.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask in a nonjudgmental way what makes taking them hard
Add a fourth drug for resistant hypertension
Tell him he will have a stroke unless he takes them
Refer him to a different physician for a fresh start
Tell him you cannot keep treating him unless he adheres

questions.explanation: Answer: explore the reasons without judgment. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 268) advise trying to find the reason for nonadherence and how willing the patient is to change, without coercing him or referring him to another physician. Brown and Sinsky (Family Practice Management, 2013) point out that how the question is asked matters, because patients want to please their doctor. They also note that forgetting explains less than 30% of nonadherence; many patients make a deliberate choice based on cost, fear of side effects, or doubt that the drug helps. Once the reason is known, the plan can change, for example fewer pills taken less often or extended-release forms.

whyWrong.b: Adherence must be confirmed before hypertension is called resistant. A fourth drug adds to pills he is already not taking (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A scare tactic is a form of pressure; your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 268) advise against coercing adherence.
whyWrong.d: Referring him away does not solve the problem and is advised against (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 268).
whyWrong.e: Threatening to end care is coercion (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 268).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Ethical situations, p. 268
Brown MT, Sinsky CA. Medication Adherence: We Didn't Ask and They Didn't Tell. Fam Pract Manag 2013;20(2):25-30

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes for a routine visit. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and has taken sertraline for depression for 1 year, with good results. She says a friend told her that St. John's wort is "natural and safer," and she plans to start it next week.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Ask why she wants it, then explain its risks and interactions
Tell her herbal products are unproven and decline to discuss them
Approve it, since natural products have few interactions
Stop sertraline so she can try St. John's wort alone
Refer her to a naturopath to manage the herbal treatment

questions.explanation: Answer: explore her reasons and advise her. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 269) advise exploring the patient's reasons in a supportive, nonjudgmental way and telling her the known benefits and risks, including side effects, contraindications, and drug interactions. The interactions matter here. NCCIH rates St. John's wort as high risk for interactions because it strongly induces cytochrome P-450 enzymes and P-glycoprotein. It has documented interactions with oral contraceptives, warfarin, cyclosporine, digoxin, and others, and with some antidepressants it can increase serotonin-related side effects that may be serious.

whyWrong.b: Refusing to talk ends the conversation and may lead her to take it without advice; your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 269) advise a supportive discussion.
whyWrong.c: St. John's wort is high risk for drug interactions, including with oral contraceptives (NCCIH).
whyWrong.d: Stopping an antidepressant that works, to try an herb, risks relapse and was not the plan of a shared discussion (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Handing her off avoids the discussion of risks and interactions that her own physician should have (standard teaching).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Ethical situations, p. 269
NCCIH: Herb-Drug Interactions: What the Science Says

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is in the intensive care unit 2 days after a motorcycle crash with a severe head injury. Today he was declared dead by brain death criteria after a complete neurologic examination and an apnea test done according to hospital policy. When a nurse touches his foot, his leg pulls back. His parents say, "He is still moving," and ask that the ventilator be continued indefinitely.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Gently explain that he died and the movement is a reflex
Keep the ventilator on indefinitely, as his family requests
Repeat the apnea test every day until the family accepts it
Tell them the movement suggests he may recover
Turn off the ventilator now without any further discussion

questions.explanation: Answer: explain gently that brain death is death. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 269) advise gently telling the family that he cannot recover, that brain death is equal to death, and that the movement is a spinal reflex, not a voluntary act. The case can be taken to the ethics committee about the futility of continuing support. StatPearls (Brain Death Criteria) explains that in the United States the Uniform Determination of Death Act defines death to include irreversible loss of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem. It also says some spinal reflexes, such as leg flexion, can still occur and are compatible with brain death. The team should be supportive and make religious accommodations if the family wishes (StatPearls).

whyWrong.b: Brain death is death, so support is not continued indefinitely; a dispute goes to the ethics committee (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 269).
whyWrong.c: Repeating the test does not change a confirmed diagnosis and does not address the family's grief (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Spinal reflexes are compatible with brain death and do not mean recovery is possible (StatPearls).
whyWrong.e: The family needs explanation and support first (StatPearls).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Ethical situations, p. 269
StatPearls: Brain Death Criteria

questions.stem: Vincristine is a chemotherapy drug that is fatal if injected into the spinal fluid. At one hospital, it was twice ordered by mistake as an intrathecal (spinal) dose in the same year. Both orders were caught by a pharmacist before the drug was given. The safety committee wants the change that is most likely to prevent this error from happening again.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following interventions is most likely to be effective?

options.text: An order system that blocks any route other than IV
Yearly training on chemotherapy safety for all staff
A bright warning label on every vincristine bag
A checklist read aloud before each chemotherapy dose
A written policy that disciplines staff who make errors

questions.explanation: Answer: a forcing function. Why: A forcing function is a design that makes the wrong action impossible. Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 273) call forcing functions the most effective human factors design. ISMP's hierarchy of effectiveness (2026) agrees. Forcing functions, barriers, and automation are high-leverage. Standardization, warnings, alerts, and checklists are medium-leverage. Rules, policies, and education are low-leverage because they depend on people remembering. ISMP gives this very example: a hard stop in the electronic health record that does not allow the IV route of a vinca alkaloid to be changed. That vincristine given into the spinal fluid is fatal is standard teaching.

whyWrong.b: Education and training are low-leverage because they rely on memory and attention (ISMP).
whyWrong.c: Warnings and alerts are medium-leverage; they can be missed or ignored (ISMP).
whyWrong.d: Checklists are medium-leverage. They make processes more reliable but still depend on people (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 273; ISMP).
whyWrong.e: Rules and policies are low-leverage (ISMP), and blame works against a safety culture in which staff can report concerns without fear (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 273).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Quality and safety, p. 273
ISMP: Implement High-Leverage and Layered Risk-Reduction Strategies Using ISMP's Hierarchy of Effectiveness (2026)

questions.topic: Human development: sleep in older adults
questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman says that over the past few years her sleep has changed. It takes her longer to fall asleep, she wakes up several times during the night, and she wakes at 4:30 AM and cannot get back to sleep. She goes to bed around 9:30 PM. She feels rested during the day, her mood is good, and her husband says she does not snore. She does crossword puzzles daily, and her memory is unchanged.
questions.leadIn: Compared with a young adult, which of the following is an expected change in her sleep?
questions.explanation: Answer: less slow-wave sleep. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 270) list the sleep changes of normal aging: less REM sleep and less slow-wave sleep, a longer time to fall asleep, and more early-morning awakenings. The same page notes that intelligence does not decline with normal aging. MSD Manual (Overview of Sleep) agrees that older adults spend less time in deep sleep, wake up more often and more easily, and tend to fall asleep and wake up early. She functions well during the day and has no signs of depression or sleep apnea, so this pattern fits normal aging.

whyWrong.b: Sleep latency (time to fall asleep) gets longer with age (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 270).
whyWrong.c: REM sleep decreases with age (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 270).
whyWrong.d: Early-morning awakenings increase with age (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 270; MSD).
whyWrong.e: More awakenings and less deep sleep mean lower sleep efficiency (standard teaching).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: The well patient (changes in the elderly), p. 270
MSD Manual Consumer Version: Overview of Sleep

questions.topic: Human development: a child's understanding of death
questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl's grandfather died of a heart attack 2 weeks ago. Her parents told her that "Grandpa went to sleep and won't wake up." Since then she has refused to go to bed and cries at bedtime. She keeps asking when Grandpa will come back. Her parents ask the pediatrician how to talk with her.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Explain plainly that Grandpa died and will not come back
Keep telling her that Grandpa is asleep so she will not be upset
Tell her she is too young to understand death
Keep her away from the funeral and avoid talking about him
Wait until she is older to talk about his death

questions.explanation: Answer: explain plainly that he died. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 269) note that between about 5 and 7 years of age, children start to grasp that death lasts forever, that the body stops working completely, and that every living thing eventually dies. They advise a direct, concrete description of the death, without clichés or euphemisms, along with reassurance that the child is not to blame, acceptance of her fears and feelings, and play and healthy ways of remembering. HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics) warns that saying someone "went to sleep" can make children, who take words literally, afraid of going to sleep. That is what happened here.

whyWrong.b: Saying he is asleep is the euphemism causing her fear of bedtime (HealthyChildren.org).
whyWrong.c: At 6 she is starting to understand that death is permanent (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 269).
whyWrong.d: Shutting down talk about him goes against naming her feelings and helping her remember him in her own way (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 269).
whyWrong.e: A direct, concrete explanation now is advised, not a delay (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 269).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Ethical situations (child and death), p. 269
HealthyChildren.org (AAP): How Children Understand Death: What to Say When a Loved One Dies

questions.stem: A healthy boy is brought for his 12-month well-child visit. He was born at term weighing 3.4 kg (7.5 lb). He has been breastfed and started solid foods at 6 months. He has had no illnesses, and his length and head circumference have followed the 50th percentile.
questions.leadIn: If his weight has followed the usual pattern, which of the following is closest to his weight now?
questions.explanation: Answer: about 10 kg. Why: MSD Manual (Physical Growth of Infants and Children) gives the usual pattern for term infants. They lose 5 to 8% of birth weight in the first days and are back to birth weight by about 2 weeks. Birth weight roughly doubles by about 5 months and triples by 1 year, so 3.4 kg × 3 ≈ 10 kg. In the first year, length increases by about 25 cm and head circumference grows by about 1 cm a month (MSD).

whyWrong.a: About 5 kg is less than double his birth weight; most infants reach double (about 7 kg) by about 5 months (MSD).
whyWrong.b: About 7 kg is double his birth weight, which is expected at about 5 months, not 12 months (MSD).
whyWrong.d: About 14 kg is about four times birth weight, more than the usual tripling by 1 year (MSD).
whyWrong.e: About 17 kg is five times birth weight and would mean far faster weight gain than the usual pattern (MSD).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Physical Growth of Infants and Children

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of breast development for 6 months and new pubic hair. Over the past year, her height has risen from the 50th to the 90th percentile. She has no headaches, vision changes, or seizures. Examination shows Tanner stage 3 breasts and stage 2 pubic hair, normal visual fields, and no skin spots. An x-ray of the left hand shows a bone age of 10 years. A morning serum LH level is in the pubertal range. Pelvic ultrasonography shows an enlarged uterus and normal ovaries with no mass.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Granulosa cell tumor of the ovary

questions.explanation: Answer: idiopathic central precocious puberty. Why: MSD Manual defines precocious puberty as puberty starting before age 8 in girls or before age 9 in boys, and notes that these cutoffs are being reconsidered. In the central type, the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis switches on early, so LH is in the pubertal range; a morning LH level is the best first test. Bone age is often advanced and growth speeds up. Most girls with the central type have no cause found, while a brain lesion is more common in boys. MSD advises MRI for girls younger than 6 and for all boys, but not routinely for girls aged 6 to 8 without neurologic signs. Treatment with a GnRH agonist, such as leuprolide or a histrelin implant, can help preserve adult height (MSD).

whyWrong.b: A hypothalamic hamartoma causes central puberty, but most girls aged 6 to 8 have no cause found and do not need routine MRI (MSD).
whyWrong.c: McCune-Albright syndrome causes peripheral puberty with low LH; it comes with café-au-lait spots and bone lesions (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: An estrogen-producing ovarian tumor causes peripheral puberty with suppressed LH and an ovarian mass on ultrasound (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Outside estrogen causes peripheral puberty, and LH stays low (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Precocious Puberty

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought for a well-child visit. He was born at term and has been healthy. His parents have no concerns, but they ask which skills most children his age have. The physician uses the CDC milestone checklists, which list skills that most children reach by each age.
questions.leadIn: By 18 months, most children can do which of the following?

options.text: Walk alone without holding on to anything
Put two words together, such as "more milk"

questions.explanation: Answer: walk alone. Why: CDC's milestone checklists (Learn the Signs. Act Early.) list skills that 75% or more of children reach by each age, so missing one is a reason to look more closely. By 18 months these include walking without holding on to anyone or anything, trying to say three or more words besides "mama" or "dada," following one-step directions without gestures, scribbling, and climbing on and off a couch or chair without help. Putting two words together and kicking a ball are 2-year milestones, using a fork is a 3-year milestone, and hopping on one foot is a 5-year milestone (CDC).

whyWrong.b: Saying two words together, such as "more milk," is a 2-year milestone (CDC).
whyWrong.c: Kicking a ball is a 2-year milestone (CDC).
whyWrong.d: Hopping on one foot is a 5-year milestone (CDC).
whyWrong.e: Eating with a fork is a 3-year milestone (CDC).

sources.title: CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.: Milestones by 18 Months
CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.: Milestones by 2 Years
CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.: Milestones by 3 Years
CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.: Milestones by 5 Years

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of frequent infections. Since age 8 months he has had six ear infections and two episodes of pneumonia, one caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and one by Haemophilus influenzae. His maternal uncle died of an infection as a child. His tonsils are very small, and no lymph nodes can be felt. Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM are all very low. Flow cytometry shows that less than 1% of his lymphocytes are CD19+ B cells; T-cell counts are normal.
questions.leadIn: A mutation in which of the following genes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: BTK (X-linked, or Bruton, agammaglobulinemia). Why: MSD Manual explains that a mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase blocks B-cell maturation, so B cells are nearly absent and all immunoglobulin classes are very low. Affected boys have recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria, very small tonsils, and no lymph nodes. Treatment is lifelong immune globulin replacement, and live vaccines must not be given (MSD). Your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes (p. 464) add that infections begin after about 6 months, when the mother's IgG fades, that T cells are normal, and that enteroviral infections and Giardia are typical.

whyWrong.b: CD40 ligand mutations cause hyper-IgM syndrome; B cells are present and IgM is normal or high (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: ADA deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency with very low T cells as well (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: CYBB mutations cause X-linked chronic granulomatous disease, a phagocyte killing defect with normal antibodies (MSD).
whyWrong.e: IL2RG mutations cause X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, with absent T and NK cells (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Chapter 7 Immunology

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has had several skin abscesses and an abscess in a neck lymph node, all growing Staphylococcus aureus. Last year he had a liver abscess. He is now admitted with pneumonia, and Aspergillus fumigatus grows from a lung biopsy that also shows granulomas. Immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte counts are normal. In a dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry test, his neutrophils do not become fluorescent after stimulation.
questions.leadIn: His neutrophils are most likely unable to do which of the following?

options.text: Produce superoxide during the respiratory burst
Roll along endothelium using sialyl Lewis X
Migrate out of vessels using CD18-containing integrins
Convert hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid

questions.explanation: Answer: produce superoxide (chronic granulomatous disease, CGD). Why: MSD Manual explains that CGD is a defect in NADPH oxidase, so phagocytes cannot make superoxide and other reactive oxygen compounds to kill microbes. More than half of cases are X-linked. Infections are caused by catalase-producing organisms such as S. aureus, E. coli, Serratia, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and fungi, and Aspergillus infection is the leading cause of death. Granulomas can form and block the gut or urinary tract. Diagnosis is by the DHR flow test; prevention uses trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and an azole antifungal, often with interferon gamma, and a stem cell transplant from an HLA-identical sibling is usually successful (MSD). Your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes (p. 473) explain why catalase matters: catalase-negative bacteria leave their own hydrogen peroxide in the phagosome, which the neutrophil can still use to kill them, while catalase-positive organisms break it down.

whyWrong.b: Rolling with sialyl Lewis X fails in leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2 (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A CD18 integrin defect is leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1, with delayed cord separation and no pus (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Failure of phagosome-lysosome fusion occurs in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, with albinism and giant granules (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Myeloperoxidase deficiency blocks hypochlorous acid formation; it is usually mild, and superoxide production is normal (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Chapter 7 Immunology

questions.stem: A 2-day-old boy has twitching of his face and hands. He was born at term. A murmur is heard, and echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus. He has low-set ears, a small jaw, and a short groove above the lip. Serum calcium is 6.4 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), and parathyroid hormone is low. A chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow.
questions.leadIn: Abnormal development of which of the following structures most likely caused his condition?

options.text: First pharyngeal arch and first pouch

questions.explanation: Answer: the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches (DiGeorge syndrome). Why: MSD Manual explains that DiGeorge syndrome results from abnormal development of the pharyngeal pouches around week 8 of gestation. Most cases are due to a deletion at chromosome 22q11, and a few involve 10p13. Underdeveloped parathyroid glands cause hypocalcemic tetany, typically at 24 to 48 hours of life. Conotruncal heart defects such as interrupted aortic arch, truncus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot are common. A missing or small thymus causes low T cells and infections. Complete DiGeorge syndrome, with no thymus, is treated with cultured thymus tissue transplant or stem cell transplant (MSD). Your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes (p. 466) describe the same 22q11 microdeletion, with failed development of third and fourth pouch structures and absent thymus and parathyroid glands.

whyWrong.b: The first arch forms the jaw muscles and two middle ear bones, and the first pouch forms the middle ear cavity (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The second pouch forms the palatine tonsil, not the thymus or parathyroids (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The thyroglossal duct is the path of the thyroid's descent; it can leave a midline neck cyst (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The fourth and sixth arches form laryngeal cartilages and muscles (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: DiGeorge Syndrome
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Chapter 7 Immunology

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a sudden drop in blood pressure, wheezing, and hives within minutes of starting a red blood cell transfusion for bleeding after childbirth. The transfusion is stopped and she is treated with epinephrine. She has celiac disease and frequent sinus infections. Serum IgA is undetectable (less than 7 mg/dL), and IgG and IgM levels are normal.
questions.leadIn: If she needs red blood cells in the future, which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

options.text: Washed red cells or cells from IgA-deficient donors
Usual red cells after premedication with diphenhydramine
Irradiated red cells to prevent graft-versus-host disease
Leukoreduced red cells to prevent febrile reactions

questions.explanation: Answer: washed red cells. Why: MSD Manual describes selective IgA deficiency as the most common primary immunodeficiency, with IgA below 7 mg/dL and normal IgG and IgM. Most people have no symptoms, but some have recurrent sinus and lung infections, and it is linked to celiac disease and autoimmune diseases. Some patients make antibodies against IgA and can have anaphylaxis when given blood products or immune globulin that contain IgA. MSD says that only washed packed red cells should be used when red cells are needed, and that other blood components should come from IgA-deficient donors. Red cells from IgA-deficient donors are also an accepted choice (standard teaching). Your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes (p. 465) give the same warning that IgA in transfused blood can cause fatal anaphylaxis and that gamma-globulin should not be used.

whyWrong.b: Immune globulin does not replace IgA and can trigger anaphylaxis in patients with anti-IgA antibodies (MSD; your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes, p. 465).
whyWrong.c: Premedication does not prevent anaphylaxis caused by anti-IgA antibodies (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease but does not remove IgA (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Leukoreduction removes white cells, not the IgA in the plasma (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Selective IgA Deficiency
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Chapter 7 Immunology

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease receives a kidney from a deceased donor. Within minutes after the vascular clamps are released, the new kidney turns mottled and dark blue and makes no urine. A biopsy shows clots in the small vessels, fibrinoid necrosis of the arteriole walls, and many neutrophils.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Preformed recipient antibodies against donor antigens
Recipient CD8 T cells activated by donor MHC
Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues
Gradual intimal thickening of arteries from chronic injury
Antibodies formed weeks after the transplant

questions.explanation: Answer: preformed antibodies (hyperacute rejection). Why: Your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes (pp. 475-476) describe hyperacute rejection as starting within minutes. It is a type II hypersensitivity reaction in which the recipient already has antibodies against donor antigens, such as ABO blood group or HLA antigens, and these antibodies activate complement and cause widespread clotting in the graft's vessels, so the graft must be removed. MSD Manual (Kidney Transplantation) lists its timing as minutes to hours and its cause as HLA incompatibility, and says that hyperacute rejection usually means the transplant has failed. Crossmatching before transplant aims to prevent it (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: CD8 T cells activated against donor MHC cause acute cellular rejection, which usually starts 1 to 4 weeks after transplant (your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes, p. 476).
whyWrong.c: Donor T cells attacking the recipient is graft-versus-host disease, usually after stem cell transplant (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Slow thickening of the graft's arteries is chronic rejection, which develops over months to years (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Antibodies made after transplant cause acute humoral rejection, not a reaction within minutes (your El-Husseiny Micro & Immuno notes, p. 476).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Chapter 7 Immunology
MSD Manual Professional: Kidney Transplantation

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of trouble swallowing for 1 year. It began with solid food and now also happens with water. She often wakes at night coughing up undigested food from dinner, and she has lost 5 kg (11 lb). Proton pump inhibitor therapy did not help. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus that narrows smoothly to a beak-like point at the gastroesophageal junction. Manometry shows no peristalsis in the esophageal body and incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.
questions.leadIn: Loss of which of the following is the most likely cause of her condition?

options.text: Inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus
Smooth muscle in the lower esophagus from fibrosis
Striated muscle in the upper esophagus
Interstitial cells of Cajal in the stomach
Squamous mucosa from chronic acid injury

questions.explanation: Answer: inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus (achalasia). Why: MSD Manual explains that achalasia is thought to result from loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of the esophagus. Dysphagia for both solids and liquids is the main symptom, often with regurgitation of undigested food at night. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus that is beak-like at the lower esophageal sphincter, and manometry, the preferred test, shows incomplete sphincter relaxation and no peristalsis. Chagas disease can cause the same picture by destroying autonomic ganglia, and the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is higher than in the general population. Treatment options are pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy, peroral endoscopic myotomy, or botulinum toxin for patients who cannot have the others; no treatment restores peristalsis (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 22-23) add that the lost neurons are the inhibitory (nonadrenergic, noncholinergic) ones that normally let the sphincter relax.

whyWrong.b: Fibrosis of esophageal smooth muscle, as in systemic sclerosis, weakens the sphincter and causes reflux rather than a tight sphincter (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Weak striated muscle in the upper esophagus causes trouble starting a swallow (oropharyngeal dysphagia), not a beak-shaped lower narrowing (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Loss of interstitial cells of Cajal in the stomach is linked to gastroparesis, not to a tight lower esophageal sphincter (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Acid injury can cause a peptic stricture, which mainly blocks solids, and her symptoms did not respond to acid suppression (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Achalasia
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Achalasia, pp. 22-23

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with heartburn several times a week for 15 years has upper endoscopy. He is obese and smokes. Endoscopy shows a 4-cm tongue of salmon-colored mucosa extending up from the gastroesophageal junction into the distal esophagus. Biopsy specimens are taken from this area.
questions.leadIn: The biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Signet ring cells invading the wall

questions.explanation: Answer: columnar epithelium with goblet cells (Barrett esophagus). Why: MSD Manual describes Barrett esophagus as replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus by metaplastic columnar epithelium after long-standing reflux, and calls it a precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma. Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 24-25) explain that the biopsy must show goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), which mark the path from metaplasia to dysplasia to adenocarcinoma, and list central obesity, smoking, and hiatal hernia among the risk factors. Recent change: your Osmosis GI notes suggest yearly endoscopy for nondysplastic Barrett esophagus. MSD now advises surveillance every 3 to 5 years when there is no dysplasia, and endoscopic ablation for confirmed low-grade or high-grade dysplasia (unless life-limiting illness is present).

whyWrong.b: Many eosinophils in squamous mucosa suggest eosinophilic esophagitis, not Barrett metaplasia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Normal squamous lining would not look salmon-colored; Barrett mucosa is metaplastic columnar epithelium (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Signet ring cells are typical of diffuse-type gastric cancer (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 59), not of Barrett metaplasia.
whyWrong.e: Noncaseating granulomas suggest Crohn disease (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 64).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Barrett's Esophagus, pp. 24-25

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of crampy right lower abdominal pain, nonbloody diarrhea, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss over 5 months. He smokes. He has a painful, draining opening beside his anus. Colonoscopy shows deep linear ulcers and a cobblestone pattern in the terminal ileum and in two separate segments of the colon, with normal bowel in between. The rectum is normal. A biopsy specimen shows a noncaseating granuloma.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the inflammation in this disease?

options.text: Transmural, with skip areas between segments
Mucosal only, continuous upward from the rectum
Surface pseudomembranes of fibrin and neutrophils

questions.explanation: Answer: transmural inflammation with skip areas (Crohn disease). Why: MSD Manual describes Crohn disease as a chronic transmural inflammatory bowel disease that usually affects the distal ileum and colon. Diseased segments are sharply separated from normal bowel (skip areas). The ileum is involved in about 80% of cases, and transmural inflammation causes strictures and fistulas; perianal fistulas and abscesses occur in about 20%. Noncaseating granulomas are a hallmark when found, but most patients do not have them on biopsy. Malabsorption can cause vitamin B12 and vitamin D deficiency (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 62-64) describe the same picture (cobblestoning, skip lesions, fistulas, noncaseating granulomas) and link it to NOD2 variants and a Th1 response, with smoking as a risk factor. Recent change: your Osmosis GI notes list sulfasalazine and antibiotics as first treatments. MSD now says 5-ASA drugs such as mesalamine lack efficacy and should not be used for Crohn disease; mild disease is treated with budesonide, and moderate to severe disease with biologics such as anti-TNF agents.

whyWrong.b: Continuous mucosal inflammation starting in the rectum describes ulcerative colitis (MSD; your Osmosis GI notes, p. 69).
whyWrong.c: Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli suggest intestinal tuberculosis, not Crohn disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Flask-shaped ulcers with trophozoites are typical of Entamoeba histolytica colitis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Pseudomembranes are typical of Clostridioides difficile colitis after antibiotics (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Crohn Disease
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Crohn's Disease, pp. 62-64

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had bloody diarrhea, urgency, and cramping in the left lower abdomen on and off for 3 years. Colonoscopy shows red, friable mucosa with shallow ulcers that begins at the anal verge and continues without interruption to the splenic flexure. The terminal ileum is normal. Biopsy specimens show crypt abscesses and inflammation limited to the mucosa and submucosa. She asks whether any treatment can cure her disease.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is curative for this condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: total proctocolectomy (ulcerative colitis). Why: MSD Manual explains that ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum and extends upward without gaps, and that inflammation involves the mucosa and submucosa unless disease is severe. Because the disease is limited to the colon and rectum, MSD states that total proctocolectomy is curative and restores normal life expectancy, although up to 25% of patients later develop small-bowel inflammation that looks like Crohn disease. Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 67-69) list crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps, toxic megacolon, colon cancer risk, and extraintestinal problems such as arthritis and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Colon cancer risk rises with the duration and extent of disease, so MSD advises surveillance colonoscopy once disease has lasted more than 8 years (from diagnosis if PSC is present). Correction: your Osmosis GI notes (p. 68) say colectomy is done only if disease is localized; MSD describes total proctocolectomy as curative, used for severe or refractory disease and for dysplasia or cancer.

whyWrong.b: Mesalamine controls mild to moderate disease but does not remove the diseased colon, so it is not curative (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Infliximab can induce and maintain remission but does not cure the disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Metronidazole is used for Crohn disease and its perianal complications (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 64), not to cure ulcerative colitis.
whyWrong.e: Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum, so removing one segment leaves diseased mucosa behind (MSD).

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because of crampy abdominal pain and vomiting. CT shows a small-bowel intussusception with a polyp at its leading point. She has dark brown-blue spots on her lips and the inside of her cheeks that have been present since early childhood. Her father had the same spots and was treated for pancreatic cancer at age 48. The resected polyp is a hamartoma with branching bands of smooth muscle.
questions.leadIn: A germline mutation in which of the following genes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: STK11 (Peutz-Jeghers syndrome). Why: MSD Manual describes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome as an autosomal dominant disease; most cases (about 66 to 94%) have a germline mutation in the STK11 (LKB1) tumor suppressor gene. Hamartomatous polyps form in the stomach, small intestine, and colon and can bleed or cause obstruction and intussusception. Dark macules appear on the lips, gums, mouth, hands, and feet, and most (except those inside the cheek) fade by puberty. The risk of GI cancers (pancreatic, gastric, small bowel, colorectal) and non-GI cancers (breast, lung, uterine, ovarian, testicular) is markedly increased (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 20) also name STK11 (LKB1) and intussusception. Correction: your Osmosis GI notes (p. 20) list intravenous drug use, bicuspid aortic valve, diabetes, high blood pressure, and smoking as causes; those are risk factors for infective endocarditis and do not apply here. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is inherited (MSD).

whyWrong.b: APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis, with hundreds of adenomas rather than hamartomas (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 16).
whyWrong.c: MUTYH mutations cause an autosomal recessive form of adenomatous polyposis (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 16).
whyWrong.d: SMAD4 mutations cause juvenile polyposis syndrome, without lip and mouth pigmentation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: MLH1 is a mismatch repair gene in Lynch syndrome, which causes few polyps and no pigmented spots (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is referred after his mother died of colon cancer at age 41. He has a hard, painless lump on his jaw that is an osteoma, and several epidermoid cysts on his back. Genetic testing shows the same pathogenic APC variant his mother had. Colonoscopy shows several hundred small adenomatous polyps covering the colon and rectum; biopsies show low-grade dysplasia and no cancer.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of his colon?

options.text: Yearly colonoscopy, removing every polyp that is found
Daily celecoxib in place of any surgery
Repeat colonoscopy at age 40, when cancer risk rises
Remove only the largest polyps and recheck in 5 years

questions.explanation: Answer: prophylactic proctocolectomy. Why: MSD Manual explains that familial adenomatous polyposis is autosomal dominant and is diagnosed when there are more than 100 adenomas, which can carpet the colon and rectum. Colorectal cancer develops before age 40 in nearly all untreated patients, so colectomy should be done soon after diagnosis; total proctocolectomy removes the colon and rectal cancer risk. The extracolonic findings once called Gardner syndrome include desmoid tumors, osteomas of the skull or jaw, sebaceous cysts, and adenomas elsewhere in the GI tract; after colectomy, duodenal surveillance and thyroid ultrasound continue (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 16-17) name the APC tumor suppressor gene, note retinal pigment changes (CHRPE), and describe Gardner syndrome as an FAP variant with prominent tumors outside the colon.

whyWrong.b: With hundreds of polyps, removing each one is not possible, and cancer will develop in nearly all patients without colectomy (MSD).
whyWrong.c: COX-2 inhibitors are listed in your Osmosis GI notes (p. 17) as medical therapy, but no drug replaces colectomy (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Nearly all untreated patients develop cancer before age 40, so waiting until 40 is far too late (MSD).
whyWrong.e: Leaving most adenomas in place would let cancer develop; colectomy is advised soon after diagnosis (MSD).

questions.stem: A 3-day-old boy with Down syndrome has not passed meconium since birth. He has had increasing abdominal distention and two episodes of green vomiting. After a rectal examination, he passes a large burst of gas and stool. A contrast enema shows a narrow rectum and sigmoid colon with a dilated colon above it.
questions.leadIn: A rectal suction biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: No ganglion cells in the submucosa
Mucosal necrosis with gas in the wall

questions.explanation: Answer: no ganglion cells (Hirschsprung disease). Why: MSD Manual describes Hirschsprung disease as a congenital absence of the Meissner (submucosal) and Auerbach (myenteric) plexuses in a segment of bowel, caused by failure of neural crest cells to migrate. The affected segment is always continuous, most often the distal colon. Most affected newborns do not pass meconium in the first 48 hours and develop distention and vomiting. About 12% have a chromosome abnormality such as Down syndrome. Contrast enema can show the transition zone, and rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells is the definitive test. Enterocolitis is a life-threatening complication, and treatment is surgical, with a pull-through procedure (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 125) add RET proto-oncogene mutations and increased acetylcholinesterase staining in the biopsy.

whyWrong.b: Thick meconium blocking normal bowel is meconium ileus, typical of cystic fibrosis; ganglion cells are present (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Transmural granulomas suggest Crohn disease, not a newborn bowel obstruction (MSD Crohn page).
whyWrong.d: Mucosal necrosis with gas in the bowel wall suggests necrotizing enterocolitis, mostly in premature infants (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A blind-ending jejunum is jejunal atresia, which would not narrow the rectum and sigmoid (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a large amount of painless, bright red and maroon blood in his diaper. He has no abdominal pain or vomiting, and his abdomen is soft. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower abdomen.
questions.leadIn: Failure of which embryonic structure to close most likely caused his bleeding?
questions.explanation: Answer: the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct (Meckel diverticulum). Why: MSD Manual explains that a Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum, containing all layers of the bowel wall, on the antimesenteric side of the ileum. It is a remnant of the vitelline duct, which normally closes by about week 6 of gestation. It often contains ectopic gastric tissue, whose acid ulcerates the nearby ileum and causes painless bright red rectal bleeding in children. The technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan detects the gastric mucosa in most bleeding children, and treatment is surgical resection (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 130) give the "rule of 2s": symptoms before age 2, about 2% of people, about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, about 2 inches long, and 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic). Other source: MSD gives a prevalence of under 1% to about 3% and places it within about 200 cm of the ileocecal valve.

whyWrong.b: A patent urachus connects the bladder to the umbilicus and leaks urine; it does not bleed into the bowel (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum of the liver (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: A patent processus vaginalis causes an indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of severe epigastric pain that began 6 hours after a large fatty meal and goes straight through to her back. She has vomited three times. She drinks alcohol rarely. Serum lipase is 5 times the upper limit of normal, and ALT is 3 times normal. Ultrasonography shows many gallstones in the gallbladder and a slightly dilated common bile duct.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following events most directly starts the injury to her pancreas?

options.text: Activation of trypsin inside acinar cells
Autoimmune attack on the islet beta cells
Bacterial infection spreading up the duct
Fibrosis and calcification of the ducts
Tumor growing into the main pancreatic duct

questions.explanation: Answer: activation of trypsin inside acinar cells. Why: MSD Manual explains that gallstones and alcohol cause most cases of acute pancreatitis. Early in the disease, enzymes such as trypsin, phospholipase A2, and elastase become active inside the pancreas (intra-acinar activation) and digest the gland. Diagnosis needs 2 of 3 findings: typical pain, lipase or amylase more than 3 times the upper limit of normal, and typical imaging. Bruising around the umbilicus (Cullen sign) or flanks (Grey Turner sign) is uncommon and signals a poor outlook (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 154) describe how a stone lodged at the sphincter of Oddi blocks the duct, pressure builds, and trypsinogen is converted to trypsin, starting autodigestion. Recent change: your Osmosis GI notes (p. 155) list complete restriction of food and antibiotics. MSD now says early enteral feeding lowers complications, mild cases can start a low-fat soft diet when tolerated, and guidelines do not recommend prophylactic antibiotics.

whyWrong.b: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells causes type 1 diabetes, not acute pancreatitis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Infection is a later complication (infected necrosis), not the starting event (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Ductal fibrosis and calcification are features of chronic pancreatitis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A tumor can block the duct, but this patient's gallstones and sudden pain point to gallstone pancreatitis (MSD).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Acute Pancreatitis
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Pancreatitis (Acute), pp. 154-155

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because his skin and eyes have turned yellow over 3 weeks. He has dark urine, pale stools, itching, and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He has smoked for 45 years. Diabetes was diagnosed 6 months ago. He has no abdominal pain. A nontender, enlarged gallbladder can be felt below the right costal margin. Serum direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are high. CT shows a 3-cm mass in the head of the pancreas with a dilated bile duct and pancreatic duct.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A stone in the common bile duct
Acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreatic tail

questions.explanation: Answer: ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas. Why: MSD Manual explains that pancreatic cancer is mainly ductal adenocarcinoma, arising from duct cells 9 times more often than from acinar cells. About 80% occur in the head of the gland, and head tumors cause obstructive jaundice in 80 to 90% of patients. Smoking and chronic pancreatitis are key risk factors, and the cancer causes diabetes in up to half of patients. CA 19-9 is used to follow known disease, not to screen. Head tumors that can be removed are treated with a Whipple procedure, but most patients have advanced disease at diagnosis and 5-year survival is low (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 58) add the Courvoisier sign (a nontender, palpable gallbladder from slow bile duct blockage), migratory clots from hypercoagulability, and spread to left supraclavicular and periumbilical nodes.

whyWrong.b: A hilar cholangiocarcinoma blocks bile above the cystic duct, so the gallbladder would not distend; CT shows a pancreatic mass (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A common bile duct stone usually causes pain, and repeated gallstone inflammation leaves a scarred, small gallbladder (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The mass is in the head, and tail tumors do not block the bile duct; acinar carcinomas are much rarer than ductal ones (MSD).
whyWrong.e: A pseudocyst follows pancreatitis and is a fluid collection, not a solid mass with weight loss (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Pancreatic Cancer
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Pancreatic Cancer, p. 58

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of tiredness, low libido, and aching knuckles of both hands for 1 year. Diabetes was diagnosed 2 years ago. His skin is a grayish tan color, and his liver edge is felt 4 cm below the costal margin. Serum transferrin saturation is 78%, ferritin is 1,850 ng/mL, and ALT is mildly elevated. Genetic testing shows homozygosity for the C282Y variant of the HFE gene.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is most likely decreased in this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: hepcidin. Why: StatPearls explains that hereditary hemochromatosis type 1 is autosomal recessive and most often caused by the C282Y variant of HFE. The defect leads to low hepcidin production or hepcidin resistance; because hepcidin normally limits iron absorption from food, too much iron is absorbed. Transferrin saturation above 45% or a high ferritin is the mainstay of diagnosis. Iron builds up in organs and causes cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, diabetes, skin darkening, cardiomyopathy, hypogonadism, and arthritis of the knuckle joints. Women often present later because menstrual blood loss removes iron (StatPearls). Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 109-110) describe the same organ damage and show iron in hepatocytes staining blue with Prussian blue. Other source: your Osmosis GI notes list deferoxamine first under medications. StatPearls says phlebotomy is first-line, and iron chelation is less effective and used mainly when phlebotomy is not possible.

whyWrong.b: Iron absorption is increased because hepcidin, which normally limits it, is low (StatPearls).
whyWrong.c: Transferrin saturation is high (78% here); above 45% supports the diagnosis (StatPearls).
whyWrong.d: Iron builds up in hepatocytes and stains blue with Prussian blue (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 109).
whyWrong.e: Ferritin is high, reflecting increased body iron stores (StatPearls).

sources.title: StatPearls: Hemochromatosis
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Hemochromatosis, pp. 109-110

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B has a routine surveillance ultrasound that shows a new 4-cm liver mass. He feels well. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is 900 ng/mL. On multiphase contrast CT, the mass lights up brightly in the arterial phase and appears darker than the surrounding liver on delayed images (washout).
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: hepatocellular carcinoma. Why: MSD Manual explains that hepatocellular carcinoma usually arises as a complication of cirrhosis. Hepatitis B carriers have more than 100 times the usual risk, and hepatitis B can cause this cancer even without cirrhosis; aflatoxins in food add to risk in subtropical regions. An alpha-fetoprotein above 400 ng/mL is found in about 40 to 65% of patients and is otherwise rare. People with cirrhosis are commonly screened with ultrasound and AFP every 6 months, and diagnosis rests on multiphase imaging showing arterial enhancement with washout on delayed images (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 55-56) list the same risk factors (hepatitis B and C, cirrhosis, hemochromatosis, alcohol, aflatoxin) and call AFP the classic marker. Recent change: your Osmosis GI notes list sorafenib and nivolumab for systemic treatment. MSD now prefers atezolizumab plus bevacizumab, or tremelimumab plus durvalumab, over sorafenib as first-line therapy for advanced disease.

whyWrong.b: A hemangioma is a benign vascular mass that does not raise AFP (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign lesion with a central scar, usually in young women without cirrhosis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Hepatocellular adenoma occurs mainly in young women using oral contraceptives and does not raise AFP this high (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Colon cancer metastases are usually multiple and do not raise AFP (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Hepatocellular Carcinoma, pp. 55-56

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of 6 months of sudden episodes of red flushing of his face and neck, cramping, and watery diarrhea. Twice he has had wheezing during an episode. A murmur of tricuspid regurgitation is heard. CT shows a 2-cm mass in the terminal ileum and several masses in the liver. His 24-hour urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) level is high.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains why his symptoms appeared only after the tumor spread?

options.text: Liver metastases bypass the liver's serotonin breakdown
The ileal tumor makes more serotonin as it grows larger
The tumor turns most dietary tryptophan into extra niacin
His lungs have lost the ability to inactivate serotonin
Gastrin from the tumor triggers histamine release

questions.explanation: Answer: liver metastases release their products directly into the systemic circulation. Why: MSD Manual explains that a serotonin-producing intestinal neuroendocrine tumor usually does not cause carcinoid syndrome until it spreads to the liver. Products from a gut tumor enter the portal circulation, where blood and liver enzymes quickly destroy them (for serotonin, hepatic monoamine oxidase); liver metastases release them straight into the systemic circulation. Flushing is the most common sign, cramps and diarrhea are often the main complaint, and only a few patients wheeze. Endocardial fibrosis causes right-sided valve disease (pulmonic stenosis and tricuspid regurgitation); left-sided lesions are rare because the lungs destroy serotonin. A high urine 5-HIAA confirms the diagnosis, and somatostatin analogs (octreotide or lanreotide) are first-line for symptoms (MSD). Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 45-46) note that the ileum is a common site and give the mnemonic of flushing, wheezing, right-sided valve lesions, and diarrhea.

whyWrong.b: Tumor size is not the reason; while the tumor stays in the gut, the liver breaks down its serotonin (MSD).
whyWrong.c: The tumor diverts tryptophan toward serotonin, which can rarely cause niacin deficiency (pellagra), the opposite of extra niacin (MSD).
whyWrong.d: The lungs still inactivate serotonin, which is why left-sided valve lesions are rare (MSD).
whyWrong.e: Gastrin-driven neuroendocrine tumors arise from enterochromaffin-like cells in the stomach (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 45), not in the ileum.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Carcinoid Syndrome
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Carcinoid Tumor, pp. 45-46

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is in the hospital 2 days after heart valve surgery, during which she had a long period of low blood pressure. She develops sudden crampy pain in the left side of her abdomen with an urgent need to defecate, followed by several bloody, loose stools. Her pain matches the mild tenderness found on examination. CT shows a thickened colon wall at the splenic flexure.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

options.text: Low blood flow to a watershed area of the colon
An embolus blocking the superior mesenteric artery
A toxin made by Clostridioides difficile
Transmural granulomatous inflammation of the colon
Bleeding from a vessel beside a diverticulum

questions.explanation: Answer: low flow to a watershed area (ischemic colitis). Why: StatPearls (Bowel Ischemia) explains that nonocclusive causes, such as low blood pressure and vasoconstricting drugs, account for almost 95% of colonic ischemia. Watershed areas, the splenic flexure (Griffiths point) and the rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point), account for about 70% of cases. Patients, usually older than 60, have sudden crampy left-sided pain with an urgent need to defecate, and rectal bleeding or bloody diarrhea is more common than in small-bowel ischemia. Colonoscopy within 48 hours is preferred, and mild cases need only supportive care (StatPearls). Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 83-84) list the same sites, note risk after aortic surgery or myocardial infarction, and describe thumbprinting on imaging.

whyWrong.b: An embolus to the superior mesenteric artery causes acute mesenteric ischemia, with severe pain out of proportion to the examination (StatPearls).
whyWrong.c: C. difficile colitis usually follows antibiotic use and causes watery diarrhea, not sudden pain after low blood pressure (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Transmural granulomatous inflammation is Crohn disease, which develops over months (MSD Crohn page).
whyWrong.e: Diverticular bleeding is usually painless (standard teaching).

sources.title: StatPearls: Bowel Ischemia
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Ischemic Colitis, pp. 83-84

questions.stem: A 4-week-old boy, the family's first child, is brought to the physician because of forceful vomiting after every feeding for 4 days. The vomit is milk without green color, and he is hungry again right after vomiting. At 1 week of age he was given erythromycin after exposure to pertussis. He has dry lips and fewer wet diapers. A firm, olive-sized mass is felt in the upper abdomen just to the right of midline.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following sets of laboratory findings is most likely?

options.text: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, normal anion gap
Metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap from lactate
Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis with low sodium
Respiratory alkalosis with a normal chloride level

questions.explanation: Answer: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Why: MSD Manual explains that vomiting of stomach contents loses hydrochloric acid and fluid, causing a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Pyloric stenosis usually appears at 3 to 6 weeks of age and is rare after 12 weeks. Boys are affected about 5 times as often as girls, firstborn boys most of all, and macrolide antibiotics such as erythromycin in the first few weeks of life raise the risk. Vomiting is forceful and nonbilious, the infant stays hungry, and an olive-sized mass may be felt. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle about 3 mm or thicker. Fluids and electrolytes are corrected first, then a pyloromyotomy is done (MSD). Correction: your Osmosis GI notes (p. 171) say vomiting starts at or soon after birth; MSD gives a usual onset of 3 to 6 weeks of life.

whyWrong.b: A normal anion gap acidosis comes from losing bicarbonate, as in diarrhea, not from vomiting stomach acid (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Lactic acidosis can occur late in severe shock, but acid loss from vomiting causes alkalosis (MSD).
whyWrong.d: High potassium and acidosis suggest adrenal problems such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, not pyloric stenosis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The problem is metabolic, from acid loss, and chloride is low (MSD).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal System (Emily's file), Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis, p. 171

questions.stem: Researchers study whether working with aromatic amine dyes is linked to bladder cancer. They enroll 50 patients with bladder cancer and 50 people of similar age without it, and ask everyone about past work with these dyes. Thirty of the patients with cancer and 10 of the people without cancer report working with the dyes.
questions.leadIn: What is the odds ratio for dye exposure in this study?
questions.explanation: Answer: 6.0. Why: This is a case-control study: people are chosen by whether they have the disease, then asked about past exposure, so the odds ratio is the right measure (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 256). In a 2 × 2 table, a = exposed cases (30), b = exposed controls (10), c = unexposed cases (20), and d = unexposed controls (40). The odds ratio is (a/c) ÷ (b/d) = ad/bc = (30 × 40) ÷ (10 × 20) = 1,200 ÷ 200 = 6.0 (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258). StatPearls explains that an odds ratio above 1 means greater odds of the event in the exposed group, that relative risk cannot be calculated in a case-control study, and that the odds ratio approaches the relative risk when the disease is rare.

whyWrong.a: 0.17 is the inverse, bc/ad = 200 ÷ 1,200; it would wrongly suggest the dyes protect against cancer (standard teaching).
whyWrong.b: 1.5 is 30/20, the odds of exposure among cases alone, without dividing by the odds among controls (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).
whyWrong.c: 3.0 divides the percentage exposed (60% ÷ 20%), which treats the data like a cohort study; that is not the odds ratio (StatPearls).
whyWrong.e: 8.0 does not come from the ad/bc formula; with these numbers, ad/bc = 1,200 ÷ 200 = 6.0 (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Observational studies, p. 256; Quantifying risk, p. 258
StatPearls: Odds Ratio

questions.stem: In a cohort study, 2,000 adults who use tanning beds and 2,000 adults who do not are followed for 10 years. Over that time, 12% of tanning-bed users and 3% of nonusers are diagnosed with a skin cancer.
questions.leadIn: What is the attributable risk of skin cancer due to tanning-bed use?
questions.explanation: Answer: 9%. Why: Attributable risk is the difference in risk between the exposed and unexposed groups: 12% − 3% = 9% (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258). It tells you how much of the risk in the exposed group is due to the exposure. The relative risk, used in cohort studies, is the ratio instead: 12% ÷ 3% = 4 (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258). StatPearls (Relative Risk) points out that a relative risk alone gives no information about absolute risk, which is why the risk difference is also reported.

whyWrong.a: 3% is the risk in the unexposed group, not the extra risk from exposure (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).
whyWrong.b: 4 is the relative risk (12 ÷ 3), a ratio with no units, not a difference in percentages (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).
whyWrong.d: 12% is the total risk in the exposed group, which includes the baseline risk everyone has (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).
whyWrong.e: 15% adds the two risks; attributable risk subtracts them (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Quantifying risk, p. 258
StatPearls: Relative Risk

questions.stem: A cross-sectional study finds that people who carry a cigarette lighter are 6 times as likely to have lung cancer as people who do not. When the researchers split the data into smokers and nonsmokers, carrying a lighter shows no link to lung cancer in either group.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the original association?
questions.explanation: Answer: confounding by smoking. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 261) describe confounding as a factor that is related to both the exposure and the outcome, is not on the causal pathway, and distorts the apparent effect of the exposure. Smoking is linked to carrying a lighter and causes lung cancer, so it created the association. StatPearls (Principles of Causation) defines a confounder the same way and lists randomization in the study design and stratification in the analysis as ways to address it. Here, stratifying by smoking made the association disappear, which is the classic sign of confounding.

whyWrong.b: In effect modification the exposure has different effects in different subgroups; here there was no effect in either group (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 261).
whyWrong.c: Selection bias comes from how participants are chosen, so the groups differ from the population; stratifying by smoking would not remove it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Recall bias occurs when people with a disease remember past exposures differently; carrying a lighter now is not a remembered exposure (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Lead-time bias makes survival look longer when disease is found earlier by screening (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 261).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Bias and study errors, p. 261
StatPearls: Principles of Causation

questions.stem: A study randomly assigns 300 adults with type 2 diabetes to one of three drugs: metformin, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, or an SGLT2 inhibitor. After 6 months, the researchers want to know whether the mean hemoglobin A1c differs among the three groups.
questions.leadIn: Which statistical test is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Answer: ANOVA. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 264) explain that a t-test compares the means of 2 groups, ANOVA compares the means of 3 or more groups, and the chi-square and Fisher exact tests compare proportions of categorical outcomes rather than means. StatPearls (Comparing the Means of Independent Groups) agrees that ANOVA tests whether the mean of a continuous outcome differs across three or more groups defined by one categorical variable, and that a two-sample t-test is used for two groups. Hemoglobin A1c is a continuous measurement and there are three groups, so ANOVA fits.

whyWrong.b: A t-test compares the means of only 2 groups (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 264).
whyWrong.c: Chi-square compares proportions of categorical outcomes, not mean values (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 264).
whyWrong.d: Fisher exact test compares 2 proportions in small samples (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 264).
whyWrong.e: Pearson correlation measures how strongly two continuous variables move together in a straight line (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 264), not differences among group means.

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Common statistical tests, p. 264
StatPearls: Comparing the Means of Independent Groups: ANOVA, ANCOVA, MANOVA, and MANCOVA

questions.stem: A new oral anticoagulant is approved after randomized trials in about 3,000 patients showed it worked as well as warfarin. In the 3 years after approval, about 500,000 patients take it. Reports to the manufacturer and the FDA reveal that about 1 in 20,000 users develops severe liver injury, and a boxed warning is added to the label.
questions.leadIn: During which stage of drug evaluation was this adverse effect most likely detected?
questions.explanation: Answer: phase IV (postmarketing surveillance). Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 256) describe four phases. Phase I tests safety, toxicity, and drug handling in a small number of people. Phase II tests efficacy, dosing, and side effects in a moderate number of patients. Phase III randomly compares the drug with standard care or placebo in a large number of patients. Phase IV is surveillance after approval, which finds rare or long-term adverse effects and can lead to boxed warnings or withdrawal. FDA describes phase 3 as 300 to 3,000 people and phase 4 as post-market safety monitoring after approval. An effect in 1 in 20,000 people is unlikely to appear in 3,000 trial patients but shows up once hundreds of thousands use the drug.

whyWrong.b: Phase I uses a small number of people to test safety and drug handling (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 256); far too few to find a 1-in-20,000 effect.
whyWrong.c: Phase II includes up to several hundred patients (FDA), too few to find this rare effect.
whyWrong.d: Phase III included about 3,000 patients before approval (FDA), so a 1-in-20,000 effect would likely be missed.
whyWrong.e: Animal testing comes before human studies and cannot show how often a rare effect occurs in people (standard teaching).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Clinical trial, p. 256
FDA: The Drug Development Process, Step 3: Clinical Research

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of tea-colored urine during two colds this year. Microscopic blood has been found in his urine since he was 5 years old. His maternal uncle started dialysis at age 30. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and dysmorphic red blood cells. Audiometry shows bilateral hearing loss at high frequencies. Slit-lamp examination shows a cone-shaped bulge on the front surface of both lenses.
questions.leadIn: A mutation in a gene that encodes which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: type IV collagen (Alport syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 83) describe a type IV collagen mutation that thins and splits the glomerular basement membrane, most often X-linked, with eye problems, nephritis, and nerve deafness, and a basket-weave pattern on electron microscopy. MSD lists the genes COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5, says X-linked inheritance is the most common form, and describes high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, cataracts, and anterior lenticonus (the cone-shaped bulge of the lens). Early ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy slows progression. After a transplant, the new kidney can develop anti-GBM antibody disease, usually in males (MSD). The affected uncle on the mother's side fits X-linked inheritance (standard teaching). Other source: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes name the alpha-3 chain. The X-linked form, the most common one, involves COL4A5, the gene for the alpha-5 chain on the X chromosome (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with fractures and blue sclerae, not nephritis and deafness (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome, which can move the lens out of place but does not cause hematuria or hearing loss (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Nephrin is part of the podocyte slit diaphragm; its defect causes congenital nephrotic syndrome with heavy protein loss in infancy, not hematuria with deafness (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Polycystin-1 is the PKD1 gene product in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, which causes enlarged cystic kidneys (MSD ADPKD).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Alport syndrome, p. 83
MSD Manual Professional: Alport Syndrome

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has coughed up blood for 4 days and his urine has looked dark for 1 week. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily and works stripping paint with solvents. His blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. Chest x-ray shows patchy opacities in both lower lungs. Serum creatinine is 3.9 mg/dL; it was normal 2 months ago. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts. A kidney biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli.
questions.leadIn: Immunofluorescence of the biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Granular IgG and C3 along the GBM

questions.explanation: Answer: linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM disease, or Goodpasture syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 84) place anti-GBM disease in type 1 rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, with linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. The antibodies also bind the basement membrane of the lung alveoli, which causes coughing up blood. StatPearls says the antibodies mostly target the non-collagen (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, and that smoking and hydrocarbon solvents are possible environmental triggers. Treatment is plasmapheresis followed by glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide; rituximab may replace cyclophosphamide in some cases (StatPearls).

whyWrong.b: A granular, lumpy-bumpy pattern means immune complexes, as in type 2 rapidly progressive disease after strep infection or with lupus (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 85).
whyWrong.c: Mesangial IgA deposits mark IgA nephropathy, which usually causes episodes of blood in the urine, not lung bleeding with crescents in most glomeruli (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: No deposits (pauci-immune) is type 3 disease, as in granulomatosis with polyangiitis (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 85). It can also cause lung and kidney disease, but smoking and solvent exposure are possible triggers of anti-GBM disease (StatPearls).
