whyWrong.e: Subepithelial humps are the pattern of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows a strep infection and does not cause lung bleeding (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, pp. 84-85
StatPearls: Goodpasture Syndrome

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his eyelids have been puffy every morning for 1 week. Two weeks ago, he had a cold. His ankles are swollen. Blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no blood. Serum albumin is 1.7 g/dL, and serum cholesterol is high. Serum creatinine and complement levels are normal.
questions.leadIn: If a kidney biopsy were done, which of the following findings would be most likely?

options.text: Effaced podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy
Subepithelial deposits with spikes on silver stain
Segmental sclerosis with hyalinosis on light microscopy
Linear IgG along the basement membrane
Acellular nodules in the mesangial matrix

questions.explanation: Answer: effacement (flattening) of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy, with normal glomeruli on light microscopy (minimal change disease). Why: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 89) call minimal change disease the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome among children aged 2 to 8 years, sometimes triggered by an infection, an immunization, or allergy, and rarely linked to Hodgkin lymphoma. Light microscopy is normal, immunofluorescence shows no deposits, and diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy is the key finding. MSD says it causes 70 to 90% of nephrotic syndrome in children older than 1 year and about 15% in adults, and that 80 to 90% of patients respond to high-dose prednisone, although most responders relapse.

whyWrong.b: Subepithelial deposits with spikes describe membranous nephropathy, a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults (MSD Membranous Nephropathy).
whyWrong.c: Segmental sclerosis with hyalinosis is focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 90), which is less likely in a young child with a sudden onset after a cold.
whyWrong.d: Linear IgG is anti-GBM disease, which causes a nephritic picture with blood in the urine and rising creatinine (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 84).
whyWrong.e: Acellular mesangial nodules (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) are seen in diabetic kidney disease (MSD Diabetic Nephropathy).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Minimal change disease, p. 89
MSD Manual Professional: Minimal Change Disease

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of leg swelling for 2 months. He has injected heroin for 10 years. His blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg. Urine protein is 8 g/24 h. Serum albumin is 2.2 g/dL. Tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C are negative. A kidney biopsy shows scarring in only part of the capillary tuft of some glomeruli, with glassy hyaline material in the scarred areas; the other glomeruli look normal. Electron microscopy shows effaced podocyte foot processes.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). Why: "focal" means only some glomeruli, and "segmental" means only part of each tuft. Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (pp. 90-91) list HIV, sickle cell disease, and heroin use as secondary causes, describe segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis on light microscopy, and note foot process effacement like minimal change disease. They call FSGS the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome among Hispanic and African American patients. StatPearls adds obesity as a cause, links HIV to the collapsing variant, and says APOL1 gene variants, more common in people of African descent, cause genetic FSGS. Corticosteroids are first-line only for primary FSGS; secondary FSGS is managed by treating the cause. About 50% of patients with persistent nephrotic-range protein loss reach end-stage kidney disease within 3 to 8 years (StatPearls).

whyWrong.b: Minimal change disease also shows foot process effacement, but light microscopy is normal, with no scarring (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 89).
whyWrong.c: Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits with spikes and thickened basement membranes, not segmental scars (MSD Membranous Nephropathy).
whyWrong.d: Membranoproliferative disease shows thick capillary walls with a tram-track look and often low complement, not segmental scars (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Diabetic nephropathy needs diabetes and shows mesangial nodules and basement membrane thickening (MSD Diabetic Nephropathy).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, pp. 90-91
StatPearls: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of swelling of her legs and face for 6 weeks. Urine protein is 7 g/24 h, and the urine sediment shows no red cell casts. Serum albumin is 2.0 g/dL. A kidney biopsy shows thick capillary walls; electron microscopy shows deposits on the outer (subepithelial) side of the basement membrane, with new membrane growing up between them. Serum antibodies to the phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) are strongly positive.
questions.leadIn: The antibody result most strongly suggests which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: idiopathic (primary) membranous nephropathy. Why: MSD says the M-type PLA2R is the major target antigen in membranous nephropathy, that idiopathic disease is typically PLA2R-antibody positive, and that cancer-associated disease is typically negative. Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 91) say most cases are idiopathic and are associated with IgG4 antibodies to PLA2R, a receptor found in high amounts on glomerular podocytes. Biopsy shows subepithelial deposits with spikes of basement membrane between them, and later a markedly thickened membrane. Secondary causes include drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold), hepatitis B or C, lupus, and cancer; 6 to 15% of patients have an underlying cancer. Renal vein thrombosis is more frequent than in other nephrotic diseases. For high-risk idiopathic disease, most experts favor rituximab plus corticosteroids (MSD). Other source: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes call it the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome among white adults; MSD calls it a common cause in adults.

whyWrong.b: Membranous disease linked to cancer is typically PLA2R-antibody negative (MSD), so a strongly positive test argues against a hidden tumor.
whyWrong.c: Lupus is a secondary cause (MSD), and lupus-related membranous disease is usually PLA2R-antibody negative (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Hepatitis B is a secondary cause (MSD); a strongly positive PLA2R antibody points to primary disease instead (MSD).
whyWrong.e: NSAIDs are a secondary cause (MSD); the antibody result points to primary disease (MSD), and no drug history is given.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Membranous nephropathy, p. 91
MSD Manual Professional: Membranous Nephropathy

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 16 years comes for a follow-up visit. His hemoglobin A1c is 8.9%. He has background retinopathy. His urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio has been 210 mg/g on 2 of 3 samples over 4 months. Serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no blood. A kidney biopsy is done because his kidney function has declined faster than expected.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on the biopsy?

options.text: Acellular nodules in the mesangial matrix
Basket-weave splitting of the lamina densa

questions.explanation: Answer: acellular nodules in the mesangial matrix (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, or nodular glomerulosclerosis). Why: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 94) describe mesangial sclerosis with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules as the characteristic lesion. MSD describes these as acellular nodules in the mesangial matrix, along with mesangial expansion and a thickened glomerular basement membrane. An early change is hyperfiltration (higher GFR). An albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 mg/g or more on 2 of 3 samples within 3 to 6 months shows kidney damage. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are first-line for blood pressure and protein loss, and SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended in type 2 diabetes unless eGFR is below 20 mL/min (MSD).

whyWrong.b: Crescents mean rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, which causes a fast nephritic picture with blood in the urine (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 84).
whyWrong.c: Subepithelial deposits with spikes are membranous nephropathy (MSD Membranous Nephropathy).
whyWrong.d: Mesangial IgA deposits are IgA nephropathy, which presents with blood in the urine (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A basket-weave lamina densa is Alport syndrome, an inherited type IV collagen disease (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 83).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Diabetic nephropathy, p. 94
MSD Manual Professional: Diabetic Nephropathy

questions.topic: Nephrotic syndrome: hypercoagulability and renal vein thrombosis
questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy comes to the emergency department because of sudden left flank pain and red urine for 1 day. He also noticed a new soft swelling above his left testicle that feels like a bag of worms and gets bigger when he stands. Doppler ultrasound shows a clot in the left renal vein.
questions.leadIn: Urinary loss of which of the following most likely contributed to this complication?
questions.explanation: Answer: antithrombin III. Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (pp. 87-88) say nephrotic syndrome causes a clotting tendency because antithrombin III, a natural anticoagulant, is lost in the urine. Renal vein thrombosis presents with sudden flank or abdominal pain and gross hematuria. In men, a clot in the left renal vein blocks drainage from the left testicular vein, so a left varicocele appears; the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein (standard teaching). MSD says renal vein thrombosis is more frequent in membranous nephropathy than in other nephrotic diseases, and it can lead to pulmonary embolism.

whyWrong.b: Loss of albumin lowers total calcium, but that does not cause clotting (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Loss of immunoglobulins raises the risk of infection, not clotting (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 87).
whyWrong.d: Transferrin loss can lower iron transport, but it does not cause clotting (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Loss of thyroxine-binding globulin changes thyroid test results, but it does not cause clotting (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Nephrotic syndrome complications, pp. 87-88
MSD Manual Professional: Membranous Nephropathy

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fever and right flank pain. She has had 4 urinary tract infections in the past year. Urine pH is 8.0. Urine culture grows Proteus mirabilis. CT scan shows a large branching stone that fills the right renal pelvis and several calyces.
questions.leadIn: Production of which of the following bacterial enzymes most directly caused this stone to form?
questions.explanation: Answer: urease. Why: struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones form when bacteria split urea. MSD says these stones are caused by urea-splitting bacteria such as Proteus and Klebsiella species and are about 3 times more common in women. Urease turns urea into ammonia, which makes the urine alkaline and lets magnesium ammonium phosphate crystals form (standard teaching). Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (pp. 97, 101) note that a staghorn stone in an adult is most likely struvite. The infection must be cleared and the stone removed, or it keeps growing (standard teaching). Other source: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes say struvite is about 15% of stones and the second most common type; MSD gives 5 to 15% for struvite and 18 to 24% for calcium phosphate.

whyWrong.b: Catalase protects bacteria from hydrogen peroxide and matters in chronic granulomatous disease, not stone formation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Coagulase identifies Staphylococcus aureus and is not part of stone formation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Beta-lactamase breaks down penicillins; it causes drug resistance, not stones (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Nitrate reductase makes the urine nitrite test positive, but it does not raise urine pH or form stones (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Ammonium magnesium phosphate stones, pp. 97 and 101
MSD Manual Professional: Urinary Calculi

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy comes to the emergency department because of colicky left flank pain. This is his third kidney stone in 2 years. His father also had stones as a young man. A concentrated, acidified urine sample shows flat, six-sided crystals. A urine sodium cyanide-nitroprusside test turns purple.
questions.leadIn: A defect in kidney reabsorption of which group of amino acids is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (cystinuria). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (pp. 100-101) say these four amino acids (COLA) share one transporter in the proximal tubule, so a defect in it lets all four spill into urine. Only cystine is poorly soluble, so it forms stones. The crystals are hexagonal, and the cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive because it detects the sulfur groups of cysteine. MSD says cystine stones occur only in people with cystinuria and that typical hexagonal crystals are found in a concentrated, acidified urine sample.

whyWrong.b: Loss of neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, is Hartnup disease, which causes a pellagra-like rash, not stones (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Loss of glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline is iminoglycinuria, a harmless finding that does not cause stones (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Phenylketonuria is a defect of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, not a transport defect in the kidney (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Maple syrup urine disease is a defect in breaking down leucine, isoleucine, and valine, not in kidney transport (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Cystine stones, pp. 100-101
MSD Manual Professional: Urinary Calculi

questions.topic: Acute kidney injury: acute tubular necrosis
questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is in the intensive care unit with septic shock from pneumonia. His blood pressure stayed below 80/50 mm Hg for 6 hours before it responded to fluids and norepinephrine. Over the next 3 days, his serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 3.4 mg/dL and his urine output falls. Urine microscopy shows many muddy brown granular casts and tubular epithelial cells. Fractional excretion of sodium is 3%.
questions.leadIn: Cells in which part of the nephron are most likely to have been injured?
questions.explanation: Answer: the proximal tubule (acute tubular necrosis, ATN). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 116) describe ATN as injury and death of tubular cells, the most common cause of intrinsic acute kidney injury. Dead cells plug the tubules and lower GFR. Muddy brown casts are the classic urine finding. Damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium (FENa above 2%) or concentrate urine. StatPearls says ischemia is the most common cause, that FENa below 1% favors prerenal disease and above 2% favors ATN, and that the proximal tubule was affected in over 90% of biopsies in a large review. The thick ascending limb is also prone to cast formation (StatPearls).

whyWrong.b: Podocyte injury causes nephrotic-range protein loss, not muddy brown casts and a high FENa (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The descending thin limb is not a main site of injury in ATN; the proximal tubule is affected in most cases (StatPearls).
whyWrong.d: The macula densa senses sodium chloride delivery but is not the main site of injury in ATN (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Collecting duct injury is not the typical ATN pattern; biopsies show the proximal tubule affected in over 90% of cases (StatPearls).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Acute tubular necrosis, p. 116
StatPearls: Acute Tubular Necrosis

questions.topic: Acute kidney injury: acute interstitial nephritis
questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has been treated with intravenous ampicillin for 12 days for an infection that is now cured. She now has a temperature of 38.3°C (101°F) and a pink, flat, bumpy rash on her trunk. Her serum creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 2.5 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows white blood cells and white blood cell casts; urine culture is negative. The blood eosinophil count is high.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start prednisone and keep the ampicillin
Give IV saline and keep the ampicillin

questions.explanation: Answer: stop the ampicillin (drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 120) describe a drug allergy that damages the interstitium and tubules. Fever, a maculopapular rash, and kidney injury 1 to 3 weeks after starting a beta-lactam, an NSAID, a sulfa drug, rifampin, a diuretic, or a proton pump inhibitor strongly suggest it, and symptoms almost always resolve after the drug is stopped. MSD says beta-lactam antibiotics are the most common cause, white blood cell casts and sterile pyuria are typical, and the full triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia occurs in fewer than 10% of drug-induced cases. Treatment starts with removing the cause; corticosteroids may speed recovery and work best within 2 weeks of stopping the drug, ideally after biopsy confirmation (MSD). Other source: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes call blood eosinophilia and urine eosinophils the most important clues; MSD says urine eosinophils cannot be relied on to make or exclude the diagnosis.

whyWrong.b: She has no urgent reason for dialysis, such as severe hyperkalemia, fluid overload, or uremic symptoms (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The offending drug must be stopped first; corticosteroids are an add-on that MSD suggests only after biopsy confirmation.
whyWrong.d: Saline helps prerenal kidney injury; this is an allergic injury, and continuing the drug keeps it going (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Cyclophosphamide is used for diseases such as anti-GBM disease (StatPearls Goodpasture Syndrome), not drug-induced interstitial nephritis.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Acute interstitial nephritis, p. 120
MSD Manual Professional: Tubulointerstitial Nephritis

questions.stem: A 20-year-old Black man comes to the emergency department because of bright red urine that started suddenly this morning, followed by colicky right flank pain. He has sickle cell trait. He takes no medicines and has no fever. Urinalysis shows many red blood cells and no casts. CT scan shows small cavities at the tips of several renal pyramids and a filling defect in the right ureter.
questions.leadIn: His condition most likely began with which of the following?

options.text: Medullary ischemia from sickled red cells
Immune complex deposits in the glomeruli
Ascending bacterial infection of the renal pelvis
Crystals forming in the collecting ducts
A defect in type IV collagen

questions.explanation: Answer: ischemia of the renal medulla from sickled red cells, causing renal papillary necrosis. Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 122) list four main causes of papillary necrosis: sickle cell disease or trait, analgesic nephropathy, acute pyelonephritis or urinary obstruction, and diabetes. Sickled cells block small vessels and cause ischemia, most often in children and young adults, and sudden gross hematuria in such a patient suggests papillary necrosis. Dead papillae slough off and can block the ureter, causing colicky flank pain. The medulla has low oxygen and high salt concentration, which promotes sickling (standard teaching). MSD (Analgesic Nephropathy) describes flank pain, hematuria, and passage of a renal papilla, and notes that patients with analgesic nephropathy have a higher risk of urothelial (transitional cell) cancer.

whyWrong.b: Immune complex glomerulonephritis causes red cell casts and protein loss, not dead papillae in the medulla (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Pyelonephritis is another cause of papillary necrosis (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 122), but he has no fever, and his sickle cell trait explains the injury.
whyWrong.d: Crystal stones can block the ureter, but they do not leave cavities at the tips of the pyramids (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome, with hematuria from birth, deafness, and eye problems (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 83).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Renal papillary necrosis, p. 122
MSD Manual Professional: Analgesic Nephropathy

questions.stem: A 23-year-old military recruit is brought to the emergency department after collapsing during a long run in hot weather. His thigh muscles are tender. His urine is dark brown. A urine dipstick is 3+ for blood, but microscopy shows 0 to 2 red blood cells per high-power field. Serum creatine kinase is 48,000 U/L. Serum potassium is 6.0 mEq/L, phosphate is high, and creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL.
questions.leadIn: Which substance in the urine most likely explains the dipstick result?
questions.explanation: Answer: myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 119) explain that the dipstick blood pad reacts with the heme in both hemoglobin and myoglobin, so a positive test without red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobin. Muscle injury from crushing, long muscle activity such as seizures, or drugs releases myoglobin and electrolytes. Heme pigment damages tubules directly and narrows kidney blood vessels, causing acute tubular necrosis, and cell breakdown raises potassium, phosphate, and uric acid. MSD says a creatine kinase above 5 times the upper limit of normal is typically required for the diagnosis, lists extreme exercise, statins, and alcohol among causes, and says treatment is supportive with IV fluids plus treatment of the cause.

whyWrong.b: Bilirubin has its own dipstick pad and does not make the blood pad positive (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Porphobilinogen is seen in acute intermittent porphyria and does not react with the blood pad (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Urobilinogen has its own dipstick pad and points to liver or hemolytic disease, not muscle injury (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Ketones have their own dipstick pad and do not make the blood pad positive (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Rhabdomyolysis, p. 119
MSD Manual Professional: Rhabdomyolysis

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man comes to the physician because of dull flank pain on both sides. His blood pressure is 158/98 mm Hg. Both kidneys are large and easy to feel. Ultrasound shows many cysts in both kidneys and several in the liver. His father started dialysis at age 58, and his paternal aunt died of a brain hemorrhage at age 45. Genetic testing shows a mutation on chromosome 16.
questions.leadIn: This mutation most likely affects the gene for which protein?
questions.explanation: Answer: polycystin-1 (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, ADPKD). Why: MSD says the PKD1 gene on chromosome 16 codes for polycystin-1 and causes most cases, while PKD2 on chromosome 4 codes for polycystin-2. Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (pp. 131-132) say PKD1 causes 85% and PKD2 15% of cases, and that ADPKD is the most common hereditary cause of kidney failure in adults. MSD describes intracranial aneurysms in about 4% of young adults and up to 10% of older adults, liver cysts in most patients (usually without liver failure), mitral valve prolapse, and hypertension in 40 to 50%. Kidney failure develops in 35 to 45% by age 60. Tolvaptan, a vasopressin receptor 2 blocker, may slow kidney growth and loss of function. Correction: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 131) say PKD1 and PKD2 code for fibrocystin. They code for polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 (MSD); fibrocystin is the protein of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Fibrocystin is the protein of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, which usually shows up in infants (standard teaching), not the chromosome 16 adult disease.
whyWrong.c: The alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen is the X-linked Alport gene, which causes nephritis with deafness, not cysts (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 83).
whyWrong.d: Tuberin is the TSC2 gene product in tuberous sclerosis, which can cause kidney cysts but also skin, brain, and heart lesions (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The VHL gene is on chromosome 3 and causes von Hippel-Lindau disease with renal cell cancer (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 135) and kidney cysts (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, pp. 131-132
MSD Manual Professional: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of blood in his urine and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. A firm mass is felt in the right flank. Hemoglobin is 18.6 g/dL, and serum calcium is 11.9 mg/dL. CT scan shows a 9-cm solid mass in the right kidney with tumor extending into the renal vein and inferior vena cava. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his high hemoglobin?

options.text: JAK2 mutation in marrow stem cells

questions.explanation: Answer: erythropoietin made by the tumor (renal cell carcinoma). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (pp. 135-137) say tumor cells can secrete hormones such as erythropoietin (causing polycythemia), PTHrP (causing hypercalcemia), renin, or ACTH. The tumor can grow into the renal vein and inferior vena cava, spread to the lungs and bone, and is resistant to chemotherapy and radiation. MSD says smoking doubles the risk, von Hippel-Lindau disease is a familial risk factor, hematuria is the most common sign, polycythemia can result from increased erythropoietin activity, and hypercalcemia is common. Recent change: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes list aldesleukin (IL-2) immunotherapy for advanced disease. MSD now names immune checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1 or PD-L1 antibodies, often in first-line combinations) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib and cabozantinib as main options, and says only about 10 to 20% of patients respond to IL-2.

whyWrong.b: Volume loss can raise hemoglobin a little by concentrating the blood, but not to 18.6 g/dL; the tumor itself is the more direct cause (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A JAK2 mutation causes polycythemia vera, a bone marrow disease that is not linked to a kidney mass (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Lung metastases are common in this cancer (MSD), but his oxygen saturation is normal, so low oxygen does not explain it.
whyWrong.e: Carbon monoxide from smoking can raise hemoglobin slightly, but not this much; a kidney tumor making erythropoietin explains it better (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Renal cell carcinoma, pp. 135-137
MSD Manual Professional: Renal Cell Carcinoma

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because her mother felt a lump in her belly while bathing her. The girl was born without irises in both eyes and has delayed speech. She has a smooth, firm mass in the left flank that does not cross the midline. Ultrasound shows a solid mass arising from the left kidney.
questions.leadIn: Deletion of which of the following genes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: WT1 (Wilms tumor with WAGR syndrome). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (pp. 137-138) describe Wilms tumor as the most common kidney cancer of early childhood (ages 2 to 4), caused by loss of the WT1 or WT2 tumor suppressor genes on chromosome 11. It usually presents as a smooth, one-sided belly mass that does not cross the midline, often found by a caregiver. WAGR complex (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and intellectual disability) comes from a WT1 deletion; Denys-Drash syndrome comes from a WT1 mutation, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome from WT2. MSD says it usually appears before age 5, a painless abdominal mass is the most frequent finding, and the tumor has blastemal, stromal, and epithelial parts. Nephrectomy is usually done instead of biopsy, and cure rates are about 85 to 95% when the tumor is confined to the kidney (MSD).

whyWrong.b: MYCN amplification is linked to neuroblastoma (standard teaching), which forms an irregular mass that can cross the midline (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 137).
whyWrong.c: RB1 loss causes retinoblastoma, a tumor of the retina, not aniridia with a kidney mass (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: VHL loss causes von Hippel-Lindau disease with renal cell carcinoma in adults (MSD Renal Cell Carcinoma).
whyWrong.e: APC loss causes familial adenomatous polyposis with many colon polyps, not a kidney tumor (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Wilms tumor, pp. 137-138
MSD Manual Professional: Wilms Tumor

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man who grew up farming irrigated fields in Egypt comes to the physician because of painless red urine for 2 months. He has never smoked and has never worked with dyes. Cystoscopy shows a mass in the bladder wall. Biopsy shows invasive cancer made of malignant squamous cells that produce keratin.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying risk factor?
questions.explanation: Answer: chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection. Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 139) explain that long-term irritation of the bladder leads to squamous metaplasia, then dysplasia, then squamous cell carcinoma. Their listed risk factors are Schistosoma haematobium infection (common in the Middle East), chronic cystitis, smoking, and long-standing stones, and it presents with painless hematuria. MSD says urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma causes more than 90% of bladder cancers, and squamous cell carcinoma is linked to parasitic infection or chronic irritation, as in schistosomiasis, long-term catheter use, or bladder stones. Diagnosis is by cystoscopy and biopsy (MSD). Schistosoma haematobium is common in Africa, including Egypt (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Aromatic amines (aniline dyes) raise bladder cancer risk (MSD), mainly urothelial carcinoma, and he never worked with dyes.
whyWrong.c: Long-term cyclophosphamide raises bladder cancer risk (MSD), but he has no history of taking it.
whyWrong.d: HPV is the main cause of cervical squamous cancer and is not a main risk factor for bladder cancer (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Phenacetin is one of the risk factors your El-Husseiny nephrology notes list for urothelial carcinoma (p. 139), not squamous cell carcinoma, and he has no history of overuse.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Bladder squamous cell carcinoma, p. 139
MSD Manual Professional: Bladder Cancer

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome comes to the physician because of muscle weakness for 3 weeks. Serum studies show: sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, chloride 115 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 15 mEq/L. Arterial pH is 7.30. Urine pH is 6.5. Abdominal x-ray shows calcium deposits in both kidneys.
questions.leadIn: Impaired function of which of the following is the most likely cause of her acid-base disorder?

options.text: Bicarbonate reclaiming in the proximal tubule
Na-K-2Cl transport in the thick ascending limb
Na-Cl transport in the distal convoluted tubule

questions.explanation: Answer: hydrogen ion secretion by alpha-intercalated cells (type 1, or distal, renal tubular acidosis). Why: her anion gap is 140 - (115 + 15) = 10, so this is a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 129) say type 1 RTA is a defect in the ability of alpha-intercalated cells to secrete H+, so urine pH stays above 5.5 despite acidosis, potassium is low, and calcium phosphate stones are more likely. Causes include amphotericin B, analgesic nephropathy, urinary tract anomalies, and autoimmune disease. MSD says type 1 RTA is impaired H+ secretion in the distal tubule with urine pH above 5.5, often with hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, and low urine citrate, which can lead to nephrocalcinosis and stones. MSD lists Sjögren syndrome among causes and treats it with sodium bicarbonate or sodium citrate.

whyWrong.b: Proximal (type 2) RTA is a bicarbonate reabsorption defect; once bicarbonate is depleted the urine pH falls below 5.5 (MSD), unlike her pH of 6.5.
whyWrong.c: Low aldosterone effect is type 4 RTA, which causes high potassium, not low (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Loss of Na-K-2Cl transport is Bartter syndrome, which causes metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, pp. 126-127).
whyWrong.e: Loss of Na-Cl transport is Gitelman syndrome, which causes metabolic alkalosis and low urine calcium (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 127).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Renal tubular acidosis, p. 129
MSD Manual Professional: Renal Tubular Acidosis

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man comes for a follow-up visit because of high blood pressure found at a sports physical. His blood pressure is 168/104 mm Hg. His father had high blood pressure starting at age 22. Serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L, and bicarbonate is 32 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are both low.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drugs is most likely to correct his blood pressure and potassium?
questions.explanation: Answer: amiloride (Liddle syndrome). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 128) describe Liddle syndrome as an autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation that increases the activity of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting tubule. The result is hypertension, low potassium, and metabolic alkalosis that look like hyperaldosteronism, but aldosterone is very low. Amiloride blocks the sodium channel. MSD says the overactive channels are on the luminal membrane of the collecting tubule, that the disorder usually appears before age 35 with low renin and aldosterone, and that triamterene and amiloride are both effective while spironolactone does not help.

whyWrong.b: Spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor, but aldosterone is already low and the channel works without it, so spironolactone does not help (MSD).
whyWrong.c: Hydrochlorothiazide would lower blood pressure a little but make potassium loss worse (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Furosemide would increase potassium loss and worsen the alkalosis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Dexamethasone treats glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, in which aldosterone is high, not low (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Liddle syndrome, p. 128
MSD Manual Professional: Liddle Syndrome

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man comes to the physician 3 weeks after cardiac catheterization for chest pain. His serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 2.7 mg/dL. He has a lacy purple pattern on the skin of both legs, and several painful blue toes, but his foot pulses are normal. The blood eosinophil count is high, and serum C3 is low. Eye examination shows bright yellow plaques in the retinal arteries.
questions.leadIn: A kidney biopsy would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Needle-shaped clefts in small renal arteries
Necrotic tubule cells with granular casts
Fibrinoid necrosis with onion-skinning of arterioles
Linear IgG along the basement membrane

questions.explanation: Answer: needle-shaped clefts in small arteries (cholesterol emboli, or renal atheroembolism). Why: Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 134) explain that a disrupted plaque showers cholesterol crystals and debris into small arteries, most often after cardiac catheterization or other vascular procedures. Signs can be immediate or delayed by more than 30 days. Skin signs are most common: blue toes with normal pulses, livedo reticularis (a lacy pattern), gangrene, and ulcers. Hollenhorst plaques are bright yellow emboli in retinal arteries. MSD says eosinophilia, eosinophils in the urine, and short-lived low complement may be present, and that the crystals dissolve during tissue processing, leaving biconcave, needle-shaped clefts in the blocked vessels. No treatment removes existing emboli; care aims to prevent more, and anticoagulation may make it worse (MSD). Your El-Husseiny nephrology notes add statins and say many patients never regain normal kidney function.

whyWrong.b: Granular casts and dead tubule cells are acute tubular necrosis (StatPearls Acute Tubular Necrosis), which does not explain blue toes, retinal plaques, or low complement (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Eosinophil-rich interstitial infiltrate is drug-induced interstitial nephritis (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 120); the eosinophilia here comes from cholesterol emboli (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Fibrinoid necrosis with onion-skinning is malignant hypertension, which needs a very high blood pressure (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Linear IgG is anti-GBM disease, which causes nephritis and lung bleeding (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 84).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Atheroembolic renal disease, p. 134
MSD Manual Professional: Renal Atheroembolism

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because she cannot get back to her life since her husband died suddenly 14 months ago. Nearly every day for the past several months, she has longed intensely for him. She says it feels as if part of her died with him, she still cannot believe he is gone, and she avoids the park where they walked. She has stopped going to her book club and feels that life has no meaning without him. Her family says her grief is far longer and deeper than is usual in their community. Outside of thoughts about him, she enjoys her grandchildren and does not feel worthless.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: prolonged grief disorder. Why: DSM-5-TR (pp. 322-323) requires a close person's death at least 12 months earlier (6 months for children and adolescents). For at least the last month, the person has had, nearly every day, intense yearning for the person or preoccupation with them. At least 3 of 8 other symptoms are also present, such as feeling that part of oneself has died, disbelief, avoiding reminders, intense emotional pain, trouble rejoining activities, emotional numbness, feeling that life is meaningless, and intense loneliness. The reaction must cause distress or impairment and clearly exceed cultural norms. She has yearning plus at least 5 of these symptoms, 14 months after the death. Prolonged grief disorder was added in the DSM-5-TR (2022) (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Normal grief can be intense, but hers is past 12 months, impairs her, and clearly exceeds the norms of her community, which defines the disorder (DSM-5-TR, p. 323).
whyWrong.c: Major depressive disorder involves low mood or loss of pleasure that spreads beyond thoughts of the loss, often with worthlessness; she still enjoys her grandchildren and does not feel worthless (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Adjustment disorder is used when a stress reaction fits no more specific diagnosis; her picture fits prolonged grief exactly (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: PTSD centers on intrusive memories, nightmares, and hyperarousal tied to a traumatic event, not yearning for the person who died (MSD PTSD).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Prolonged grief disorder, pp. 322-323
MSD Manual Professional: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the physician by his parents because he has been acting strangely for 10 weeks. He says that the FBI has put a chip in his tooth and that he hears two voices commenting on what he does. He has stopped showering and speaks very little, with a flat face. He has had no episodes of depression or mania. Urine toxicology screen is negative, and physical examination and laboratory studies are normal. Before these 10 weeks, he was doing well in college.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features

questions.explanation: Answer: schizophreniform disorder. Why: DSM-5-TR (p. 111) requires 2 or more core symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), at least one of them delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, for an episode of 1 month or longer but shorter than 6 months. MSD likewise defines it as schizophrenia-like symptoms lasting at least 1 month and under 6 months; beyond 6 months the diagnosis is likely schizophrenia, and treatment is antipsychotics with supportive care, continued for at least 12 months after symptoms resolve. Mood disorders with psychosis must be ruled out. If the person has not yet recovered, the diagnosis is called provisional. He has delusions, hallucinations, and negative symptoms (flat affect, little speech, poor self-care) for 10 weeks. Schizophrenia requires the disturbance to last at least 6 months (DSM-5-TR, pp. 113-114).

whyWrong.b: Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month; once psychotic symptoms last 1 month or longer, another diagnosis applies (DSM-5-TR, p. 111).
whyWrong.c: Schizophrenia needs continuous signs for at least 6 months (DSM-5-TR, p. 114); he has had symptoms for only 10 weeks.
whyWrong.d: Delusional disorder involves delusions without prominent hallucinations or negative symptoms, and functioning is usually intact (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: He has had no manic or depressive episodes, which must be ruled out before diagnosing schizophreniform disorder (DSM-5-TR, p. 111).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Schizophreniform disorder, p. 111; schizophrenia, pp. 113-114
MSD Manual Professional: Schizophreniform Disorder

questions.topic: Somatic symptom disorders: functional neurological symptom disorder
questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she suddenly could not move her right leg after an argument with her partner 6 hours ago. She lies on the stretcher and cannot push her right heel down into the examiner's hand. When she is asked to lift her left leg against resistance, her right hip pushes down with full strength. Reflexes and sensation are normal, and the toes point down when the soles are stroked. MRI of the brain and spine is normal. She is not seeking time off work or money, and nothing suggests she is faking the weakness.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder). Why: the finding is Hoover's sign. DSM-5-TR (p. 361) describes it as weak hip extension that returns to normal strength when the other hip flexes against resistance. It is a positive sign showing that the weakness does not fit known neurological disease. The diagnosis is not made just because tests are normal, and it can coexist with neurological disease. DSM-5-TR (p. 362) says la belle indifférence (lack of concern about the symptom) is not specific enough to diagnose it, and (p. 363) that about 1 in 5 people with functional seizures also have epilepsy. MSD says the symptoms develop without conscious intent, often start suddenly after stress, and affect women in 60 to 80% of cases. Explaining the diagnosis is a key treatment, and cognitive behavioral therapy and physical therapy help some people (MSD).

whyWrong.b: Factitious disorder requires deliberate falsification with deception, even without external reward (DSM-5-TR, pp. 367-368); nothing here suggests she is faking.
whyWrong.c: Malingering is intentional feigning for an external incentive such as money, avoiding work, or drugs (DSM-5-TR, p. 835); she seeks no gain.
whyWrong.d: Multiple sclerosis would show upper motor neuron signs and lesions on MRI; Hoover's sign shows the weakness does not match neurological disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Illness anxiety disorder is worry about having a serious illness with few or no symptoms; she has a sudden, clear deficit (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Functional neurological symptom disorder, pp. 361-363
MSD Manual Professional: Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is referred by his attorney for evaluation of severe neck pain after a minor car crash 4 months ago. He has a lawsuit pending against the other driver. He says he cannot turn his head at all and cannot work. In the waiting room, he was seen turning his head freely to talk to the man next to him. He refuses to sign a release for his previous medical records. Neurologic examination and imaging are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Answer: malingering. Why: DSM-5-TR (p. 835) describes malingering as intentionally producing false or grossly exaggerated symptoms for an external incentive, such as money, avoiding work or military duty, evading prosecution, or getting drugs. It should be strongly suspected with a medicolegal context (such as referral by an attorney), a large gap between claimed disability and objective findings, poor cooperation, or antisocial personality disorder. He has all of the first three. MSD contrasts this with factitious disorder, in which the deception is deliberate but the aim is to take on the sick role, with no obvious external incentive such as money or time off work. Malingering is not itself a mental disorder (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Factitious disorder is deception without an obvious external reward (DSM-5-TR, p. 835); his pending lawsuit is an external reward.
whyWrong.c: Functional neurological symptom disorder is not intentionally produced, and the external incentive here points away from it (DSM-5-TR, p. 835).
whyWrong.d: Somatic symptom disorder involves real distress and excessive worry about symptoms, not deliberate exaggeration for gain (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Illness anxiety disorder is fear of having a serious disease with few symptoms, not feigned disability (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Malingering, p. 835
MSD Manual Professional: Factitious Disorder Imposed on Self

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has been admitted 4 times in 6 months for episodes of hypoglycemia with sweating and drowsiness. Every episode began while his mother, a nurse, was alone with him. She is very attentive, knows his chart in detail, and is friendly with the staff. During the latest episode, his serum insulin was high and his C-peptide was very low. No episodes occur when she is away.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for the mother?
questions.explanation: Answer: factitious disorder imposed on another (formerly factitious disorder by proxy). Why: DSM-5-TR (pp. 367-368) describes falsifying or causing illness in another person, with identified deception, and presenting that person as ill, even when there is no obvious external reward. The perpetrator, not the victim, receives the diagnosis, and the victim may receive an abuse diagnosis. MSD says the caregiver, usually a parent, may harm the child with drugs or other agents, often appears deeply concerned and protective, and the child has frequent hospitalizations without a firm diagnosis. High insulin with low C-peptide means the insulin came from outside the body, because the pancreas releases C-peptide along with its own insulin (standard teaching). Child protective services should be contacted (MSD).

whyWrong.b: Factitious disorder imposed on self means falsifying one's own illness; here she causes illness in her son (DSM-5-TR, p. 367).
whyWrong.c: Malingering requires an external incentive such as money (DSM-5-TR, p. 835); none is present.
whyWrong.d: Delusional disorder involves a fixed false belief; her behavior is deliberate deception, not a delusion (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Illness anxiety disorder is worry about one's own health, not causing illness in another (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Factitious disorder, pp. 367-368; malingering, p. 835
MSD Manual Professional: Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man comes to the physician because he feels lonely. He works night shifts doing data entry and has turned down two promotions because they would require leading team meetings, where he fears he would be criticized. He would like to have friends and a girlfriend but does not join coworkers for lunch unless he is sure they like him. He sees himself as dull and inferior to others. He has felt this way since his teens. He has no odd beliefs.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: avoidant personality disorder. Why: DSM-5-TR (pp. 764-765) describes a long-standing pattern of shyness with others, feeling inadequate, and being very sensitive to being judged, starting by early adulthood. Examples include avoiding jobs with a lot of contact with people because of fear of criticism or rejection, getting involved with people only when sure of being liked, and seeing oneself as inept or inferior; at least 4 of 7 features are needed. The key contrast is that he wants relationships but fears rejection. In schizoid personality disorder, the person neither wants nor enjoys close relationships (DSM-5-TR, pp. 741-742). MSD puts it this way: schizoid patients are isolated because they are not interested in others, while avoidant patients long for contact but are hypersensitive to rejection or criticism. Group cognitive behavioral therapy focused on social skills is considered effective (MSD).

whyWrong.b: Schizoid personality disorder means not wanting or enjoying close relationships (DSM-5-TR, pp. 741-742); he wants friends and a partner.
whyWrong.c: Schizotypal personality disorder includes odd beliefs, magical thinking, and eccentric behavior (standard teaching); he has none.
whyWrong.d: Dependent personality disorder centers on needing others to make decisions and fear of being alone, not avoiding people (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Paranoid personality disorder centers on distrust and suspicion that others mean harm, not fear of criticism (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Avoidant personality disorder, pp. 764-765; schizoid personality disorder, pp. 741-742
MSD Manual Professional: Avoidant Personality Disorder (AVPD)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician after cutting her forearms when her boyfriend said he might leave. She describes intense relationships that swing from adoring people to hating them; last week she called her therapist perfect, and today she says the therapist is useless. She often feels empty, spends money impulsively, and is terrified of being alone. She has no psychotic symptoms and is not depressed most of the time.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Answer: dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) for borderline personality disorder. Why: MSD describes intolerance of being alone, fear of abandonment, a shift from idealizing to devaluing people (black-and-white thinking), feeling empty, and impulsivity with self-harm. The suicide risk is 40 times that of the general population, and about 8 to 10% of patients die by suicide (MSD). Psychotherapy is the mainstay of treatment, and DBT, a cognitive-behavioral therapy that combines individual and group sessions, is one option. Medications do not consistently help the core symptoms and are mainly used for coexisting conditions such as depression (MSD).

whyWrong.b: MSD says benzodiazepines are not recommended in borderline personality disorder because of dependence, overdose, and diversion.
whyWrong.c: MSD says stimulants are not recommended because of dependence, overdose, and diversion; she has no ADHD.
whyWrong.d: Electroconvulsive therapy is for severe depression or catatonia, not the core features of a personality disorder (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Medications are not consistently effective for core borderline symptoms (MSD), and she has no psychosis that would call for long-term antipsychotics.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with major depressive disorder has trouble sleeping and has lost 6 kg (13 lb) over 3 months because of poor appetite. Her physician chooses an antidepressant that often causes sedation and weight gain and has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs. She takes it at bedtime.
questions.leadIn: This drug's antidepressant effect comes mainly from blocking which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors (mirtazapine). Why: MSD says mirtazapine blocks alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors as well as 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors. It causes weight gain and sedation through histamine H1 blockade and has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs and SNRIs. Alpha-2 autoreceptors normally act as a brake on norepinephrine release, so blocking them increases norepinephrine and serotonin release (standard teaching). Its sedation and appetite effects can help an older patient with insomnia and weight loss. Correction: your Pharmacology High Yield notes (PDF p. 60) say mirtazapine blocks 5-HT1A plus alpha-2. MSD lists alpha-2, 5-HT2, and 5-HT3, not 5-HT1A. Buspirone is the drug that acts on 5-HT1A receptors, as a partial agonist (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Blocking the serotonin transporter is how SSRIs work; SSRIs cause more sexual side effects than mirtazapine (MSD).
whyWrong.c: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors block breakdown of monoamines and need dietary tyramine limits (standard teaching); this is not mirtazapine's action.
whyWrong.d: Blocking norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake is bupropion's action, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (MSD), which does not cause weight gain (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: MSD does not list 5-HT1A among mirtazapine's targets; buspirone is the 5-HT1A drug (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Medications for Treatment of Depression
Pharmacology High Yield (Emily's file), Atypical antidepressants, PDF p. 60

questions.topic: Eating disorders: bulimia nervosa and bupropion
questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman comes to the physician because she binge eats and then makes herself vomit 4 times a week. This has gone on for 8 months. Her BMI is 22 kg/m2. She has swollen glands in front of both ears, worn enamel on the back of her front teeth, and scars on the backs of her fingers. Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. She also wants to quit smoking and asks for a pill that could help both her mood and smoking.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: bupropion. Why: MSD says bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, is contraindicated in patients who have bulimia or are seizure-prone, and it can raise seizure risk with other drugs. Electrolyte problems from purging add to the seizure risk (standard teaching). She has bulimia nervosa: MSD notes that patients are typically of normal weight, and that vomiting can erode dental enamel, swell the parotid glands, scar the backs of the hands, and cause low potassium. Cognitive behavioral therapy is the treatment of choice, and fluoxetine is often used in adults (MSD).

whyWrong.b: Fluoxetine is often used to treat bulimia nervosa in adults (MSD Bulimia Nervosa).
whyWrong.c: SSRIs such as sertraline do not carry bupropion's contraindication in bulimia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Nicotine replacement is a safe option to help her stop smoking (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Varenicline is a smoking-cessation drug without bupropion's seizure contraindication in eating disorders (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Medications for Treatment of Depression
MSD Manual Professional: Bulimia Nervosa

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician 5 weeks after giving birth because of low mood, loss of interest, guilt, poor concentration, and trouble sleeping for 3 weeks. She has no psychotic symptoms or thoughts of harming herself or her baby. She is prescribed an oral drug to take once daily in the evening with a fatty meal for 14 days and is told not to drive for at least 12 hours after each dose.
questions.leadIn: This drug most likely acts by enhancing the activity of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: GABA-A receptors (zuranolone). Why: FDA approved zuranolone (Zurzuvae) on 4 August 2023 as the first oral drug for postpartum depression in adults, taken once daily in the evening with a fatty meal for 14 days. Before that, drug treatment for postpartum depression was only available as an IV injection given in certain health care facilities (FDA). The boxed warning says it impairs driving, so patients should not drive for at least 12 hours after a dose. The label says its mechanism is thought to be positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors. Recent change: zuranolone was approved in 2023, so older review sources may not list it.

whyWrong.b: Blocking NMDA receptors is how esketamine works (standard teaching); MSD lists esketamine nasal spray for treatment-resistant depression, not a 14-day oral course.
whyWrong.c: Blocking the serotonin transporter is how SSRIs work; that is a different drug class (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: D2 blockade is the action of antipsychotics, used for psychosis, which she does not have (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Mu opioid receptors are not a target of depression treatment (standard teaching).

sources.title: FDA: FDA Approves First Oral Treatment for Postpartum Depression (4 Aug 2023)
FDA label: Zurzuvae (zuranolone) capsules, 2023

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for 4 months, and her psychosis has improved. She now has no menstrual periods and a milky discharge from both nipples. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Serum prolactin is high. She has no tremor or rigidity.
questions.leadIn: Blocking dopamine receptors in which pathway most likely caused these findings?

options.text: Chemoreceptor trigger zone in the medulla

questions.explanation: Answer: the tuberoinfundibular pathway. Why: dopamine released from the hypothalamus into the pituitary portal blood normally inhibits prolactin release. Blocking D2 receptors there raises prolactin, causing galactorrhea and missed periods (standard teaching). MSD says second-generation antipsychotics block dopamine and serotonin receptors, which lowers the risk of motor (extrapyramidal) side effects. Most raise prolactin only slightly or not at all, except risperidone, which raises it as much as first-generation drugs and can cause galactorrhea (MSD). Correction: your Pharmacology High Yield notes (PDF p. 52) say atypical antipsychotics have no action on D2. MSD says they do block dopamine receptors, which is why risperidone can raise prolactin and why atypicals can still cause motor side effects, though less often.

whyWrong.b: Nigrostriatal D2 blockade causes motor (extrapyramidal) side effects such as rigidity and tremor (standard teaching); she has none.
whyWrong.c: Mesolimbic D2 blockade is thought to cause the antipsychotic effect on positive symptoms (standard teaching), not high prolactin.
whyWrong.d: The mesocortical pathway is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms (standard teaching), not prolactin release.
whyWrong.e: Blocking D2 in the chemoreceptor trigger zone gives an antinausea effect (standard teaching), not high prolactin.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Antipsychotic Medications
Pharmacology High Yield (Emily's file), Antipsychotics, PDF p. 52

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia has had little improvement despite adequate trials of haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine. Two months ago he attempted suicide. His psychiatrist starts the antipsychotic most likely to help treatment-resistant illness and to reduce suicidal behavior.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following must be monitored regularly while he takes this drug?
questions.explanation: Answer: blood cell counts, specifically the neutrophil count (clozapine). Why: MSD says clozapine helps about 40% of patients who do not respond to first-generation antipsychotics and reduces suicidality. Its most serious adverse effect is agranulocytosis, in fewer than 1% of patients, so blood counts are checked often. Clozapine can also cause dose-related seizures, metabolic syndrome, and myocarditis (MSD). Recent change: FDA removed the clozapine REMS program, effective 13 June 2025 (announced 27 Aug 2025). Prescribers and pharmacies no longer have to enroll in it or report ANC results, but FDA still recommends monitoring the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) as the label directs. FDA says the risk of severe neutropenia is greatest in the first months of treatment and never goes away.

whyWrong.b: Slit-lamp exams are not the standard monitoring test for clozapine; its key risk is low neutrophils (MSD).
whyWrong.c: Thyroid tests are monitored with lithium (standard teaching), not clozapine.
whyWrong.d: Creatine kinase is checked when neuroleptic malignant syndrome is suspected (standard teaching), not routinely with clozapine.
whyWrong.e: Hearing tests are not part of antipsychotic monitoring (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Antipsychotic Medications
FDA Drug Safety Communication: FDA removes REMS program for clozapine (27 Aug 2025)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia had severe rigidity with one antipsychotic and breast enlargement with another. He is switched to a newer capsule that combines two drugs. One of them acts in the brain without affecting dopamine D2 receptors. The other stays outside the brain and is added to reduce nausea, vomiting, and other side effects of the first.
questions.leadIn: The antipsychotic drug in this combination acts mainly on which receptors?
questions.explanation: Answer: muscarinic (cholinergic) receptors, with xanomeline-trospium (Cobenfy). Why: FDA approved it on 26 September 2024 as the first antipsychotic for schizophrenia that targets cholinergic receptors instead of dopamine receptors. MSD says it is the first antipsychotic with no effect on D2 receptors, it improves both positive and negative symptoms in trials, and trospium is a peripheral anticholinergic that counters xanomeline's cholinergic side effects. Xanomeline is a muscarinic receptor agonist (standard teaching). FDA lists nausea, indigestion, constipation, vomiting, and high blood pressure among common side effects, and urinary retention, moderate or severe kidney or liver disease, gastric retention, and untreated narrow-angle glaucoma as contraindications. Recent change: approved in 2024, so it is not in older review sources.

whyWrong.b: MSD says this is the first antipsychotic with no effect on D2 receptors.
whyWrong.c: Histamine H1 blockade causes sedation and weight gain with some antipsychotics (standard teaching); it is not this drug's main action.
whyWrong.d: NMDA blockade is linked to ketamine and esketamine (standard teaching), not this antipsychotic.
whyWrong.e: Opioid receptors are not a target of antipsychotics (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Antipsychotic Medications
FDA: FDA Approves Drug with New Mechanism of Action for Treatment of Schizophrenia (26 Sep 2024)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with opioid use disorder who has injected heroin for 3 years asks for treatment. He is started on a film placed under the tongue that contains buprenorphine and naloxone.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the main reason naloxone is included in this product?

options.text: To block withdrawal symptoms on day 1

questions.explanation: Answer: to discourage injection. Why: MSD says naloxone is inactive when buprenorphine-naloxone is taken under the tongue, but it causes acute withdrawal if the product is injected. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu opioid receptor with a ceiling effect that limits breathing suppression and sedation. Its strong binding to the receptor protects against overdose when other opioids are used (MSD). Low-dose induction lets buprenorphine start without precipitating withdrawal. Methadone, a full agonist, can prolong the QTc interval (MSD). Recent change: MSD notes that U.S. rules on prescribing buprenorphine, including extra training requirements, were relaxed after December 2022.

whyWrong.b: Buprenorphine's own ceiling effect, as a partial agonist, limits respiratory depression (MSD); naloxone is inactive when taken under the tongue.
whyWrong.c: Naloxone does not lengthen buprenorphine's action (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Naloxone in this product is inactive when taken as directed (MSD), so it does not treat constipation.
whyWrong.e: Naloxone causes withdrawal rather than blocking it when injected (MSD).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Opioid Use Disorder

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who has misused oxycodone daily for 2 years wants to stop and asks for a monthly extended-release naltrexone injection. His last oxycodone dose was 20 hours ago. He has mild yawning and a runny nose.
questions.leadIn: If naltrexone is injected today, which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: precipitated opioid withdrawal. Why: naltrexone is an opioid receptor antagonist; given while oxycodone is still bound to receptors, it pushes the opioid off and causes sudden, severe withdrawal (standard teaching). MSD says naltrexone cannot be given within 7 days of the last full dose of an opioid agonist. MSD names buprenorphine (a partial agonist) and methadone (a full agonist) as other treatments for opioid use disorder.

whyWrong.b: Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors, so it does not cause respiratory depression (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Serotonin syndrome comes from serotonergic drugs, not naltrexone (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Liver failure is not the expected result of a single dose given too early (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A disulfiram-like reaction follows alcohol with drugs such as metronidazole, not naltrexone with opioids (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Opioid Use Disorder

questions.topic: Eating disorders: anorexia nervosa and refeeding syndrome
questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl with restricting-type anorexia nervosa is admitted to the hospital. Her BMI is 14.6 kg/m2. Her pulse is 42/min, blood pressure falls when she stands, and she has fine downy hair on her back. Nutrition is started. On the third day, she becomes weak and confused and has new swelling of her ankles.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: hypophosphatemia (refeeding syndrome). Why: MSD describes refeeding syndrome as a potentially serious metabolic problem marked by low phosphate and other electrolyte abnormalities, seen rarely and mostly in the most undernourished patients. Feeding starts at about 30 to 40 kcal/kg/day and is raised gradually (MSD). Feeding raises insulin, which drives phosphate into cells to make ATP, so blood phosphate falls (standard teaching). DSM-5-TR (p. 381) defines anorexia nervosa by restricted intake causing significantly low weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and a disturbed view of body weight or shape; restricting type means no bingeing or purging in the last 3 months. A BMI under 15 is extreme severity (DSM-5-TR, p. 381). MSD lists slow heart rate, low blood pressure (especially on standing), low body temperature, and lanugo hair as common, and recommends family-based treatment for children and adolescents.

whyWrong.b: High sodium is not the hallmark of refeeding; low phosphate is (MSD).
whyWrong.c: Refeeding lowers rather than raises electrolytes, with low phosphate as the hallmark (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Refeeding moves potassium into cells, lowering it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Phosphate falls during refeeding, it does not rise (MSD).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Anorexia Nervosa
DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Anorexia nervosa, p. 381

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student comes to the physician because she falls asleep in class and while studying, even after a full night of sleep. When she laughs hard, her knees buckle and her jaw goes slack for a few seconds, but she stays awake and aware. She sometimes sees vivid figures in her room just as she falls asleep and occasionally wakes up unable to move. A multiple sleep latency test shows an average sleep latency of 4 minutes and REM sleep at the start of 3 naps.
questions.leadIn: Loss of which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.text: Dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta
Serotonin neurons of the raphe nuclei
Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis

questions.explanation: Answer: hypocretin (orexin) neurons in the hypothalamus (narcolepsy type 1). Why: MSD says type 1 narcolepsy is thought to be due to hypocretin deficiency, with low hypocretin-1 in spinal fluid, possibly from autoimmune destruction of hypocretin-making cells in the lateral hypothalamus, and it is strongly linked to certain HLA types. Cataplexy is brief weakness triggered by strong emotion such as laughter, with consciousness preserved. Hallucinations at sleep onset and sleep paralysis are also typical. Polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test shows an average sleep latency of 8 minutes or less and REM periods at sleep onset. Oxybates or pitolisant treat cataplexy, modafinil is added for sleepiness, and classic stimulants are third- or fourth-line (MSD).

whyWrong.b: Loss of substantia nigra dopamine neurons causes Parkinson disease, with tremor and rigidity, not cataplexy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Raphe serotonin neurons are not the lesion in narcolepsy, which is caused by hypocretin deficiency (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Loss of nucleus basalis cholinergic neurons is linked to Alzheimer disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Pineal melatonin affects circadian timing, not cataplexy or sleep-onset REM (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Narcolepsy

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician 10 days after she was assaulted while walking home. Since then she has had nightmares and vivid flashbacks of the attack, avoids the street where it happened, feels as if things around her are unreal, sleeps poorly, and startles at small noises. She had no mental health problems before.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: acute stress disorder. Why: DSM-5-TR (p. 315) limits acute stress disorder to symptoms lasting 3 days to 1 month after a traumatic event. MSD says PTSD can only be diagnosed at least 1 month after the trauma, and acute stress disorder can progress to PTSD. MSD groups PTSD symptoms into intrusions (unwanted memories, nightmares), avoidance, negative changes in thinking and mood, and changes in arousal. If symptoms last beyond 1 month, the diagnosis becomes PTSD. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy has the strongest evidence for PTSD (MSD).

whyWrong.b: PTSD can only be diagnosed at least 1 month after the trauma (MSD); it has been 10 days.
whyWrong.c: Adjustment disorder is used when a stress reaction fits no more specific diagnosis; her trauma symptoms fit acute stress disorder (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Generalized anxiety disorder is broad, ongoing worry for at least 6 months, not trauma-linked flashbacks (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Panic disorder involves unexpected panic attacks and worry about having more, not flashbacks of a trauma (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Acute stress disorder, p. 315
MSD Manual Professional: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)

questions.stem: A 41-year-old veteran has had posttraumatic stress disorder for 2 years. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy and sertraline have helped his daytime symptoms, but he still has nightmares about combat several nights a week that wake him in a sweat.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to add?
questions.explanation: Answer: prazosin. Why: MSD says prazosin appears helpful in reducing nightmares in PTSD, SSRIs improve PTSD symptoms, and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy has the strongest evidence. Prazosin blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, reducing the effect of norepinephrine, which is thought to drive nightmares and arousal (standard teaching). MSD advises that benzodiazepines be used sparingly, if at all.

whyWrong.b: MSD advises benzodiazepines be used sparingly, if at all, in PTSD.
whyWrong.c: Haloperidol is for psychosis; he has no psychotic symptoms (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Methylphenidate is a stimulant that would worsen arousal and sleep (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, not PTSD nightmares (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with major depressive disorder has taken sertraline for 3 months. His mood, sleep, and energy are much better, but he now has great difficulty reaching orgasm, which upsets him and his partner. He wants to keep treating his depression.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate change in his treatment?
questions.explanation: Answer: switch to bupropion. Why: MSD says sexual dysfunction, especially difficulty reaching orgasm, occurs in more than half of patients taking SSRIs, and that lowering the dose or changing to a serotonin modulator or a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor may help. Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (MSD). Bupropion does not increase serotonin, which is why it rarely causes sexual side effects (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Paroxetine is another SSRI and would likely cause the same problem (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Venlafaxine is an SNRI; MSD says mirtazapine has fewer sexual effects than SSRIs and SNRIs, meaning SNRIs also cause them.
whyWrong.d: Stopping an SSRI abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms and risks relapse; he wants to keep treatment (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A benzodiazepine does not treat the sexual side effect and adds dependence risk (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Medications for Treatment of Depression

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man comes to the physician because of shortness of breath with exertion that has slowly worsened over 2 years. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. His older brother had a liver transplant at age 45. Breath sounds are decreased at both lung bases. Spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 that does not improve after a bronchodilator. CT of the chest shows emphysema that is worst in both lower lobes. Serum ALT is mildly increased.
questions.leadIn: A liver biopsy from this patient is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Iron deposits stained with Prussian blue

questions.explanation: Answer: PAS-positive globules in liver cells (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 91) explain that alpha-1 antitrypsin is the main blocker of neutrophil elastase. When it is missing, elastase digests the alveolar walls of the whole acinus (panacinar emphysema), worst in the lower lobes. The misfolded protein gets stuck inside liver cells, so a biopsy shows pink PAS-positive globules, and smoking greatly raises the risk of lung damage. MSD adds that the protein is made in the liver, that the PI*ZZ genotype causes more than 95% of severe cases, and that the trapped protein forms polymers in liver cells, which can cause newborn cholestasis; your El-Husseiny respiratory notes also link it to cirrhosis. MSD advises testing for this condition in people who develop emphysema before about age 50, as in this smoker with an early, lower-lobe pattern and a family history of liver failure. Selected patients can receive replacement (augmentation) therapy with the protein (MSD).

whyWrong.b: Mallory-Denk bodies are tangled keratin in liver cells, seen mainly in alcohol-related liver disease; they do not explain early lower-lobe emphysema (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Iron deposits point to hemochromatosis, which affects the liver, heart, pancreas, and skin, not the lungs (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Ground-glass liver cells hold hepatitis B surface antigen; hepatitis B does not cause emphysema (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Copper buildup is Wilson disease, which affects the liver and brain, not the lungs (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, p. 91
MSD Manual Professional: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman comes to the physician because of episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and cough that are worse at night and after she visits a friend who has cats. She had eczema as a child. Expiratory wheezes are heard in both lungs. A complete blood count shows eosinophilia. Microscopy of her sputum shows coiled mucus casts and many tiny, double-pointed, needle-shaped crystals.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following cytokines most directly drives the growth and survival of the cells that form these crystals?
questions.explanation: Answer: interleukin-5 (IL-5). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 94) list the classic sputum findings in asthma: Curschmann spirals (coiled mucus casts made from shed airway lining cells), eosinophils, and Charcot-Leyden crystals, which form when eosinophils break down. MSD explains that Th2 cells, eosinophils, and mast cells fill the airway wall in allergic asthma, that IL-5 drives eosinophil maturation and survival, and that IL-13 adds to eosinophil buildup, mucus gland growth, and scarring. MSD names atopy (the tendency to make IgE to allergens) as the strongest known risk factor for asthma, which fits her eczema and cat trigger.
