Drugs that block IL-5 are used for severe eosinophilic asthma (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: IL-4 pushes T cells toward the Th2 type and switches B cells to make IgE (MSD), but it is not the main growth signal for eosinophils.
whyWrong.c: IL-2 makes T cells divide; it does not directly drive eosinophil growth (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: IL-17 comes from Th17 cells and mainly recruits neutrophils, which fits neutrophil-rich, low-T2 asthma rather than this eosinophilic picture (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Interferon-gamma is a Th1 cytokine that activates macrophages and tends to hold back Th2 responses (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Asthma, p. 94
MSD Manual Professional: Asthma

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because he and his wife have not conceived after 2 years of trying. He has had a daily cough with large amounts of thick sputum since childhood and frequent sinus infections. His heart sounds are loudest to the right of the sternum. Semen analysis shows a normal sperm count, but the sperm do not move. CT of the chest shows dilated, thick-walled bronchi.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: the dynein arms of cilia (primary ciliary dyskinesia, Kartagener syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 96) list Kartagener syndrome among the causes of bronchiectasis, a permanent widening of the airways, and explain that it comes from an inherited dynein arm defect that stops cilia from beating. MSD says primary ciliary dyskinesia causes sinusitis, ear infections, and male infertility, and gives Kartagener syndrome as dextrocardia, sinus disease, and situs inversus (mirror-image organs, so the heart sits on the right). The triad usually taught for exams is situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis (standard teaching). MSD adds that CT shows thick, widened airways (tram lines and signet-ring signs). Sperm tails are built like cilia, so they cannot swim even when the count is normal (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: CFTR defects (cystic fibrosis) also cause bronchiectasis and male infertility, but the infertility comes from a missing vas deferens with no sperm in the semen, and CF does not put the heart on the right (standard teaching). MSD notes CF bronchiectasis favors the upper lobes.
whyWrong.c: NADPH oxidase defects cause chronic granulomatous disease, with catalase-positive infections and granulomas, not immotile sperm or a right-sided heart (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes lower-lobe emphysema and liver disease, not sinus disease or situs inversus (MSD Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency).
whyWrong.e: Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia, with bacterial infections from low antibody levels but normal cilia (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Bronchiectasis, p. 96
MSD Manual Professional: Bronchiectasis

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician because of slowly worsening shortness of breath for 3 years. He installed pipe insulation in shipyards for 30 years and smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Fine crackles are heard at both lung bases, and he has clubbing of the fingers. CT of the chest shows scarring in both lower lobes and calcified plaques on the pleura over the diaphragm. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows golden-brown, dumbbell-shaped rods that turn blue with Prussian blue stain.
questions.leadIn: This patient is at greatest risk of death from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 100) describe asbestosis as scarring that is worst in the lower lobes, with ferruginous (asbestos) bodies, golden-brown rods that stain with Prussian blue, and calcified plaques on the parietal pleura. The same pages say lung cancer develops in about 25% of heavily exposed workers and is the leading cause of death in this group. Smoking multiplies the risk: about 6-fold with asbestos alone and about 60-fold with asbestos plus smoking. MSD agrees that asbestos and smoking act together and adds that asbestosis usually appears 20 to 40 years after exposure.

whyWrong.b: Mesothelioma is less common than lung cancer in asbestos workers, although it is more specific for heavy asbestos exposure (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 101).
whyWrong.c: Raised tuberculosis risk is linked to silica, which damages macrophages, not to asbestos (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 102).
whyWrong.d: Progressive massive fibrosis means large, merging upper-lobe scars from coal or silica dust, not lower-lobe asbestos scarring (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune reaction to inhaled organic material, such as bird proteins, not mineral fibers (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Asbestosis, p. 100; mesothelioma, p. 101; silicosis, p. 102
MSD Manual Professional: Asbestosis

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician because of shortness of breath and a dull, constant ache in the right side of his chest for 3 months. He worked replacing brake linings and building insulation from age 20 to 35. He has never smoked. Chest x-ray shows a large right pleural effusion. CT shows thick, lumpy pleura that wraps around the whole right lung. Fluid removed from the chest is bloody, and its cytology does not show a diagnosis.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: malignant pleural mesothelioma. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 101) describe mesothelioma as a rare cancer of the pleura that is more specific for heavy asbestos exposure than lung cancer. MSD gives a latency of 30 to 50 years after exposure, says the risk does not depend on smoking, and lists shortness of breath and non-pleuritic chest pain as the usual first symptoms. MSD also says up to 90% of patients have an effusion, usually on one side and bloody, that fluid cytology is usually not diagnostic, so a pleural biopsy is needed, and that median survival is only about 6 to 18 months. Other source: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes call asbestos the only known environmental risk factor. MSD also lists other mineral fibers, radiation therapy for lymphoma, and SV40 virus as possible causes.

whyWrong.b: Lung adenocarcinoma can spread to the pleura, but in a never-smoker, decades after asbestos work, a rind of tumor wrapping the lung points to mesothelioma (MSD).
whyWrong.c: Tuberculous pleurisy causes fever and a lymphocyte-rich effusion; it does not form a thick, lumpy rind around the lung (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Benign pleural plaques are calcified collagen patches on the parietal pleura (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 100); they do not cause a large bloody effusion or a mass encasing the lung.
whyWrong.e: Small cell lung cancer is a central airway tumor of smokers (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 114), not a tumor that spreads along the pleura.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Mesothelioma, p. 101; asbestosis, p. 100
MSD Manual Professional: Mesothelioma

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of a cough and shortness of breath that have worsened over 1 year. For 15 years he has cut and polished engineered stone kitchen countertops. Chest x-ray shows many small nodules in both upper lobes and enlarged hilar lymph nodes with thin rims of calcium around their edges.
questions.leadIn: This patient is at greatest risk of which of the following infections?
questions.explanation: Answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (pp. 101-102) explain that silica from foundries, sandblasting, and mining causes upper-lobe scarring and eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes. Silica is thought to break open the phagolysosomes of macrophages and impair them, which raises the risk of tuberculosis. MSD describes recent outbreaks in workers who cut engineered stone, says the eggshell pattern is typical but not unique to silicosis, and says that because the risk of mycobacterial disease is higher, these patients should be tested and treated for latent tuberculosis. MSD also notes that silica is a known human carcinogen.

whyWrong.b: Pneumocystis infects people with weak T-cell immunity, such as advanced HIV, not people with silicosis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Haemophilus influenzae commonly infects airways in chronic bronchitis, but silica's main infection risk is mycobacteria (MSD).
whyWrong.d: Aspergillus can grow in old lung cavities, but silica's specific link is to tuberculosis because of macrophage damage (MSD).
whyWrong.e: Histoplasma is acquired from soil with bird or bat droppings and is not tied to silica exposure (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Silicosis, pp. 101-102
MSD Manual Professional: Silicosis

questions.stem: A 31-year-old Black woman comes to the physician because of a dry cough, tiredness, and blurred vision in her right eye for 2 months. She has red, painful nodules on both shins. Chest x-ray shows enlarged lymph nodes at both lung roots. Serum calcium is 11.6 mg/dL, and serum PTH is low. Biopsy of a lymph node shows tight clusters of macrophage-derived cells and giant cells without central necrosis.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's high calcium level?

options.text: PTH-related peptide made by tumor cells
Excess PTH from a parathyroid adenoma
Low calcium excretion from a CASR defect

questions.explanation: Answer: calcitriol (active vitamin D) made by macrophages in the granulomas (sarcoidosis). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (pp. 103-104) describe sarcoidosis as a CD4 T-cell disease of unknown cause in which these cells release interferon-gamma and TNF, leading to non-caseating granulomas. It is more common in young adults, women, and African Americans, and causes hilar lymph node enlargement, uveitis, erythema nodosum, raised serum ACE, and high calcium because the granuloma cells have 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity. Steroids are the treatment, but the disease often clears on its own. MSD agrees that macrophages make calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), notes that ACE levels are not specific, and describes Lofgren syndrome (hilar nodes, erythema nodosum, and joint pain).

whyWrong.b: PTH-related peptide causes high calcium in squamous cell lung cancer (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 116), but a biopsy of non-caseating granulomas fits sarcoidosis.
whyWrong.c: A parathyroid adenoma would raise PTH; here PTH is low because high calcium suppresses it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Bone metastases can raise calcium, but this young woman has granulomas, eye and skin signs, and no tumor (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (a calcium-sensing receptor defect) causes mild lifelong high calcium with normal or high PTH and no organ disease (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Sarcoidosis, pp. 103-104
MSD Manual Professional: Sarcoidosis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted with severe acute pancreatitis. On day 2, he becomes short of breath and needs intubation. With PEEP of 8 cm H2O and FiO2 of 0.6, arterial PO2 is 72 mm Hg. Chest x-ray shows patchy opacities in both lungs. Echocardiography shows normal heart function, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 9 mm Hg.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the fluid in this patient's alveoli?

options.text: Blocked lymphatic drainage of the lungs

questions.explanation: Answer: a leaky alveolar-capillary membrane (acute respiratory distress syndrome, ARDS). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (pp. 105-106) explain that ARDS follows direct lung injury or a distant insult such as sepsis, burns, or pancreatitis. Damage to the lining cells makes the capillaries leak protein-rich fluid into the alveoli, so the wedge pressure stays normal, unlike in heart failure. The criteria are bilateral opacities, onset within 1 week, a PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300, and no cardiac cause. His ratio is 72/0.6 = 120, which MSD places in the moderate range (over 100 and up to 200 with PEEP of at least 5). Treatment is to fix the cause and ventilate with low tidal volumes and higher PEEP. MSD gives a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg ideal body weight or less, a plateau pressure below 30 cm H2O, and prone positioning for at least 12 hours a day in moderate to severe disease. Recent change: MSD reports that a consensus panel proposed widening the Berlin definition to include patients on high-flow oxygen of at least 30 L/min, an SpO2/FiO2 ratio of 315 or less when SpO2 is 97% or less, and ultrasound to confirm bilateral opacities.

whyWrong.b: High capillary hydrostatic pressure is cardiogenic edema, which would raise the wedge pressure; his is normal (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 105).
whyWrong.c: Low oncotic pressure, as in nephrotic syndrome, makes fluid shift slowly and does not cause sudden respiratory failure after pancreatitis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Blocked lymph drainage, as with cancer in the lymphatics, causes slow interstitial fluid buildup, not sudden alveolar flooding (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Strongly negative pleural pressure causes edema only in special cases, such as after a blocked airway is suddenly opened (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Acute respiratory distress syndrome, pp. 105-106
MSD Manual Professional: Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure (AHRF), Including Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of confusion and a cough for 3 weeks. He has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 45 years. Serum sodium is 121 mEq/L, and his urine is inappropriately concentrated. CT of the chest shows a large mass beside the right main bronchus and enlarged nodes in the mediastinum. Biopsy shows sheets of small, dark cells with very little cytoplasm and many mitoses. The cells stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin.
questions.leadIn: This tumor most likely arose from which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: Answer: neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells (small cell lung carcinoma). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (pp. 114-115) describe small cell carcinoma as a central tumor of smokers that arises from neuroendocrine cells and is made of small dark cells with scant cytoplasm that stain for markers such as chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD56. It can make ACTH (Cushing syndrome) or ADH (SIADH, which explains his low sodium), and it can trigger antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels (Lambert-Eaton syndrome). It is treated with chemotherapy and radiation rather than surgery. MSD gives it about 15% of lung cancers, says 70% to 80% of patients already have metastases at diagnosis, and lists SIADH and Lambert-Eaton syndrome among its paraneoplastic effects. MSD says surgery plays a limited role, and that chemotherapy and immunotherapy, with or without radiation, are given depending on stage.

whyWrong.b: Club cells line small bronchioles and are not the source of a central neuroendocrine tumor (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Adenocarcinoma, a peripheral tumor that forms glands, arises from alveolar lining cells (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 115); these cells stain for neuroendocrine markers instead.
whyWrong.d: Squamous cell carcinoma is also central, but it shows keratin pearls and causes high calcium through PTHrP, not SIADH (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 116).
whyWrong.e: Mesothelial cells give rise to mesothelioma, a pleural tumor linked to asbestos (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 101).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Small cell lung carcinoma, pp. 114-115
MSD Manual Professional: Lung Carcinoma

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a cough, thirst, and constipation for 1 month. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. Serum calcium is 13.1 mg/dL, and serum PTH is low. CT of the chest shows a mass at the left hilum, with a central cavity, arising from a main bronchus.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of this mass is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Small cells with scant cytoplasm and molding
Mucin-producing glands at the lung edge

questions.explanation: Answer: keratin pearls and intercellular bridges (squamous cell carcinoma). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 116) describe squamous cell carcinoma as a central, hilar tumor of smokers that can cavitate and that causes high calcium by making PTH-related peptide (PTHrP); under the microscope it shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. MSD agrees that hypercalcemia in squamous cell carcinoma comes from tumor PTHrP. The low PTH here shows that the parathyroid glands are not the cause.

whyWrong.b: Small cells with scant cytoplasm are small cell carcinoma, which causes SIADH or Cushing syndrome rather than high calcium (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 114).
whyWrong.c: Glands with mucin describe adenocarcinoma, which usually grows in the lung periphery (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 115).
whyWrong.d: Large cell carcinoma is undifferentiated and can make beta-hCG, which causes gynecomastia (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 117); it is not linked to PTHrP.
whyWrong.e: Non-caseating granulomas mark sarcoidosis, where high calcium comes from macrophage vitamin D (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 103), not from a cavitating mass in a smoker.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, pp. 116-117
MSD Manual Professional: Lung Carcinoma

questions.topic: Lung cancer: adenocarcinoma and targeted therapy
questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman who has never smoked comes to the physician because of a cough for 2 months. She has clubbing of the fingers. CT of the chest shows a 3-cm mass at the edge of the right upper lobe and several bone lesions. Biopsy shows malignant glands that contain mucin. Tumor testing shows an activating mutation in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: osimertinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that blocks mutant EGFR. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 115) call adenocarcinoma the most common primary lung cancer overall, more common in women and in people who have never smoked. It grows in the lung periphery, forms glands that often make mucin, and is linked to clubbing (hypertrophic osteoarthropathy). MSD says adenocarcinoma makes up about 40% of lung cancers and is the most common type in never-smokers. It names osimertinib as the treatment of choice for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer, with amivantamab plus lazertinib as another option.

whyWrong.b: MSD lists alectinib or lorlatinib for tumors with an ALK gene rearrangement, which this tumor does not have.
whyWrong.c: Imatinib blocks BCR-ABL and KIT, so it treats chronic myeloid leukemia and gastrointestinal stromal tumors (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Trastuzumab is an antibody against HER2, used mainly in HER2-positive breast and stomach cancers (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Rituximab is an antibody against CD20 on B cells, used for B-cell lymphomas and some autoimmune diseases (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Adenocarcinoma of the lung, p. 115
MSD Manual Professional: Lung Carcinoma

questions.topic: Lung cancer: Pancoast tumor and Horner syndrome
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of severe pain in his right shoulder for 2 months that spreads toward his armpit and down the inner side of his arm. He has smoked for 40 years. His right hand grip is weak, and the small muscles of the right hand are wasted. His right upper eyelid droops, his right pupil is smaller than the left, and his right forehead stays dry when he sweats. Chest x-ray shows a mass at the top of the right lung.
questions.leadIn: Tumor invasion of which of the following structures best explains this patient's eye and sweating findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: the cervical sympathetic ganglia (Horner syndrome from a Pancoast tumor). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 119) explain that a tumor in the superior sulcus at the lung apex can invade nearby neck structures. Shoulder pain spreading to the armpit and arm, with hand weakness and wasting, comes from the lower brachial plexus. Ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the same side come from the cervical sympathetic ganglia. Pressure on the subclavian vessels can swell the arm, and spread to the recurrent laryngeal or phrenic nerve causes hoarseness or a paralyzed diaphragm. MSD agrees that apical tumors, usually non-small cell cancers, invade the brachial plexus, pleura, or ribs, and that involvement of the sympathetic chain or stellate ganglion causes ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

whyWrong.b: An oculomotor nerve lesion causes ptosis with a large pupil and an eye turned down and out, not a small pupil and dry skin (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The lower brachial plexus explains his shoulder pain and hand weakness, but not the eye or sweating signs (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 119).
whyWrong.d: The recurrent laryngeal nerve controls voice; its invasion causes hoarseness (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 119).
whyWrong.e: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; its invasion paralyzes half of the diaphragm (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 119).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Pancoast syndrome, p. 119
MSD Manual Professional: Lung Carcinoma

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of diarrhea, poor weight gain, and white plaques in his mouth that keep coming back. His newborn screening test showed very low T-cell receptor excision circles. His mother's brother died of infections at 7 months of age. Chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow. Flow cytometry shows almost no T cells and no NK cells, with B cells present but not working.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.text: Common gamma chain of interleukin receptors
Adenosine deaminase in the purine salvage pathway
CD40 ligand on helper T cells
Bruton tyrosine kinase in B cells

questions.explanation: Answer: the common gamma chain shared by many interleukin receptors (X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, SCID). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 469) say the IL-2 receptor gamma chain defect is the most common, X-linked form of SCID, and that adenosine deaminase deficiency is second. Infants have bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections, thrush, diarrhea, and failure to thrive in the first year. Tests show low T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs), no thymic shadow, and no T cells, and the treatment is a bone marrow transplant. MSD says symptoms usually start by 6 months of age, that newborn screening uses TRECs, and that a stem cell transplant restores immunity in 90% to 100% of patients. The affected uncle on his mother's side fits X-linked inheritance (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is the second most common cause (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 469). It is autosomal recessive, so it would not explain an affected maternal uncle, and it removes B cells as well as T cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: CD40 ligand defects cause hyper-IgM syndrome, in which T cells are present but cannot help B cells switch antibody class (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 470).
whyWrong.d: Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause X-linked agammaglobulinemia, with no B cells but normal T cells and a normal thymus (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome) can remove the thymus, but it also causes low calcium, heart defects, and facial changes, and NK cells are normal (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Severe combined immunodeficiency, p. 469
MSD Manual Professional: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has had repeated sinus infections and pneumonia. Her parents say she has walked with a wide, unsteady gait since she first began walking. Examination shows small, spidery red blood vessels on the whites of both eyes and on her ears. Serum IgA is very low, and serum alpha-fetoprotein is high.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following cellular processes is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: repair of DNA double-strand breaks (ataxia-telangiectasia). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (pp. 469-470) describe an autosomal recessive mutation in the ATM gene, so cells cannot repair double-strand DNA breaks and are very sensitive to x-rays. The triad is cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, and sinus and lung infections from IgA deficiency, with a higher risk of lymphoma and leukemia. MSD says ataxia is often the first sign and starts when children begin to walk, telangiectasias usually appear between ages 4 and 6, IgA is low in about 80% of patients, and a high alpha-fetoprotein level is a diagnostic clue. MSD adds that cancers, such as leukemia, lymphoma, brain tumors, and stomach cancer, usually appear after age 10. Other source: your El-Husseiny immunology notes list low IgA, IgG, and IgE; MSD lists low IgA and IgE.

whyWrong.b: Nucleotide excision repair fails in xeroderma pigmentosum, which causes severe sun damage and skin cancers, not ataxia or IgA deficiency (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, with colon and endometrial cancers in adults (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Base excision repair defects (such as MUTYH) cause colon polyps, not ataxia or immune deficiency (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Lysosomal trafficking defects cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome, with albinism, giant granules, and neuropathy (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Ataxia-telangiectasia, pp. 469-470
MSD Manual Professional: Ataxia-Telangiectasia

questions.stem: A 7-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever, fast breathing, and low oxygen levels. A bronchoalveolar lavage sample shows Pneumocystis jirovecii. He had watery diarrhea from Cryptosporidium at 5 months. Serum IgM is high, and serum IgG, IgA, and IgE are very low. A lymph node biopsy shows no germinal centers.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.text: CD40 ligand on helper T cells
Bruton tyrosine kinase in B cells
Common gamma chain of interleukin receptors

questions.explanation: Answer: CD40 ligand on helper T cells (X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 470) explain that helper T cells without working CD40 ligand cannot give B cells the second signal they need to switch classes, so only IgM is made, IgG, IgA, and IgE are very low, and no germinal centers form. Infants have severe pyogenic infections and opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium, and CMV. MSD confirms that the X-linked form is caused by a CD40 ligand (CD154) defect and lists treatment with immune globulin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole to prevent Pneumocystis, and a stem cell transplant when possible.

whyWrong.b: Bruton tyrosine kinase defects stop B cells from forming, so all antibody classes, including IgM, are low (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Common gamma chain defects cause SCID, with no T cells and no thymic shadow (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 469), not a high IgM level.
whyWrong.d: WAS protein defects cause eczema, small platelets, and infections, with high IgE and IgA (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, pp. 470-471).
whyWrong.e: CD18 defects cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency, with no pus and late cord separation, not low IgG with high IgM (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, pp. 471-472).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Hyper-IgM syndrome, p. 470
MSD Manual Professional: Hyper-IgM Syndrome

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of bloody stools and many small purple spots on his skin. He has had eczema since early infancy and 5 ear infections. His platelet count is 28,000/mm3, and a blood smear shows that the platelets are unusually small. Serum IgE and IgA are high, and IgM is low.
questions.leadIn: The protein affected in this patient's condition normally controls which of the following?

options.text: Platelet binding to von Willebrand factor

questions.explanation: Answer: reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (pp. 470-471) describe an X-linked mutation in the WAS gene, so white cells and platelets cannot rearrange their actin skeleton. The triad is thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections (WATER), with high IgE and IgA and fewer, smaller platelets, and the treatment is an HLA-matched bone marrow transplant. MSD confirms the WASP protein, small platelets, and low IgM, notes that about 10% of patients develop a cancer after age 10, and says a stem cell transplant is curative.

whyWrong.b: NADPH oxidase defects cause chronic granulomatous disease, with catalase-positive infections but normal platelets (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Defective platelet binding to von Willebrand factor (Bernard-Soulier syndrome) gives large, not small, platelets and no eczema or immune defect (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Double-strand break repair is the defect in ataxia-telangiectasia, which causes ataxia and telangiectasias, not small platelets (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, pp. 469-470).
whyWrong.e: Failed lysosome fusion is Chediak-Higashi syndrome, with albinism, giant granules, and neuropathy (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, pp. 470-471
MSD Manual Professional: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome

questions.stem: A 5-week-old girl is brought to the physician because the skin around her umbilical cord stump is red and swollen. The cord stump is still attached. Her leukocyte count is 42,000/mm3 with mostly neutrophils. The red area is not warm to the touch and has no pus. Her parents are first cousins.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: CD18, the shared beta-2 chain of white cell integrins such as LFA-1 (leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (pp. 471-472) explain that this autosomal recessive defect stops white cells from sticking tightly to blood vessel walls and moving into tissue. Neutrophils pile up in the blood, but none reach the infection, so no pus forms. Signs include skin and mucosal infections, poor wound healing, omphalitis, and late separation of the umbilical cord. MSD names the ITGB2 gene for CD18, notes a high white cell count, and says a stem cell transplant is the only effective treatment. Other source: your El-Husseiny immunology notes define late cord separation as more than 30 days; MSD uses more than 3 weeks.

whyWrong.b: NADPH oxidase defects (chronic granulomatous disease) let neutrophils reach tissues, so abscesses and granulomas form (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Lysosomal trafficking defects (Chediak-Higashi syndrome) cause albinism, giant granules, and neuropathy, and the neutrophil count is low (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is common and usually mild; neutrophils still reach tissue and form pus (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Terminal complement deficiency causes repeated Neisseria infections, not late cord separation (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 433).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Leukocyte adhesion deficiency, pp. 471-472
MSD Manual Professional: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of fever, a stiff neck, and a spreading purple rash. Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-negative diplococci. He had the same type of meningitis at age 14. His older brother had a blood infection with the same organism. His blood counts and serum immunoglobulin levels are normal.
questions.leadIn: This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following?

options.text: Early complement components C1 through C4

questions.explanation: Answer: terminal complement components C5 through C9, which form the membrane attack complex. Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 433) say terminal complement deficiency raises the risk of repeated Neisseria bloodstream infections, while early deficiencies (C1 to C4) cause sinus and lung infections and, with C3 loss, immune complex disease. MSD's table lists C5 to C9 deficiencies as autosomal recessive and linked to repeated meningococcal infections and spread-out gonococcal infection. Patients should get meningococcal vaccines, and drugs that block C5, such as eculizumab, carry the same Neisseria risk (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Early component deficiency causes repeated pyogenic sinus and lung infections, and C3 loss adds immune complex disease (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 433).
whyWrong.c: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, with swelling from bradykinin and low C4, not infections (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 433).
whyWrong.d: Missing decay-accelerating factor (with CD59) causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, with complement destroying red cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: CD18 defects cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency, with skin infections and no pus in infancy (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, pp. 471-472).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Complement protein deficiencies, p. 433
MSD Manual Professional: Complement Deficiencies (table)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is being treated with chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia. He receives a unit of platelets donated by his son that was not irradiated. Two weeks later, he has a fever and a red rash that spreads from his palms to his whole body. He then has watery and bloody diarrhea and turns yellow. Serum bilirubin and liver enzymes are high, and his blood counts fall sharply.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.text: Donor T cells attacking the recipient's tissues
Recipient antibodies against donor ABO antigens
Bacterial contamination of the platelet unit

questions.explanation: Answer: donor T cells attacking the recipient's tissues (transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, GVHD). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 478) explain that GVHD can follow bone marrow or liver transplants or transfusion of blood that was not irradiated, usually in a host with a very weak immune system. Donor T cells see the host's MHC molecules as foreign and attack, mainly the skin, liver, and gut, so blood products for immunocompromised patients should be irradiated. MSD says the reaction starts 4 to 30 days after the transfusion, with fever, rash, diarrhea, liver injury, and pancytopenia from bone marrow failure, and has a death rate over 90%. MSD adds that blood from first-degree relatives should also be irradiated, because donor and recipient can share HLA types.

whyWrong.b: ABO antibodies cause an acute hemolytic reaction within about an hour of the transfusion (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 462), not weeks later.
whyWrong.c: Donor antibodies against recipient white cells cause transfusion-related acute lung injury, with breathing trouble within 6 hours (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 462).
whyWrong.d: Antibodies against IgA in an IgA-deficient recipient cause an allergic or anaphylactic reaction within minutes to hours (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 462).
whyWrong.e: Bacterial contamination of platelets causes fever and shock during or soon after the transfusion, not rash and liver failure weeks later (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Graft-versus-host disease, p. 478; transfusion reactions, p. 462
MSD Manual Professional: Complications of Transfusion

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a large, painless swelling on her neck that drains pus when opened. She has had several similar skin abscesses that were not red or warm, and two pneumonias that left air-filled cysts in her lungs. She has had an itchy rash since infancy, and she broke her arm after a minor fall. Her face is coarse, and none of her baby teeth have fallen out. Culture of the pus grows Staphylococcus aureus. Serum IgE is 5,200 IU/mL, and she has eosinophilia.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: STAT3 signaling needed to make Th17 cells (autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome, or Job syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 467) explain that STAT3 mutations leave too few Th17 cells, so neutrophils are not recruited to infections. The features follow the ABCDEF pattern: cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained baby teeth, coarse facies, skin rash (eczema), high IgE with eosinophils, and fractures after minor trauma. MSD confirms the STAT3 defect and faulty Th17 development, lists lung cysts (pneumatoceles), and uses an IgE level over 2000 IU/mL to support the diagnosis. Treatment is lifelong antibiotics against staph, usually trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (MSD). Other source: MSD says the very high IgE is thought to be a result of the disease, not its cause.

whyWrong.b: NADPH oxidase defects (chronic granulomatous disease) cause catalase-positive infections and granulomas, but not high IgE, retained teeth, or fractures (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: WAS protein defects affect boys and cause small platelets with bleeding along with eczema (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, pp. 470-471).
whyWrong.d: CD18 defects cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency, with no pus at all and late cord separation (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, pp. 471-472); this girl's abscesses drain pus.
whyWrong.e: IL-12 receptor defects cause severe mycobacterial infections with low interferon-gamma (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 466), not staph abscesses with high IgE.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome), pp. 466-467
MSD Manual Professional: Hyper-IgE Syndrome

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of weight loss, a racing heart, and heat intolerance for 3 months. Her eyes look as if she is staring, and both eyes bulge forward. The skin over both shins is thick and firm, with an orange-peel texture. Her thyroid gland is smoothly and evenly enlarged. Serum TSH is very low, and free T4 is high. A radioactive iodine uptake scan shows high uptake spread evenly through the gland.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.text: Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor
Release of stored hormone from inflammation

questions.explanation: Answer: IgG antibodies that switch on the TSH receptor (Graves disease). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 75-76) explain that thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) binds and activates the TSH receptor, so the gland grows evenly and makes too much hormone while TSH falls. T cells in the orbit and the skin of the shins drive fibroblasts to lay down glycosaminoglycans, which pushes the eyes forward (ophthalmopathy) and thickens the shin skin (pretibial myxedema). Radioactive iodine uptake is high and diffuse. MSD agrees that the antibody is stimulatory, calls the eye disease specific to Graves disease, and notes that the skin change rarely occurs without the eye disease. MSD also explains that uptake is low when thyrotoxicosis comes from thyroiditis or extra iodine.

whyWrong.b: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are the marker of Hashimoto thyroiditis, which usually causes hypothyroidism (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 71).
whyWrong.c: A TSH-secreting adenoma would cause high or normal TSH, not suppressed TSH, and would not cause eye or shin changes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: A single hot nodule shows uptake in one spot, not even uptake across the gland (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 76).
whyWrong.e: Hormone leaking from an inflamed gland (thyroiditis) gives low radioactive iodine uptake (MSD Hyperthyroidism).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Graves disease, pp. 75-76
MSD Manual Professional: Hyperthyroidism

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman comes to the physician because of tiredness, weight gain, and constipation for 1 year. Her thyroid gland is firm, rubbery, and mildly enlarged without tenderness. Serum TSH is high, free T4 is low, and antibodies against thyroid peroxidase are strongly positive. A fine-needle biopsy shows many lymphocytes and plasma cells with germinal centers and large follicular cells with pink, granular cytoplasm.
questions.leadIn: This patient has an increased risk of which of the following neoplasms?
questions.explanation: Answer: primary B-cell lymphoma of the thyroid. Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (p. 71) call Hashimoto thyroiditis the most common cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate. It is an autoimmune disease that is more common in women. Biopsy shows lymphocytes and plasma cells with germinal centers and Hurthle cells (large pink cells with granular cytoplasm), and antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin are present. The same page links it to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR5 and to a higher risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, usually of B cells. MSD agrees on the lymphocytic infiltrate with lymphoid follicles and the high thyroid peroxidase antibodies, says thyroid lymphoma is a rare complication, and notes that most patients need lifelong levothyroxine. Chronic B-cell stimulation in the gland is thought to be the soil for the lymphoma (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Medullary carcinoma comes from calcitonin-making C cells and is linked to RET mutations, not to autoimmune thyroiditis (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 82).
whyWrong.c: Anaplastic carcinoma is a rapidly growing, deadly tumor (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 83); Hashimoto disease is not its classic risk factor (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause of very high calcium and has no link to Hashimoto thyroiditis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Follicular adenoma is a benign encapsulated nodule; it is not a known result of chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Hashimoto thyroiditis, p. 71
MSD Manual Professional: Hashimoto Thyroiditis

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of severe pain in the front of her neck that spreads to her jaw and ears for 1 week. She had a sore throat and runny nose 3 weeks ago. She feels shaky and has palpitations. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). Her thyroid is enlarged and very tender. Serum TSH is low, free T4 is high, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 88 mm/h. Radioactive iodine uptake is almost zero.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of this patient's thyroid would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Lymphocytes with germinal centers and Hurthle cells
Tall follicular cells with scalloped colloid
Dense fibrosis spreading beyond the capsule
Papillae with clear nuclei and psammoma bodies

questions.explanation: Answer: granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells (subacute, or de Quervain, thyroiditis). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (p. 72) describe a likely post-viral thyroiditis that follows an upper respiratory infection and causes fever, a high ESR, and a painful, tender gland. Damage to the follicles releases stored hormone, so the patient is briefly thyrotoxic, but iodine uptake is low because no new hormone is being made. A hypothyroid phase may follow, and most people return to normal. Biopsy shows mixed inflammation with giant cells around broken pieces of colloid. MSD agrees that a virus is the likely cause, that uptake is low (often near 0) early on, and that biopsy shows giant cells and disrupted follicles. MSD treats mild cases with NSAIDs or aspirin, moderate to severe cases with glucocorticoids, and symptoms with a short course of a beta-blocker. Other source: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes say the hypothyroid phase is permanent in about 15% of cases; MSD gives no figure and says lasting hypothyroidism happens when follicle damage is extensive.

whyWrong.b: Lymphocytes with germinal centers and Hurthle cells describe Hashimoto thyroiditis, which is painless (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 71).
whyWrong.c: Tall, crowded cells with scalloped colloid describe Graves disease, which has high iodine uptake (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 76).
whyWrong.d: Dense fibrosis that spreads into nearby neck tissue is Riedel thyroiditis, a hard, painless gland (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 72).
whyWrong.e: Papillae with clear nuclei and psammoma bodies describe papillary thyroid cancer, which is not painful or febrile (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, pp. 79-80).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Subacute thyroiditis, p. 72
MSD Manual Professional: Subacute Thyroiditis

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a firm lump in the right side of his neck for 2 months. He has had watery diarrhea for several weeks. Ultrasound shows a 2.5-cm solid nodule in the right thyroid lobe. Fine-needle aspiration shows sheets of spindle-shaped and polygonal cells. Pink material between the cells turns apple-green under polarized light after Congo red staining.
questions.leadIn: Measurement of which of the following serum substances is most useful for diagnosing this tumor and following it after surgery?
questions.explanation: Answer: calcitonin (medullary thyroid carcinoma). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (p. 82) explain that this tumor comes from the parafollicular C cells, which make calcitonin. The cells are polygonal or spindle shaped and lie in amyloid made from calcitonin, which stains with Congo red. Activating RET mutations are strongly linked to the tumor, and most cases are sporadic, with the rest familial, as in MEN 2. MSD calls serum calcitonin, which is greatly raised, the best test, and says pheochromocytoma must be ruled out with plasma metanephrines and removed before thyroid surgery. Treatment is total thyroidectomy with removal of the central neck lymph nodes (MSD). Other source: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes give 80% sporadic and 20% familial; MSD says 25% are familial.

whyWrong.b: Thyroglobulin is the tumor marker for papillary and follicular cancers, which come from follicular cells, not C cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: PTH would be followed in parathyroid disease; in MEN 2A, parathyroid overgrowth can occur with this tumor, but PTH does not track the thyroid cancer (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: TSH reflects pituitary control of follicular cells and is not made by C cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker for liver cancer and yolk sac tumors (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Medullary carcinoma, p. 82
MSD Manual Professional: Thyroid Cancers

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician because his rings and shoes no longer fit. His wife says his face has changed over 5 years and that he snores loudly. His jaw juts forward, his teeth have spread apart, and his hands are large and thick. He has numbness in the thumb and first two fingers of both hands. Blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg, and fasting glucose is 128 mg/dL.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following findings would best confirm the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Growth hormone that stays high after oral glucose
Low IGF-1 with high growth hormone levels
Serum prolactin more than 5 times normal
Cortisol not suppressed by low-dose dexamethasone
Low TSH with low free T4

questions.explanation: Answer: growth hormone that does not fall after an oral glucose load (acromegaly). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 18-19) explain that acromegaly comes from too much growth hormone after the growth plates close, almost always from a pituitary macroadenoma. Bones thicken rather than lengthen, so the hands, feet, jaw, and brow enlarge, and soft tissue growth causes a big tongue, a deep voice, carpal tunnel syndrome, and heart enlargement. IGF-1 causes most of the damage, while growth hormone itself causes insulin resistance. IGF-1 is the screening test, and failure of growth hormone to fall after oral glucose confirms the diagnosis. MSD agrees that IGF-1 should be measured when acromegaly is suspected and that normal people suppress growth hormone to below 1 ng/mL within 2 hours of a 75-g glucose drink. MSD adds that sleep apnea occurs in 40% to 50% of patients, that surgery is first-line, and that somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide), the growth hormone receptor blocker pegvisomant, and cabergoline are drug options.

whyWrong.b: Low IGF-1 with high growth hormone is growth hormone resistance (Laron dwarfism), which causes short stature (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 20).
whyWrong.c: A prolactin level more than 5 times normal points to a prolactinoma (MSD Prolactinoma); prolactinomas cause galactorrhea and low sex hormones, not large hands and jaw.
whyWrong.d: Failure of cortisol to suppress with dexamethasone points to Cushing syndrome, which causes central obesity and thin skin, not bone overgrowth (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Low TSH with low T4 shows central hypothyroidism, which would cause tiredness and cold intolerance, not acral growth (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Acromegaly, pp. 18-19
MSD Manual Professional: Gigantism and Acromegaly

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has had no menstrual periods for 7 months and has a milky discharge from both nipples. A pregnancy test is negative. She takes no medications. Her visual fields are normal. Serum prolactin is 210 ng/mL (normal, under 25). MRI shows an 8-mm pituitary mass.
questions.leadIn: The most appropriate drug for this patient works by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Answer: stimulating dopamine receptors (a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (p. 21) explain that dopamine from the hypothalamus constantly holds back prolactin release, that prolactin suppresses GnRH and so stops ovulation, and that dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine shrink prolactinomas. MSD says prolactin is the hormone most often made in excess by pituitary tumors, that women typically have galactorrhea with missed or irregular periods, and that prolactinoma levels are usually more than 5 times normal. MSD calls cabergoline the treatment of choice because it is easier to tolerate, and advises stopping it once a pregnancy test is positive unless the tumor is invasive or presses up against the optic chiasm, when continuing it may be wiser. Dopamine acts on D2 receptors on the lactotroph cells (standard teaching). Other source: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes name bromocriptine; MSD prefers cabergoline.

whyWrong.b: Dopamine blockers, such as most antipsychotics, raise prolactin and can cause this picture (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 21).
whyWrong.c: Somatostatin analogs such as octreotide treat acromegaly (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 19), not prolactinoma.
whyWrong.d: Growth hormone receptor blockers (pegvisomant) treat acromegaly by lowering IGF-1 (MSD Gigantism and Acromegaly).
whyWrong.e: Estrogen receptor blockers such as tamoxifen are used in breast cancer and do not shrink prolactinomas (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Prolactin, p. 21
MSD Manual Professional: Prolactinoma

questions.topic: Posterior pituitary: central diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency)
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is admitted after a motorcycle crash with a skull base fracture. Two days later, he is passing about 7 L of urine a day and is very thirsty. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L, and serum glucose is normal. Urine osmolality is 110 mOsm/kg. After 6 hours without water, urine osmolality is 140 mOsm/kg. One hour after desmopressin is given, urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's polyuria?

options.text: Too little ADH from the posterior pituitary
Kidney tubules that do not respond to ADH
Drinking more water than the kidneys can excrete
Osmotic diuresis from glucose in the urine
Too much ADH released from the posterior pituitary

questions.explanation: Answer: too little ADH (central diabetes insipidus, now called arginine vasopressin deficiency). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 29-31) explain that central DI comes from damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary from stroke, tumors, trauma, low oxygen, or infiltration, causing large volumes of dilute urine and high sodium. In a water deprivation test, the urine stays dilute. Desmopressin then raises urine osmolality by more than 50% in central DI but barely changes it in nephrogenic DI. Here it rose from 140 to 480, more than tripling. Treatment is desmopressin. MSD lists skull fractures, pituitary or hypothalamic surgery, and tumors among causes, gives the same over-50% rise after vasopressin, and warns that too much desmopressin can cause water retention and low sodium. Recent change: MSD now titles this condition arginine vasopressin deficiency, with central diabetes insipidus in brackets; the kidney form is now arginine vasopressin resistance.

whyWrong.b: Kidneys that ignore ADH (nephrogenic DI) would show little change after desmopressin (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 31).
whyWrong.c: Primary polydipsia concentrates the urine during water deprivation and causes low, not high, sodium (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, pp. 30-31).
whyWrong.d: Glucose in the urine causes osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus, but his glucose is normal (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Too much ADH (SIADH) causes concentrated urine and low sodium (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, pp. 32-33).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Diabetes insipidus, pp. 29-31
MSD Manual Professional: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (Central Diabetes Insipidus)

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for 12 years. She comes to the physician because she urinates large amounts day and night and is always thirsty. Serum sodium is 143 mEq/L, and glucose is normal. During a water deprivation test, her urine stays dilute, and urine osmolality rises by only 8% after desmopressin. Her psychiatrist wants her to stay on lithium because it has kept her well.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to reduce this patient's urine output?
questions.explanation: Answer: amiloride. Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 29-31) list lithium as a cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, in which the collecting duct does not respond to ADH, so desmopressin barely changes urine osmolality. The same pages say treatment includes fixing the cause, thiazides, NSAIDs, and amiloride, which is used for lithium-induced disease because it blocks lithium from entering collecting duct cells through the sodium channel. MSD now calls this condition arginine vasopressin resistance (formerly nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), names lithium as the main drug cause, says urine osmolality rises only minimally after vasopressin, and lists a low-salt, low-protein diet, thiazides, indomethacin, and amiloride as ways to reduce urine output. Other source: MSD lists amiloride as an option but does not say it is specific to lithium; your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes do.

whyWrong.b: Desmopressin replaces ADH, which works in central DI; here the kidney cannot respond to it (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 31).
whyWrong.c: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that would increase urine output and does not help nephrogenic DI (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Demeclocycline blocks ADH action and itself causes nephrogenic DI; it is used for SIADH (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, pp. 30, 33).
whyWrong.e: Tolvaptan blocks V2 receptors and is used for SIADH (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 33); it would make water loss worse.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Diabetes insipidus, pp. 29-31; SIADH, p. 33
MSD Manual Professional: Arginine Vasopressin Resistance

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman taking an SSRI for depression is admitted with confusion. Serum sodium is 114 mEq/L, serum osmolality is 240 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 520 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium is 48 mEq/L. She has no edema and is not dehydrated. Thyroid and adrenal tests are normal. She receives hypertonic saline, and her serum sodium rises to 128 mEq/L in the first 24 hours. Three days later, she has slurred speech, trouble swallowing, and weakness in all four limbs.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this patient's new neurologic findings?

options.text: Myelin loss from overly fast sodium correction
Embolic stroke in the posterior circulation

questions.explanation: Answer: osmotic demyelination syndrome from correcting her sodium too fast. Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 32-33) describe SIADH as too much ADH, from causes that include small cell lung cancer, lung and brain diseases, and drugs such as SSRIs, carbamazepine, and cyclophosphamide. The result is low sodium with concentrated urine, urine sodium over 20 mEq/L, and no edema or dehydration. Severe symptoms are treated with hypertonic saline, but correction must be slow to avoid osmotic demyelination (formerly called central pontine myelinolysis). MSD lists the same drug and disease causes, requires normal thyroid and adrenal function for the diagnosis, and advises raising sodium by no more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours. Her sodium rose 14 mEq/L. Damage to the pons a few days later causes slurred speech, trouble swallowing, and weakness of all four limbs (standard teaching). MSD adds that oral tolvaptan should be used for less than 30 days because of liver toxicity. Other source: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes restrict fluid to 800-1,000 mL/day; MSD says restriction to 250-500 mL/day is usually needed.

whyWrong.b: Cerebral edema comes from low sodium that falls quickly or is not corrected; her sodium had risen when the new signs began (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: An embolic stroke could cause similar signs, but the timing right after a fast sodium rise points to demyelination (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, eye movement problems, and an unsteady gait, usually in people with alcohol use disorder or malnutrition (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, fever, sweating, and muscle jerks, not slurred speech with limb weakness (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), SIADH, pp. 32-33
MSD Manual Professional: Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH Secretion (SIADH)

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the physician after muscle cramps and tingling around her mouth. She is short for her age, has a round face, and has had learning difficulties. Her 4th and 5th knuckles are missing when she makes a fist, and firm calcium deposits are felt under the skin of her arms. Tapping in front of her ear makes her facial muscles twitch. Serum calcium is low, phosphate is high, and PTH is high.
questions.leadIn: This patient's condition is most likely caused by a mutation affecting which of the following?

options.text: Gs alpha protein coupled to the PTH receptor
Development of the third pharyngeal pouch

questions.explanation: Answer: the Gs alpha subunit (from the GNAS gene) that links the PTH receptor to adenylyl cyclase (pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 94-95) explain that an inactivating GNAS mutation inherited from the mother makes the kidney and bone resistant to PTH, so calcium is low, phosphate is high, and PTH is high. These children have Albright hereditary osteodystrophy: short 4th and 5th digits, short stature, a round face, calcium deposits under the skin, and developmental delay. When the same mutation comes from the father, the body features appear but blood tests are normal (pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism), because only the mother's copy works in the kidney. Twitching of the face when the facial nerve is tapped (Chvostek sign) shows low calcium. MSD agrees on target-organ resistance to PTH, the Gs alpha (GNAS1) defect, low calcium with high phosphate, and the imprinting pattern. Other source: MSD says the 1st, 4th, and 5th metacarpals are short; your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes name the 4th and 5th.

whyWrong.b: A defective calcium-sensing receptor causes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, with high, not low, calcium (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency causes vitamin D-dependent rickets, with low phosphate and bone deformities rather than short 4th and 5th digits (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Failed third pharyngeal pouch development (DiGeorge syndrome) causes low calcium with low PTH, not high PTH (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: AIRE mutations cause autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, with hypoparathyroidism (low PTH), candidiasis, and adrenal failure (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Hypocalcemia signs and pseudohypoparathyroidism, pp. 94-95
MSD Manual Professional: Hypocalcemia

questions.stem: A 34-year-old nurse is brought to the emergency department because she was found confused and sweaty at work. Serum glucose is 36 mg/dL, and her symptoms resolve with IV dextrose. She has had 3 similar episodes in 2 months. She does not have diabetes. During an episode, serum insulin is very high, C-peptide is very low, and proinsulin is low. A screen for sulfonylureas is negative.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypoglycemia?

options.text: Injection of insulin by the patient
Secret use of a sulfonylurea drug

questions.explanation: Answer: surreptitious (secret) insulin injection. Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 115-116, 118) name the two main causes of hypoglycemia with high insulin in a person without diabetes: an insulinoma or secret use of insulin or a sulfonylurea. C-peptide, proinsulin, and a sulfonylurea screen tell them apart. Insulinoma, the most common islet cell tumor, raises both insulin and C-peptide, because the beta cell releases them together, and it is linked to MEN 1. MSD explains that injected insulin carries no C-peptide or proinsulin, so these stay normal or low with secret insulin use, whereas in insulinoma C-peptide is at least 0.6 ng/mL and proinsulin is at least 5 pmol/L. MSD adds that insulinoma is diagnosed with a supervised fast of up to 72 hours and that 98% of patients have symptoms within 48 hours. Access to insulin through her work supports this answer (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: An insulinoma releases insulin with C-peptide, so both would be high (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 118).
whyWrong.c: Sulfonylureas make the patient's own beta cells release insulin (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 115), so C-peptide would be high (standard teaching), and the drug screen is negative.
whyWrong.d: Adrenal insufficiency can cause low glucose, but insulin would be low, not high (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Glucagon raises glucose; a glucagonoma causes high blood sugar and a migrating rash (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Hypoglycemia, pp. 115-116; insulinoma, p. 118
MSD Manual Professional: Insulinoma

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man comes to the physician because of burning upper abdominal pain and diarrhea for 6 months despite taking a proton pump inhibitor. Endoscopy shows several ulcers in the second part of the duodenum, and fasting serum gastrin is very high. Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL, and PTH is high. He has had low libido, and serum prolactin is high. His father had kidney stones and peptic ulcers.
questions.leadIn: A mutation in a gene encoding which of the following is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: menin (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1). Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (pp. 120-121) describe MEN 1 as autosomal dominant with tumors of the parathyroid, pituitary (often prolactin or GH), and pancreas, including gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), insulinoma, and VIPoma, caused by mutation of the MEN1 gene that makes menin, a tumor suppressor. MSD agrees and adds that hyperparathyroidism occurs in at least 95% of patients, with symptom-free high calcium as its most common form, that gastrinoma is the most common functioning pancreatic tumor and insulinoma the second, and that 25% to 90% of the pituitary tumors are prolactinomas. MSD advises offering genetic testing to first-degree relatives and treating the hyperparathyroidism with subtotal parathyroidectomy.

whyWrong.b: RET mutations cause MEN 2A and 2B, with medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma rather than gastrinoma and prolactinoma (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 121).
whyWrong.c: Von Hippel-Lindau mutations cause brain and retinal hemangioblastomas, kidney cancer, and pheochromocytoma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Neurofibromin mutations cause neurofibromatosis type 1, with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Calcium-sensing receptor defects cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, not ulcers or pituitary tumors (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), MEN 1, pp. 120-121
MSD Manual Professional: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia, Type 1 (MEN 1)

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease comes to the physician for a follow-up visit. He has taken metformin for 9 years. His estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) has fallen to 24 mL/min/1.73 m2. He is scheduled for a CT scan with iodinated contrast next week.
questions.leadIn: Continuing metformin in this patient most increases his risk of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: lactic acidosis. Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (p. 140) explain that metformin lowers glucose mainly by blocking gluconeogenesis in the liver, is first-line for type 2 diabetes, causes modest weight loss, and does not cause hypoglycemia. Its main side effects are stomach upset and lactic acidosis: the gut makes extra lactate, and the liver, with gluconeogenesis blocked, cannot clear it. Kidney failure raises this risk. MSD agrees that lactic acidosis is very rare but says metformin should not be used in people at risk of acidosis, such as those with significant kidney disease, and should be held for surgery, IV contrast, and serious illness. MSD also notes it can lower vitamin B12. Recent change: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes define kidney failure by serum creatinine (1.5 mg/dL in men or 1.4 mg/dL in women). The 2017 FDA label instead uses eGFR: metformin is contraindicated below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, should not be started at 30-45, and should be stopped at or before an iodinated contrast study in people with an eGFR of 30-60.

whyWrong.b: Metformin does not raise insulin, so it does not cause hypoglycemia on its own (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 140).
whyWrong.c: SGLT2 inhibitors, not metformin, can cause ketoacidosis, sometimes with near-normal glucose (MSD Medications for Diabetes Mellitus Treatment).
whyWrong.d: Fluid retention and worsening heart failure are side effects of thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 142).
whyWrong.e: Pancreatitis is a listed side effect of GLP-1 analogs (your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes, p. 143).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Metformin, p. 140; other diabetes drugs, pp. 142-143
MSD Manual Professional: Medications for Diabetes Mellitus Treatment
FDA label: Glucophage and Glucophage XR (metformin), 2017

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with untreated Graves disease is brought to the emergency department 1 day after an emergency appendectomy. She is agitated and confused. Temperature is 40.3°C (104.5°F), pulse is 162/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 148/62 mm Hg. She has had diarrhea since surgery. Free T4 is very high, and TSH is undetectable. Propranolol and IV hydrocortisone are started.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following should be given at least 1 hour before potassium iodide in this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: propylthiouracil (PTU), given before iodine. Why: your El-Husseiny endocrinology notes (p. 77) describe thyroid storm as a rare but serious worsening of poorly treated hyperthyroidism after stress such as infection, trauma, or surgery, with fever, agitation, delirium, diarrhea, and fast irregular heart rhythms, which can be fatal. Treatment uses 4 drugs: propranolol for symptoms and to slow T4-to-T3 conversion, PTU to block new hormone synthesis, iodine to block hormone release, and glucocorticoids to slow T4-to-T3 conversion. Iodine is given at least an hour after PTU so the gland does not use the iodine to make more hormone. MSD agrees, listing PTU 600 mg by mouth before iodine and then saturated potassium iodide every 6 hours, and says PTU is preferred in storm because high doses also block peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. MSD gives hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours or dexamethasone, and says propranolol lowers the heart rate within minutes when given IV.

whyWrong.b: Levothyroxine is thyroid hormone; giving it would make thyrotoxicosis worse (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Radioactive iodine destroys the gland over weeks to months, too slowly for storm, and is avoided right before or during it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Acetaminophen can be used for fever, but it does not need to come before iodine and does not stop hormone synthesis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia after certain anesthetics, which causes rigidity and high CO2, not a thyroid storm (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Endocrinology (Emily's file), Thyroid storm, p. 77
MSD Manual Professional: Hyperthyroidism

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man who worked outdoors as a farmer for 50 years comes to the physician because of several rough, scaly, pink patches on his forehead, nose, and the backs of his hands. They feel like sandpaper. He has fair skin and red hair. A biopsy of one patch shows atypical keratinocytes in the lower epidermis and retained nuclei in the stratum corneum, without invasion of the dermis.
questions.leadIn: If left untreated, these lesions are most likely to progress to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Why: your Osmosis dermatology notes (pp. 1-2) describe actinic keratoses as small, rough, scaly patches caused by repeated sun exposure. UVB damages keratinocytes and causes mutations such as in p53, leading to dysplastic cells, and the biopsy shows atypia with parakeratosis (nuclei kept in the stratum corneum). Risk factors are fair skin, older age, sun-exposed sites, immunosuppression, albinism, xeroderma pigmentosum, and HPV. The main complication is change into squamous cell carcinoma, with a quoted likelihood of 0.03% to 20%. Treatment options include topical 5-fluorouracil or imiquimod, cryotherapy, scraping, and photodynamic therapy. MSD says cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma can arise in an existing actinic keratosis and is linked to cumulative UV damage.

whyWrong.b: Basal cell carcinoma is sun-related but arises without a scaly precursor lesion like this one (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Melanoma comes from melanocytes, not from keratinocyte atypia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Seborrheic keratosis is a benign, stuck-on, waxy growth, not the outcome of actinic damage (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare neuroendocrine skin cancer that does not arise from actinic keratoses (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Dermatology (Emily's file), Actinic keratosis, pp. 1-2
MSD Manual Professional: Squamous Cell Carcinoma

questions.topic: Skin cancer: cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
questions.stem: A 61-year-old man who had a kidney transplant 12 years ago and takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate comes to the physician because of a growing, crusted sore on his lower lip for 3 months. It bleeds easily. He smoked for 30 years. Examination shows a firm, 1.5-cm ulcerated nodule on the lower lip. A biopsy shows nests of atypical keratinocytes invading the dermis.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is most likely to be seen within the tumor nests?

options.text: Palisading basal cells with peripheral clefts
Small blue cells with neuroendocrine granules

questions.explanation: Answer: keratin pearls (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma). Why: your Osmosis dermatology notes (pp. 29-31) describe squamous cell carcinoma as the second most common skin cancer, arising from keratinocytes that resist cell death and divide often. Causes and risk factors include UV light, HPV, actinic keratosis, immunosuppression, fair skin, and tobacco, which raises the risk of lip and mouth cancers. Well-differentiated tumors are made of polygonal pink cells that form keratin pearls. MSD defines it as a cancer of epidermal keratinocytes that invades the dermis, lists chronic immunosuppression as a risk factor, and says it is more likely to spread than basal cell carcinoma. MSD treats low-risk lesions with excision with 4- to 6-mm margins and prefers Mohs surgery for high-risk lesions. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer in organ transplant recipients (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Palisading basal cells with clefts around the nests describe basal cell carcinoma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Atypical melanocytes along the junction describe melanoma, not keratinocyte nests (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Small blue cells with neuroendocrine granules describe Merkel cell carcinoma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Spindle cells forming slit-like vessels describe Kaposi sarcoma, which is also more common after transplant but is a vascular tumor caused by HHV-8 (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Dermatology (Emily's file), Squamous cell carcinoma, pp. 29-31
MSD Manual Professional: Squamous Cell Carcinoma

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of an itchy rash that has come and gone since infancy. When he was a baby, it was on his cheeks and the outer parts of his arms and legs. Now he has thick, dry, scratched plaques in the creases of both elbows and behind both knees. He has asthma and seasonal allergies, and his mother has hay fever. Serum IgE is high.
questions.leadIn: A loss-of-function mutation in the gene for which of the following proteins most likely contributes to this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: filaggrin, a protein needed for the skin barrier (atopic dermatitis). Why: your Osmosis dermatology notes (pp. 10-11) describe an itchy, relapsing rash in people with atopy and high IgE. A broken skin barrier, as from filaggrin mutations, lets antigens in, and Th2 cells release IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, which drive IgE and recruit mast cells and eosinophils. In children under 2, the rash is on the cheeks and extensor surfaces. In older children it is on the flexures, with thick, lichenified plaques. Complications include Staphylococcus aureus infection and eczema herpeticum. MSD calls loss-of-function filaggrin mutations a major predisposing factor in many patients, describes the same age pattern, and names atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma as the atopic triad. MSD says topical corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment, with calcineurin inhibitors, dupilumab (which blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling), and oral JAK inhibitors for harder cases.

whyWrong.b: Desmoglein 3 is the target of antibodies in pemphigus vulgaris, which causes fragile blisters and mouth sores (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Type VII collagen defects cause dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, with blisters and scarring from minor friction (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Bullous pemphigoid antigens are targets of antibodies in bullous pemphigoid, a disease of older adults with tense blisters (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Tyrosinase defects cause oculocutaneous albinism, with pale skin and hair, not itchy rashes (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Dermatology (Emily's file), Atopic dermatitis, pp. 10-11
MSD Manual Professional: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the physician because of very itchy bumps on his wrists and shins for 2 months. Examination shows flat-topped, shiny, purple, many-sided papules. Some are in a line along a scratch. The inside of both cheeks shows white, lace-like lines. He used injection drugs 20 years ago.
questions.leadIn: A skin biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Bandlike lymphocytes at the basal layer
Neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum
