questions.explanation: Answer: a dense band of lymphocytes along the dermal-epidermal junction (lichen planus). Why: your Osmosis dermatology notes (pp. 32-33) describe lichen planus with the 6 Ps (planar, purple, polygonal, pruritic papules and plaques), lace-like Wickham striae, the Koebner phenomenon (new lesions at sites of injury), and spread on the flexor wrists, elbows, ankles, and shins. Biopsy shows interface dermatitis, with lymphocytes along the junction, a sawtooth pattern, and dying basal cells (Civatte bodies). CD8 T cells react to altered antigens in the basal layer. MSD calls it a T-cell-mediated autoimmune attack on basal keratinocytes, describes Wickham striae as a hallmark of the oral form, and links it to hepatitis B and C and to drugs such as beta-blockers, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and thiazides. His past injection drug use makes hepatitis C testing reasonable (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum (Munro microabscesses) are typical of psoriasis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A subepidermal blister with eosinophils describes bullous pemphigoid (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Acantholysis above the basal layer describes pemphigus vulgaris (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Noncaseating granulomas describe sarcoidosis, which can cause skin papules but not Wickham striae (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Dermatology (Emily's file), Lichen planus, pp. 32-33
MSD Manual Professional: Lichen Planus

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of white patches on the backs of her hands and around her mouth that have grown over 1 year. The patches have sharp edges and appear on both sides of the body. Under a Wood lamp, they glow bright white. She takes levothyroxine for Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of a white patch is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Absence of melanocytes in the basal layer
Normal melanocytes that cannot make tyrosinase
Fungal hyphae in the stratum corneum
Lymphocytes around dermal blood vessels only

questions.explanation: Answer: no melanocytes in the affected skin (vitiligo). Why: your Osmosis dermatology notes (p. 41) describe vitiligo as loss of pigment because melanocytes are destroyed, likely by an autoimmune process, leaving sharply bordered white patches. The non-segmental type is symmetric and keeps spreading, and the segmental type is one-sided and stable. Risk factors include a personal or family history of Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, lupus, celiac disease, and Addison disease. Treatment includes topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and phototherapy. MSD says melanocytes are missing in affected areas, that up to 30% of patients have other autoantibodies, most strongly Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis, and that a Wood lamp makes the chalk-white patches easier to see. MSD prefers narrowband UVB for widespread disease. Recent change: MSD lists a topical JAK inhibitor, ruxolitinib cream, as a treatment option, which your Osmosis dermatology notes do not mention.

whyWrong.b: Normal melanocytes that lack working tyrosinase describe albinism, which is present from birth and affects all of the skin (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Fungal hyphae point to tinea versicolor, which causes scaly, lighter patches, often on the trunk (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Extra melanin in basal cells causes darker, not white, patches, as in melasma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A light perivascular infiltrate alone does not explain total pigment loss with sharp borders (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Dermatology (Emily's file), Vitiligo, p. 41
MSD Manual Professional: Vitiligo

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of sores around his nose and mouth for 1 week. They began as small blisters that broke open and now have honey-colored crusts. Several children at his daycare have similar sores. A culture grows beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive gram-positive cocci in chains.
questions.leadIn: This patient is at greatest risk of developing which of the following complications in the next few weeks?
questions.explanation: Answer: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Why: your Osmosis dermatology notes (p. 50) describe impetigo as a very contagious infection of the upper epidermis in children, caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. In the common non-bullous form, a red bump becomes a blister that breaks and forms a yellow crust. Risk factors include warm, humid weather, eczema, and daycare. Complications are cellulitis and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. MSD describes honey-colored crusts, says staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cause the bullous form, and warns that children aged 2 to 4 years can develop glomerulonephritis after skin infection with nephritogenic group A strep, which antibiotics are unlikely to prevent. MSD treats localized impetigo with a topical antibiotic such as mupirocin for 5 to 7 days. Bacitracin sensitivity identifies group A strep (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Rheumatic fever follows group A strep throat infection, not skin infection (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Scalded skin syndrome comes from S. aureus exfoliative toxins, but this culture grew strep (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Toxic shock syndrome causes fever, low blood pressure, and a sunburn-like rash; it is not the expected course of simple impetigo (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Erythema nodosum can follow strep throat but is not the main risk after impetigo (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Dermatology (Emily's file), Impetigo, p. 50
MSD Manual Professional: Impetigo and Ecthyma

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with obesity comes to the physician because of pain in her right knee and in several finger joints for 2 years. The pain is worse at the end of the day and after walking, and morning stiffness lasts about 15 minutes. There are hard, bony swellings at several distal interphalangeal joints. The knee has crepitus but is not warm. X-rays show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis. Synovial fluid from the knee has 600 leukocytes/mm3.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the primary process underlying this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: wear-and-tear breakdown of joint cartilage (osteoarthritis). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 134-135) call osteoarthritis the most common arthritis and describe it as wear and tear of cartilage. Risk factors include age, female sex, obesity, and joint injury. It is often asymmetric, and the bony nodes at the DIP joints (Heberden nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard nodes) are osteophytes. Bone under worn cartilage becomes polished (eburnation), with subchondral sclerosis and cysts, and joint fluid has fewer than 2000 white cells per microliter. MSD agrees that morning stiffness usually lasts less than 30 minutes, describes Heberden and Bouchard nodes, and gives a synovial fluid white count of 2000/µL or less. MSD favors topical NSAIDs first for hand and knee osteoarthritis.

whyWrong.b: A pannus of inflamed synovium is rheumatoid arthritis, which causes morning stiffness over 1 hour and spares the DIP joints (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 136-137).
whyWrong.c: Urate crystals cause gout, with sudden, red, very painful attacks, often of the big toe (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 144).
whyWrong.d: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals cause pseudogout, with acute attacks, often of the knee, and calcium lines in cartilage on X-ray (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 145-146).
whyWrong.e: HLA-B27 enthesitis fits ankylosing spondylitis, which affects the spine and sacroiliac joints of young men (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 141).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Osteoarthritis, pp. 134-135
MSD Manual Professional: Osteoarthritis (OA)

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman who smokes comes to the physician because of pain and swelling in both hands and wrists for 4 months. Each morning her hands are stiff for about 2 hours. Both wrists and the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints are swollen and tender, and the distal interphalangeal joints are normal. Rheumatoid factor is negative.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following blood tests is most specific for this patient's most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies, for rheumatoid arthritis. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 136-137) list female sex, smoking, and HLA-DR4 as risk factors. The disease affects the MCP, PIP, and wrist joints on both sides, spares the DIP joints, and causes morning stiffness of more than 1 hour. The same pages explain that T cells react to citrullinated peptides, that rheumatoid factor is an IgM antibody against the Fc part of IgG, and that anti-CCP is more specific than rheumatoid factor. They also advise a plain neck X-ray to look for a slipped C1-C2 joint before a patient with rheumatoid arthritis is intubated or put under anesthesia (p. 137). MSD gives anti-CCP 'high specificity (90%) and sensitivity (approximately 77 to 86%),' says rheumatoid factors are present in approximately 70% of patients, names the wrists and the second and third MCP joints as most commonly involved, and says stiffness typically lasts more than 60 minutes. So a negative rheumatoid factor does not rule out the disease.

whyWrong.b: Antinuclear antibodies are sensitive for lupus but are not specific for any one disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The sedimentation rate shows inflammation in general but does not point to any one disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are specific for lupus, not rheumatoid arthritis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Uric acid relates to gout, which starts with sudden attacks, usually in one joint (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 144).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Rheumatoid arthritis, pp. 136-137
MSD Manual Professional: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department at 3 AM because of severe pain in his left big toe that woke him from sleep. The evening before, he drank several beers with a large dinner. He takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, hot, swollen, and too tender to touch. Fluid is drawn from the joint.
questions.leadIn: Polarized light microscopy of the fluid is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent (gout). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 144-145) explain that gout comes from monosodium urate crystals. About 90% of cases come from poor kidney excretion of uric acid, and thiazide and loop diuretics raise urate. Attacks often strike the big toe (podagra) after alcohol or a large meal. Under polarized light the crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent, looking yellow when lined up with the compensator's slow ray. Acute attacks are treated with NSAIDs such as indomethacin, glucocorticoids, or colchicine, and urate is lowered long term with allopurinol or febuxostat. MSD agrees that the crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent, says decreased excretion is by far the most common cause of high urate, and sets a serum urate goal below 6 mg/dL.

whyWrong.b: Rhomboid, weakly positive crystals are calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout), which most often affects the knee of older adults (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 145-146).
whyWrong.c: Envelope-shaped calcium oxalate crystals appear in urine, for example after ethylene glycol poisoning, not in gouty joints (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Hexagonal cystine crystals are found in urine in cystinuria (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Septic arthritis can look similar, but a night attack after alcohol in a man on a thiazide fits gout; the fluid should still be cultured (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Gout, pp. 144-145
MSD Manual Professional: Gout

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a swollen, painful right knee for 2 days. He has type 2 diabetes, bronze-colored skin, and an enlarged liver, and his serum ferritin and transferrin saturation are both very high. The knee is warm and swollen. An X-ray shows thin lines of calcium within the knee cartilage. Fluid from the joint shows rhomboid crystals.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following substances is most likely deposited in this patient's joint?
questions.explanation: Answer: calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 145-146) link calcium pyrophosphate deposition to hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and joint injury, mostly after age 50, with the knee affected in more than half of cases. X-rays show calcium in the cartilage (chondrocalcinosis), and the crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent (blue when lined up with the compensator's slow ray). Treatment uses NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids, and colchicine can also prevent attacks. This man's bronze skin, diabetes, and iron overload point to hemochromatosis. MSD also lists hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and low magnesium as linked conditions and describes rhomboid or rod-shaped crystals. Other source: MSD says the crystals are 'not birefringent, or are weakly positively birefringent,' so a weak or absent signal does not rule out the diagnosis.

whyWrong.b: Urate crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent, and gout most often starts in the big toe (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 144-145).
whyWrong.c: Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals are too small to see as separate crystals on routine light microscopy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Cholesterol crystals appear in long-standing effusions, not with chondrocalcinosis and hemochromatosis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Homogentisic acid darkens cartilage in alkaptonuria and does not form rhomboid crystals (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Pseudogout, pp. 145-146
MSD Manual Professional: Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of low back pain and stiffness for 1 year. The stiffness is worst in the morning, lasts about 1 hour, and gets better with exercise but not with rest. He also has pain at the back of both heels. Chest expansion is reduced. X-rays show erosions and fusion of both sacroiliac joints.
questions.leadIn: This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
questions.explanation: Answer: anterior uveitis. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 141-142) describe ankylosing spondylitis as inflammation of the sacroiliac joints and spine in young men that can fuse the vertebrae into a 'bamboo spine.' Stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes and improves with exercise, inflammation where tendons attach to bone (enthesitis) causes heel pain, and chest expansion falls. The notes report anterior uveitis in 20-30% of these patients, with eye pain, blurred vision, and light sensitivity, and they also list apical lung fibrosis and aortitis with aortic regurgitation. MSD reports HLA-B27 in 90% of White patients, says the disease is 3 times more common in men, with onset usually between ages 20 and 40, and says recurrent anterior uveitis is common. MSD starts treatment with NSAIDs and moves to TNF or IL-17 inhibitors when needed.

whyWrong.b: Mitral stenosis follows rheumatic fever; ankylosing spondylitis affects the aortic valve instead (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 142).
whyWrong.c: Optic neuritis suggests multiple sclerosis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Retinal detachment is not a typical complication of ankylosing spondylitis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Bilateral hilar lymph nodes point to sarcoidosis (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Ankylosing spondylitis, pp. 141-142
MSD Manual Professional: Ankylosing Spondylitis

questions.stem: A newborn boy has short arms and legs, a large head with a prominent forehead, and a trunk of normal length. His parents are of average height, and there is no family history of short stature. The father is 52 years old.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this child's condition?

options.text: Mutation in a type I collagen gene

questions.explanation: Answer: an activating (gain-of-function) mutation in FGFR3. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 116-117) explain that an activating FGFR3 mutation slows the cartilage growth plates, so bones that grow by endochondral ossification (long bones) stay short, while bones made by membranous ossification (skull) grow normally. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and intelligence, life span, and fertility are normal. Most cases are new mutations linked to older fathers (standard teaching). MSD calls achondroplasia the most common short-limbed dwarfism and confirms autosomal dominant FGFR3 mutations. Recent change: MSD says vosoritide, a C-type natriuretic peptide analog, improves growth in children with achondroplasia, while growth hormone is generally not effective.

whyWrong.b: FGFR3 normally slows bone growth; the disease comes from too much signaling, not too little (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 116).
whyWrong.c: Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, with long limbs (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Type I collagen mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with fragile bones (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 46).
whyWrong.e: Growth hormone deficiency causes proportionate short stature, usually noticed after infancy (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Achondroplasia, pp. 116-117
MSD Manual Professional: Osteochondrodysplasias

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he does not follow objects with his eyes or turn toward sounds. He has had two fractures from minor falls. His liver and spleen are enlarged. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, leukocyte count is 3,200/mm3, and platelet count is 60,000/mm3. X-rays show very dense bones throughout the skeleton, with a 'bone within a bone' look in the vertebrae.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following processes is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: bone resorption by osteoclasts (osteopetrosis). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 119-120) explain that osteopetrosis comes from osteoclasts that cannot resorb bone. Bone becomes dense but brittle, so it breaks. Thick bone crowds out the marrow, causing low blood counts and blood cell production outside the marrow (enlarged liver and spleen), and it narrows openings in the skull, compressing the nerves for vision and hearing and sometimes causing hydrocephalus. One form comes from carbonic anhydrase II deficiency, which also causes renal tubular acidosis. X-rays show a bone-in-bone look, and bone marrow transplant can cure it, since osteoclasts come from monocytes. MSD describes the severe infant form with palsies of cranial nerves II, III, and VII, an enlarged liver and spleen, and pancytopenia, and lists stem cell transplantation and interferon gamma as treatments.

whyWrong.b: Poor osteoblast function would make bones thin, not dense (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with thin, fragile bones and blue sclerae (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 46).
whyWrong.d: Poor mineralization is rickets, which softens and bows bones rather than making them dense (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 120-121).
whyWrong.e: Growth plate signaling defects such as FGFR3 mutations cause short limbs, not dense bones and low blood counts (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 116-117).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Osteopetrosis, pp. 119-120
MSD Manual Professional: Osteosclerosis (Osteopetrosis)

questions.stem: A 16-month-old girl is brought to the physician because her legs have become bowed since she started walking. She has been fed only breast milk without supplements and rarely goes outside. Exam shows bowed legs, widened wrists, and a row of bumps where her ribs meet the rib cartilage. Serum calcium is low-normal, phosphate is low, alkaline phosphatase is high, and parathyroid hormone is high.
questions.leadIn: A bone biopsy would most likely show which of the following?

options.text: Thin trabeculae of normally mineralized bone

questions.explanation: Answer: too much osteoid that is not mineralized (rickets). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 120-121) define rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults as defective mineralization of osteoid, most often from lack of vitamin D, which lowers calcium and phosphate. Bone biopsy shows an excess of unmineralized osteoid. Children develop a pigeon chest and a rachitic rosary (bumps where the ribs meet cartilage). MSD describes craniotabes, a rachitic rosary, and bowed legs, with low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, and normal or high PTH, and diagnoses it by measuring 25-hydroxyvitamin D. High PTH keeps calcium near normal but makes the kidneys waste phosphate, and breast milk is low in vitamin D (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Thin but normally mineralized trabeculae describe osteoporosis, where calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase are normal (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A mosaic pattern of lamellar bone is Paget disease of bone, a disease of older adults (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Dense bone with retained cartilage fits osteopetrosis, from defective osteoclasts (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 119-120).
whyWrong.e: Fibrous tissue with woven bone fits fibrous dysplasia (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Rickets and osteomalacia, pp. 120-121
MSD Manual Professional: Vitamin D Deficiency and Dependency

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of pain and swelling just above her right knee for 4 months. An X-ray shows a large lytic lesion with a 'soap-bubble' look in the end (epiphysis) of the distal femur, reaching up to the joint surface. There is no sclerotic rim.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of the lesion is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Osteoclast-like giant cells among mononuclear cells
Malignant spindle cells that lay down osteoid directly
Sheets of small, round, blue cells
A cartilage cap over a bony stalk
A small nidus of woven bone ringed by sclerosis

questions.explanation: Answer: osteoclast-like giant cells mixed with mononuclear cells (giant cell tumor). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 130) place giant cell tumor in young adults, in the epiphysis of the distal femur or proximal tibia, with a soap-bubble look on X-ray. The tumor's mononuclear cells make RANKL, which draws in the osteoclast-like giant cells. The tumor is locally aggressive and may recur. MSD places it in people in their 20s and 30s, describes a lytic lesion in the epiphysis with no sclerotic rim, notes spread to the lungs in 4 to 7%, and says these tumors are 'notorious for their tendency to recur.' MSD treats it with curettage and lists denosumab, a RANKL inhibitor, for tumors that cannot be removed.

whyWrong.b: Osteoid made by malignant cells defines osteosarcoma, usually in the metaphysis of teenagers (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Small round blue cells fit Ewing sarcoma, often in the diaphysis of children (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: A cartilage-capped bony stalk is an osteochondroma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A small nidus with surrounding sclerosis is an osteoid osteoma, which causes night pain relieved by NSAIDs (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Giant cell tumor, p. 130
MSD Manual Professional: Benign Bone Tumors and Cysts

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a fracture of his left femur after tripping while walking. He has had 3 earlier fractures from minor falls, and child protective services was contacted after one of them. His sclerae are blue. His mother had several fractures as a child and now has hearing loss.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: type I collagen (osteogenesis imperfecta). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 46) explain that osteogenesis imperfecta usually comes from autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 that leave less normal type I collagen. Patients have many fractures from small injuries, which can be mistaken for child abuse, plus blue sclerae, weak teeth (dentinogenesis imperfecta), and hearing loss, and bisphosphonates help. MSD says COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations cause more than 85% of cases, that inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, and that hearing loss affects up to 70% of patients. Thin sclerae let the dark layer underneath show through, which makes them look blue (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Type III collagen defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with fragile vessels and organs (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 47).
whyWrong.c: Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome, with kidney disease, hearing loss, and eye problems, not fractures (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome, with tall stature and lens dislocation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Low lysyl oxidase activity from copper deficiency is Menkes disease, with kinky hair and low muscle tone (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 48).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Osteogenesis imperfecta, p. 46
MSD Manual Professional: Osteogenesis Imperfecta

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of sudden, severe abdominal pain. A CT scan shows a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm. She has bruised easily all her life, and her skin is thin, with veins easily seen through it. Her small joints are only mildly loose. Her father died suddenly at age 35 of a ruptured aorta.
questions.leadIn: A mutation affecting which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: type III collagen (vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 47) describe Ehlers-Danlos syndromes as collagen disorders with stretchy skin, easy bruising, loose joints, and aneurysms. The hypermobile type is the most common, the classical type comes from type V collagen, and the vascular type comes from type III collagen. MSD says the vascular type is caused by COL3A1 mutations and can lead to rupture of arteries, bowel, or uterus. Type III collagen is plentiful in blood vessels and hollow organs, which explains where they tear (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with fractures and blue sclerae (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 46).
whyWrong.c: Type IV collagen forms basement membranes; its defects cause Alport syndrome (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome, with tall stature and lens dislocation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Low lysyl oxidase activity from copper deficiency is Menkes disease, which shows up in infant boys (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 48).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, p. 47
MSD Manual Professional: Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of poor feeding, floppiness, and seizures. He was well at birth. His scalp hair is sparse, brittle, and kinky, and he is small for his age. Imaging shows long, twisted arteries in the brain. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low.
questions.leadIn: Reduced activity of which of the following enzymes best explains his abnormal blood vessels?
questions.explanation: Answer: lysyl oxidase (Menkes disease). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 48) describe Menkes disease as an X-linked disorder of the ATP7A copper transporter, so copper is poorly absorbed from the gut. Lysyl oxidase needs copper to cross-link collagen, so its activity drops and connective tissue weakens. Babies have kinky hair, poor growth, and low muscle tone. MSD describes affected males with sparse, steely or kinky hair, intellectual disability, and arterial rupture, with low serum copper and ceruloplasmin. MSD treats it with copper histidine injections and notes that most children die by age 10.

whyWrong.b: Prolyl hydroxylase needs vitamin C; its failure causes scurvy, with bleeding gums (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 243).
whyWrong.c: Procollagen peptidase deficiency causes a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 47).
whyWrong.d: Tyrosinase uses copper to make pigment, but low pigment does not explain fragile arteries (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Homogentisate dioxygenase deficiency causes alkaptonuria, with dark urine and dark cartilage (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Menkes disease, p. 48
MSD Manual Professional: Copper Deficiency

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man who lives alone is brought to the physician by his daughter because of easy bruising and bleeding gums for 2 months. He eats mostly tea, toast, and canned meat. His gums are swollen, purple, and bleed when touched. There are small bleeds around the hair follicles on his legs, and the hairs are coiled. A cut on his hand from a month ago has not healed.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following steps in collagen synthesis is most likely impaired?
questions.explanation: Answer: hydroxylation of proline and lysine (scurvy). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 243) explain that vitamin C is needed for the enzymes that add hydroxyl groups to proline and lysine in collagen. Without it, collagen is weak, causing gum disease, easy bruising, small skin bleeds, bleeding around hair follicles, bleeding into joints, corkscrew hairs, and poor wound healing. MSD notes that 'follicular hyperkeratosis, coiled hair, and perifollicular hemorrhages may develop,' describes gums that are swollen, purple, spongy, and friable, and says wounds heal poorly. MSD usually makes the diagnosis clinically and treats adults with 500 to 1000 mg of vitamin C by mouth daily for 1 to 2 weeks.

whyWrong.b: Glycosylation of hydroxylysine does not need vitamin C (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Failure to cut the procollagen end peptides causes a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 47).
whyWrong.d: Cross-linking by lysyl oxidase needs copper and fails in Menkes disease (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 48).
whyWrong.e: Making the collagen chains on ribosomes does not depend on vitamin C (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Vitamin C, p. 243
MSD Manual Professional: Vitamin C Deficiency

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a burning apartment building. He is confused and then has a seizure. Pulse oximetry reads 97% on supplemental oxygen. Arterial blood gas shows a pH of 7.18 with a high anion gap, and serum lactate is 14 mmol/L. Central venous blood has an unusually high oxygen content.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?
questions.explanation: Answer: hydroxocobalamin. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 155) explain that cyanide binds cytochrome a/a3 (complex IV of the electron transport chain) and stops aerobic respiration, and they add that cells then switch to anaerobic metabolism, causing severe lactic acidosis (p. 156). Antidotes include nitrites, which turn hemoglobin into methemoglobin, hydroxocobalamin, and sodium thiosulfate. MSD agrees that cyanide enters mitochondria and inactivates cytochrome oxidase, causing lactic acidosis and higher-than-usual venous oxygen content, because the tissues cannot extract oxygen from the blood. MSD notes that hydroxocobalamin is generally considered as effective as nitrite plus thiosulfate and that, unlike nitrites, it does not decrease oxygen-carrying capacity, which matters when carbon monoxide poisoning is also present. Fire victims can breathe in both gases (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Nitrites work by making methemoglobin, which lowers oxygen-carrying capacity in a patient who may also have carbon monoxide poisoning (MSD).
whyWrong.c: Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia; it does not remove cyanide (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Atropine and pralidoxime treat organophosphate poisoning (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Fomepizole treats methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Electron transport chain poisons, pp. 155-156
MSD Manual Professional: Systemic Asphyxiant Chemical Warfare Agents

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a lump in her left breast that she noticed 2 months ago. It is not painful and does not change with her menstrual cycle. Exam shows a 2-cm, smooth, round, rubbery mass that moves easily under the fingers. There is no skin change, nipple discharge, or enlarged axillary lymph node.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: fibroadenoma. Why: your Elnemr breast pathology notes (p. 5) describe fibroadenoma as a benign tumor of young women, a well-defined, rubbery mass that slips under the fingers (a 'breast mouse'). Under the microscope it is biphasic, with ducts and fibrous stroma; the stroma either surrounds the ducts (pericanalicular) or squeezes them into slits (intracanalicular). Cancer arising in a fibroadenoma is extremely rare. MSD describes fibroadenomas as smooth, rounded, mobile, painless masses in women of reproductive age, notes that simple fibroadenomas do not appear to raise breast cancer risk, and removes them if they grow or cause symptoms.

whyWrong.b: Phyllodes tumors are usually large, with very cellular, leaf-like stroma (your Elnemr breast pathology notes, p. 6).
whyWrong.c: Intraductal papillomas sit in the large ducts and usually cause nipple discharge (your Elnemr breast pathology notes, p. 6).
whyWrong.d: Invasive cancer usually forms a hard, fixed mass in older women (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Fibrocystic change causes lumpy, tender breasts that change with the menstrual cycle (standard teaching).

sources.title: Dr. Elnemr Reproductive Pathology: Breast (Emily's file), Fibroadenoma, p. 5
MSD Manual Professional: Breast Masses (Breast Lumps)

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a mass in her right breast that has grown quickly over 3 months. Exam shows a 7-cm, firm, mobile mass with stretched, shiny skin over it. Core biopsy shows ducts lined by epithelium and a very cellular stroma that overgrows them and pushes into them to form leaf-like projections. The stromal cells show marked atypia and many mitoses, and the tumor edge infiltrates the surrounding fat.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Wide local excision with clear margins
Observation with repeat ultrasound in 6 months
Shelling the mass out along its edge

questions.explanation: Answer: wide excision with clear margins. Why: your Elnemr breast pathology notes (p. 6) describe phyllodes tumor as a large biphasic tumor in which the stroma is very cellular and grows into leaf-like projections. Most are benign but tend to come back after removal, and they are graded benign, borderline, or malignant by cell atypia, mitoses, necrosis, and the tumor's border. Marked atypia, many mitoses, stromal overgrowth, and an infiltrative edge make this tumor malignant. MSD groups phyllodes tumors with breast cancers of the supporting stroma and notes that they do not express hormone receptors. For malignant phyllodes tumors, MSD recommends wide local excision to negative margins or mastectomy and says lymph node surgery is not indicated. Shelling out the mass leaves tumor behind and invites recurrence (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Watching a fast-growing 7-cm mass only delays treatment (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: MSD says lymph node surgery is not indicated for malignant phyllodes tumors (MSD Breast Cancer).
whyWrong.d: MSD notes that phyllodes tumors do not express hormone receptors, so tamoxifen would not help (MSD Breast Cancer).
whyWrong.e: Shelling out the tumor leaves tumor at the edge, and these tumors tend to recur (your Elnemr breast pathology notes, p. 6).

sources.title: Dr. Elnemr Reproductive Pathology: Breast (Emily's file), Phyllodes tumor, p. 6
MSD Manual Professional: Breast Cancer

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of bloody discharge from her right nipple for 3 weeks. The discharge comes from a single duct. No mass is felt in either breast, and there are no skin changes or enlarged lymph nodes. Mammography is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: intraductal papilloma. Why: your Elnemr breast pathology notes (p. 6) describe intraductal papilloma as a small tumor (under 3 cm) in the large milk ducts beneath the nipple that causes serous or bloody nipple discharge. It has branching fibrovascular cores covered by epithelial cells with an outer layer of myoepithelial cells. A papilloma without atypia carries only a slight cancer risk, while multiple papillomas with atypia carry a significant risk. MSD calls intraductal papilloma 'the most common cause of a bloody nipple discharge without a breast mass' and notes that cancer causes fewer than 15% of nipple discharge cases.

whyWrong.b: Duct ectasia usually causes thick, sticky discharge from several ducts in older women (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A prolactinoma causes milky discharge from both breasts, often with missed periods (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Paget disease of the nipple causes a scaly, eczema-like rash of the nipple (your Elnemr breast pathology notes, p. 11).
whyWrong.e: Fat necrosis usually forms a firm mass after an injury, not bloody discharge (standard teaching).

sources.title: Dr. Elnemr Reproductive Pathology: Breast (Emily's file), Duct papilloma, p. 6
MSD Manual Professional: Nipple Discharge

questions.topic: Breast: Paget disease of the nipple
questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an itchy, scaly, red patch on her left nipple and areola for 3 months. It has not improved with a steroid cream. No breast mass is felt. A biopsy of the nipple skin shows large cells with plenty of pale, clear cytoplasm scattered within the epidermis.
questions.leadIn: This finding most strongly suggests which of the following?

options.text: Allergic contact dermatitis of the nipple
Melanoma in situ of the areola
Psoriasis of the nipple and areola

questions.explanation: Answer: an underlying ductal carcinoma. Why: your Elnemr breast pathology notes (p. 11) explain that Paget disease of the breast is an eczema-like rash of the nipple caused by Paget cells in the epidermis, on top of a ductal carcinoma that may be in situ or invasive. Paget cells are large, with clear cytoplasm, and the outlook depends on the underlying carcinoma. MSD describes a one-sided eczematous to psoriasiform plaque of the nipple and areola, says about 90% of cases are linked to ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive cancer, diagnoses it by biopsy, and bases treatment on the associated cancer plus removal of the nipple and areola. A one-sided nipple rash that does not heal with steroid cream needs a biopsy (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Contact dermatitis is usually on both sides, gets better with steroid cream, and has no Paget cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Melanoma in situ is made of atypical melanocytes, which usually make pigment (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ shows atypical keratinocytes through the full thickness of the epidermis, not scattered large clear cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Psoriasis is usually on both sides, with plaques elsewhere, and shows no Paget cells (standard teaching).

sources.title: Dr. Elnemr Reproductive Pathology: Breast (Emily's file), Paget disease of the breast, p. 11
MSD Manual Professional: Paget Disease of the Nipple

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man comes to the physician because of tender swelling under both nipples for 3 months. He has heart failure and takes furosemide, lisinopril, metoprolol, spironolactone, and isosorbide dinitrate. Exam shows a tender, rubbery disc of tissue under each areola. His testes are normal in size, and liver tests are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of his medications is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Answer: spironolactone. Why: your Elnemr breast pathology notes (p. 14) explain that gynecomastia is normal (physiologic) in newborns, at puberty, and in older men, and becomes pathologic with too much estrogen (liver failure, estrogen treatment for prostate cancer, estrogen-making tumors), with testicular atrophy, or with drugs such as digitalis. MSD says the mechanism is usually 'a decrease in androgen effect or an increase in estrogen effect' and names spironolactone, anabolic steroids, and antiandrogens as key drug causes. Spironolactone blocks androgen receptors as well as aldosterone receptors, and switching to the more selective eplerenone is a common fix (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Furosemide is not a typical cause of gynecomastia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril are not a typical cause of gynecomastia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Beta-blockers such as metoprolol are not a typical cause of gynecomastia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Nitrates such as isosorbide dinitrate are not a typical cause of gynecomastia (standard teaching).

sources.title: Dr. Elnemr Reproductive Pathology: Breast (Emily's file), Gynecomastia, p. 14
MSD Manual Professional: Gynecomastia

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 33 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after sudden abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding began. She has chronic hypertension and used cocaine earlier today. Her uterus is firm, tender, and contracting often. The fetal heart rate tracing shows late decelerations. Abdominal ultrasound shows a placenta high in the fundus, well away from the cervix, and no clot is seen behind it.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: placental abruption. Why: your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes (pp. 47-49) define placental abruption as early separation of a normally placed placenta. Bleeding is usually visible but can be hidden behind the placenta. Risk factors include a previous abruption, hypertension, blunt trauma, smoking, and cocaine. It is the most common cause of painful bleeding late in pregnancy and the most common cause of DIC in pregnancy, and no finger exam should be done until placenta previa is ruled out. MSD lists the same risk factors (cocaine carries a risk of up to 10%), says the uterus 'may be painful, tender, and irritable to palpation,' and warns that 'normal ultrasonographic findings do not rule out placental abruption.' Here the ultrasound has ruled out previa, and the painful, tender uterus with fetal distress points to abruption.

whyWrong.b: Placenta previa causes painless bleeding, and this ultrasound shows the placenta far from the cervix (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Vasa previa bleeds when the membranes rupture, and the blood lost is fetal, so the mother usually stays stable (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Uterine rupture usually happens with a prior uterine scar and causes contractions to stop (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A bloody show is a small amount of blood and does not cause a rigid, tender uterus (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials of Obstetrics (Emily's file), Abruptio placentae, pp. 47-49
MSD Manual Professional: Placental Abruption (Abruptio Placentae)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is stung by a bee while gardening. Within 10 minutes he has hives over his trunk, swelling of his lips, wheezing, and lightheadedness. His blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg and pulse is 128/min. He had only a local reaction to a bee sting 1 year ago.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this reaction?

options.text: Antigen cross-linking IgE bound to mast cells
IgG binding to antigens on red cell surfaces
Bradykinin excess from C1 inhibitor deficiency

questions.explanation: Answer: venom cross-links IgE that is already bound to mast cells (type I hypersensitivity). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (pp. 450-452) explain that a first exposure makes IgE, which sits on high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure the antigen cross-links that IgE, and the cells degranulate within minutes, releasing histamine and tryptase (tryptase in the blood shows that mast cells have fired). Leukotrienes and chemokines follow hours later. The mediators widen blood vessels, make them leak, and narrow the airways, which causes anaphylactic shock, and without prompt epinephrine it can be fatal. MSD agrees that antigen meeting IgE on basophils and mast cells releases histamine, leukotrienes, and other mediators, and calls epinephrine 'the cornerstone of treatment for anaphylaxis,' given intramuscularly into the outer thigh. MSD notes that serum tryptase, preferably measured within 2 hours, can confirm the diagnosis, and that glucocorticoids have no proven role.

whyWrong.b: Immune complexes activating complement describe type III reactions such as serum sickness, which start days, not minutes, after exposure (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 458).
whyWrong.c: Cytokines from sensitized T cells cause type IV reactions, which take 1 to 3 days to appear (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: IgG against red cell antigens is a type II reaction, causing hemolysis rather than hives and wheezing (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Hereditary angioedema comes from too much bradykinin, not IgE, and causes swelling without hives (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Type I hypersensitivity, pp. 450-452
MSD Manual Professional: Anaphylaxis

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fever, an itchy rash, and aching joints for 2 days. Nine days ago she started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Her temperature is 38.4°C. There are raised, red, itchy welts on her trunk and limbs, tender lymph nodes in her neck and groin, and pain with movement of her wrists and knees. Serum C3 is low.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this patient's condition?

options.text: Drug cross-linking IgE on mast cells
Antibodies against her own red blood cells
Direct toxic injury to the liver and joints

questions.explanation: Answer: drug-antibody immune complexes that activate complement (serum sickness, a type III reaction). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 458) call serum sickness the prototype immune complex disease. Antibodies form against a foreign protein, and 1 to 2 weeks later antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissues and activate complement. The result is fever, urticaria, joint pain, glomerulonephritis, swollen lymph nodes, and a low C3 level 5-10 days after exposure. Serum sickness-like reactions follow some drugs, including monoclonal antibodies and sulfonamides, and some infections, such as hepatitis B. MSD describes serum sickness as 'a type III hypersensitivity reaction due to medication-antibody complexes and complement activation' that typically starts 7 to 10 days after exposure, names beta-lactam and sulfonamide antibiotics among the most common causes, and says symptoms are self-limited, lasting 1 to 2 weeks.

whyWrong.b: IgE cross-linking causes type I reactions within minutes of exposure, not after 9 days, and does not lower C3 (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, pp. 450-451).
whyWrong.c: T cells attacking keratinocytes cause SJS/TEN, with painful blisters, skin peeling, and mouth sores rather than hives and low complement (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Antibodies against red cells cause hemolytic anemia, not fever, hives, and joint pain with low complement (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Direct drug toxicity does not explain low complement, hives, and swollen nodes (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Serum sickness, p. 458
MSD Manual Professional: Drug Hypersensitivity

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man received a kidney from a deceased donor 3 weeks ago. Since then, his serum creatinine has risen from 1.3 to 2.6 mg/dL, and his urine output has fallen. Ultrasound shows normal blood flow and no blocked ureter. A biopsy of the transplanted kidney shows a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes in the interstitium, invading the tubules and the walls of small arteries.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this injury?

options.text: Recipient T cells reacting to donor MHC molecules
Preformed recipient antibodies against donor blood groups
Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues
Smooth muscle growth narrowing graft arteries
Recurrence of the original kidney disease

questions.explanation: Answer: recipient T cells reacting to donor MHC molecules (acute cellular rejection). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 476) place acute rejection weeks to months after transplant, usually 1 to 4 weeks. It is mostly cell mediated: recipient CD8 and CD4 T cells are activated against donor MHC molecules (a type IV reaction), while antibody-mediated (humoral) acute rejection is less common. Biopsy shows a dense lymphocytic infiltrate in the graft with vasculitis of graft vessels, and immunosuppressive drugs are aimed mainly at preventing this form. MSD describes acute rejection as a new T-cell response to donor histocompatibility antigens, with a mononuclear cell infiltrate, and says it often reverses with stronger immunosuppression.

whyWrong.b: Preformed antibodies cause hyperacute rejection, which clots the graft within minutes to hours of surgery (MSD; standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Donor T cells attacking the host is graft-versus-host disease, mostly after bone marrow or liver transplants (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 478).
whyWrong.d: Intimal smooth muscle growth narrowing arteries is chronic rejection, which develops over months to years (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 477).
whyWrong.e: Recurrent disease would not cause a dense T-cell infiltrate attacking tubules and vessels 3 weeks after transplant (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Acute rejection, p. 476
MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Transplantation

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman who had a lung transplant 3 years ago comes to the physician because of a dry cough and shortness of breath that have slowly worsened over 6 months. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. She has no fever. Spirometry shows a new obstructive pattern with a steadily falling FEV1. A biopsy shows scarring that narrows and blocks the small airways (bronchioles).
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: chronic rejection (bronchiolitis obliterans after a lung transplant). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 477) describe chronic rejection as starting months to years after transplant, with both cellular and antibody components (type II and type IV reactions). Recipient T cells respond to donor MHC presented by recipient cells, and the cytokines they release cause smooth muscle growth in vessel walls and scarring of the organ, so the picture is dominated by narrowed, scarred arteries. MSD says chronic rejection typically occurs months to years after transplant, shows neointimal proliferation of smooth muscle cells ('transplantation atherosclerosis'), lists obliterative bronchiolitis with cough and dyspnea as its form in the lung, and says there is no established treatment.

whyWrong.b: Acute cellular rejection usually appears weeks after transplant, with a dense lymphocyte infiltrate rather than slow airway scarring (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 476).
whyWrong.c: Hyperacute rejection occurs within 48 hours, from preformed antibodies (MSD Overview of Transplantation).
whyWrong.d: CMV pneumonitis is an infection with fever and interstitial infiltrates, not slowly progressive airway scarring (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Graft-versus-host disease mostly follows bone marrow or liver transplants and targets skin, liver, and gut (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 478).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Chronic rejection, p. 477
MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Transplantation

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has had pneumonia twice and sinus infections 4 times in the past 2 years. She also has recurrent watery diarrhea, and stool tests last year showed Giardia. Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM are all low. Flow cytometry shows a normal number of circulating B cells. She did not make protective antibodies after pneumococcal and tetanus vaccines.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this patient's condition?

options.text: B cells that fail to mature into plasma cells
Absent B cells from a BTK gene mutation
Failed class switching from a CD40 ligand defect
Absent thymus with low T cells

questions.explanation: Answer: B cells that cannot mature into antibody-making plasma cells (common variable immunodeficiency). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 465) describe CVID as a defect in B-cell differentiation with many causes, starting in the late teens or acquired in the 20s and 30s. Plasma cells and immunoglobulins are low, and patients have sinus and lung infections, bronchiectasis, more autoimmune disease, and a higher lymphoma risk. MSD defines CVID by low immunoglobulins with phenotypically normal B cells, usually diagnosed between ages 20 and 40, and requires low IgG plus low IgA or IgM and an impaired response to vaccines. MSD lists autoimmune cytopenias and granulomatous inflammation as complications, says gastric carcinoma or lymphoma occurs in 10% of patients, and treats it with immune globulin (IgG) replacement.

whyWrong.b: A BTK mutation (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) leaves almost no B cells and appears in infant boys after maternal antibody wanes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A CD40 ligand defect (hyper-IgM syndrome) causes normal or high IgM, not low IgM (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Selective IgA deficiency leaves IgG and IgM normal (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 465).
whyWrong.e: Thymic aplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) presents in infancy with low T cells, low calcium, and heart defects (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Common variable immunodeficiency, p. 465
MSD Manual Professional: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID)

questions.stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes for 2 months. She received the BCG vaccine at birth. Cultures of a lymph node and bone marrow grow Mycobacterium bovis (BCG strain). Her lymphocyte count, immunoglobulin levels, and neutrophil oxidative burst test are normal. Her T cells make very little interferon-gamma when stimulated.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.text: CD40 ligand on helper T cells

questions.explanation: Answer: the interleukin-12 (IL-12) receptor. Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 466) describe IL-12 receptor deficiency as an autosomal recessive defect in the Th1 response. They explain (p. 437) that IL-12 pushes naive helper T cells to become Th1 cells, whose interferon-gamma activates macrophages to kill intracellular microbes such as mycobacteria, and that these patients are treated with IFN-gamma. Without this loop, IFN-gamma is low, and children get disseminated mycobacterial and fungal infections, sometimes after the live BCG vaccine. MSD lists Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease as caused by defects in the genes for the IFN-gamma receptor, IL-12, or the IL-12 receptor, with mycobacterial infections of varying severity.

whyWrong.b: NADPH oxidase loss (chronic granulomatous disease) gives an abnormal oxidative burst test, which is normal here (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes SCID, with very low lymphocyte counts and low antibodies (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Bruton tyrosine kinase defects leave few B cells and low immunoglobulins, which are normal here (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: CD40 ligand defects block class switching and mainly cause high IgM with low IgG and IgA (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), IL-12 and IL-12 receptor deficiency, pp. 437, 466
MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Immunodeficiency Disorders

questions.topic: Graft-versus-host disease after stem cell transplant
questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia received an allogeneic stem cell transplant from his HLA-matched sister 5 weeks ago. He now has a red, itchy rash on his palms, soles, and trunk, watery diarrhea, and a serum bilirubin of 4.1 mg/dL. A skin biopsy shows lymphocytes attacking the basal layer of the epidermis. His physician explains that the immune process causing these symptoms may also have a benefit.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes that benefit?

options.text: Donor T cells also attack leftover leukemia cells
Host T cells are destroyed, preventing graft rejection
Donor B cells make antibodies against infections
Cytokines from the rash suppress the bone marrow
Host natural killer cells are activated by the rash

questions.explanation: Answer: donor T cells also attack leukemia cells that survived treatment (graft-versus-tumor effect). Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (p. 478) explain that graft-versus-host disease follows allogeneic bone marrow transplants, lymphocyte-rich organs such as the liver, or transfusion of non-irradiated blood. Immune-competent donor T cells (both CD4 and CD8) see host MHC antigens as foreign (a type IV reaction). The skin, liver, and gut are hit hardest, causing a maculopapular rash, jaundice, and diarrhea. The same reaction can help in leukemia, because donor cells also attack the tumor (graft-versus-tumor effect). MSD describes acute GVHD as donor immune cells attacking recipient tissue, causing fever, rash, hepatitis with high bilirubin, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, and notes a graft-versus-tumor effect that may reduce relapse rates. MSD lists methotrexate and cyclosporine for prevention and methylprednisolone for treatment.

whyWrong.b: Pre-transplant conditioning, not GVHD, removes host immune cells; the attacking cells in GVHD come from the donor (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: GVHD is driven by donor T cells, not by protective donor antibodies (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 478).
whyWrong.d: Suppressing the bone marrow would be harmful, not a benefit, and is not how GVHD helps (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The attacking cells in GVHD are donor T cells, not host natural killer cells (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 478).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Graft-versus-host disease, p. 478
MSD Manual Professional: Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man had a kidney transplant 4 months ago. His medications are tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and a low dose of prednisone. He now has a fine tremor of his hands, his fasting glucose has risen to 142 mg/dL, and his serum creatinine has slowly increased. A blood level of one of his drugs is above the target range. Biopsy of the graft shows no rejection.
questions.leadIn: The drug most likely responsible for his tremor and rising creatinine works by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Inhibits mTOR, blocking the response to IL-2
Inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, blocking purine synthesis
Blocks the IL-2 receptor alpha chain (CD25)
Blocks CD80/CD86 costimulation of T cells

questions.explanation: Answer: tacrolimus, which inhibits calcineurin and so lowers IL-2 transcription. Why: your El-Husseiny immunology notes (pp. 481-482) explain that tacrolimus binds FK506-binding protein and cyclosporine binds cyclophilin, and that both block calcineurin, a phosphatase that normally activates NFAT so T cells can make IL-2. Both drugs are highly nephrotoxic, especially at higher doses. Tacrolimus resembles cyclosporine but has a higher risk of diabetes and neurotoxicity, without the gum overgrowth or hirsutism that cyclosporine causes. MSD agrees that calcineurin inhibitors block the T-cell transcription needed for cytokine production, calls nephrotoxicity the most serious dose-dependent adverse effect of cyclosporine, lists tremor, diabetes, and hypertension, and says tacrolimus is more prone to induce diabetes.

whyWrong.b: Blocking mTOR is how sirolimus works; it is not nephrotoxic, and it causes low blood counts and high lipids (your El-Husseiny immunology notes, p. 482).
whyWrong.c: Blocking IMP dehydrogenase is how mycophenolate works; its main side effects are gut upset and low blood counts, not tremor or nephrotoxicity (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Blocking CD25 is how basiliximab works; MSD reports anaphylaxis as its only adverse effect (MSD Overview of Transplantation).
whyWrong.e: Blocking costimulation is how belatacept works, and it is used to avoid calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity (MSD Overview of Transplantation).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Immunosuppressant drugs, pp. 481-482
MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Transplantation

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy comes to the physician because of pimples on his face, chest, and upper back for 1 year. Exam shows open and closed comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) and many red papules and pustules. He plays football and wears a helmet and shoulder pads most days.
questions.leadIn: The bacterium involved in his inflamed lesions contributes mainly by which of the following?

options.text: Breaking sebum down into free fatty acids
Making a toxin that splits desmoglein 1
Invading the dermis to form deep abscesses
Making a superantigen that activates T cells
Inducing keratinocytes to make extra melanin

questions.explanation: Answer: breaking sebum down into irritating free fatty acids. Why: your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book) (pp. 171-172) explain that acne is chronic inflammation of hair follicles and their sebaceous glands. Androgens raise sebum production, and extra keratin plugs the follicles, forming comedones. The plugged, oily, low-oxygen follicle lets the normal skin bacterium grow, and its lipases break sebum into proinflammatory fatty acids, which produce pustules and nodules. Risk factors include higher androgen levels, oily hair products, and friction from tight sports gear. Treatment includes benzoyl peroxide and vitamin A derivatives. MSD names excess sebum, follicular plugging, and colonization by Cutibacterium acnes among the 4 major factors, describes the bacterium 'breaking down sebum into free fatty acids that irritate the follicular epithelium,' and then an inflammatory response by neutrophils and lymphocytes. Recent change: MSD uses the bacterium's newer name, Cutibacterium acnes; your notes use its older name, Propionibacterium acnes.

whyWrong.b: A toxin that splits desmoglein 1 is the exfoliative toxin of Staphylococcus aureus in scalded skin syndrome and bullous impetigo (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Deep dermal abscesses are typical of S. aureus boils, not comedonal acne (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Superantigens are made by S. aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes and cause toxic shock (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Extra melanin causes dark spots after inflammation but is not how the bacterium drives acne (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Acne vulgaris, pp. 171-172
MSD Manual Professional: Acne Vulgaris

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an intensely itchy rash for 3 months. Exam shows clusters of small blisters and scratched, crusted bumps on both elbows, both knees, and her buttocks. She has mild bloating after meals but no diarrhea. Her hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with a low ferritin.
questions.leadIn: Direct immunofluorescence of skin next to a lesion is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Granular IgA in the tips of dermal papillae
Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane
IgG in a net-like pattern between keratinocytes
Linear IgA along the basement membrane
No immune deposits in the skin

questions.explanation: Answer: granular IgA deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae (dermatitis herpetiformis). Why: your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book) (p. 179) describe dermatitis herpetiformis as autoimmune IgA deposition at the tips of the dermal papillae, with itchy papules, vesicles, and blisters on both sides on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), the upper back, and the buttocks. Biopsy shows small collections of neutrophils and fibrin at the papillary tips. The disease is strongly linked to celiac disease, and a gluten-free diet improves both the gut and the skin. MSD says almost all patients have celiac disease on histology, describes granular IgA deposition in the dermal papillary tips, uses IgA anti-tissue and anti-epidermal transglutaminase antibodies for diagnosis, and treats with dapsone or sulfapyridine plus a gluten-free diet. Her iron deficiency hints at silent celiac malabsorption (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane is bullous pemphigoid, with tense blisters in older adults (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A net-like IgG pattern between keratinocytes is pemphigus vulgaris, with fragile blisters and mouth sores (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Linear IgA along the basement membrane is linear IgA bullous dermatosis, often triggered by vancomycin (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis is defined by IgA deposits in the skin (your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book), p. 179).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Dermatitis herpetiformis, p. 179
MSD Manual Professional: Dermatitis Herpetiformis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man had a melanoma removed from his back 3 years ago. He now has several new nodules in his lungs and liver. A biopsy of a liver nodule shows metastatic melanoma, and genetic testing of the tumor shows a BRAF V600E mutation.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drug combinations specifically targets the signaling pathway activated by this mutation?

options.text: BRAF inhibitor combined with MEK inhibitor
EGFR inhibitor combined with a platinum drug

questions.explanation: Answer: a BRAF inhibitor combined with a MEK inhibitor. Why: your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book) (p. 187) explain that melanoma is a cancer of melanocytes, which come from the neural crest. BRAF is a protein kinase in the growth-signaling pathway, and the BRAF V600E mutation, found in 40-60% of melanomas, switches that pathway on, driving melanocyte growth, survival, and spread. The notes add that depth of invasion (Breslow thickness) is the most important predictor of spread. MSD lists combination BRAF and MEK inhibitors (for example, dabrafenib with trametinib, encorafenib with binimetinib, or vemurafenib with cobimetinib) for BRAF-mutated melanoma when standard immunotherapy cannot be given, and lists anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4, and anti-LAG-3 checkpoint inhibitors as the main immunotherapies for metastatic melanoma. MEK sits just downstream of BRAF in the same pathway, so blocking both gives a deeper block (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: EGFR inhibitors target EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, not BRAF-mutant melanoma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Hedgehog inhibitors such as vismodegib treat advanced basal cell carcinoma (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: BCR-ABL inhibitors such as imatinib treat chronic myeloid leukemia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Anti-HER2 antibodies such as trastuzumab treat HER2-positive breast and stomach cancers (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Melanoma, p. 187
MSD Manual Professional: Melanoma

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of small bumps on his trunk and arms for 3 months. Exam shows 15 firm, pink, dome-shaped papules, each 2 to 4 mm across with a small central dimple. His younger sister has similar bumps. He is otherwise healthy.
questions.leadIn: A biopsy of one papule is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions
Koilocytes with clear halos around their nuclei
Fungal hyphae in the stratum corneum
Nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading

questions.explanation: Answer: large inclusions in the cytoplasm of keratinocytes (molluscum bodies). Why: your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book) (p. 193) describe molluscum contagiosum as firm, pink, umbilicated papules caused by a poxvirus, with cytoplasmic inclusions in infected keratinocytes called molluscum bodies. It is most common in children and also affects sexually active adults and people with weak immune systems. MSD describes pink, dome-shaped, waxy or pearly umbilicated papules from a poxvirus, common among children, with characteristic inclusion bodies on biopsy or smear. MSD says it spreads by direct contact, autoinoculation, and fomites, that people with HIV may get widespread infection, and that most lesions clear on their own within 6 months to 2 years. Poxviruses replicate in the cytoplasm, which is why the inclusions sit there (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions (Tzanck smear) point to herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Koilocytes are the hallmark of human papillomavirus, as in common warts (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Hyphae in the stratum corneum suggest tinea, which forms scaly rings rather than dimpled papules (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Palisading basaloid nests describe basal cell carcinoma, a tumor of older, sun-damaged skin (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Molluscum contagiosum, p. 193
MSD Manual Professional: Molluscum Contagiosum

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss, early fullness after meals, and dark skin in his armpits over 2 months. He has a BMI of 21 kg/m2 and a normal fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c. Exam shows dark, velvety, thickened skin in both axillae and on the back of his neck. He has iron deficiency anemia.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: gastric adenocarcinoma. Why: your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book) (p. 198) describe acanthosis nigricans as epidermal thickening that causes symmetric, dark, thickened skin, mostly in the axillae and on the neck. It is linked to insulin resistance (type 2 diabetes) and to cancer of the internal organs, especially gastric adenocarcinoma. MSD says acanthosis nigricans most often reflects impaired glucose tolerance 'but it may reflect internal cancer, especially if onset is rapid and distribution is widespread,' and lists it as a paraneoplastic skin sign of gastrointestinal cancer, along with the sudden appearance of many seborrheic keratoses (Leser-Trélat sign). This lean man with normal glucose, weight loss, early satiety, and iron deficiency fits a stomach cancer (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Adrenal insufficiency darkens skin creases, scars, and gums evenly, without velvety thickening (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Hemochromatosis gives a diffuse bronze color with diabetes and liver disease, not velvety plaques (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Insulin resistance is the most common cause, but this lean man has normal glucose and alarm symptoms (MSD Paraneoplastic Syndromes).
whyWrong.e: Small cell lung cancer is linked to hormone syndromes such as SIADH and Cushing syndrome, not acanthosis nigricans (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Acanthosis nigricans, p. 198
MSD Manual Professional: Paraneoplastic Syndromes

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of painful red lumps on both shins for 1 week. Three weeks ago she had a sore throat with fever. She takes no medications and is not pregnant. Exam shows several tender, warm, red, raised nodules, 2 to 4 cm across, on the front of both lower legs. There are no ulcers. Her antistreptolysin O titer is high.
questions.leadIn: A deep biopsy of a nodule is most likely to show inflammation centered in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: the septa of the subcutaneous fat (septal panniculitis). Why: your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book) (p. 199) describe erythema nodosum as painful, raised, inflamed lesions of the subcutaneous fat, usually on the front of the shins. It is often idiopathic but can be linked to sarcoidosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, tuberculosis, streptococcal infections, leprosy, and inflammatory bowel disease. MSD calls it a form of panniculitis with tender red or violet nodules, mainly on the shins, names streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, and inflammatory bowel disease as the most common causes, says up to about 50% of cases are idiopathic, and notes that it almost always clears on its own in about 3 to 6 weeks. The inflammation sits in the fibrous septa between fat lobules (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Inflamed dermal vessel walls describe leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which causes palpable purpura (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Damage to the basal layer is seen in lichen planus and lupus, not in tender shin nodules (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Inflamed hair follicles and oil glands are acne (your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book), p. 171).
whyWrong.e: Erythema nodosum is a disease of the subcutaneous fat, not the superficial dermis (your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book), p. 199).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Erythema nodosum, p. 199
MSD Manual Professional: Erythema Nodosum

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student comes to the physician because of a rash on her trunk for 10 days. It began as a single 4-cm, pink, oval, scaly patch on her chest. A week later, many smaller oval patches appeared on her chest and back, lined up along skin creases. Each patch has a fine ring of scale just inside its border. Her palms and soles are clear, and she feels well.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Answer: reassurance, with relief of itching if needed (pityriasis rosea). Why: your El-Husseiny skin notes (in the musculoskeletal book) (p. 200) describe a first large 'herald patch,' with more scaly red plaques arriving a few days later, often in a Christmas tree pattern on the trunk, with collarette scale. It may be idiopathic or linked to viral infection and clears on its own in 6 to 8 weeks. MSD describes a single 2- to 10-cm herald patch, a Christmas tree-like pattern on the back, and a collarette of scale. Other source: MSD says the rash usually clears within 5 weeks and rarely returns. MSD also says no specific treatment is usually needed beyond anti-itch measures. MSD advises a blood test for syphilis when the palms or soles are involved, when no herald patch is seen, or when the pattern is unusual.

whyWrong.b: Terbinafine treats tinea; tinea can look like a single patch but does not spread in a Christmas tree pattern (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Penicillin treats secondary syphilis, which usually involves the palms and soles and has no herald patch (MSD Pityriasis Rosea; standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Oral steroids are not needed for a self-limited rash (MSD Pityriasis Rosea).
whyWrong.e: There is no bacterial infection to treat (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Pityriasis rosea, p. 200
MSD Manual Professional: Pityriasis Rosea

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he is behind in his milestones. He has coarse facial features, a large tongue, stiff joints, an umbilical hernia, and noisy breathing at night. His corneas are cloudy, and his liver and spleen are enlarged. Urine shows high levels of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: alpha-L-iduronidase (Hurler syndrome, MPS I). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 204) describe Hurler syndrome as an autosomal recessive deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase, so heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate build up in lysosomes. Findings are developmental delay, coarse 'gargoyle' features, airway obstruction, corneal clouding, and an enlarged liver and spleen. MSD's mucopolysaccharidosis table lists cloudy corneas, stiff joints, heavy facial features, a large tongue, intellectual disability, heart disease, hernias, and sleep apnea for Hurler syndrome. Hunter syndrome, by contrast, is milder and spares the corneas.

whyWrong.b: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency is Hunter syndrome, which is X-linked and does not cloud the corneas (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 204).
