whyWrong.c: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency is Gaucher disease, with bone pain and big spleen but no corneal clouding or coarse facies (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Hexosaminidase A deficiency is Tay-Sachs disease, with a cherry-red macula and no enlarged organs (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency is Fabry disease, with burning pain and angiokeratomas (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Mucopolysaccharidoses, p. 204
MSD Manual Consumer Version: Types of Mucopolysaccharidoses (table)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of hyperactive, aggressive behavior and delayed speech. He has coarse facial features, stiff joints, and an enlarged liver and spleen. His corneas are clear on slit-lamp exam. Urine shows high levels of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. Enzyme testing shows deficient iduronate-2-sulfatase.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: X-linked recessive (Hunter syndrome, MPS II). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 204) describe Hunter syndrome as an X-linked recessive deficiency of iduronate-2-sulfatase, with the same stored substances as Hurler syndrome (heparan and dermatan sulfate). It looks like a mild Hurler syndrome plus aggressive behavior, without corneal clouding; the memory hook is that 'Hunters see clearly and aggressively aim for the X.' MSD's mucopolysaccharidosis table describes Hunter syndrome as similar to Hurler syndrome but milder and without cloudy corneas, with normal intelligence in the mild form and death before age 15 in the severe form. Because it is X-linked, nearly all patients are boys (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Autosomal recessive inheritance fits Hurler syndrome, which clouds the corneas (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 204).
whyWrong.c: Most lysosomal storage diseases are recessive, not dominant (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Mitochondrial disorders pass only from the mother and mainly affect muscle and brain energy use, not glycosaminoglycan breakdown (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: X-linked dominant disorders affect girls as well as boys and are rare among storage diseases (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Mucopolysaccharidoses, p. 204
MSD Manual Consumer Version: Types of Mucopolysaccharidoses (table)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a red, scaly rash on his face, neck, and the backs of his hands that gets worse in the summer. After a recent fever he had several days of unsteady walking, which then improved. His diet is limited. Urinalysis shows large amounts of neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, with normal amounts of proline and hydroxyproline.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this patient's skin and neurologic findings?

options.text: Too little tryptophan to make niacin
Too little tyrosine to make melanin
Too much cystine forming kidney stones
Too little thiamine for pyruvate dehydrogenase

questions.explanation: Answer: too little tryptophan available to make niacin (Hartnup disease). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 238) explain that Hartnup disease is an autosomal recessive defect of the neutral amino acid transporter in the kidney tubules and gut. Neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, are lost in the urine and poorly absorbed, so less tryptophan is turned into niacin, causing pellagra-like symptoms: a rash on sun-exposed skin and neurologic problems, most often ataxia, that come and go. Proline, hydroxyproline, and arginine in the urine are normal, which separates it from Fanconi syndrome. Treatment is nicotinic acid or nicotinamide with a high-protein diet. The notes (p. 237) list the three Ds of pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia). MSD confirms a mutation in the sodium-dependent neutral amino acid transporter, a pellagra-like rash on sun-exposed skin, cerebellar ataxia, attacks triggered by sunlight, fever, or medications, and diagnosis by excess neutral amino acids except proline and hydroxyproline in the urine, and treats attacks with oral nicotinamide.

whyWrong.b: Low tyrosine is not the problem in Hartnup disease, and lack of melanin would cause pale skin, not a sun-triggered rash (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Excess cystine in the urine is cystinuria, a defect of the dibasic amino acid transporter that causes kidney stones (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: High homocysteine causes clots and lens dislocation (homocystinuria), not a sun-triggered rash (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy, without a photosensitive rash (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Niacin and Hartnup disease, pp. 237-238
MSD Manual Professional: Hartnup Disease

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman and her two children are brought to the emergency department in January because all three have had headaches, nausea, and dizziness since the morning. They have been heating their home with a gas space heater. The family dog has also been sluggish. The mother's pulse oximetry reading is 99% on room air.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following findings is most likely in the mother's arterial blood?

options.text: Low PaO2 with low hemoglobin oxygen saturation

questions.explanation: Answer: a high carboxyhemoglobin level with a normal PaO2. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 155) explain that carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin, pushing oxygen off, and also binds cytochrome a/a3 less tightly than cyanide. Symptoms include headache, nausea, and fast heart and breathing rates, and it is treated with oxygen. MSD explains that CO has a greater affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, and inhibits mitochondrial respiration. Headache and nausea can start at levels of 10 to 20%. 'The pulse oximeter cannot differentiate normal hemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin,' so the reading looks falsely normal, and diagnosis needs a carboxyhemoglobin level measured with a CO-oximeter. MSD treats with 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask, which shortens CO's half-life from about 4.5 hours on room air to about 1.5 hours, and considers hyperbaric oxygen in severe cases. PaO2 reflects oxygen dissolved in plasma, which CO does not change (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: PaO2 measures dissolved oxygen, which stays normal because her lungs work normally (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Methemoglobin comes from oxidizing drugs such as dapsone or nitrites, not from a space heater, and PaO2 stays normal in methemoglobinemia too (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: CO blocks oxygen binding to hemoglobin but does not lower the amount of hemoglobin (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Her breathing is not depressed; early CO poisoning causes fast breathing, not CO2 retention (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Electron transport chain poisons, p. 155
MSD Manual Professional: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of daily headaches and blurred vision for 1 month. For 6 months she has taken large doses of a vitamin A supplement she bought online to clear her acne. Her hair has become thin and coarse, and her skin is dry. Exam shows swelling of both optic discs and a mildly enlarged liver. MRI of the brain shows no mass.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her headaches?
questions.explanation: Answer: pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) from vitamin A toxicity. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 246) explain that taking more than 10 times the recommended daily amount of vitamin A can cause toxicity. Chronic toxicity brings hair loss, dry skin, high lipids, liver damage, an enlarged liver and spleen, and vision problems, and papilledema points to benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri). Vitamin A also causes birth defects, so before isotretinoin (a vitamin A derivative) is started, pregnancy must be ruled out and two methods of birth control used. MSD lists sparse, coarse hair as an early sign of chronic toxicity, followed by severe headache, idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), and weakness, notes liver toxicity and an enlarged liver, and says the treatment is to stop vitamin A, after which recovery is generally complete. MSD also notes that eating too much carotene causes carotenemia, not vitamin A toxicity.

whyWrong.b: Migraine does not cause swollen optic discs or an enlarged liver (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Bacterial meningitis causes fever and neck stiffness over hours to days, not a month of headaches with hair loss (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Tension-type headache does not cause papilledema (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Pituitary apoplexy is a sudden, severe headache from bleeding into a pituitary tumor, and the MRI shows no mass (standard teaching).
