MSD Manual Professional: Vitamin A Toxicity

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with Down syndrome is brought to the physician by his sister because he has become more forgetful over 1 year. He now gets lost in his group home and can no longer do tasks he once did on his own, such as making a sandwich. He had an atrioventricular septal defect repaired in infancy. Serum TSH, vitamin B12, and a hearing test are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains why this condition began at an early age in this patient?

options.text: Extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene
Expansion of CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene
Prion protein misfolding that spreads between neurons
Deficiency of thiamine from a poor diet

questions.explanation: Answer: an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (pp. 101-102) explain that about 95% of Down syndrome comes from trisomy 21 by meiotic nondisjunction, almost always in the mother's egg, with older maternal age as a risk factor. About half of babies have heart defects, most often atrioventricular septal defects and VSDs, and 10-15% have gut anomalies such as duodenal atresia. Chromosome 21 carries the APP gene, and the extra copy is thought to speed amyloid buildup, causing early Alzheimer disease. ALL and AML are also more common. MSD agrees that about 95% of cases come from nondisjunction, usually of the maternal chromosome, notes an increased risk of Alzheimer disease at an early age, recommends yearly assessment starting at age 40, and lists hypothyroidism as common, which is why the TSH was checked.

whyWrong.b: CAG repeat expansion causes Huntington disease, with chorea and a family history, not Down syndrome dementia (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Prion disease progresses over months with myoclonus and is not linked to trisomy 21 (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Vascular dementia follows strokes in people with vascular risk factors; it does not explain a steady decline tied to trisomy 21 (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, usually with heavy alcohol use, eye movement problems, and ataxia (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Down syndrome, pp. 101-102
MSD Manual Professional: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of constant hunger and weight gain. As a newborn he was very floppy and fed so poorly that he needed a feeding tube. Now he searches for food at night and is obese. He has small hands and feet, a small penis with undescended testes, and mild intellectual disability. DNA methylation testing of chromosome 15 shows only the maternal pattern.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.text: Expanded CGG repeat in the FMR1 gene

questions.explanation: Answer: loss of the paternally inherited 15q11-q13 region (Prader-Willi syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (pp. 80-81) explain that in genomic imprinting one parent's copy of a gene is silenced by DNA methylation, so only the other copy works. In the Prader-Willi region, the maternal genes are normally silenced, so the disease appears when the paternal copy is deleted or mutated. About 25% of cases come from maternal uniparental disomy, in which both chromosome 15s come from the mother. Findings are hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability, hypogonadism, and hypotonia. MSD's microdeletion table lists a paternal deletion at 15q11 and describes hypotonia, poor feeding, and poor growth in infancy, then obesity, hypogonadism, small hands and feet, intellectual disability, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors in childhood. A maternal-only methylation pattern fits either a paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Losing the maternal copy of this region causes Angelman syndrome, with seizures, frequent laughter, and severe intellectual disability (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 81).
whyWrong.c: FMR1 CGG repeat expansion causes fragile X syndrome, with large ears and large testes, not hyperphagia (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 97).
whyWrong.d: A 7q11.23 deletion is Williams syndrome, with elfin facies, friendliness, and supravalvular aortic stenosis (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 109).
whyWrong.e: A 22q11 deletion causes DiGeorge syndrome, with thymic and parathyroid defects and heart anomalies (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 109).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Genomic imprinting, pp. 80-81
MSD Manual Professional: Examples of Microdeletion Syndromes (table)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she does not speak any words and has had several seizures. She walks with a stiff, jerky, unsteady gait, often flaps her hands, and laughs frequently, even when nothing seems funny. Her head is small. Genetic testing shows a deletion on chromosome 15q11-q13.
questions.leadIn: This deletion most likely involves the copy of chromosome 15 inherited from which parent, and which gene?
questions.explanation: Answer: the maternal copy, affecting UBE3A (Angelman syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 81) explain that the paternal UBE3A gene is normally silenced by imprinting, so the brain depends on the maternal copy. Angelman syndrome happens when the mother's copy is lost (by deletion) or carries a mutation, and about 5% of cases come from paternal uniparental disomy. Children laugh at odd times (the 'happy puppet' picture) and have seizures, an unsteady gait (ataxia), and severe intellectual disability. MSD's microdeletion table lists a maternal deletion at 15q11 with seizures, puppet-like ataxia, frequent laughter, hand flapping, and severe intellectual disability.

whyWrong.b: The paternal UBE3A copy is already silenced in the brain, so losing it does not cause Angelman syndrome (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 81).
whyWrong.c: FMR1 is on the X chromosome, and its silencing causes fragile X syndrome (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 97).
whyWrong.d: Losing paternal genes in this region, such as SNRPN, causes Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonia, hyperphagia, and obesity (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 80); the SNRPN example is standard teaching.
whyWrong.e: MECP2 is on the X chromosome, and its mutation causes Rett syndrome, with loss of skills after normal early development (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Angelman syndrome, p. 81
MSD Manual Professional: Examples of Microdeletion Syndromes (table)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of learning problems and delayed speech. He avoids eye contact, flaps his hands when excited, and has frequent tantrums. He has a long, narrow face, a prominent forehead and chin, and large, protruding ears. His mother went through menopause at age 36. A maternal uncle has intellectual disability.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this patient's condition?

options.text: CGG repeat expansion that silences FMR1
CAG repeat expansion that makes a toxic protein
CTG repeat expansion in an untranslated region
GAA repeat expansion that lowers frataxin

questions.explanation: Answer: a CGG repeat expansion that silences the FMR1 gene by methylation (fragile X syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 97) explain that fragile X syndrome comes from the FMR1 gene on Xq (the X chromosome's long arm) and is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. The CGG repeat expands during oogenesis. A premutation is still under 200 repeats, while more than 200 repeats (full mutation) cause hypermethylation and shut the gene off. Features include a long, thin face, large jaw, large protruding ears, a prominent forehead, large testes after puberty, mild to moderate intellectual disability, severe language delay, behavior problems, and autistic features. MSD agrees that full mutations have more than 200 CGG repeats and premutations have 55 to 200, and notes that women with the premutation may have premature ovarian failure, sometimes with menopause in the mid-30s, as his mother did.

whyWrong.b: CAG repeat expansions make toxic polyglutamine proteins, as in Huntington disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A CTG repeat in the DMPK gene causes myotonic dystrophy, with grip myotonia, cataracts, and balding (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 96); its untranslated-region location is standard teaching.
whyWrong.d: GAA repeat expansion lowers frataxin in Friedreich ataxia, with ataxia, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Loss of the paternal 15q11-q13 region causes Prader-Willi syndrome, with hyperphagia and obesity (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 80).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Fragile X syndrome, p. 97
MSD Manual Professional: Fragile X Syndrome

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of trouble letting go of objects he grips and weakness in his hands for 3 years. After a handshake, he cannot open his hand for several seconds. He has droopy eyelids, a long thin face, frontal balding, and small testes. Slit-lamp exam shows cataracts. His father had similar problems and died suddenly at age 52.
questions.leadIn: This patient is at greatest risk of sudden death from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: a cardiac arrhythmia. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 96) explain that myotonic dystrophy type 1 is autosomal dominant and comes from a CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the DMPK gene. It causes myotonia (slow muscle relaxation, as when a patient cannot release a handshake), muscle wasting, cataracts, testicular atrophy, frontal balding, and arrhythmia; the memory hook is cataracts, toupee (early balding), and gonadal atrophy. MSD agrees that type 1 involves a CTG repeat in DMPK on chromosome 19 with autosomal dominant inheritance, describes delayed relaxation after muscle contraction, ptosis, distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, and small testes in men, and says cardiac arrhythmias raise the risk of premature death.

whyWrong.b: Aortic dissection is a risk in Marfan and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, not myotonic dystrophy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Pulmonary embolism is not a typical cause of death in myotonic dystrophy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Brain aneurysms are linked to polycystic kidney disease and some connective tissue diseases, not myotonic dystrophy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Myotonic dystrophy is linked to endocrine problems, but sudden death in this family points to the heart (MSD Myotonic Dystrophy).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Myotonic dystrophy type 1, p. 96
MSD Manual Professional: Myotonic Dystrophy

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a cleft lip and palate, very small eyes, an extra finger on each hand, and a punched-out defect of the scalp skin. A loud heart murmur is heard. Her karyotype is 47,XX,+13.
questions.leadIn: Brain imaging is most likely to show which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: holoprosencephaly, failure of the forebrain to split into two hemispheres. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 105) list the features of Patau syndrome (trisomy 13): severe intellectual disability, small eyes (microphthalmia), a small head (microcephaly), rocker-bottom feet, cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, cutis aplasia (missing patches of skin), congenital heart disease, polycystic kidneys, and omphalocele, with death usually by age 1. MSD agrees that trisomy 13 usually comes from nondisjunction, lists holoprosencephaly among its common midline anomalies, along with cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, microphthalmia, and scalp defects, says 57 to 80% of infants have severe heart anomalies, and says about 10% survive beyond the first year.

whyWrong.b: Dandy-Walker malformation is a cystic fourth ventricle with a small cerebellar vermis, not the typical trisomy 13 brain defect (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Periventricular calcifications suggest congenital cytomegalovirus infection (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Arnold-Chiari II malformation goes with lumbosacral myelomeningocele (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Lissencephaly (smooth brain) comes from a neuronal migration defect, as in Miller-Dieker syndrome (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Patau syndrome, p. 105
MSD Manual Professional: Trisomy 13

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a heart murmur. She has a broad forehead, full cheeks, a wide mouth, and a small upturned nose. She has mild intellectual disability but talks a lot and is very friendly with strangers. Serum calcium is 11.4 mg/dL. Echocardiography shows narrowing of the aorta just above the aortic valve.
questions.leadIn: The deleted region in this patient most likely includes the gene for which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: elastin (Williams syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 109) describe Williams syndrome as a congenital microdeletion on the long arm of chromosome 7 that includes the elastin gene. Findings are 'elfin' facies, intellectual disability, high calcium because the body responds more strongly to vitamin D, good language skills, an unusually friendly manner with strangers, and vessel narrowing, such as supravalvular aortic stenosis and renal artery stenosis. MSD's microdeletion table lists a deletion at 7q11.23 with aortic stenosis, intellectual disability, elfin facies, and transient high calcium in infants. Losing one elastin copy weakens and thickens arterial walls, which narrows the aorta (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, with tall stature and aortic root dilation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Type I collagen mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with fractures and blue sclerae (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: TBX1 lies in the 22q11 region deleted in DiGeorge syndrome, with thymic and parathyroid defects (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 109); the gene name is standard teaching.
whyWrong.e: Dystrophin mutations cause Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Williams syndrome, p. 109
MSD Manual Professional: Examples of Microdeletion Syndromes (table)

questions.stem: A newborn boy has a weak, high-pitched cry that sounds like a mewing kitten. He has a low birth weight, a small head, a round face, widely spaced eyes, and poor muscle tone. A murmur from a ventricular septal defect is heard.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following chromosome findings is most likely?

options.text: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
Deletion on the long arm of chromosome 7

questions.explanation: Answer: a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (cri-du-chat syndrome, 5p-). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 109) describe cri-du-chat syndrome as a congenital deletion of 5p with microcephaly, moderate to severe intellectual disability, a high-pitched, cat-like cry, epicanthal folds, and heart defects such as VSD. MSD describes a high-pitched, mewing cry like a kitten's in the newborn period, hypotonia, low birth weight, microcephaly, a round face with wide-set eyes, frequent heart anomalies, and markedly delayed development, and notes that many children survive into adulthood with significant disability.

whyWrong.b: A 7q deletion is Williams syndrome, with elfin facies and supravalvular aortic stenosis (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 109).
whyWrong.c: A 22q11 deletion is DiGeorge syndrome, with thymic aplasia, low calcium, and conotruncal heart defects (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 109).
whyWrong.d: Trisomy 13 causes holoprosencephaly, cleft lip, and polydactyly (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 105).
whyWrong.e: A paternal 15q11 deletion is Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonia and later hyperphagia (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 80).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Cri-du-chat syndrome, p. 109
MSD Manual Professional: Chromosomal Deletion Syndromes

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy in a refugee camp is brought to a clinic because of swelling of his legs and face for 3 weeks. Since he was weaned 6 months ago, he has eaten mainly maize porridge. He is irritable. He has puffy eyelids, pitting edema of both legs, a protruding abdomen, an enlarged liver, peeling patches of skin, and sparse, light-colored hair. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this patient's edema?

options.text: Low plasma oncotic pressure from low albumin
Kidney sodium retention from nephrotic syndrome

questions.explanation: Answer: low plasma oncotic pressure from low albumin (kwashiorkor). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 249) describe kwashiorkor as protein malnutrition causing skin lesions (thickening and patchy color change), edema from low plasma oncotic pressure, and a fatty liver from too little apolipoprotein synthesis, often in a small child with a swollen abdomen (MEALS: malnutrition, edema, anemia, liver, skin). Marasmus, by contrast, is a calorie deficit with muscle wasting and no edema. MSD describes kwashiorkor as the edematous form linked to protein deficiency, with peripheral and periorbital edema from low serum albumin, leaky cell membranes, an enlarged liver, a protruding abdomen, skin that becomes hyperpigmented and fissured, and blond, sparse, brittle hair. MSD warns that refeeding can cause dangerous shifts in fluid and electrolytes, including low phosphate.

whyWrong.b: Thiamine deficiency can cause wet beriberi with high-output heart failure, but not the skin, hair, and liver changes here (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Nephrotic syndrome causes edema with heavy proteinuria, not a poor diet with skin and hair changes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Filarial lymphatic blockage causes firm swelling of one limb over years, not generalized edema in a malnourished child (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Excess ADH lowers sodium but does not cause pitting edema (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Protein-energy malnutrition, p. 249
MSD Manual Professional: Protein-Energy Undernutrition (PEU)

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis comes to the physician because of an unsteady gait for 6 months. She has not taken her pancreatic enzymes or vitamins regularly. Exam shows loss of vibration and position sense in her feet, absent ankle reflexes, and a positive Romberg sign. Hemoglobin is 10.6 g/dL with a high reticulocyte count. Serum vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which of the following is the most likely cause of her findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: vitamin E. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 247) explain that vitamin E is an antioxidant that protects red cells and membranes from free radical damage. Deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, acanthocytes, muscle weakness, and demyelination of the posterior columns and spinocerebellar tracts. The nerve findings resemble B12 deficiency, but there is no megaloblastic anemia, no high methylmalonic acid, and no hypersegmented neutrophils. MSD lists fat malabsorption, including cystic fibrosis, as a cause, describes mild hemolytic anemia and spinocerebellar ataxia with loss of reflexes and of vibration and position sense, explains that vitamin E prevents lipid peroxidation of cell membranes, and treats malabsorption-related deficiency with oral alpha-tocopherol 15 to 25 mg/kg daily.

whyWrong.b: B12 deficiency causes similar spinal cord signs, but with megaloblastic anemia and high methylmalonic acid (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 247).
whyWrong.c: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and dry eyes, not ataxia and hemolysis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Vitamin D deficiency causes soft bones and low phosphate, not posterior column loss (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy or beriberi, not hemolysis (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Vitamin E, p. 247
MSD Manual Professional: Vitamin E Deficiency

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a rash, hair loss, and diarrhea that began soon after he was weaned from breast milk. Exam shows red, scaly, crusted plaques around his mouth, nose, and eyes, over his diaper area, and on his fingers and toes, with swelling around the nails. His scalp hair is thin. He is irritable and below the 5th percentile for weight.
questions.leadIn: Supplementation with which of the following is most likely to resolve this condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: zinc (acrodermatitis enteropathica). Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (pp. 248-249) explain that zinc is needed by more than 100 enzymes and forms zinc-finger motifs in transcription factors. Deficiency causes delayed wound healing, weak immunity, hypogonadism, loss of adult body hair, poor taste and smell, and acrodermatitis enteropathica. MSD describes acrodermatitis enteropathica as a rare autosomal recessive disorder of zinc malabsorption, with a psoriasis-like rash around the eyes, nose, and mouth, on the buttocks and perineum, and on the hands and feet, plus hair loss, paronychia, poor immunity, diarrhea, and poor growth. MSD says elemental zinc 1 to 3 mg/kg by mouth daily usually brings complete remission, and notes that biotin, riboflavin, and essential fatty acid deficiencies can look similar. MSD also says the symptoms usually begin after infants are weaned from breast milk.

whyWrong.b: Biotin deficiency can cause a similar rash and hair loss, but MSD lists it as a mimic; the timing at weaning and the pattern fit zinc (MSD Zinc Deficiency).
whyWrong.c: Niacin deficiency (pellagra) causes a rash on sun-exposed skin with diarrhea and dementia, not a rash around body openings (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and dry eyes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Copper deficiency causes kinky hair and low muscle tone (Menkes disease), not this rash (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Zinc, pp. 248-249
MSD Manual Professional: Zinc Deficiency

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because he is sleepy and sweaty. The night before, he drank leftover mixed drinks after a family party and ate nothing for breakfast. He is difficult to wake. His fingerstick glucose is 36 mg/dL, and his blood alcohol level is elevated. He wakes up after IV dextrose.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his low blood glucose?

options.text: Alcohol stimulating insulin release from beta cells
Alcohol blocking glucose absorption in the gut
Kidney glucose loss from tubular injury

questions.explanation: Answer: a high NADH/NAD+ ratio in the liver that blocks gluconeogenesis. Why: your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (pp. 250-251) explain that alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase both make NADH, so ethanol raises the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the liver. This pushes pyruvate to lactate (lactic acidosis) and oxaloacetate to malate, which stops gluconeogenesis and causes fasting hypoglycemia, and it pushes acetyl-CoA into ketone production. Page 251 also notes that fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and disulfiram blocks acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. MSD warns that young children who drink alcohol are at significant risk of hypoglycemia because alcohol impairs gluconeogenesis and their smaller glycogen stores are quickly used up, and advises a fingerstick glucose to rule out hypoglycemia. After an overnight fast, glycogen is low, so the liver depends on gluconeogenesis (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Alcohol does not cause hypoglycemia by raising insulin; insulin falls when glucose is low (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Alcohol does not block glucose absorption, and he ate nothing to absorb (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Glycogen runs low from fasting and small stores in children, not from destruction by acetaldehyde (MSD Alcohol Toxicity and Withdrawal).
whyWrong.e: Kidney glucose loss would not cause this, and alcohol does not injure the tubules this way (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Ethanol metabolism, pp. 250-251
MSD Manual Professional: Alcohol Toxicity and Withdrawal

questions.stem: A 48-year-old dairy farmer comes to the physician because of episodes of fever, chills, cough, and shortness of breath. The episodes start about 6 hours after he forks moldy hay in the barn and clear within 2 days. He does not smoke. Chest CT shows patchy ground-glass opacities and small centrilobular nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows many lymphocytes, with more CD8 than CD4 cells.
questions.leadIn: A lung biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Poorly formed granulomas around small airways
Ferruginous bodies in a fibrotic interstitium
Birefringent particles in hilar fibrotic nodules

questions.explanation: Answer: loosely formed, non-necrotizing granulomas around the small airways (hypersensitivity pneumonitis, farmer's lung). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 102) describe hypersensitivity pneumonitis as a mixed type III and type IV hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled organic antigens, often in farmers and bird keepers. Fever, cough, and shortness of breath start hours after exposure and resolve once the exposure stops, while chronic exposure leads to interstitial fibrosis. Noncaseating granulomas form, as they also do in berylliosis. MSD names thermophilic actinomycetes in hay dust as the cause of farmer's lung, describes dyspnea 4 to 8 hours after exposure, lists poorly formed non-necrotizing granulomas on biopsy, and describes a lavage lymphocytosis above 40% with a CD4/CD8 ratio below 1. MSD calls antigen avoidance the most important part of long-term care and uses glucocorticoids for acute disease.

whyWrong.b: Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli mean tuberculosis, which does not come and go with hay exposure (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Ferruginous bodies mark asbestosis, from asbestos fibers, not organic dust (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 102).
whyWrong.d: Birefringent particles in fibrotic nodules with eggshell node calcification mark silicosis (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 102).
whyWrong.e: Hyaline membranes are the pattern of ARDS, not repeated short episodes after hay exposure (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, p. 102
MSD Manual Professional: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because he falls asleep while driving and at work. His wife says he snores loudly and sometimes stops breathing for several seconds before gasping. He has obesity (BMI 36 kg/m2), a neck circumference of 46 cm, and hypertension that is hard to control. His daytime arterial blood gas is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his breathing pauses at night?

options.text: Upper airway collapse as muscles relax in sleep
Loss of brainstem drive to breathe during sleep
Fluid in the alveoli from heart failure while lying flat
Weak diaphragm from a phrenic nerve injury

questions.explanation: Answer: collapse of the upper airway as its muscles relax during sleep (obstructive sleep apnea). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (pp. 111-112) describe obstructive sleep apnea as breathing effort against a blocked airway, with normal daytime PaO2. In adults, extra tissue around the throat narrows the airway, and in children large tonsils and adenoids do. The airway-opening muscles weaken as a person falls asleep, so the narrowed airway collapses, causing loud snoring, pauses, and daytime sleepiness. Each pause causes brief high CO2 and low oxygen. MSD agrees that the upper airway collapses repeatedly during sleep, notes OSA is 7 times more common with obesity, lists a large neck circumference as a risk factor, links it strongly to hypertension and atrial fibrillation, and calls polysomnography the gold standard for diagnosis, with an AHI of 5 or more per hour plus symptoms. MSD treats it with CPAP and weight loss, and uses hypoglossal nerve stimulation for patients who cannot tolerate CPAP.

whyWrong.b: Loss of brainstem drive causes central sleep apnea, with pauses without breathing effort, often with heart failure or opioids (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Bronchoconstriction causes wheezing, as in asthma, not snoring with pauses (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Fluid in the alveoli from heart failure causes shortness of breath when lying flat, not snoring with pauses (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Phrenic nerve injury weakens the diaphragm, with breathlessness when lying down, but does not cause snoring with pauses (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Obstructive sleep apnea, pp. 111-112
MSD Manual Professional: Obstructive Sleep Apnea

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and fainting while climbing stairs. Her mother had the same condition. Exam shows a loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound and a right ventricular heave. Right heart catheterization shows a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg and a normal pulmonary artery wedge pressure. She shows no response to vasodilator testing. Genetic testing finds a BMPR2 mutation.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following drugs treats her condition by blocking the receptor for a vasoconstrictor that is overactive in this disease?
questions.explanation: Answer: bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 109) describe primary (heritable) pulmonary arterial hypertension in young women, often from an inherited inactivating mutation in BMPR2 with autosomal dominant inheritance and variable penetrance. A second hit then raises endothelin (a vasoconstrictor) and lowers nitric oxide and prostacyclin (vasodilators), leading to vessel narrowing, smooth muscle growth, fibrosis, and clots in the small pulmonary arteries. MSD agrees that BMPR2 mutations cause 75% of heritable PAH, inherited as autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, describes higher endothelin-1 and thromboxane activity with lower prostacyclin and nitric oxide. Recent change: MSD defines pulmonary hypertension by a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mm Hg; your notes use the older cutoff of more than 25 mm Hg. The 48 mm Hg here fits both. MSD treats patients who respond to vasodilator testing with a calcium channel blocker, and otherwise uses oral endothelin-receptor antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan), PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogs, riociguat, and sotatercept.

whyWrong.b: Sildenafil blocks PDE5, raising cGMP to boost the nitric oxide pathway; it does not block a vasoconstrictor receptor (MSD Pulmonary Hypertension; standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Epoprostenol replaces the missing vasodilator prostacyclin rather than blocking a vasoconstrictor (MSD Pulmonary Hypertension).
whyWrong.d: Riociguat stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase (MSD Pulmonary Hypertension).
whyWrong.e: Calcium channel blockers are used only when vasodilator testing is positive, which it was not (MSD Pulmonary Hypertension).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Primary pulmonary hypertension, p. 109
MSD Manual Professional: Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is admitted with fever, a productive cough, and right-sided chest pain for 5 days. Chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate with a moderate pleural effusion. Thoracentesis shows cloudy fluid. Pleural fluid protein is 4.4 g/dL (serum 6.6 g/dL), and pleural fluid LDH is 520 U/L (serum 280 U/L; upper limit of normal 220 U/L).
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the formation of this effusion?

options.text: Leak of lymph from the thoracic duct

questions.explanation: Answer: increased capillary permeability from inflammation (an exudate). Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 123) explain that transudates are low in protein and clear, caused by high hydrostatic pressure (heart failure) or low oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis). Exudates are high in protein and cloudy, caused by inflammation that makes vessel walls leaky, as with cancer, pneumonia, collagen vascular disease, or trauma, and they must be drained because of the risk of infection. Chylothorax is milky fluid high in triglycerides from thoracic duct injury. MSD's Light's criteria call fluid an exudate when the pleural fluid to serum protein ratio is 0.5 or more, the LDH ratio is 0.6 or more, or fluid LDH is at least two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum. This fluid meets all three (protein ratio 0.67, LDH ratio 1.9). MSD names pneumonia, cancer, pulmonary embolism, and tuberculosis as the most common causes of exudates, and heart failure as the most common cause of transudates.

whyWrong.b: High hydrostatic pressure, as in heart failure, makes a low-protein transudate (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 123).
whyWrong.c: Low oncotic pressure, as in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis, also makes a transudate (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 123).
whyWrong.d: Thoracic duct leaks make milky fluid high in triglycerides (chylothorax) (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 123).
whyWrong.e: Ascites moving through the diaphragm (hepatic hydrothorax) makes a transudate in someone with cirrhosis (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Pleural effusions, p. 123
MSD Manual Professional: Pleural Effusion

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of pain in the upper right abdomen and nausea for 1 day. Blood pressure is 162/106 mm Hg. She has 2+ protein in her urine and tenderness under the right ribs. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, platelet count is 62,000/mm3, AST is 340 U/L, and LDH is 900 U/L. A blood smear shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes).
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Platelet transfusion and waiting until 37 weeks
Plasma exchange for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Oral labetalol and repeat labs in 1 week
Liver biopsy to find the cause of hepatitis

questions.explanation: Answer: give magnesium sulfate and deliver promptly (HELLP syndrome). Why: your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes (p. 81) describe HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) as a form of severe preeclampsia. Right upper abdominal pain comes from the swollen liver stretching its capsule, and the blood smear shows schistocytes. It is twice as common in women who have been pregnant before. Management is prompt delivery at any gestational age, IV magnesium sulfate to prevent seizures, continued for 24 hours after delivery, plus blood pressure drugs, and steroids may speed recovery of liver enzymes and platelets. Complications include DIC, abruption, fetal death, ascites, and liver rupture. MSD classifies HELLP as a severe form of preeclampsia, defines it by LDH of 600 IU/L or more, aminotransferases more than twice normal, and platelets below 100,000/µL, says it may present without hypertension or proteinuria in up to 15% of patients, says to deliver immediately once it is diagnosed, and gives magnesium sulfate to prevent seizures in preeclampsia with severe features.

whyWrong.b: Waiting puts the mother at risk of DIC, abruption, and liver rupture; HELLP calls for delivery at any gestational age (your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes, p. 81).
whyWrong.c: Plasma exchange treats TTP, which does not cause this pregnancy-linked picture of high blood pressure, protein in the urine, and liver injury (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Outpatient treatment with repeat labs delays the delivery that HELLP requires (your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes, p. 81).
whyWrong.e: A liver biopsy is not needed and is risky with low platelets (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials of Obstetrics (Emily's file), HELLP syndrome, p. 81
MSD Manual Professional: Preeclampsia and Eclampsia

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 0, at 8 weeks' gestation comes for her first prenatal visit. Her last two pregnancies ended at 19 and 20 weeks after painless cervical dilation and bulging membranes, with no contractions, bleeding, or infection. Five years ago she had a large cone biopsy of the cervix for high-grade dysplasia. Ultrasound shows a single healthy fetus.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Strict bed rest from 16 weeks onward

questions.explanation: Answer: a planned (history-indicated) cerclage at 13 to 14 weeks. Why: your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes (p. 56) define cervical insufficiency as a cervix that cannot hold a pregnancy to viability without contractions or labor. Causes include trauma from forceful dilation during second-trimester abortion, cervical tears from a rapid delivery, deep cervical conization, and DES exposure. With one or more unexplained second-trimester losses, serial transvaginal ultrasound of the cervix after 16-20 weeks can help, and an elective cerclage at 13-14 weeks is appropriate once ultrasound shows a normal fetus. A McDonald cerclage is removed at 36-37 weeks. MSD defines the condition as painless cervical dilation causing second-trimester loss, lists a prior cone biopsy (particularly when 1.7 to 2.0 cm or more of the cervix was removed) as a risk factor, and places a cerclage when the cervix is under 2.5 cm before 24 weeks in uncertain cases. Other source: MSD says a history-indicated cerclage is usually placed in the first trimester or before pregnancy.

whyWrong.b: Bed rest has not been shown to prevent loss from cervical insufficiency (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Tocolytics such as nifedipine stop contractions; cervical insufficiency happens without contractions (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Routine cultures do not fix a weak cervix; infection is excluded before an urgent cerclage (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Waiting for contractions misses the problem, because the cervix opens without them (your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes, p. 56).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials of Obstetrics (Emily's file), Cervical insufficiency, p. 56
MSD Manual Professional: Cervical Insufficiency

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 39 weeks' gestation in labor has a sudden gush of fluid as her membranes rupture. The fetus is in breech presentation. Within a minute, the fetal heart rate drops from 140/min to 70/min and stays there. On vaginal exam, a pulsating loop of umbilical cord is felt in the vagina.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Elevate the presenting part; urgent cesarean
Gently replace the cord back inside the uterus
Start oxytocin to speed vaginal delivery
Apply fundal pressure to deliver quickly
Continue monitoring and recheck in 1 hour

questions.explanation: Answer: lift the presenting part off the cord and proceed to immediate cesarean delivery. Why: your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes (p. 116) call umbilical cord prolapse an obstetric emergency, because cord compression cuts off fetal oxygen and can kill the fetus. Prolapse can be occult, partial, or complete. Risk factors are rupture of membranes when the presenting part is not snug against the cervix, and malpresentation. Management is to avoid holding the cord or pushing it back, place the patient in the knee-chest position, lift the presenting part, avoid touching the cord, and perform an immediate cesarean delivery. MSD agrees that overt prolapse occurs with ruptured membranes and is more common with breech presentation or a transverse lie, that monitoring may show severe bradycardia or severe variable decelerations, and that the presenting part should be gently lifted and held off the cord while cesarean delivery proceeds. MSD adds that changing the woman's position and a single dose of IV terbutaline may help.

whyWrong.b: Trying to push the cord back is advised against and wastes time (your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes, p. 116).
whyWrong.c: Oxytocin strengthens contractions, which squeeze the cord harder (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Fundal pressure pushes the fetus down onto the cord and is not safe here (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Persistent fetal bradycardia with a prolapsed cord needs action now, not observation (your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes, p. 116).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials of Obstetrics (Emily's file), Prolapsed umbilical cord, p. 116
MSD Manual Professional: Umbilical Cord Prolapse

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 29 weeks' gestation is admitted with preterm labor. She receives corticosteroids and a tocolytic drug. After 4 days of the tocolytic, ultrasound shows a lower amniotic fluid volume, and fetal echocardiography shows narrowing of the ductus arteriosus.
questions.leadIn: The tocolytic drug most likely acts by inhibiting which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: cyclooxygenase (indomethacin, a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor). Why: your El-Husseiny obstetrics notes (p. 68) explain that prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors such as indomethacin relax uterine muscle by lowering prostaglandin production. Side effects include oligohydramnios, closure of the ductus arteriosus before birth, and neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis, and they should not be used after 32 weeks. MSD agrees that tocolytics can usually delay labor at least 48 hours so that corticosteroids can be given, recommends a prostaglandin inhibitor only when the fetus is 32 weeks or less because these drugs may narrow or close the ductus arteriosus early, and warns of transient oligohydramnios and fetal kidney damage with more than 48 hours of use. MSD also advises IV magnesium sulfate before 32 weeks for fetal neuroprotection. The fetal ductus stays open because of prostaglandins, and the fetal kidney needs them for urine output (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Blocking L-type calcium channels is how nifedipine works; it does not narrow the ductus (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Oxytocin receptor blockers such as atosiban are not linked to ductal narrowing (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Magnesium sulfate, which blocks NMDA receptors, is given for fetal neuroprotection rather than causing ductal narrowing (MSD Preterm Labor; standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: PDE5 inhibitors are not tocolytics (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials of Obstetrics (Emily's file), Tocolytics, p. 68
MSD Manual Professional: Preterm Labor

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped his antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago comes to the emergency department because of headache, nausea, and fever for 2 weeks. Today his partner noticed he was confused. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 45/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a mildly increased leukocyte count with mostly lymphocytes, a high protein concentration, and a low glucose concentration. An India ink preparation of the fluid shows round budding yeasts, each surrounded by a wide clear zone.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following features of this organism is most responsible for the clear zone seen on this stain?

options.text: Mycolic acid in the cell wall

questions.explanation: Answer: a thick polysaccharide capsule (Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 196-197) explain that Cryptococcus causes disease in people with weak cell-mediated immunity, such as those with HIV, sarcoidosis, leukemia, or high-dose steroid use, and that meningitis is its most common presentation, with headache, nausea, vomiting, and confusion. The CSF shows low glucose, high protein, and a low leukocyte count with lymphocytes. India ink darkens the background but not the yeast, so the thick capsule shows up as a clear ring around each cell. The capsular antigen test (latex agglutination) is more sensitive and specific than the stain, and treatment is amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole. MSD agrees that cryptococcosis defines advanced HIV infection, usually with CD4 counts under 100/mcL, that India ink shows the capsule as a halo, and that the capsular antigen lateral flow assay has sensitivity and specificity above 99%. MSD gives liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine for the first 2 weeks, then oral fluconazole for 8 weeks.

whyWrong.b: Mycolic acid makes Mycobacterium tuberculosis acid-fast; it does not cause a clear zone on India ink (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Pseudohyphae and germ tubes point to Candida albicans, which rarely causes meningitis in this setting (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Spherules with endospores are the tissue form of Coccidioides, which is linked to the US Southwest (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Septate hyphae branching at acute angles are Aspergillus, a mold rather than a budding yeast (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Cryptococcus neoformans, pp. 196-197
MSD Manual Professional: Cryptococcosis

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of constipation for 4 days and poor feeding for 2 days. His mother says his suck and cry have become weak. His grandmother has been dipping his pacifier in honey. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). He has drooping eyelids, a weak gag, poor head control, and low muscle tone in all four limbs.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this infant's weakness?

options.text: Blocked acetylcholine release from nerve endings
Blocked glycine release from spinal inhibitory neurons
Loss of anterior horn cells from a viral infection
Demyelination of peripheral nerves after an infection

questions.explanation: Answer: blocked release of acetylcholine from nerve endings (infant botulism). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 70-72) explain that infant botulism usually comes from eating C. botulinum spores, for example in honey (more than 12% of honey samples contain spores). The spores germinate in the infant's gut, which does not yet have competing flora, and the bacteria make toxin there. Adult botulism, by contrast, comes from eating toxin already made in canned food. It affects babies aged 2 weeks to 6 months, with constipation, a weak suck, and general weakness, and severe cases look 'floppy'. The toxin acts at the neuromuscular junction to block acetylcholine release, and like tetanus toxin it cleaves SNARE proteins. Almost all infants recover. MSD agrees that most infant cases come from swallowed spores, typically in honey, with toxin made in the gut, and that the toxin irreversibly blocks acetylcholine release at peripheral nerve endings. MSD treats infant botulism types A and B with human botulinum immune globulin (BabyBIG).

whyWrong.b: Antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, which is not caused by eating honey (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Blocking glycine and GABA release from inhibitory neurons is how tetanus toxin causes spastic paralysis, not floppiness (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 68).
whyWrong.d: Poliovirus destroys anterior horn cells and causes asymmetric flaccid weakness with fever, not constipation and bulbar weakness after honey (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness after an infection and is rare at this age (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Clostridium tetani and C. botulinum, pp. 68, 70-72
MSD Manual Professional: Botulism

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever, headache, and confusion for 2 days. This morning she said she smelled burning rubber and then had a generalized seizure. She has trouble understanding speech. She takes no medications. MRI of the brain shows swelling of the right temporal lobe. Cerebrospinal fluid shows increased lymphocytes, many red blood cells, and a high protein concentration.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: HSV-1 (herpes simplex virus type 1), causing encephalitis. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 248-250) explain that HSV-1 stays latent in the trigeminal ganglion and that, among sporadic (non-epidemic) encephalitis, HSV-1 is the leading cause of death. The virus reaches the brain along the olfactory tract or after reactivation in the trigeminal ganglion. Patients have headache, fever, mental status changes, and seizures, and temporal lobe damage can cause receptive aphasia and personality changes. Imaging shows a swollen temporal lobe with bleeding and tissue death (hemorrhagic necrosis), the diagnosis is made by CSF PCR, and untreated mortality is 70%. MSD agrees that most cases are due to HSV-1, notes that olfactory seizures with foul smells point to temporal lobe involvement, and describes MRI edema in the orbitofrontal and temporal areas. MSD explains that hemorrhagic necrosis puts red blood cells into the CSF, calls CSF PCR particularly sensitive and specific, and starts IV acyclovir promptly, usually for 14 days.

whyWrong.b: Enteroviruses are a common cause of viral meningitis, which usually lacks focal temporal lobe signs and bloody CSF (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Pneumococcal meningitis gives a CSF with many neutrophils and low glucose, not a focal temporal lobe lesion (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: West Nile virus is spread by mosquitoes and can cause encephalitis with flaccid weakness, but it does not favor the temporal lobe (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in people with weak immunity, with slow white-matter damage and no fever (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Herpes simplex virus, pp. 248-250
MSD Manual Professional: Encephalitis

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of high fever, cough, and watery diarrhea for 3 days. He returned from a cruise 5 days ago. He smokes and has COPD. He is confused. His temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F). Serum sodium is 128 mEq/L. A chest x-ray shows consolidation of the right lower lobe. A sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils but few organisms.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: a urine antigen test for Legionella pneumophila. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 116-117) describe Legionella as a gram-negative rod that stains poorly on Gram stain, lives in water (air conditioning systems, hot water tanks), and spreads by aerosols. It grows inside cells, so cell-mediated immunity matters, and it is cultured on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with cysteine and iron. Suspect it after a cruise or hotel stay when pneumonia comes with fever above 39°C, confusion, and diarrhea, especially in smokers and people with chronic lung disease. Hyponatremia is common and thought to come from inappropriate ADH or kidney tubule damage. The sputum shows many neutrophils but few organisms, the diagnosis is most often made by urine antigen, and treatment is levofloxacin or azithromycin. MSD agrees that infection comes from inhaling aerosols of contaminated water, is more frequent and severe in smokers, people with COPD, and older adults, and causes diarrhea, confusion, and hyponatremia. MSD notes the urine antigen test detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1, and treats with a respiratory fluoroquinolone or azithromycin.

whyWrong.b: Cold agglutinins point to Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which causes a milder 'walking pneumonia' in young adults (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 170).
whyWrong.c: An acid-fast stain looks for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which causes a slower illness with weight loss and upper lobe disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The heterophile (Monospot) test diagnoses Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 254).
whyWrong.e: Cryptococcal antigen is tested in suspected Cryptococcus infection, usually meningitis in people with advanced HIV (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, pp. 196-197).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Legionella, pp. 116-117
MSD Manual Professional: Legionella Infections

questions.stem: A 19-year-old military recruit comes to the physician because of a sore throat, low-grade fever, tiredness, and a dry, hacking cough for 10 days. Several others in his barracks have similar symptoms. He looks well. Chest x-ray shows patchy interstitial infiltrates in both lower lobes that look worse than expected from his exam. When a sample of his blood in an EDTA tube is placed on ice, the red cells clump, and the clumps disappear when the tube is warmed.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains why amoxicillin would not treat this infection?

options.text: The organism has no cell wall
The organism lives only inside cells
The organism has altered penicillin-binding proteins
The organism pumps the drug out of the cell

questions.explanation: Answer: the organism has no cell wall (Mycoplasma pneumoniae). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 169-170) explain that mycoplasmas are the smallest free-living bacteria and have no peptidoglycan cell wall, so beta-lactam drugs do not work and the organisms do not show up on Gram stain. They are the only bacteria with sterols in their cell membrane. They spread by droplets among people in close contact, such as families, military recruits, and medical school classes, and attach to airway cells with the P1 protein. They cause 'walking pneumonia' with a persistent dry cough, and the x-ray looks worse than the patient. Cross-reacting IgM antibodies (cold agglutinins) clump red cells in the cold, which can be shown at the bedside with an EDTA tube and ice, and can cause mild hemolysis. MSD agrees that mycoplasmas lack a cell wall, so drugs that target cell-wall synthesis, such as penicillins and cephalosporins, are ineffective, and describes outbreaks in congregate settings such as schools and summer camps. MSD also explains that cold agglutinins are almost always IgM and react below 37°C, and lists mycoplasmal pneumonia as a cause of cold agglutinin disease.

whyWrong.b: Beta-lactamase production explains penicillin resistance in organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, which have a cell wall to target (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Obligate intracellular bacteria include Chlamydia and Rickettsia; Mycoplasma is extracellular (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, pp. 162, 169).
whyWrong.d: Altered penicillin-binding proteins explain MRSA and resistant pneumococci, not organisms that have no cell wall at all (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Efflux pumps are a common cause of tetracycline resistance, not the reason beta-lactams fail here (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Mycoplasma, pp. 169-170
MSD Manual Professional: Mycoplasmas
MSD Manual Professional: Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia

questions.stem: Public health officials identify a new influenza A strain whose hemagglutinin and neuraminidase are unlike those of any strain that has circulated in people. Genetic testing suggests it arose in a pig that was infected with a human influenza A strain and a swine influenza A strain at the same time. Within months it spreads worldwide and makes many young adults ill, because few people have antibodies against it.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following processes most likely produced this strain?

options.text: Point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene
Transduction of genes by a phage

questions.explanation: Answer: reassortment of genome segments (antigenic shift). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (p. 296) explain that the influenza genome is segmented, so when one cell is infected with two different strains, some new virions carry a mix of segments from both. This antigenic shift happens only in influenza A, for example when human and swine influenza A viruses reassort, and it makes a new virus that the population has no immunity to, which is what causes pandemics. Yearly epidemics are caused by both influenza A and B. Influenza also damages the airway lining, so bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) often follows. MSD defines antigenic drift as minor, progressive mutations in existing H and NA antigens and antigenic shift as a rare, abrupt, major change from new combinations of H and/or NA that arises from reassortment of the viral genome. MSD explains that shift can cause pandemics because antibodies against other strains give little protection, and that hemagglutinin binds host sialic acid while neuraminidase removes it so new virions can leave the cell.

whyWrong.b: Point mutations in hemagglutinin cause antigenic drift, the small yearly changes behind seasonal epidemics, not a brand-new H and N (MSD Influenza).
whyWrong.c: Phenotypic mixing swaps coat proteins for one generation without changing the genome, so it cannot create a lasting new strain (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Complementation lets one virus supply a missing protein for another, but neither genome changes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Transduction moves bacterial genes by bacteriophage; it does not occur between influenza viruses (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Influenza virus, p. 296
MSD Manual Professional: Influenza

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who injects drugs comes to the physician for follow-up. Two months ago he had fatigue, dark urine, and jaundice. He now feels better, and his jaundice has faded. Serum ALT has fallen from 1,450 U/L to 210 U/L. Tests show: HBsAg negative; anti-HBs negative; IgM anti-HBc positive; IgM anti-HAV negative; anti-HCV negative.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes this patient's hepatitis B status?

options.text: Acute infection in the window period
Resolved infection from many years ago

questions.explanation: Answer: acute hepatitis B infection in the window period. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 303-304) explain that people who inject drugs are at high risk and that more than 95% of infected adults have an acute illness that resolves. HBsAg is the first marker and stays positive through the symptomatic phase. Anti-HBs appears after vaccination or after HBsAg clears and lasts for life, but there is a gap between HBsAg disappearing and anti-HBs appearing, called the window period. IgM anti-HBc is present during that window, which makes it the most specific marker of acute hepatitis B, while IgG anti-HBc means past or chronic infection. HBeAg means active replication and high infectivity. MSD agrees that HBsAg appears during the incubation period and disappears during convalescence, that anti-HBs appears weeks or months later after recovery, and that IgM anti-HBc is a sensitive marker of acute infection that is occasionally the only marker, reflecting the window between loss of HBsAg and appearance of anti-HBs.

whyWrong.b: Vaccination gives anti-HBs alone, because the vaccine contains only HBsAg; this patient has no anti-HBs (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 304; standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Chronic infection keeps HBsAg positive, with IgG rather than IgM anti-HBc (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 304).
whyWrong.d: An old resolved infection shows anti-HBs with IgG anti-HBc, not IgM anti-HBc (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 304).
whyWrong.e: A person never infected or vaccinated has no hepatitis B markers, but this patient has IgM anti-HBc (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Hepatitis B virus, pp. 303-304
MSD Manual Professional: Hepatitis B, Acute

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who has taken omeprazole for reflux for 6 years comes to the emergency department because of sudden, painless, profuse watery diarrhea for 1 day. She returned 2 days ago from a trip to an area with a cholera outbreak. Her stools are gray and cloudy with flecks of mucus. Her blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg and pulse is 124/min. Stool microscopy shows no leukocytes or red blood cells, and culture grows curved, gram-negative, oxidase-positive rods. Her husband ate the same meals and is well.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following most likely made her more susceptible than her husband?

options.text: Reduced gastric acid killing of bacteria
Recent antibiotic loss of normal colonic flora
Low serum IgA from a primary defect
Absent spleen after an old injury
Reduced bile salt secretion with age

questions.explanation: Answer: less stomach acid to kill the bacteria (Vibrio cholerae). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 122-123) describe V. cholerae as a comma-shaped, oxidase-positive, gram-negative rod with 'shooting star' motility. It is sensitive to stomach acid, so a large dose (more than 10^7 organisms) is normally needed to cause disease, but with achlorhydria, including achlorhydria from long-term proton pump inhibitor use such as omeprazole, very few organisms are needed. The toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs, raising cAMP and pushing chloride and water into the gut. This causes sudden, massive 'rice-water' diarrhea that can lead to shock. Because the bacteria do not invade the gut wall, stool microscopy shows no leukocytes or red cells, and prompt oral rehydration is needed. MSD agrees that hypochlorhydria and achlorhydria, including from acid-suppressing drugs, predispose to cholera, that the toxin makes the small bowel secrete large amounts of isotonic fluid, that stools are often white liquid without fecal matter (rice-water stool), and that few or no white cells are found because the organisms do not invade. MSD treats mild cases with oral rehydration solution.

whyWrong.b: Antibiotics that kill normal colonic flora raise the risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis, not cholera (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Selective IgA deficiency is often silent and is classically linked to Giardia, not to cholera after a shared meal (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: An absent spleen raises the risk from encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus and Salmonella, not Vibrio cholerae (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 139).
whyWrong.e: Lower bile salt output is not a known risk factor for cholera (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Vibrio cholerae, pp. 122-123
MSD Manual Professional: Cholera

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, headache, abdominal pain, and constipation for 9 days. His fever has risen a little each day. He returned 10 days ago from visiting relatives in South Asia. His temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F) and pulse is 78/min. Faint pink spots that fade with pressure are seen on his abdomen, and the tip of his spleen is palpable. Leukocyte count is 3,800/mm3. Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains how this organism spreads through the body?

options.text: It invades only the intestinal lining cells
It spreads from cell to cell using actin tails
It travels along nerves to reach the brain
It stays on the gut surface and makes a toxin

questions.explanation: Answer: it survives inside macrophages (Salmonella Typhi, typhoid fever). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 137-139) explain that typhoid fever is caused only by Salmonella Typhi or Paratyphi and, in developed countries, is suspected after travel to Asia, Africa, or Latin America. The bacteria cross the gut lining through enterocytes and the M cells over Peyer patches, are taken up by macrophages, and survive inside them. The macrophages carry them to the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, causing hepatosplenomegaly and bacteremia. Early symptoms are mild cramping with fever and diarrhea or constipation, followed by salmon-colored 'rose spots'. Inflammation of Peyer patches can cause bleeding or perforation, and bacteria that settle in the gallbladder can make a person a chronic carrier. The Vi capsule helps the bacteria resist phagocytosis. MSD agrees that typhoid in the US occurs mainly in returning travelers, describes pink, blanching rose spots in crops on the chest and abdomen, prolonged fever with relative bradycardia, early constipation, splenomegaly, and leukopenia, and notes hemorrhage or perforation, usually of the distal ileum. MSD adds that about 3% of untreated patients become gallbladder carriers and that blood cultures are usually positive only in the first 2 weeks.

whyWrong.b: Nontyphoidal Salmonella invade the intestinal lining cells rather than macrophages and cause gastroenteritis, not a 9-day fever with rose spots (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 137).
whyWrong.c: Actin-tail spread from cell to cell is how Listeria and Shigella move, not Salmonella Typhi (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Travel along nerves to the brain is typical of rabies virus and herpesviruses, not a bacterium causing fever and splenomegaly (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Staying on the gut surface and making a toxin describes Vibrio cholerae, which causes watery diarrhea without bacteremia (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 123).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Salmonella, pp. 137-139
MSD Manual Professional: Typhoid Fever

questions.topic: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli and hemolytic uremic syndrome
questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she is pale and has passed very little urine for 1 day. One week ago, 3 days after eating a hamburger at a county fair, she had abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhea with little fever, which has since stopped. She has scattered petechiae. Hemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL, platelet count is 38,000/mm3, and serum creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL. A blood smear shows many fragmented red cells.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her illness?
questions.explanation: Answer: Escherichia coli O157:H7 (enterohemorrhagic E. coli) causing hemolytic uremic syndrome. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (p. 145) explain that enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), also called Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, makes a Shiga-like toxin that inactivates the 60S ribosomal subunit, stopping protein synthesis and killing cells. EHEC causes bloody diarrhea without invading the gut wall and can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). HUS is the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, low platelets from consumption, and kidney failure. O157:H7 is the most common strain, outbreaks have come from undercooked beef (hamburger), and this strain does not ferment sorbitol. MSD agrees that EHEC makes Shiga toxin and causes bloody diarrhea, that fever is usually absent or low grade, and that outbreaks follow undercooked ground beef. MSD notes that up to 22% of cases, mostly in children under 5 and adults over 60, are complicated by HUS, that antibiotics have not been shown to prevent HUS, and that fluoroquinolones are suspected of raising toxin release and HUS risk.

whyWrong.b: Enterotoxigenic E. coli causes watery traveler's diarrhea through cAMP and cGMP toxins, not bloody diarrhea with HUS (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 145).
whyWrong.c: Salmonella Typhi causes typhoid fever, with a long fever, rose spots, and splenomegaly (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, pp. 137-138).
whyWrong.d: Vibrio cholerae causes massive watery rice-water diarrhea without blood (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 123).
whyWrong.e: Campylobacter jejuni causes bloody diarrhea with fever and is linked to Guillain-Barré syndrome, but it is not the classic cause of HUS (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Escherichia coli, p. 145
MSD Manual Professional: Infection by Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Other Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC)

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman comes to the clinic for routine screening. She has had a small amount of vaginal discharge for 2 weeks but no pain. She has had two new sexual partners this year and uses condoms inconsistently. Pelvic examination shows a friable cervix with yellow mucopurulent discharge. A Gram stain of the discharge shows neutrophils but no organisms. A nucleic acid amplification test is positive for an organism that cannot be grown on standard laboratory agar.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following features of this organism best explains why it cannot be grown on standard agar?

options.text: It must use ATP from host cells
It needs cholesterol in its medium
It needs charcoal yeast with iron
It grows only at 42 degrees C
It requires factors X and V

questions.explanation: Answer: it must use ATP made by host cells (Chlamydia trachomatis). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 162-164) explain that chlamydiae are obligate intracellular bacteria that cannot make ATP and are not seen on Gram stain, because their cell wall lacks muramic acid. They have two forms. The elementary body is the small, metabolically inactive, infectious form that enters the cell by phagocytosis. Inside the cell it becomes a reticulate body, which divides by binary fission and then matures back into elementary bodies that are released when the cell bursts. Serotypes D through K cause urethritis and cervicitis, the most common bacterial STD in the US, and chronic or repeated infection can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy. MSD agrees that chlamydiae are obligate intracellular bacteria that depend on the host cell for 3 of their 4 nucleoside triphosphates and use host ATP directly for energy, and that the elementary body is the infectious form while the reticulate body is the replicative form. MSD adds that C. trachomatis causes most mucopurulent cervicitis, that women are usually asymptomatic, that NAAT is the preferred test, and that treatment is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 7 days.

whyWrong.b: A cholesterol-enriched medium is needed for Mycoplasma, which has sterols in its membrane but makes its own ATP (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, pp. 162, 169).
whyWrong.c: Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with cysteine and iron is used to grow Legionella (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 116).
whyWrong.d: Growth at 42°C on selective media is a feature of Campylobacter jejuni (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 118).
whyWrong.e: Factors X (hemin) and V (NAD+) are needed to grow Haemophilus influenzae (standard teaching).
