MSD Manual Professional: Chlamydiae
MSD Manual Professional: Urogenital Chlamydial Infections

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of vaginal itching, burning, and discharge for 1 week. The discharge is yellow-green, frothy, and smells fishy. She has one male sexual partner. Speculum examination shows small red spots on the cervix. A saline wet mount of the discharge, examined right away, shows motile, pear-shaped organisms with flagella.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Metronidazole for her and her partner
Fluconazole for her and her partner
Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for both of them
Acyclovir for her and her partner

questions.explanation: Answer: metronidazole for her and her sexual partner (trichomoniasis). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 216, 347) explain that Trichomonas vaginalis spreads by sexual contact and cannot live outside the body because it does not form cysts. It causes vaginitis with a foul-smelling, greenish discharge, itching, and burning, and should not be confused with bacterial vaginosis from Gardnerella vaginalis. Diagnosis is by seeing motile trophozoites on a wet mount, and the cervix can look like a 'strawberry'. Treatment is metronidazole for the patient and the partner. MSD agrees that women can have a copious, yellow-green, frothy discharge with a fishy odor, and that red 'strawberry' spots come from small bleeding points on the vaginal walls and cervix. MSD says the wet mount should be examined right away, because trichomonads may be motile then, and that NAATs are more sensitive than microscopy or culture in women. MSD treats women with metronidazole 500 mg by mouth twice a day for 7 days, and says recent sex partners should be seen and treated.

whyWrong.b: Fluconazole treats vulvovaginal candidiasis, which causes a thick, white discharge without a fishy odor (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Clindamycin cream treats bacterial vaginosis, and treating only her would let her partner reinfect her (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline treats gonorrhea and chlamydia, which do not show motile flagellated organisms on a wet mount (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Acyclovir treats genital herpes, which causes painful vesicles and ulcers rather than a frothy discharge (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Trichomonas vaginalis, pp. 216, 347
MSD Manual Professional: Trichomoniasis

questions.stem: A newborn boy is small for gestational age. Examination shows petechiae, jaundice, a small head, and an enlarged liver and spleen. He fails his newborn hearing screen, and an eye examination shows chorioretinitis. CT of the head shows calcifications lining the lateral ventricles. During the pregnancy, his mother had a week of fever, tiredness, and swollen glands, and a Monospot test at the time was negative.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: cytomegalovirus (congenital CMV infection). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 254, 257) explain that CMV spreads through saliva, sex, blood transfusion, and from mother to fetus, and is the most common infection passed in utero in the US. It is also the most common cause of a mononucleosis-like illness with a negative Monospot test. Congenital infection ranges from no visible problems to severe cytomegalic inclusion disease, with jaundice, a small head, an enlarged liver and spleen, purpura from low platelets ('blueberry muffin baby'), and brain damage. Babies can also have chorioretinitis, sensorineural deafness, periventricular calcifications, and seizures. MSD agrees that CMV is the most common congenital viral infection and lists microcephaly, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, periventricular calcifications, chorioretinitis, and sensorineural hearing loss. MSD diagnoses it by PCR of urine or saliva collected within the first 3 weeks of life, and notes that 6 months of oral valganciclovir modestly protects hearing and improves development.

whyWrong.b: Congenital toxoplasmosis also causes chorioretinitis, but its calcifications are scattered through the brain and it often causes hydrocephalus; it is linked to cat feces or undercooked meat (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Congenital rubella classically causes cataracts, deafness, and a patent ductus arteriosus (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Congenital syphilis causes a runny nose, a rash on the palms and soles, and bone changes, not periventricular calcifications (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy causes fetal anemia and hydrops fetalis, not periventricular calcifications (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 240).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus, pp. 254, 257
MSD Manual Professional: Congenital and Perinatal Cytomegalovirus Infection (CMV)

questions.stem: An 18-year-old college student comes to the physician because of fever, sore throat, and tiredness for 1 week. Two days ago he was given amoxicillin for presumed strep throat, and today he has an itchy red rash over his trunk and arms. His tonsils are enlarged with white exudate, the lymph nodes at the back of his neck are swollen, and the tip of his spleen is palpable. Leukocyte count is 14,000/mm3 with 55% lymphocytes. The blood smear shows many large lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm.
questions.leadIn: These large lymphocytes on his blood smear are most likely which of the following?

options.text: CD8+ T cells reacting to infected B cells
B cells infected with the virus

questions.explanation: Answer: CD8+ T cells reacting to infected B cells (Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 254-255) explain that EBV spreads through saliva and infects throat cells and B cells, binding to CD21 on B cells with its gp350 protein. Infected B cells are activated in large numbers and make heterophile antibodies, and this is followed by a strong T-cell response, which shows up as many atypical lymphocytes in the blood. Typical features are fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, an enlarged liver and spleen, atypical lymphocytes, and a positive Monospot test (IgM heterophile antibodies that clump horse red cells). Patients should avoid contact sports until the spleen shrinks because it can rupture, and amoxicillin can cause a typical maculopapular rash. MSD agrees that EBV infects B lymphocytes and that the atypical lymphocytes come mainly from CD8+ T cells responding to the infection, and notes that heterophile antibodies are present in only 50% of children aged 2 to 5. MSD advises avoiding heavy lifting and contact sports for 1 month and until the splenomegaly resolves. Recent change: MSD says the rash was once thought to be rare unless antibiotics such as ampicillin were given, but newer data suggest rash occurs in up to about 20% of patients and that antibiotics may not raise that rate further.

whyWrong.b: EBV does infect B cells, but the large atypical lymphocytes on the smear are mostly the CD8+ T cells responding to them (MSD Infectious Mononucleosis).
whyWrong.c: Activated monocytes do not make up the lymphocytosis of mononucleosis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Heterophile antibodies come from widespread B-cell activation, but the atypical cells on the smear are T cells (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 254).
whyWrong.e: Leukemic blasts would suggest leukemia, which does not follow a sore throat with an amoxicillin rash and usually lowers normal blood counts (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Epstein-Barr virus, pp. 254-255
MSD Manual Professional: Infectious Mononucleosis

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the physician because he has been very pale and tired for 4 days. One week ago he had a runny nose and a low-grade fever. He has no pain. His hemoglobin is 4.1 g/dL (his usual level is 8 g/dL), his reticulocyte count is 0.2% (his usual level is 12%), and his leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. His spleen is not palpable.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following cells is most likely infected by the cause of this crisis?

options.text: Splenic macrophages that trap red cells
Hematopoietic stem cells in the marrow

questions.explanation: Answer: erythroid (red cell) precursors in the bone marrow, infected by parvovirus B19 (transient aplastic crisis). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 239-240) explain that parvovirus B19 is the smallest DNA virus, has single-stranded DNA and no envelope, and spreads by the respiratory route. It enters red cell precursors through the P blood group antigen (globoside), and immature erythroid cells are the most vulnerable, so the virus mainly targets the bone marrow. B19 causes fifth disease, aplastic crisis in sickle cell anemia, and hydrops fetalis. In sickle cell disease, killing the red cell precursors cuts off the supply of reticulocytes needed to replace the short-lived sickle cells, so the hemoglobin falls while the reticulocyte count stays at or below the low end of normal. MSD agrees that parvovirus B19 is a single-stranded DNA virus that causes temporary suppression of red cell production, that transient aplastic crisis is usually seen in children with hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease, and that these children need a CBC and reticulocyte count. MSD adds that infection in pregnancy can cause severe fetal anemia with hydrops, with the highest risk of fetal death in the first half of pregnancy.

whyWrong.b: The P antigen is also found on megakaryocytes, but his platelet count is normal, and the problem is anemia with no reticulocytes, which points to red cell precursors (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, pp. 239-240).
whyWrong.c: Splenic sequestration causes a sudden drop in hemoglobin with an enlarging spleen and a high reticulocyte count (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Loss of erythropoietin-producing cells happens in chronic kidney disease and does not start suddenly after a cold (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Damage to hematopoietic stem cells (aplastic anemia) would lower white cells and platelets too, but his are normal (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Parvovirus B19, pp. 239-240
MSD Manual Professional: Erythema Infectiosum

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man from Connecticut comes to the physician because his right knee has been swollen for 3 weeks. The swelling has come and gone over the past month. Four months ago, after a hiking trip, he had a large red ring-shaped rash on his thigh that cleared in the center. Six weeks later, he had a left facial droop that went away on its own. He was not treated for either. The right knee is warm and swollen with a moderate effusion. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F).
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme arthritis). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 159-160) explain that this large spirochete is spread by Ixodes deer ticks, often during camping or hiking in New England, and moves from the skin through the blood to the heart, joints, and nervous system. Stage 1 is erythema migrans, a red, ring-shaped rash with central clearing that grows outward from the bite. Stage 2 brings carditis with AV block, facial nerve palsy (which can be bilateral), and moving joint and muscle pains. Stage 3 brings encephalopathy and chronic arthritis. The mnemonic is 'FACE': facial palsy, arthritis, cardiac block, and erythema migrans. Doxycycline is first line, with amoxicillin as an alternative and ceftriaxone for severe illness, CNS signs, or heart block. MSD agrees that I. scapularis carries Lyme disease in the northeastern and north central US, that erythema migrans is the first sign and the best clinical indicator, that Bell palsy can be bilateral, and that AV block can occur. MSD describes Lyme arthritis as intermittent swelling and pain in a few large joints, especially the knees, recurring for several years, and notes doxycycline is avoided in children under 8.

whyWrong.b: Disseminated gonococcal infection causes arthritis with tenosynovitis and skin pustules in sexually active people, not after a ring-shaped rash and facial palsy (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis is usually acute, very painful, and comes with high fever (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Rocky Mountain spotted fever causes fever with a rash that starts at the wrists and ankles; it does not cause months of knee swelling (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Syphilis causes a painless chancre and then a rash on the palms and soles, not erythema migrans (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Borrelia burgdorferi, pp. 159-160
MSD Manual Professional: Lyme Disease

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl with sickle cell disease is brought to the physician because of fever and pain in her left lower leg for 5 days. Her pain is not like her usual pain crises. Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F). The middle of the left tibia is swollen, warm, and very tender. MRI shows bone marrow edema with a small abscess. Blood cultures grow a motile gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose, is oxidase-negative, and makes hydrogen sulfide.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: Salmonella species (osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (p. 139) explain that blockage of small vessels in sickle cell disease causes repeated infarcts of the spleen, leaving it unable to work (functional asplenia). Without a working spleen, encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus, Neisseria, and Salmonella) are harder to clear, and the Salmonella Vi capsule protects it from phagocytosis. In sickle cell anemia, Salmonella leads the list of osteomyelitis causes, followed by E. coli and then S. aureus, because vaso-occlusive crises leave small areas of dead bone where bacteria can settle. Salmonella bacteremia can spread to bones, joints, lungs, and meninges. MSD agrees, listing Salmonella species as a cause of blood-borne osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease, liver disease, or weak immunity. The lab features in the stem (motile, non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, H2S-producing) are standard teaching for Salmonella.

whyWrong.b: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is oxidase-positive and causes osteomyelitis in people who inject drugs or after puncture wounds (MSD Osteomyelitis; standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: E. coli is the second most common cause in sickle cell disease, but it ferments lactose (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 139; standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive coccus in clusters, so it does not fit a gram-negative rod (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Pasteurella multocida infects tissues after cat or dog bites and is not linked to sickle cell disease (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Salmonella and sickle cell disease, p. 139
MSD Manual Professional: Osteomyelitis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a sore on her right index finger for 3 weeks. She works in a garden center and pricked the finger on a rosebush a few days before it began. The sore started as a red bump and then broke down into a painless ulcer. Over the past week, a line of firm red nodules has appeared up the back of her hand and forearm. She feels well otherwise.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the most likely cause?

options.text: Dimorphic fungus that forms cigar-shaped yeast
Weakly acid-fast branching filaments in soil
Acid-fast rod that grows best in cool water
Mold with septate hyphae branching at acute angles
Gram-negative rod spread by a cat scratch

questions.explanation: Answer: a dimorphic fungus that forms cigar-shaped yeast in tissue (Sporothrix schenckii). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (p. 185) explain that Sporothrix grows as a mold in nature, on the bark of trees, shrubs, garden plants, and plant debris, and as cigar-shaped yeast in tissue. It enters through breaks in the skin, often from a thorn prick, and spreads along the lymph channels, so sporotrichosis ('rose gardener's disease') is common in gardeners. The first lesion is a red nodule at the injury that later ulcerates, followed by nodules along the draining lymphatics. Biopsy shows a granuloma, diagnosis is by culture, and treatment is itraconazole or amphotericin B. MSD agrees that sporotrichosis is a skin infection caused by dimorphic fungi of the genus Sporothrix, which live on rose and barberry bushes, in sphagnum moss, hay, and mulch. MSD describes skin nodules that spread along the lymphatics and break down into ulcers ('sporotrichoid spread'), says culture of tissue gives the definitive diagnosis, and calls itraconazole the treatment of choice for lymphocutaneous disease.

whyWrong.b: Nocardia is weakly acid-fast and lives in soil; it more often causes lung or brain infection in people with weak immunity (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Mycobacterium marinum can also spread along lymphatics, but it comes from fish tanks or water, not a rose thorn (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Aspergillus is a mold with septate hyphae that mainly infects the lungs (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Bartonella henselae causes cat scratch disease with a papule and swollen regional lymph nodes after a cat scratch (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Sporothrix schenckii, p. 185
MSD Manual Professional: Sporotrichosis

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy who has not been vaccinated is brought to the physician because of fever for 4 days, a hacking cough, a runny nose, and red, watery eyes. Yesterday a red, blotchy rash began on his face in front of and below the ears and has spread down to his trunk. His temperature is 40.0°C (104°F). Tiny white spots on a red base are seen on the inside of his cheeks opposite the molars.
questions.leadIn: In addition to supportive care, which of the following should be given to lower this child's risk of complications and death?
questions.explanation: Answer: vitamin A (measles). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (p. 287) explain that measles (rubeola) is caused by a paramyxovirus. Its classic sign is Koplik spots, small white, bluish, or gray specks on the inside of the cheek next to the molars, like grains of sand on a red base. Koplik spots with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis (the '3 Cs') make measles likely, and a maculopapular rash then starts at the head and neck and spreads downward over 1-2 days. Vitamin A lowers measles deaths in malnourished or vitamin-deficient children, helps prevent eye damage (keratitis and corneal ulcers), and lowers the risk of pneumonia and encephalitis. Complications include encephalitis (about 1 in 1,000), giant cell pneumonia in people with weak immunity, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later, and measles is prevented by the live MMR vaccine. MSD agrees that the prodrome is fever, coryza, a hacking cough, and conjunctivitis, describes Koplik spots as grains of white sand with red rings opposite the upper molars, and says the rash starts on the face in front of and below the ears and spreads downward. Other source: MSD says vitamin A lowers measles illness and death and recommends it for all children with measles, not only those who are malnourished.

whyWrong.b: Acyclovir treats herpes simplex and varicella-zoster infections; it does not treat measles (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Aspirin is avoided in children with viral illnesses because of the risk of Reye syndrome (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Zinc is used for diarrhea in children and for zinc deficiency, not to lower measles deaths (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Penicillin does not act on viruses; antibiotics are used only if a bacterial infection follows (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Measles, p. 287
MSD Manual Professional: Measles

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man who moved from rural Bolivia 10 years ago comes to the physician because of shortness of breath with exertion and palpitations for 1 year. Last month he fainted once. For several years he has had trouble swallowing both solids and liquids. Echocardiography shows enlargement of all four chambers and an aneurysm at the left ventricular apex. A barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus that narrows at the lower end.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following was most likely the route of this patient's infection?

options.text: Insect feces rubbed into a bite wound
Bite of an infected female sand fly
Bite of a tsetse fly in East Africa
Bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito
Eating undercooked pork with larval cysts

questions.explanation: Answer: feces from a triatomine ('kissing') bug rubbed into a bite wound (Chagas disease from Trypanosoma cruzi). Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology notes (pp. 214-215) explain that T. cruzi is spread by the reduviid ('kissing') bug, which leaves infected feces at a painless bite, and is endemic in rural Central and South America. Inside cells the parasite becomes amastigotes that multiply in almost any tissue. The heart is hit hardest in the acute phase, with myocyte necrosis, fibrosis, and lymphocytic infiltrates, and one-sided swelling around the eye (Romaña sign) can appear. In the chronic phase the parasite destroys the nerve plexuses of the esophagus, colon, and ureters, causing achalasia, megacolon, and megaureter. Diagnosis is by finding trypomastigotes on a blood smear, and treatment is benznidazole or nifurtimox. MSD agrees that infected bugs leave feces with trypomastigotes on the skin while biting, that the infection is endemic in 21 Latin American countries, and that chronic cardiomyopathy often brings enlargement of all chambers and apical aneurysms, with heart failure, fainting, or sudden death from heart block or ventricular arrhythmia. MSD describes megaesophagus with dysphagia and megacolon with long periods of constipation, and notes benznidazole is generally better tolerated than nifurtimox.

whyWrong.b: Sand flies spread Leishmania, which causes kala-azar or skin ulcers, not cardiomyopathy with megaesophagus (your El-Husseiny microbiology notes, p. 215).
whyWrong.c: Tsetse flies spread Trypanosoma brucei, which causes African sleeping sickness, not Chagas disease (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria, which causes cyclic fevers and hemolysis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Eating undercooked pork with larval cysts spreads Taenia solium, which can cause cysticercosis (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Trypanosoma cruzi, pp. 214-215
MSD Manual Professional: Chagas Disease

questions.stem: A 1-day-old boy is evaluated because he does not move his right arm. He weighed 4.6 kg (10.1 lb) at birth, and the delivery was complicated by shoulder dystocia that needed strong sideways pulling on the head. His right arm lies against his side, turned inward at the shoulder, with the elbow straight and the forearm pronated. He grasps a finger firmly with both hands. The Moro reflex is absent on the right.
questions.leadIn: Injury to which of the following structures is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.text: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
Radial nerve in the spiral groove
Axillary nerve at the humeral neck
Long thoracic nerve on the chest wall

questions.explanation: Answer: the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (Erb palsy). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 24) describe Erb palsy as a stretch or tear of the upper trunk (C5-C6 roots), caused in babies by sideways pulling on the neck during delivery and in adults by trauma. The muscles that lose power explain the posture, often called the 'waiter's tip': without the deltoid and supraspinatus the arm cannot abduct and hangs at the side, without the infraspinatus it cannot rotate outward so it turns inward, and without the biceps the elbow stays straight and the forearm pronated. The hand muscles come from C8-T1, so the grasp is normal. Other source: MSD's Birth Injuries page describes Erb palsy as an upper plexus injury of C5 to C7 (one level lower than your notes), with the shoulder held in adduction and internal rotation and the forearm pronated. MSD links plexus injuries to sideways stretching of the neck during shoulder dystocia, and says treatment of Erb palsy is usually supportive, with physical therapy and protective positioning.

whyWrong.b: A lower trunk (C8-T1) injury, or Klumpke palsy, weakens the small muscles of the hand and causes a claw hand, so the grasp would be weak (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A radial nerve injury in the spiral groove causes wrist drop, with weak wrist and finger extension, and does not stop shoulder movement (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor, so it would not explain the straight elbow and pronated forearm (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 7).
whyWrong.e: The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior; injury causes a winged scapula, not this arm posture (standard teaching).

El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Axillary nerve, p. 7
MSD Manual Professional: Birth Injuries

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man comes to the emergency department after a rugby tackle forced his raised, outward-turned left arm backward. The left shoulder has lost its rounded outline, and there is a fullness at the front of the armpit. X-rays show the head of the humerus in front of and below the glenoid. After the shoulder is put back in place, he has numbness over a patch of skin on the outer upper arm, and he cannot raise his arm away from his side.
questions.leadIn: Weakness of which other muscle is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: teres minor, because the axillary nerve was injured. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 30) explain that the glenohumeral joint dislocates more often than any other joint because its socket is shallow, that most shoulder dislocations are anterior, and that they usually follow a blow to an arm that is abducted and turned outward. The axillary nerve is the nerve most often injured. It supplies the deltoid (abduction past about 15 degrees) and teres minor (outward rotation), and it carries feeling from the skin over the deltoid (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 7). Loss of the deltoid outline points to an anterior dislocation. MSD's Shoulder Dislocations page agrees that shoulder dislocations are anterior in at least 95% of patients, that the mechanism is abduction and external rotation, and that axillary nerve injury causes decreased sensation over the deltoid.

whyWrong.b: The supraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve, which is not the nerve that wraps around the humeral neck (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The serratus anterior is supplied by the long thoracic nerve; weakness causes a winged scapula (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The biceps is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, which carries feeling from the side of the forearm, not the shoulder (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve and is not affected by an axillary nerve injury (standard teaching).

questions.topic: Ulnar nerve injury at the elbow
questions.stem: A 41-year-old accountant comes to the physician because of tingling in his right little finger and the inner half of his ring finger for 2 months. He spends most of the day resting his elbows on a hard desk. On examination, the muscles between the bones on the back of his hand look thin, and pain shoots into his little finger when the back of the inner elbow is tapped. Sensation over the thumb and index finger is normal.
questions.leadIn: Weakness of which of the following movements is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Lifting the arm out to the side
Bending the thumb at its tip joint

questions.explanation: Answer: spreading the fingers apart, from an ulnar nerve injury at the elbow. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 19-21) explain that the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, where only a thin layer of soft tissue covers it (the 'funny bone'), so this is a common place for injury. In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, the medial two lumbricals, the adductor of the thumb, and all the interossei: the dorsal interossei spread the fingers apart and the palmar interossei bring them together. It carries feeling from the fifth digit and the inner half of the fourth. A lesion at the elbow weakens finger spreading and closing, and a distal lesion can cause an ulnar claw. MSD's Mononeuropathies page agrees that ulnar palsy at the elbow is often caused by trauma in the ulnar groove, causes a sensory deficit in the fifth digit and medial half of the fourth digit, and weakens the thumb adductor, fifth digit abductor, and interossei. MSD adds that severe chronic ulnar palsy causes a clawhand deformity.

whyWrong.b: Wrist extension comes from muscles supplied by the radial nerve; a radial injury causes wrist drop (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Elbow flexion comes mainly from the biceps and brachialis, supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Lifting the arm out to the side needs the deltoid, supplied by the axillary nerve (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 7).
whyWrong.e: Bending the thumb tip uses the flexor pollicis longus, supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has tripped over her right toes for 1 week. She has lost 14 kg (31 lb) over 4 months on a strict diet, and she often sits for hours with her right leg crossed over her left knee. She cannot lift her right foot or turn its sole outward. Pointing the foot downward and turning the sole inward are normal. Sensation is decreased over the top of the right foot. Ankle reflexes are normal.
questions.leadIn: Compression at which of the following sites most likely caused these findings?

options.text: Outer side of the neck of the fibula
Tarsal tunnel behind the medial ankle
L5 nerve root in the lower spine
Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
Sciatic nerve deep in the buttock

questions.explanation: Answer: the outer side of the fibular neck, where the common peroneal (fibular) nerve lies just under the skin. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 49-51) explain that the common peroneal nerve is the nerve most often injured in the leg because it wraps around the fibular neck close to the surface, and that pressure there (long surgery, leg crossing, a tight cast) or a fibular neck fracture can damage it. Its deep branch supplies the front of the leg (lifting the foot and toes) and its superficial branch supplies the outer compartment (turning the sole outward), and together they carry feeling from most of the top of the foot. Injury causes foot drop, a high-stepping gait, and numbness on top of the foot, while pointing the foot down and turning it inward still work because the tibial nerve is spared. MSD's Mononeuropathies page agrees that the nerve is typically compressed against the lateral aspect of the fibular neck, names emaciated bedbound patients and thin people who habitually cross their legs as the people most affected, and says it causes footdrop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion.

whyWrong.b: The tarsal tunnel holds the tibial nerve; compression causes burning and numbness of the sole, not foot drop (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: An L5 root lesion can cause foot drop, but it usually also weakens turning the sole inward and causes back pain spreading down the leg (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The tibial nerve controls pointing the foot down and turning it inward, which are normal here (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 51).
whyWrong.e: A sciatic nerve lesion would also weaken the hamstrings and the calf, so pointing the foot down and the ankle reflex would be affected (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Common peroneal (fibular) nerve, pp. 49-51
MSD Manual Professional: Mononeuropathies

questions.topic: Scaphoid fracture and its blood supply
questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman comes to the physician 2 days after she fell onto her outstretched right hand while skating. She has a dull ache on the thumb side of the wrist. There is tenderness in the hollow between the two thumb tendons on the back of the wrist. X-rays of the wrist show no fracture.
questions.leadIn: If this injury is not treated, which complication is she at greatest risk for?

options.text: Death of bone in the proximal pole
Median nerve compression at the wrist
Death of bone in the lunate
Ulnar nerve injury in Guyon's canal

questions.explanation: Answer: death of bone (avascular necrosis) in the proximal pole of the scaphoid. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 36) explain that the scaphoid, the biggest bone in the first row of carpal bones, is the most often fractured carpal bone, and that the usual cause is a fall on an outstretched hand. Persistent pain and tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox after a fall should suggest it. A branch of the radial artery enters near the distal pole, so blood reaches the proximal pole in a backward (retrograde) direction, and a fracture can easily cut it off. This puts the bone at risk of avascular necrosis and nonunion. MSD's Scaphoid (Navicular) Fractures page agrees that these fractures usually come from the wrist being bent back, typically in a fall on an outstretched hand, lists tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox as a sign, and says that only around 70% of these fractures show on the first x-rays, so a normal film does not rule it out. MSD notes that the fracture can disrupt the blood supply to the proximal scaphoid, so osteonecrosis is a common complication, and that many nondisplaced fractures are treated with a thumb spica cast for up to 6 to 8 weeks.

whyWrong.b: Median nerve compression is carpal tunnel syndrome, which causes numbness of the thumb side of the hand (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 39).
whyWrong.c: Avascular necrosis of the lunate (Kienböck disease) is a separate condition and does not follow from a scaphoid fracture (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Ulnar nerve injury in Guyon's canal is linked to a fracture of the hook of the hamate, on the little-finger side of the wrist (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 20).
whyWrong.e: The dinner-fork deformity is from a distal radius (Colles) fracture, which would usually show on x-ray (standard teaching).

questions.topic: Carpal tunnel syndrome: spared thenar sensation
questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because she wakes at night with burning and tingling in her right thumb, index finger, and middle finger. Shaking her hand helps. Tapping the front of the wrist reproduces the tingling, and so does holding both wrists fully bent for 1 minute. Sensation is decreased on the palm side of the first three fingers, but it is normal over the skin of the fleshy pad at the base of the thumb.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the normal sensation over the pad at the base of the thumb?

options.text: Its palmar cutaneous branch runs outside the tunnel
The recurrent motor branch carries this sensation
The ulnar nerve supplies the skin over the thenar area
The superficial radial nerve supplies this palm skin
Sensory fibers resist pressure better than motor ones

questions.explanation: Answer: the median nerve's palmar cutaneous branch reaches the hand outside the carpal tunnel. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 39) describe the carpal tunnel as the space between the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament), carrying the median nerve with the long finger flexor tendons. The syndrome is linked to pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism, diabetes, and dialysis-related amyloidosis. It causes pain and tingling in the median nerve area that is worse at night, Tinel and Phalen signs, and later thenar muscle wasting. Feeling over the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch enters the hand outside the tunnel. The median nerve normally carries feeling from the thenar eminence and the lateral three and a half fingers (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 14). MSD's Carpal Tunnel Syndrome page agrees that it is compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, lists pregnancy-induced edema, diabetes, hypothyroidism, and rheumatoid arthritis as risk factors, and describes waking at night with numbness and tingling. MSD adds that thenar atrophy and weak thumb opposition and abduction may develop late, and that treatment includes a lightweight neutral wrist splint, especially at night.

whyWrong.b: The recurrent branch of the median nerve is purely motor to the thenar muscles and carries no skin sensation (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 16).
whyWrong.c: The ulnar nerve carries feeling from the medial one and a half fingers and the hypothenar side, not the thenar pad (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 19).
whyWrong.d: The superficial radial nerve supplies the back of the hand near the thumb, not the thenar skin of the palm (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Nerve compression usually causes sensory symptoms early; thenar weakness tends to appear later, so this does not explain a spared patch (standard teaching).
