questions.stem: A boy born at term is deeply cyanotic 3 hours after birth. His mother has type 2 diabetes. His oxygen saturation is 62% and does not improve with 100% oxygen. There is no murmur. A chest x-ray shows an egg-shaped heart with a narrow upper mediastinum. Echocardiography shows that the aorta comes off the right ventricle while the pulmonary artery leaves the left ventricle.
questions.leadIn: Abnormal development of which of the following embryologic processes most likely caused this condition?

options.text: Spiral growth of the aorticopulmonary septum
Fusion of the endocardial cushions in the AV canal
Forward shift of the infundibular septum
Division of the truncus into two vessels
Closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth

questions.explanation: Answer: spiral growth of the aorticopulmonary septum (transposition of the great arteries). Why: your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes (pp. 6-7) explain that in the fifth week, ridges in the truncus twist around each other to form a spiral aorticopulmonary septum, which divides the truncus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Neural crest cells moving into the endocardial cushions help build this septum. If the septum grows straight instead of spiraling, the aorta comes off the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk off the left ventricle. Your notes group this with tetralogy of Fallot and persistent truncus arteriosus as cyanotic defects tied to failed neural crest migration. MSD's TGA page agrees on the anatomy, explaining that it creates independent, parallel pulmonary and systemic circulations, so the baby survives only if blood mixes through openings between the two sides. MSD notes that severe cyanosis occurs within hours of birth, that murmurs may be absent, and that the chest x-ray may show an egg-on-a-string shape with a narrow upper mediastinum. Treatment is a PGE1 infusion to keep the ductus open, balloon atrial septostomy if needed, and an arterial switch operation typically done during the first week of life.

whyWrong.b: Failed fusion of the endocardial cushions causes atrioventricular septal defects, linked to Down syndrome, which are not cyanotic at first (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Forward (anterosuperior) shift of the infundibular septum causes tetralogy of Fallot, which usually has a harsh pulmonic stenosis murmur and a boot-shaped heart (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Complete failure to divide the truncus gives persistent truncus arteriosus, one vessel leaving both ventricles, not two switched vessels (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, p. 6).
whyWrong.e: Closure of the ductus is normal after birth; in transposition it makes cyanosis worse, which is why PGE1 is given, but it is not the cause (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, p. 10).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Cardiovascular System (Emily's file), Septation of the truncus arteriosus, pp. 6-7
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Cardiovascular System (Emily's file), Fetal-postnatal derivatives, p. 10
MSD Manual Professional: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA)

questions.stem: A girl born at 28 weeks' gestation is 5 days old in the neonatal intensive care unit. She now needs more oxygen. Her pulses are bounding, and her pulse pressure is wide. A continuous murmur is heard best below the left clavicle at the upper left sternal border. Echocardiography shows blood flowing from the aorta into the pulmonary artery through a fetal vessel that has not closed.
questions.leadIn: This vessel develops from which of the following embryologic structures?
questions.explanation: Answer: the left sixth aortic arch, which forms the ductus arteriosus. Why: your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes (pp. 10-11) explain that each pharyngeal arch has its own aortic arch: the third forms the common carotid and proximal internal carotid arteries, the fourth forms part of the aortic arch on the left and the proximal right subclavian artery on the right, and the sixth forms the proximal pulmonary arteries and, on the left only, the ductus arteriosus. In the fetus the ductus lets blood skip the lungs by flowing from the pulmonary artery to the aorta. It normally closes after birth as oxygen rises and prostaglandin E2 falls, and it then becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. If it stays open, blood shunts left to right. Indomethacin (a prostaglandin blocker) can close it, while prostaglandin E1 or E2 keeps it open. MSD's PDA page agrees that PDA is very common among preterm infants, that the rise in PaO2 and fall in prostaglandins close it, and that with no other defects the shunt is left to right, from aorta to pulmonary artery. MSD describes a continuous murmur heard best at the upper left sternal border with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure, and lists indomethacin or ibuprofen to close it.

whyWrong.b: The left fourth arch forms part of the true aortic arch (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, p. 11).
whyWrong.c: The third arches form the common carotid and proximal internal carotid arteries (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, pp. 10-11).
whyWrong.d: The second arches form the stapedial and hyoid arteries, which mostly regress (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, pp. 10-11).
whyWrong.e: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis; the ductus venosus, not the ductus arteriosus, links it to the IVC (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, p. 10, and standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Cardiovascular System (Emily's file), Fetal-postnatal derivatives and aortic arch derivatives, pp. 10-11
MSD Manual Professional: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)

questions.topic: Right coronary artery: inferior MI with bradycardia
questions.stem: A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of crushing chest pain for 1 hour. He is sweaty and lightheaded. His pulse is 42/min and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with sinus bradycardia. Coronary angiography shows that the posterior descending artery arises from the vessel that is blocked.
questions.leadIn: Occlusion of which of the following arteries most likely explains both the ECG changes and the slow heart rate?
questions.explanation: Answer: the right coronary artery. Why: your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes (pp. 18-19) explain that the right coronary artery gives off the sinoatrial (SA) nodal artery as one of its first branches, so a blockage can cause bradycardia or heart block. In most people it ends as the posterior descending artery, which feeds the bulk of the left ventricle's underside (inferior wall), the back third of the septum, and the AV node. Your notes say the posterior descending artery comes from the right coronary artery in 85% of people (right dominance), the circumflex does in about 8% (left dominance), and both do in about 7%. The LAD supplies the front wall and front two-thirds of the septum and is the most common site of blockage. StatPearls' Inferior Myocardial Infarction page agrees that leads II, III, and aVF show the inferior wall, and that heart block and bradycardia may occur because the right coronary artery perfuses the SA node and the AV node. StatPearls adds that if the right ventricle is also infarcted, nitrates should be avoided and fluids given, because these patients depend on preload. Other source: StatPearls puts the right coronary share at 80%, with the circumflex supplying the inferior wall in the other 20%, slightly different from the figures in your notes.

whyWrong.b: The LAD supplies the front wall and apex, so its blockage gives ST elevation in the front (precordial) leads, not II, III, and aVF (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, p. 19).
whyWrong.c: The circumflex supplies the lateral wall and gives rise to the posterior descending artery only in left-dominant hearts; here the blocked vessel gives rise to the posterior descending artery and the SA node is affected (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, pp. 18-19).
whyWrong.d: A left main blockage affects both the LAD and circumflex areas and usually causes shock with widespread ECG changes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Diagonal branches come off the LAD and supply the anterolateral wall (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Cardiovascular System (Emily's file), Arterial supply of the heart, pp. 18-19
StatPearls: Inferior Myocardial Infarction

questions.topic: Left atrial enlargement in mitral stenosis (Ortner syndrome)
questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman who moved from rural Nepal 3 years ago comes to the physician because of a hoarse voice for 2 months and shortness of breath when climbing stairs. She had joint pains and fever as a child. Auscultation shows a sharp sound soon after S2, followed by a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur best heard at the apex. Laryngoscopy shows a paralyzed left vocal cord.
questions.leadIn: Pressure from which enlarged heart chamber most likely explains her hoarseness?
questions.explanation: Answer: the left atrium. Why: your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes (pp. 14-15) explain that the left atrium forms most of the back (posterior) surface of the heart, with the esophagus right behind it. That is why transesophageal echo shows the left atrium and mitral valve so well. Conditions that enlarge the left atrium, such as mitral stenosis or atrial fibrillation, can press on the esophagus and cause trouble swallowing, or squeeze the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (which comes from the vagus) and cause hoarseness. The front surface is mostly the right ventricle, the right border is the right atrium, and the left border and apex are the left ventricle. MSD's Mitral Stenosis page agrees that the usual cause is rheumatic fever, that left atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation, and that hoarseness can come from compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by a dilated left atrium or pulmonary artery (Ortner syndrome). MSD describes an early diastolic opening snap followed by a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur heard best at the apex.

whyWrong.b: The left ventricle is not under extra load in pure mitral stenosis, because less blood reaches it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The right atrium forms the right border of the heart, away from the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, p. 14).
whyWrong.d: The right ventricle forms the front surface of the heart, far from the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (your El-Husseiny cardiovascular notes, p. 14).
whyWrong.e: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch, not the ascending aorta; and a dilated aorta is not part of mitral stenosis (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Cardiovascular System (Emily's file), Surface projections of the heart, pp. 14-15
MSD Manual Professional: Mitral Stenosis

questions.stem: A boy born at 37 weeks' gestation has frothy saliva in his mouth and coughs, chokes, and turns blue during his first feeding. The pregnancy was complicated by too much amniotic fluid. A feeding tube cannot be passed more than 10 cm beyond the lips. A chest and abdominal x-ray shows the tube coiled in the upper chest and air in the stomach and bowel.
questions.leadIn: Abnormal development of which of the following structures most likely caused this condition?

options.text: Neural crest cells of the bowel wall

questions.explanation: Answer: the tracheoesophageal septum. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 2) explain that the respiratory system starts in the fourth week as a single outpouching of endoderm from the front of the foregut. The trachea and foregut are open to each other at first, and a mesodermal wall, the tracheoesophageal septum, grows to separate them. Faulty growth of this septum leaves an abnormal opening between the trachea and esophagus (a tracheoesophageal fistula). Air in the stomach on x-ray tells you the lower esophagus is connected to the trachea (standard teaching). MSD's Esophageal Atresia page agrees that the anomaly is usually suspected before birth because of polyhydramnios, and that typical signs are excessive secretions, coughing and cyanosis after attempts at feeding, and aspiration pneumonia. MSD says the diagnosis is made when a nasogastric or orogastric tube cannot be passed into the stomach and by x-ray, notes that a distal fistula causes abdominal distention, and says about 20% of these infants meet criteria for VACTERL.

whyWrong.b: Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membranes causes congenital diaphragmatic hernia, with bowel in the chest and breathing trouble, not choking at feeds (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A thickened pyloric muscle causes projectile vomiting at 2 to 6 weeks of age, not choking with the first feed (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Failure of the third and fourth pouches causes DiGeorge syndrome, with a missing thymus and parathyroids (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Failed migration of neural crest cells into the bowel causes Hirschsprung disease, with delayed passage of meconium (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Lung development, p. 2
MSD Manual Professional: Esophageal Atresia

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has a large right pleural effusion. A trainee inserts a thoracentesis needle at the back of the chest, one space below the top of the fluid, aiming just under the lower edge of the rib above. Within minutes the man becomes pale, his blood pressure falls to 88/52 mm Hg, and repeat ultrasound shows fresh blood collecting in the pleural space.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following structures was most likely injured?

options.text: Intercostal artery in the costal groove
Internal thoracic artery behind the sternum
Inferior vena cava below the diaphragm
Right subclavian artery above the first rib
Azygos vein along the vertebral bodies

questions.explanation: Answer: an intercostal artery running in the groove under the rib. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (pp. 13-14) explain that the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove along the lower edge of each rib, so a thoracentesis needle is placed at the lower part of the intercostal space, just over the upper border of the rib below. Fluid collects in the costodiaphragmatic recess when the patient is upright, and your notes give safe lower limits for the needle at different lines on the chest so that abdominal organs such as the liver are not hit. MSD's How To Do Thoracentesis page agrees that the needle must be placed over the upper edge of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle at the lower edge, which includes the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve. MSD places the needle in the mid-scapular line one intercostal space below the top of the effusion, and lists pneumothorax and hemothorax from damaged intercostal vessels among the major complications.

whyWrong.b: The internal thoracic arteries run just beside the sternum at the front of the chest, far from a posterior needle site (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Going too low risks abdominal organs, but this needle was placed one space below the fluid level, and the IVC lies deep in the middle of the body (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, pp. 13-14).
whyWrong.d: The subclavian artery lies above the first rib near the base of the neck, nowhere near a low posterior thoracentesis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The azygos vein lies in the posterior mediastinum next to the spine, deep to the pleura and medial to a normal needle site (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Pleura and thoracentesis, pp. 13-14
MSD Manual Professional: How To Do Thoracentesis

questions.topic: Phrenic nerve: referred shoulder pain from the pleura
questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had fever and cough for 4 days. Today she has a sharp pain at the tip of her right shoulder that gets worse when she breathes in deeply. She has no injury, and moving the shoulder does not change the pain. A chest x-ray shows pneumonia in the lower part of the right lower lobe, touching the center of the right side of the diaphragm.
questions.leadIn: Pain fibers from the irritated area enter the spinal cord at which of the following levels?
questions.explanation: Answer: C3 to C5, through the phrenic nerve. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 13) explain that the parietal pleura has somatic nerves, so its pain is sharp and easy to localize, while the visceral pleura does not feel pain. The phrenic nerve, from the C3-C5 roots, moves the diaphragm and also brings pain signals from the pleura covering the diaphragm and the mediastinum. Irritation there is felt as pain in the C3-C5 skin area, around the lower neck and the top of the shoulder. The rest of the parietal pleura sends pain through the intercostal nerves. StatPearls' Anatomy, Thorax, Phrenic Nerves page agrees that the phrenic nerve comes from the anterior rami of C3 through C5, gives all the motor supply to the diaphragm and feeling to its central tendon, and carries touch and pain from the mediastinal pleura. StatPearls adds that pain from the diaphragm is often referred to the tip of the shoulder, called the Kehr sign.

whyWrong.b: C6 to C8 supply the lower arm and hand, not the shoulder tip, and do not carry fibers from the diaphragm (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Upper thoracic levels carry pain from the heart and upper chest wall; the central diaphragm and its pleura send pain through the phrenic nerve (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 13).
whyWrong.d: Middle intercostal nerves carry pain from the costal pleura, which would be felt in the chest wall itself, not the shoulder (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 13).
whyWrong.e: Lower intercostal nerves supply the outer edge of the diaphragm and the abdominal wall; this pain is at the shoulder tip (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 13, and standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Pleura: innervation, p. 13
StatPearls: Anatomy, Thorax, Phrenic Nerves

questions.stem: A lung biopsy from a 55-year-old man is examined. One small airway has no cartilage plates and no goblet cells. It is lined by simple cuboidal cells, some with cilia and many that are dome-shaped and non-ciliated. A thin layer of smooth muscle lies under the lining, and a few thin-walled alveoli open directly from the airway wall.
questions.leadIn: This airway segment is best described by which of the following?

options.text: First airway segment where gas exchange occurs
Last part of the airway that has cartilage plates
Airway lined by pseudostratified ciliated cells
Airway with the highest total airflow resistance
Airway whose wall is made only of alveoli

questions.explanation: Answer: the first part of the airway where gas exchange occurs, which is the respiratory bronchiole. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 4) explain that the conducting zone (nose to terminal bronchioles) warms, filters, and humidifies air but does not exchange gas, and is called anatomic dead space. Cartilage and goblet cells go only as far as the end of the bronchi, and pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells line the bronchi before giving way to cuboidal cells. The respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli) takes part in gas exchange. Respiratory bronchioles are mostly cuboidal, and cilia, the last feature to disappear, end there. Terminal bronchioles are so numerous and side by side that they have the lowest resistance. Osmosis' bronchioles and alveoli histology lesson agrees that small bronchioles lack the cartilage plates of bronchi, that terminal bronchioles contain club (Clara) cells instead of goblet cells, and that respiratory bronchioles have a mix of simple cuboidal and columnar cells with even more club cells. Club cells are the non-ciliated dome-shaped cells here; your notes say they secrete part of the surfactant and break down toxins (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 9).

whyWrong.b: Cartilage plates end with the bronchi, well before this airway (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 4).
whyWrong.c: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells line the bronchi; this airway has simple cuboidal cells (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 4).
whyWrong.d: Small airways are so many and arranged side by side that their total resistance is lowest; medium-sized bronchi have the highest (standard teaching; your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 4).
whyWrong.e: Alveolar ducts are made almost entirely of alveolar openings; this airway still has a wall of cuboidal cells and smooth muscle (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 4, and standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Respiratory tree and respiratory zone, p. 4
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Pneumocytes, p. 9
Osmosis: Bronchioles and alveoli histology

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man comes to the physician because he has fainted twice in 2 months, once while shaving his neck and once after turning his head quickly while wearing a tight shirt collar. He has a history of high cholesterol and a bruit over the right carotid artery. With ECG monitoring, gentle massage of the right carotid sinus causes a 5-second pause in the heartbeat.
questions.leadIn: The afferent signals that start this reflex travel in which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation: Answer: the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX). Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 105) describe the baroreceptor reflex as a fast nerve response to changes in blood pressure. Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus send signals along the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and those in the aortic arch send signals along the vagus nerve (CN X). Both reach the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla, which then raises parasympathetic output to the heart and lowers sympathetic output, slowing the heart and widening blood vessels. Carotid sinus receptors respond to both rises and falls in pressure, while aortic arch receptors mostly respond to rises. In atherosclerosis, the receptors can become oversensitive (carotid sinus syndrome), so even light pressure on the carotid sinus causes extreme bradycardia. StatPearls' carotid sinus hypersensitivity page agrees that carotid sinus signals travel in the glossopharyngeal nerve and aortic arch signals in the vagus. It notes the condition is about 4 times more common in men and very unlikely before age 50, and lists tight collars, shaving, and sudden neck movements as triggers. StatPearls says monitored carotid massage is the best way to diagnose it and a dual-chamber pacemaker is the cornerstone of treatment for the cardioinhibitory type.

whyWrong.b: The vagus nerve carries the afferent signal from the aortic arch and the efferent signal that slows the heart, but signals from the carotid sinus travel in CN IX (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 105).
whyWrong.c: The phrenic nerve moves the diaphragm and carries no baroreceptor fibers (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Sympathetic output is turned down in this reflex; the sympathetic chain is not the sensory limb from the carotid sinus (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 105).
whyWrong.e: The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue and has no role in blood pressure control (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Baroreceptors, p. 105
StatPearls: Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of episodes of cramping pain in the right upper abdomen for 3 months. Each episode starts about 30 minutes after a large meal of fried food and lasts about 2 hours. Ultrasound shows several gallstones in a gallbladder with a normal wall. The pain is caused by the gallbladder squeezing against a stone stuck in its outlet.
questions.leadIn: The hormone that most directly triggers this squeezing is released by which of the following cells?

options.text: I cells in the small intestine
S cells in the small intestine
G cells in the gastric antrum
K cells in the upper intestine
D cells in the pancreatic islets

questions.explanation: Answer: I cells in the small intestine, which release cholecystokinin (CCK). Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 306) list CCK as a hormone made by enteroendocrine I cells. It is released when food is eaten, especially fatty acids and amino acids, and it increases gallbladder contraction, increases the output of pancreatic enzymes, and controls how food moves from the stomach into the small intestine. A fatty meal releases CCK, the gallbladder squeezes, and a stone blocking the cystic duct causes biliary colic. StatPearls' Biochemistry, Cholecystokinin page agrees that CCK is made by I cells in the intestinal mucosa, that fatty acids and proteins stimulate its release by acting directly on I cells, and that it causes the gallbladder to contract in response to food. StatPearls adds that CCK controls the release of pancreatic digestive enzymes and can slow stomach emptying by relaxing the upper stomach.

whyWrong.b: S cells release secretin, which mainly raises bicarbonate and water secretion from the pancreas and bile ducts (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 306).
whyWrong.c: G cells in the antrum release gastrin, which raises stomach acid; it does not drive gallbladder contraction (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: K cells release GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide), which raises insulin release (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 306, and standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits the release of secretin and other gut hormones, so it would not cause this squeezing (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 306, and standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Gastrointestinal hormones, p. 306
StatPearls: Biochemistry, Cholecystokinin

questions.topic: Starling forces: edema from low oncotic pressure
questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his eyelids have been puffy every morning for 1 week and his legs are now swollen. His blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no blood. His serum albumin concentration is 1.6 g/dL (normal 3.5-5.5). Pressing on his shins leaves deep dents.
questions.leadIn: A change in which of the following capillary forces is most likely causing his swelling?

options.text: Blocked lymphatic drainage of the legs

questions.explanation: Answer: decreased plasma oncotic pressure. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (pp. 155-156) explain that fluid movement across capillaries depends on Starling forces. Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, and plasma oncotic pressure, made mainly by albumin, pulls fluid back in. At the arterial end the outward push wins, and at the venous end the inward pull wins. Lymphatics return what is left. Edema happens when these forces are out of balance: higher capillary pressure (heart failure, a blocked vein), lower plasma protein (liver failure, malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome), leaky capillaries (burns, inflammation), or poor lymph drainage. Losing albumin in the urine lowers the pull that keeps fluid in the vessels. MSD's Edema page agrees, listing decreased plasma oncotic pressure among the mechanisms of edema, with examples such as nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, liver failure, and starvation.

whyWrong.b: High capillary hydrostatic pressure causes edema in heart failure or venous blockage; his blood pressure is normal and his albumin is very low (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 156).
whyWrong.c: Leaky capillaries cause edema in burns and inflammation; there is no sign of those here (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 156).
whyWrong.d: Blocked lymph drainage (for example, from filariasis or lymph node removal) causes swelling of one area, not puffy eyelids with heavy proteinuria (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 156).
whyWrong.e: Interstitial fluid pressure is near zero normally and rises, rather than falls, as fluid builds up; a fall would not cause edema (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 155, and standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Microcirculation and Starling forces, pp. 155-156
MSD Manual Professional: Edema

questions.stem: A researcher records action potentials from cells taken from the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava. The cells fire about 75 times per minute without any stimulus. Between beats the membrane slowly depolarizes. The upstroke is slow and is followed directly by repolarization, with no plateau. Adding tetrodotoxin, which blocks fast sodium channels, does not change the upstroke.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following currents is most responsible for the upstroke in these cells?

options.text: Inward Na+ through fast Na+ channels

questions.explanation: Answer: inward calcium through L-type channels. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 121) explain that pacemaker cells set off their own action potentials (automaticity). The SA node lies in the wall of the right atrium and fires at 60 to 100 per minute, the AV node at 40 to 60, and the His bundle and Purkinje fibers at 20 to 40. In phase 4, sodium enters through 'funny' channels that open when the cell is hyperpolarized, slowly depolarizing it to threshold. Phase 0, the upstroke, is a strong inward calcium current, and phase 3 is potassium leaving the cell. Phases 1 and 2 are missing, so there is no plateau. Klabunde's CV Physiology page on sinoatrial node action potentials agrees that phase 0 depolarization is primarily caused by increased calcium conductance through L-type calcium channels, and that the phase 0 slope is much slower than in other heart cells. It adds that there are no fast sodium channels and currents operating in SA nodal cells.

whyWrong.b: Fast sodium channels make the rapid upstroke of atrial and ventricular muscle cells; tetrodotoxin had no effect here (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The funny sodium current drives the slow depolarization of phase 4, not the upstroke (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 121).
whyWrong.d: Outward potassium current causes phase 3 repolarization (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 121).
whyWrong.e: Chloride current plays no major part in the pacemaker action potential (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Action potentials in pacemaker cells, p. 121
CV Physiology (Klabunde): Sinoatrial Node Action Potentials

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is evaluated 6 weeks after a large anterior myocardial infarction. He becomes short of breath after one flight of stairs. Echocardiography shows that the left ventricle holds 150 mL at the end of diastole and 90 mL at the end of systole.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes this patient's left ventricular ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: Answer: 40%, which is in the reduced range. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 120) define stroke volume as the end-diastolic volume minus the end-systolic volume, and ejection fraction as stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, with an average of 50% to 65%. Here, stroke volume is 150 - 90 = 60 mL, and ejection fraction is 60 / 150 = 40%. StatPearls' Heart Failure and Ejection Fraction page defines heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) as an LVEF of 40% or less and preserved ejection fraction as 50% or more, so a value of 40% with symptoms fits HFrEF.

whyWrong.b: 60% comes from dividing the end-systolic volume by the end-diastolic volume (90/150); that fraction is what stays in the ventricle, not what is ejected (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: 60% is the wrong number (it is the fraction left behind), and 60% would not be reduced (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: 67% comes from dividing stroke volume by end-systolic volume (60/90); the denominator must be end-diastolic volume (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: 40% is the right number, but it is below the average range of 50% to 65% (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 120).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Stroke volume, ejection fraction, and cardiac output, p. 120
StatPearls: Heart Failure and Ejection Fraction

questions.topic: Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve: 2,3-BPG at high altitude
questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman moves from sea level to a mountain town at 3,800 m (12,500 ft). Three weeks later, a blood sample shows that the concentration of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in her red blood cells has risen.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the effect of this change?

options.text: Right shift with more O2 released to tissues
Left shift with more O2 released to tissues
Right shift with tighter O2 binding in tissues
Left shift with tighter O2 binding in tissues
No shift but a higher maximum O2 saturation

questions.explanation: Answer: the curve shifts right, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen to the tissues. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (pp. 612-614) explain that the curve is S-shaped because each oxygen that binds makes the next bind more easily. P50, the oxygen pressure at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated, measures its affinity. A right shift raises P50 and lowers affinity, so oxygen is unloaded more easily, while a left shift does the opposite. 2,3-BPG (called 2,3-DPG in your notes), a byproduct of glycolysis, binds the beta chains of deoxyhemoglobin and lowers its oxygen affinity. Its production rises when oxygen is low, for example when living at high altitude, so more oxygen is delivered to tissues. Higher CO2, lower pH (the Bohr effect), and higher temperature also shift the curve right. Fetal hemoglobin, which binds 2,3-BPG poorly, and carbon monoxide shift it left. MSD's oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve figure agrees that increased red blood cell 2,3-DPG, H+, temperature, and PCO2 shift the curve right with decreased affinity for oxygen, and that decreases in these shift it left with increased affinity.

whyWrong.b: A left shift raises affinity and makes oxygen harder to unload (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 614).
whyWrong.c: A right shift lowers affinity, so oxygen is held less tightly in the tissues, not more (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 613).
whyWrong.d: A left shift is caused by lower 2,3-BPG, higher pH, lower temperature, fetal hemoglobin, or carbon monoxide, not by a rise in 2,3-BPG (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 614).
whyWrong.e: 2,3-BPG changes affinity and shifts the curve; it does not raise the maximum saturation (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, pp. 612-614
MSD Manual Professional: Oxyhemoglobin Dissociation Curve (figure)

questions.stem: Researchers enroll 24 adults with chronic stable angina. Each participant takes drug A for 4 weeks, takes no study drug for the next 2 weeks, and then takes drug B for 4 weeks. A computer randomly decides whether each participant gets drug A or drug B first. The number of angina episodes per week is compared between the two treatment periods within each participant.
questions.leadIn: The 2-week drug-free interval is most likely meant to reduce which of the following problems?
questions.explanation: Answer: carryover of the first drug's effect into the second period. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 256) describe a crossover study as one that compares the effect of two or more treatments given in a series to the same participant. The order of treatments is randomized, and a washout period separates them. Because each participant serves as their own control, differences between people (age, sex, disease severity) are balanced out within the comparison. Penn State's STAT 509 lesson on crossover designs agrees that each patient receives different treatments in different time periods and serves as their own control, and that patients are randomized to treatment sequences. It defines the washout period as the time between treatment periods, meant to let the previous drug clear and reduce carryover, the effect of a previous treatment on later measurements. The lesson adds that the design works only for chronic, stable conditions, because a treatment that cures the patient in the first period leaves nothing for the second treatment to show, and that it can need fewer patients than a parallel design.

whyWrong.b: Each participant acts as their own control, so fixed traits like age and sex are already matched; the washout is not aimed at them (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, pp. 256, 261).
whyWrong.c: Recall bias is a problem in retrospective studies where people with a disease remember exposures differently; here episodes are counted as they happen (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 260).
whyWrong.d: Lead-time bias comes from screening finding disease earlier, making survival look longer; there is no screening here (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 261).
whyWrong.e: Selection bias is about who gets into the study; randomizing the order and the washout period do not change who was enrolled (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 260).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Observational studies (crossover study), p. 256
First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Bias and study errors, pp. 260-261
Penn State STAT 509: Lesson 15, Crossover Designs

questions.stem: A cohort study follows 400 factory workers exposed to an industrial solvent and 600 unexposed workers for 10 years. Twenty of the exposed workers and 6 of the unexposed workers develop bladder cancer.
questions.leadIn: What is the relative risk of bladder cancer in exposed compared with unexposed workers?
questions.explanation: Answer: 5.0. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 258) define relative risk as the risk of disease in the exposed group divided by the risk in the unexposed group, written as [a/(a + b)] / [c/(c + d)], and note that it is the usual measure in cohort studies. Here the risk in exposed workers is 20/400 = 0.05 (5%) and the risk in unexposed workers is 6/600 = 0.01 (1%), so the relative risk is 0.05 / 0.01 = 5.0. Exposed workers are 5 times as likely to develop bladder cancer. An RR of 1 means no association, above 1 means the exposure is linked to more disease, and below 1 means less. The CDC's Principles of Epidemiology (Lesson 3, Section 5) agrees that the risk ratio compares the risk in the group of primary interest with the risk in a comparison group, that 1.0 means identical risk, that above 1.0 means increased risk for the group in the numerator (usually the exposed group), and that below 1.0 suggests the exposure may be protective.

whyWrong.b: 5.2 is the odds ratio, (20/380) / (6/594); it is used in case-control studies and only approximates the RR when the disease is rare (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).
whyWrong.c: 0.04 is the attributable risk, the difference in risk between the groups (0.05 - 0.01), not a ratio (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).
whyWrong.d: 0.20 is the ratio turned upside down (unexposed risk divided by exposed risk) (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: 25 is the number needed to harm, 1 divided by the attributable risk (1/0.04) (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 258).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Quantifying risk, p. 258
CDC Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 3: Measures of Risk, Section 5

questions.stem: A new blood test for pulmonary embolism has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80% when compared with CT pulmonary angiography in a large validation study.
questions.leadIn: What is the positive likelihood ratio of this test?
questions.explanation: Answer: 4.5. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 257) define the likelihood ratio as how likely a given test result is in a patient with the disease compared with a patient without it. The positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity / (1 - specificity), the true-positive rate divided by the false-positive rate, and the negative likelihood ratio is (1 - sensitivity) / specificity. Here LR+ = 0.90 / (1 - 0.80) = 0.90 / 0.20 = 4.5. Your pages note that an LR+ above 10 marks a highly specific test, an LR- below 0.1 marks a highly sensitive test, and that LRs can be multiplied by the pretest odds to estimate the posttest odds. StatPearls' Diagnostic Testing Accuracy page gives the same formulas, describes LR+ as the true-positive rate divided by the false-positive rate, and notes that, unlike predictive values, likelihood ratios are not affected by disease prevalence.

whyWrong.b: 0.13 is the negative likelihood ratio, (1 - 0.90) / 0.80 = 0.125 (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 257).
whyWrong.c: 1.1 comes from dividing sensitivity by specificity (0.90/0.80); the denominator must be the false-positive rate, 1 - specificity (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: 9.0 comes from dividing sensitivity by the false-negative rate (0.90/0.10), which is not a likelihood ratio (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: 0.22 is the false-positive rate divided by sensitivity (0.20/0.90), the positive likelihood ratio turned upside down (standard teaching).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Evaluation of diagnostic tests (likelihood ratio), p. 257
StatPearls: Diagnostic Testing Accuracy: Sensitivity, Specificity, Predictive Values and Likelihood Ratios

questions.topic: Incidence vs prevalence: effect of longer survival
questions.stem: A new drug for a chronic, incurable lung disease lengthens average survival from 3 years to 7 years after diagnosis. It does not cure the disease and does not change how many people develop it each year. The drug is given to nearly everyone with the disease in a country for 10 years.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following changes is most likely over this period?

options.text: Prevalence rises; incidence stays the same
Prevalence falls; incidence stays the same
Incidence rises; prevalence stays the same
Both stay the same because nobody is cured

questions.explanation: Answer: prevalence rises while incidence stays the same. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 259) explain that incidence counts new cases in a period among people at risk, while prevalence counts all existing cases at a point in time. Prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by the average duration of the disease. Your table lists longer survival time as raising prevalence with no change in incidence, while faster recovery or higher mortality lowers prevalence, and wide vaccination lowers both. Chronic diseases have a prevalence well above their incidence because existing cases build up. Penn State's STAT 507 Lesson 3 agrees that because prevalence counts both new and existing cases, the duration of the disease affects prevalence, and that diseases that last longer will be more prevalent than those of shorter duration. Here people live longer with the disease, so more cases exist at any time, but the number of new cases is unchanged.

whyWrong.b: Prevalence falls when cases end faster, through quicker recovery or higher mortality, not when survival is longer (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 259).
whyWrong.c: Incidence depends on how many new people develop the disease, which the drug does not change (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 259).
whyWrong.d: Both fall with prevention, such as wide vaccination, which removes new cases; this drug treats existing cases (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 259).
whyWrong.e: A cure is not needed to change prevalence; any change in how long cases last changes it (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 259).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Incidence vs prevalence, p. 259
Penn State STAT 507: Lesson 3, Measurements of Disease Occurrence and Frequency

questions.stem: A cohort study of 3,000 adults reports that regular use of a sleep medication is associated with hip fracture, with a relative risk of 1.8 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.9 to 3.6. The study used an alpha of 0.05.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: The link is not statistically significant
The drug nearly doubles the risk of fracture
The drug protects against hip fracture
The p-value must be less than 0.05
A larger study would widen the interval

questions.explanation: Answer: the association is not statistically significant. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 263) describe a confidence interval as the range in which the true value is expected to fall with a set probability, with the 95% interval matching an alpha of 0.05. If the 95% interval for a relative risk or odds ratio includes 1, or the interval for a difference in means includes 0, the null hypothesis is not rejected. As the sample size grows, the interval becomes narrower. Here the interval for the relative risk (0.9 to 3.6) includes 1, the value of no effect, so the result could be due to chance and p is above 0.05. The University of Nottingham's evidence-based practice page on confidence intervals agrees that if a confidence interval includes the value that means 'no effect', you cannot rule out that the intervention has no effect, and its table gives 1 as the no-effect value for relative risk and 0 for differences.

whyWrong.b: The point estimate is 1.8, but the interval includes 1, so the study cannot claim the drug raises risk (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A protective effect would need the whole interval below 1; most of this interval lies above 1 (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: An interval that includes 1 corresponds to a p-value above 0.05, not below it (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 263).
whyWrong.e: Larger samples make confidence intervals narrower, not wider (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 263).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Confidence interval, p. 263
University of Nottingham: Assessing statistical significance from a confidence interval

questions.stem: A hospital studies hand hygiene on its medical wards. Nurses and physicians are told that trained observers will record their hand washing during a 2-week study period. Hand-washing rates during the study are 85%, compared with 45% measured by hidden electronic dispensers in the month before. One month after the observers leave, the dispenser data show a rate of 47%.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the high rate during the study period?
questions.explanation: Answer: the Hawthorne effect, a type of measurement bias. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 260) list the Hawthorne effect under measurement bias: participants change their behavior when they know they are being watched. Ways to reduce measurement bias include objective, standardized data collection planned ahead of time and the use of a placebo group. Here staff washed their hands more only while they knew observers were present, and the rate went back down after the observers left. McCambridge and colleagues' systematic review of the Hawthorne effect (Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 2014) agrees that the effect concerns research participation and the resulting awareness of being studied, with a possible impact on behavior.

whyWrong.b: The Pygmalion (observer-expectancy) effect is when the researcher's belief in a treatment changes the outcome they record, not when subjects change behavior (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 260).
whyWrong.c: Recall bias happens when people with a disease remember past exposures differently; hand washing here was directly observed (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 260).
whyWrong.d: Berkson bias is selection bias from choosing cases or controls in hospitals, where people are sicker than the general population (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 260).
whyWrong.e: Lead-time bias is when earlier detection makes survival look longer (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 261).

sources.title: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 (Emily's biostats file), Public Health Sciences: Bias and study errors (measurement bias), p. 260
McCambridge J, Witton J, Elbourne DR. Systematic review of the Hawthorne effect. J Clin Epidemiol 2014;67(3):267-277

questions.stem: Investigators send a single survey to 2,000 randomly chosen adults in a city. On the same day, each person reports whether they currently smoke and whether they currently have asthma. No one is followed over time.
questions.leadIn: This study design is best suited to measure which of the following?

options.text: Prevalence of asthma at that time
Incidence of new asthma over a year
Relative risk of asthma in smokers

questions.explanation: Answer: the prevalence of asthma at that time. Why: Your First Aid pages in the biostats file (p. 256) describe a cross-sectional study as one that measures how often a disease and its risk factors occur in the present, asking 'what is happening?' It measures disease prevalence and can show that a risk factor is associated with a disease, but it cannot establish causality. Cohort studies, which compare exposed and unexposed groups over time, give relative risk, and case-control studies, which compare people with and without the disease, give odds ratios. Penn State's STAT 507 Lesson 3 agrees that point prevalence can be estimated from a cross-sectional survey, and notes that incidence can come from a cohort study. It adds that prevalence is not generally useful for hypothesis-driven research into causes, because the cases are not new.

whyWrong.b: Incidence counts new cases over a period, which needs follow-up of people at risk, as in a cohort study (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, pp. 256, 259).
whyWrong.c: Relative risk compares the risk of developing disease in exposed vs unexposed groups followed over time, as in a cohort study (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, pp. 256, 258).
whyWrong.d: A cross-sectional study can show an association but cannot establish causality, because exposure and disease are measured at the same time (your First Aid pages in the biostats file, p. 256).
whyWrong.e: Survival after diagnosis needs people to be followed over time, for example with a Kaplan-Meier analysis (standard teaching).

questions.topic: Neural cells: oligodendrocytes in multiple sclerosis
questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of blurred vision and pain on moving her right eye for 4 days. Two years ago she had numbness of her legs that went away over a month. When she bends her neck forward, she feels an electric shock running down her back. MRI of the brain shows several bright T2 lesions next to the lateral ventricles, some radiating outward from the corpus callosum.
questions.leadIn: Damage to which of the following cell types is most directly responsible for her lesions?
questions.explanation: Answer: oligodendrocytes, the cells that make myelin in the brain and spinal cord. Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (pp. 58-59) describe multiple sclerosis as an autoimmune disease that strips myelin from nerves in the brain and spinal cord, mainly through a cell-mediated (type IV) reaction. T cells activated by myelin proteins cross the blood-brain barrier, B cells make antibodies that tag myelin, and macrophages engulf the tagged oligodendrocytes. Early on, oligodendrocytes can recover and remyelinate, but repeated attacks kill them, and myelin and axons are lost. Your notes list optic neuritis, Lhermitte sign (an electric shock down the back on bending the neck), and MRI plaques radiating from the corpus callosum (Dawson fingers), with high antibody levels in the CSF. It usually affects young adults, and women are about twice as likely to be affected. MSD's Multiple Sclerosis page agrees that MS causes scattered patches of demyelination in the brain and spinal cord with destruction of oligodendroglia. MSD notes that optic neuritis causes vision loss and eye pain with eye movement, that MRI is the most sensitive imaging test, and that oligoclonal IgG bands can usually be found in the CSF.

whyWrong.b: Schwann cells make myelin in peripheral nerves; their damage causes Guillain-Barré syndrome, not brain and spinal cord plaques (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Astrocytes support neurons and detoxify ammonia; they swell in hepatic encephalopathy rather than being the main target in MS (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 91).
whyWrong.d: Microglia are the brain's resident macrophages; they help clear damaged myelin but are not the cells that make it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and help make CSF; they do not make myelin (standard teaching).

questions.topic: Skeletal muscle: sarcomere bands during contraction
questions.stem: In a physiology lab, electron micrographs are taken of a single skeletal muscle fiber at rest and again during a strong contraction. The distance between neighboring Z lines is shorter during the contraction.
questions.leadIn: Which part of the sarcomere stays the same length during the contraction?
questions.explanation: Answer: the A band. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 85-86) define the sarcomere as the distance between two Z lines. Actin (thin filaments) attaches to the Z line, and myosin (thick filaments) attaches to the M line in the middle. The A band is the full length of the thick myosin filaments, including the parts overlapped by actin, so it keeps the same length during contraction (your notes say 'A band is Always the same length'). The I band holds only thin filaments and the H zone holds only thick filaments; both shrink as actin slides over myosin toward the M line. The Atlas of Microscopic Anatomy's plate on striated muscle agrees: the A band contains the myosin filaments plus thin filaments reaching in from the I band, the I band contains thin actin filaments, and the H zone bisects the A band and vanishes in contraction.

whyWrong.b: The I band holds only thin filaments and gets shorter as they slide over the thick filaments (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 85).
whyWrong.c: The H zone holds only thick filaments and shrinks, or disappears, during contraction (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 86).
whyWrong.d: The Z-to-Z distance is the sarcomere itself, which shortens; the stem tells you this happened (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 85).
whyWrong.e: The gap between the ends of thin filaments in the middle of the sarcomere closes during contraction; it is the same region as the H zone (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with severe narrowing of the right renal artery has high blood pressure and high plasma renin activity. A kidney biopsy specimen shows enlarged cells packed with granules in the wall of the arteriole entering each glomerulus, close to a patch of tall, crowded tubule cells.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the granular cells?

options.text: Modified smooth muscle cells that release renin
Modified tubular cells that sense filtrate NaCl
Mesangial cells that support glomerular loops
Podocytes that form the filtration slit membrane

questions.explanation: Answer: modified smooth muscle cells that release renin, the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells. Why: your El-Husseiny nephrology notes (p. 17) explain that the juxtaglomerular apparatus helps regulate kidney blood flow, GFR, and blood pressure through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. JG cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the middle layer of the afferent arteriole (and to a lesser degree the efferent arteriole). They secrete renin and act as baroreceptors, releasing more renin when kidney perfusion falls, as with a narrowed renal artery or low blood volume. The macula densa is a group of modified tubule cells at the start of the distal tubule, next to the JG cells, that senses low NaCl in the tubule fluid. The Atlas of Microscopic Anatomy's plate on juxtaglomerular cells agrees that they are a granular kind of cell in the wall of the afferent arteriole, and that low perfusion pressure leads to renin release. It calls the macula densa a group of specialized cells of the straight part of the distal tubule. Kenhub's macula densa page adds that the macula densa detects Na+ and Cl- in the tubular fluid and influences renin release from the nearby JG cells.

whyWrong.b: This describes the macula densa, the crowded tubule cells next to the granular cells; they sense NaCl but do not store renin (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 17).
whyWrong.c: Mesangial cells sit between the glomerular capillary loops, support them, and can take up debris; they are not the renin-storing cells of the arteriole wall (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Podocytes cover the outside of the glomerular capillaries and form the filtration slits; they do not make renin (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Erythropoietin is made by interstitial cells near the tubules in response to low oxygen, not by cells in the arteriole wall (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy has had fever, sore throat, and tender swollen neck lymph nodes for 2 weeks. A heterophile antibody test is positive. Because one node keeps growing, it is removed. Microscopy shows normal outer follicles but a greatly expanded zone of small and large lymphocytes between the follicles and the medulla.
questions.leadIn: Which region of the lymph node is expanded?
questions.explanation: Answer: the paracortex. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes (pp. 395-396) explain that lymph enters a node through afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus, filters through the outer cortex and its follicles, and leaves through the medulla and efferent lymphatics at the hilum. Follicles in the outer cortex are where B cells gather and multiply: primary follicles are dense and inactive, and secondary follicles have pale, active germinal centers. The paracortex, between the follicles and the medulla, houses T cells; it is underdeveloped in DiGeorge syndrome and enlarges in strong cell-mediated responses such as EBV and other viral infections (paracortical hyperplasia). The medulla has medullary cords of lymphocytes and plasma cells and medullary sinuses with macrophages. The University of Utah's WebPath lymph node image, stained for the T-cell marker CD45RO, agrees that T cells cluster around follicles and extend into the paracortex.

whyWrong.b: Primary follicles are dense, inactive B-cell areas in the outer cortex, which looked normal here (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 395).
whyWrong.c: Germinal centers are the pale active centers of secondary follicles, where B cells multiply; they are inside the follicles, not between follicles and medulla (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 395).
whyWrong.d: Medullary cords hold lymphocytes and plasma cells in the inner medulla (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 396).
whyWrong.e: The subcapsular sinus is just under the capsule, where afferent lymph first enters (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 395).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Lymph node, pp. 395-396

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has his spleen removed after a car crash. A section of the removed spleen shows small round collections of lymphocytes, each wrapped tightly around a central arteriole, surrounded by large areas of blood-filled sinusoids.
questions.leadIn: The lymphocytes forming the sheath directly around each central arteriole are mainly which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: T lymphocytes. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes (p. 398) explain that the spleen starts immune responses to antigens in the blood. Branches of the splenic artery become wrapped in lymphocytes, forming the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS), and these sheaths make up the white pulp. T cells sit in the PALS, while B cells gather in white-pulp follicles. Between the white pulp and red pulp lies the marginal zone, which holds antigen-presenting cells and special B cells that capture blood-borne antigens, and nearby macrophages remove encapsulated bacteria. The arterioles end in vascular sinusoids, which form the red pulp. That is why people without a spleen are at risk from encapsulated organisms. The Australian Immunisation Handbook's page on asplenia agrees that people with absent or poorly working spleens are at risk of life-threatening infections from encapsulated bacteria, including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b. It notes that the risk is highest in the first years after splenectomy but lasts for life, and recommends extra pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib-containing vaccines.

whyWrong.b: B cells are found in the follicles of the white pulp, next to the sheath rather than forming it (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 398).
whyWrong.c: Plasma cells are mature B cells; in the spleen they are not the cells that form the sheath around the arteriole (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 398, and standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Macrophages in the spleen clear encapsulated bacteria and old red cells, mainly in and near the marginal zone and red pulp (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 398, and standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Neutrophils circulate in the blood and are not a resident part of the white pulp (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Spleen, p. 398

questions.topic: Glial cells: astrocytes in hepatic encephalopathy
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department because of confusion and sleepiness for 2 days. He vomited blood 3 days ago. When he holds his arms out with wrists bent back, his hands flap. His serum ammonia concentration is high.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following brain cells detoxifies ammonia and swells in this condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: astrocytes. Why: Your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 91) explain that hepatic encephalopathy is brain injury from toxic substances, such as ammonia from nitrogen breakdown, that a failing liver does not remove. Astrocytes detoxify ammonia, which builds up glutamine inside them, and the resulting osmotic stress makes them swell. Other insults, such as bleeding, infection, alkalosis, other metabolic problems, or medications, can bring on an episode. The Merck Manual Consumer Version page on hepatic encephalopathy agrees that toxic substances normally removed by the liver build up in the blood and reach the brain, and that some bypass the liver through abnormal connections caused by portal hypertension. It lists digestive tract bleeding, infection, dehydration, and some drugs as triggers, describes asterixis (a flapping motion of the hands), and says lactulose lowers how much ammonia is absorbed while rifaximin acts on gut bacteria.

whyWrong.b: Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the brain and spinal cord; they are the cells damaged in multiple sclerosis (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 58).
whyWrong.c: Microglia are resident macrophages of the brain that respond to injury; they are not the main ammonia-detoxifying cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and help make CSF (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Purkinje cells are large neurons of the cerebellar cortex; alcohol can damage them, but they do not detoxify ammonia (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of tingling in his feet and weakness in his legs for 3 days. The weakness has now spread to his arms. Two weeks ago he had several days of bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken. He is weak in all four limbs, more in the legs, and reflexes are absent throughout. Sensation is only mildly reduced in the feet.
questions.leadIn: Analysis of his cerebrospinal fluid is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: High protein with a normal cell count
Many neutrophils with a low glucose
Many red cells with yellow fluid
Many lymphocytes with a low glucose

questions.explanation: Answer: high protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation). Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (pp. 196-197) describe Guillain-Barré syndrome as an acute autoimmune disease that strips myelin from peripheral nerves. Through molecular mimicry, a preceding infection, most often Campylobacter jejuni (also Mycoplasma, CMV, EBV, influenza A, Zika, and HIV), triggers antibodies and macrophages that attack peripheral myelin, slowing or blocking nerve conduction. Patients have symmetric, flaccid, ascending weakness that peaks within about 4 weeks, with lost reflexes, and the diaphragm can weaken enough to need a ventilator. The CSF shows high protein without more cells, and treatment is IVIG or plasmapheresis. MSD's Guillain-Barré Syndrome page agrees that infection is the trigger in over 50% of patients, that relatively symmetric weakness usually starts in the legs and spreads to the arms, that deep tendon reflexes are lost, and that CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (increased protein but a normal white cell count). MSD adds that forced vital capacity should be measured every 6 to 8 hours, that plasma exchange and IVIG are the treatments of choice, and that glucocorticoids are not indicated.

whyWrong.b: Many neutrophils with low glucose point to bacterial meningitis, which causes fever and a stiff neck rather than ascending weakness (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Oligoclonal bands in the CSF are typical of multiple sclerosis, which affects the brain and spinal cord, not peripheral nerves (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 59, and standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Red cells and yellow (xanthochromic) fluid suggest subarachnoid hemorrhage, which causes a sudden severe headache (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Many lymphocytes with low glucose suggest tuberculous or fungal meningitis, not an autoimmune neuropathy (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Guillain-Barré syndrome, pp. 196-197
