questions.stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because he has become forgetful and walks with short, shuffling steps as if his feet were stuck to the floor over the past 8 months. He has also started wetting himself without warning. He has no tremor. MRI of the brain shows enlarged lateral ventricles that are out of proportion to only mild widening of the sulci.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

options.text: Poor CSF absorption with large ventricles
Loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra
Many small infarcts in deep white matter
Amyloid plaques spreading through the cortex
Prion-induced spongy change of the cortex

questions.explanation: Answer: poor absorption of CSF causing enlarged ventricles (normal pressure hydrocephalus). Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 47) describe normal pressure hydrocephalus as a buildup of CSF that slowly enlarges the lateral ventricles. The name is misleading, because pressure is mildly raised but without the usual signs of high pressure. The stretched ventricles press on fibers of the corona radiata, which causes urinary incontinence, a 'magnetic' or 'glue-footed' gait, and dementia. It can be idiopathic or follow a stroke, meningitis, trauma, or a tumor, and it is most common in older people. Imaging shows large ventricles without matching cortical atrophy, a high-volume lumbar tap that improves function supports the diagnosis, and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt can help. The Merck Manual Consumer Version page on normal-pressure hydrocephalus agrees that it causes difficulty walking, urinary incontinence, and dementia, and that it is thought to occur when CSF is not reabsorbed normally. It describes a slow, unsteady, wide-legged walk with feet that seem stuck to the floor, and says that removing CSF by spinal tap makes the diagnosis more likely if it improves gait, with a shunt as the main treatment.

whyWrong.b: Loss of dopamine neurons causes Parkinson disease, with resting tremor, rigidity, and slow movement, but not early incontinence and large ventricles (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Vascular dementia from many small infarcts causes stepwise decline and white-matter lesions on MRI, not ventricles enlarged out of proportion to the sulci (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Alzheimer disease causes memory loss with widespread cortical atrophy; gait and bladder problems come late (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Prion disease (Creutzfeldt-Jakob) causes very fast dementia with myoclonus over months (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Normal pressure hydrocephalus, p. 47
Merck Manual Consumer Version: Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of daily headaches for 3 months and brief episodes of blurred vision when she stands up. For 1 week she has seen double when looking to the left. Her BMI is 37 kg/m2. Fundoscopy shows swelling of both optic discs. Her left eye does not move outward past the midline. MRI of the brain is normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 340 mm H2O with normal CSF.
questions.leadIn: Stretching of which of the following nerves most likely explains her double vision?
questions.explanation: Answer: the left abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI). Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 149) describe idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) as long-lasting high intracranial pressure without an obvious cause, most often in women of childbearing age who are overweight. It causes headache, papilledema, visual field loss, pulsatile tinnitus, brief visual disturbances, and double vision, and cranial nerve palsies, typically of CN VI because of its long course inside the skull. Imaging and CSF are normal, the opening pressure is high, and treatment includes weight loss and acetazolamide, which lowers CSF production. MSD's Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension page agrees that it typically occurs in women of childbearing age, much more often with obesity, and lists transient obscuration of vision, pulsatile tinnitus, and diplopia due to sixth cranial nerve dysfunction. MSD sets the pressure as elevated above 250 mm H2O with normal CSF composition, treats with acetazolamide or topiramate plus weight loss if needed, and warns that permanent vision loss is the most serious consequence.

whyWrong.b: An oculomotor (CN III) palsy causes a 'down and out' eye, droopy lid, and sometimes a large pupil, not weakness looking outward (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A trochlear (CN IV) palsy causes vertical double vision, worse looking down and in, as when reading or using stairs (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The optic nerve is compressed in this condition, causing papilledema and vision loss, but it carries vision, not eye movement (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 149).
whyWrong.e: The facial nerve moves the face; it does not move the eye (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, p. 149
MSD Manual Professional: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of attacks of severe, stabbing pain behind his right eye for 3 weeks. The attacks wake him at about the same time each night and last 45 minutes. During attacks his right eye waters and turns red, his right nostril runs, and his right eyelid droops. He paces the room rather than lying still. He had a similar 2-month bout last year. Having a beer at night brings on an attack.
questions.leadIn: Functional imaging during an attack is most likely to show activation of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Answer: the posterior hypothalamus. Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (pp. 134-135) describe cluster headache as one-sided pain in the area of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, with autonomic symptoms. Activation of the posterior hypothalamus, which explains the episodic, clock-like timing, leads to trigeminal stimulation and overactivity of the parasympathetic pterygopalatine ganglion, causing tearing, red eye, and a runny nose. Inflammation in the cavernous sinus wall can injure sympathetic fibers on the internal carotid artery, causing a droopy lid and small pupil. It is more common in men, attacks come once to eight times a day in bouts lasting weeks, and patients are restless and agitated. Acute treatment is oxygen or an intranasal triptan, and verapamil is used for prevention. MSD's Cluster Headache page agrees that it affects primarily men, that the pain is always one-sided around the eye and temple, often waking patients from sleep, and that patients restlessly pace. MSD lists tearing, runny nose, nasal congestion, and Horner syndrome on the same side, says alcohol triggers attacks during a cluster, and notes that the periodicity suggests hypothalamic dysfunction. MSD treats attacks with a parenteral triptan, dihydroergotamine, or 100% oxygen.

whyWrong.b: The visual cortex is where migraine aura arises from a wave of spreading cortical depression; aura is typical of migraine, not cluster headache (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The substantia nigra is affected in Parkinson disease, not in cluster headache (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The cerebellar vermis controls balance of the trunk; alcohol damages it over time, but it does not drive cluster attacks (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The hippocampus is involved in memory and is damaged early in Alzheimer disease (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Cluster headache, pp. 134-135
MSD Manual Professional: Cluster Headache

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the physician because of headaches twice a month for 2 years. Each headache starts with 20 minutes of flickering zigzag lines that spread across her vision. Then a throbbing pain develops on one side of her head and lasts most of the day, with nausea and sensitivity to light and noise. Walking up stairs makes it worse. Her neurologic examination is normal between attacks.
questions.leadIn: Release of which of the following from trigeminal sensory nerve endings most directly contributes to her headache pain?
questions.explanation: Answer: calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (pp. 136-137) explain that in migraine, overexcitable neurons start a wave of spreading depression across the cortex that releases inflammatory substances and potassium, which activate trigeminal pain fibers around blood vessels. These fibers release substance P, CGRP, and neurokinin A, causing inflammation and widening of meningeal vessels, and the pain signals travel through the trigeminal nucleus caudalis to the thalamus and cortex. The spreading depression also likely causes the aura, most often visual, such as a zigzag line that spreads outward. Migraine is one-sided, pulsating, made worse by activity, and comes with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Your notes (p. 138) list NSAIDs and acetaminophen for mild attacks, triptans and ergots for moderate to severe attacks, and beta blockers, tricyclics, and topiramate or valproate for prevention. MSD's Migraine page agrees that the trigeminovascular system is involved, with release of neuropeptides such as CGRP causing painful inflammation in cranial vessels and the dura, and that migraine is far more common in women. Recent change: MSD now also lists drugs that block CGRP. These are the gepants ubrogepant or rimegepant for attacks when triptans cannot be used, and atogepant or rimegepant, or injectable CGRP monoclonal antibodies (for example erenumab, fremanezumab, or galcanezumab), for prevention. Your notes do not include these.

whyWrong.b: Acetylcholine is released by parasympathetic fibers; it is not the main pain-producing peptide from trigeminal endings (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Glycine is an inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord; it does not cause blood vessel inflammation in the meninges (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Dopamine from the substantia nigra controls movement; dopamine blockers such as metoclopramide treat migraine nausea, but dopamine is not the trigeminal pain peptide (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Norepinephrine from sympathetic fibers narrows blood vessels; it is not released by trigeminal pain fibers (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Migraine, pp. 136-138
MSD Manual Professional: Migraine

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is stabbed in the back. MRI shows that the knife cut the left half of the spinal cord at the T10 level. He is examined 2 days later.
questions.leadIn: Which pattern of deficits is most likely below the level of the injury?

options.text: Left leg weak; left vibration lost; right pain lost
Left leg weak; right vibration lost; left pain lost
Right leg weak; left vibration lost; left pain lost
Both legs weak; vibration lost on both sides
Left leg weak only, with normal sensation

questions.explanation: Answer: weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the left, with loss of pain and temperature on the right. Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 199) describe Brown-Séquard syndrome as damage to one half of the spinal cord. Cutting the corticospinal tract causes spastic weakness on the same side below the lesion (with flaccid weakness of muscles supplied at the level of the injury). Cutting the dorsal column causes loss of vibration, position sense, and fine touch on the same side. Cutting the spinothalamic tract causes loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side. Causes include stab and gunshot wounds, fractures, tumors, and inflammatory diseases. StatPearls' Brown-Séquard Syndrome page agrees that it follows a hemisection of the spinal cord, with weakness and loss of position and vibration sense on the side of the injury and loss of pain and temperature on the other side. StatPearls explains that pain and temperature fibers cross through the anterior white commissure (they do so within a level or two of entering the cord, which is standard teaching), while dorsal column fibers cross only in the caudal medulla. It notes that knife injury is the most common traumatic mechanism and that this syndrome has the best prognosis for walking among spinal cord injuries.

whyWrong.b: This swaps the two sensory losses; the dorsal columns carry vibration on the same side, and the spinothalamic tract carries pain from the opposite side (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla, so weakness is on the same side as the cord injury, not the opposite side (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Weakness and vibration loss in both legs suggest damage across the whole cord, not one half (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Cutting half the cord also cuts the dorsal column and spinothalamic tract on that side, so sensation is affected too (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 199).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Brown-Séquard syndrome, p. 199
StatPearls: Brown-Séquard Syndrome

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because she burned both hands on a hot pan without feeling it. She has had neck pain for years. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation over her shoulders, upper back, and both arms, with normal light touch, vibration, and position sense. The small muscles of both hands are thin and weak. MRI shows the lower cerebellum extending below the foramen magnum and a fluid-filled cavity in the center of the cervical spinal cord.
questions.leadIn: Damage to which of the following structures best explains her sensory loss?

options.text: Dorsal columns of the cervical spinal cord
Lateral corticospinal tracts on both sides
Dorsal root ganglia of cervical nerves
Dorsal spinocerebellar tracts on both sides

questions.explanation: Answer: the pain and temperature fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure. Why: your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 52) describe syringomyelia as a CSF-filled cyst (syrinx) around the central canal of the spinal cord. As it grows, pressure damages the cord, and symptoms progress slowly, so diagnosis is often in adulthood. It can be congenital, linked to Chiari malformation, or acquired after trauma, tumor, or bleeding. Patients have pain, abnormal sensations, weakness, and a 'suspended' sensory level that affects only the segments involved. MRI shows the syrinx, and treatment is surgical drainage and restoring CSF flow. Pain and temperature fibers cross to the other side through the anterior white commissure (StatPearls' Brown-Séquard Syndrome page). They cross within a level or two of entering the cord, and this commissure lies just in front of the central canal (standard teaching), so a central cavity cuts these crossing fibers first. MSD's Syrinx page agrees that a syrinx is a fluid-filled cavity in the spinal cord, often linked to Chiari malformation, that it commonly begins in the cervical cord, and that pain and temperature loss occurs early in a capelike pattern over the shoulders, arms, and back, while light touch, position, and vibration are spared. MSD adds that weakness, wasting, and lost reflexes of the hands and arms follow, that MRI with gadolinium makes the diagnosis, and that surgical decompression of the foramen magnum and upper cervical cord is the only useful treatment.

whyWrong.b: Damage to the dorsal columns would cause loss of vibration and position sense, which are normal here (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Corticospinal tract damage would cause spastic weakness of the legs with brisk reflexes; her hand weakness comes from anterior horn cells next to the cavity (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Dorsal root ganglion damage would affect all types of sensation from those segments, including touch and vibration (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious position sense to the cerebellum; damage causes unsteadiness, not loss of pain and temperature (standard teaching).

MSD Manual Professional: Syrinx of the Spinal Cord or Brain Stem
StatPearls: Brown-Séquard Syndrome

questions.stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the physician because she is not growing well and her joints have become stiff. She has coarse facial features, cloudy corneas, a curved spine, and fingers that she cannot fully straighten. Blood levels of several lysosomal enzymes are many times higher than normal. Her cultured skin fibroblasts are packed with large cytoplasmic inclusions.
questions.leadIn: Failure of which of the following steps best explains these findings?

options.text: Adding N-linked sugars in the rough ER
Returning proteins to the ER in COPI vesicles
Breaking down ubiquitin-tagged proteins in proteasomes

questions.explanation: Answer: adding mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi. Why: this is I-cell (inclusion-cell) disease, also called mucolipidosis type II. Your el-husseiny biochemistry notes (pp. 43-44) explain that enzymes meant for lysosomes get a phosphate added to a mannose sugar in the Golgi by N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase. That mannose-6-phosphate tag pulls them out of the secretion pathway and sends them to lysosomes. When the phosphotransferase is defective, the enzymes are secreted out of the cell instead. So enzyme levels in the blood are high, while lysosomes inside the cells lack their enzymes and fill with undigested material (the inclusions). Your notes describe the same child: a coarse face, cloudy corneas, stiff joints, claw-like hands, a curved spine, and high blood levels of lysosomal enzymes, and the disease is often fatal in childhood. StatPearls' article on protein targeting and I-cell disease agrees that the cause is low GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase activity, that hydrolase enzymes normally get their phosphomannose targeting signal in the cis-Golgi, and that misrouted enzymes build up outside the cell. It adds that death usually comes within the first decade, at an average age of about 5 years.

whyWrong.b: N-linked glycosylation in the rough ER happens before the Golgi step; a failure there would not specifically send lysosomal enzymes into the blood (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: COPI vesicles carry proteins backward, from the Golgi to the ER; the defect here is in the Golgi tagging step that routes enzymes to lysosomes (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 44).
whyWrong.d: Proteasomes break down ubiquitin-tagged proteins in the cytoplasm; a proteasome problem would not raise lysosomal enzyme levels in the blood (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Failure of lysosomes to fuse with phagosomes is the problem in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which causes recurrent infections and albinism, not high serum lysosomal enzymes (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Biochemistry (Emily's file), Protein targeting to lysosomes and I-cell disease, pp. 43-44
StatPearls: Biochemistry, Protein Targeting and I Cell Diseases

questions.topic: Alveolar cells: type II pneumocytes in lung repair
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is treated in the ICU for severe lung injury after a bacterial pneumonia. Two weeks later, a lung biopsy is done because he is slow to come off the ventilator. Many alveolar walls have lost their normal thin lining. Instead, they are lined by plump, cube-shaped cells that are actively dividing.
questions.leadIn: The dividing cube-shaped cells are most likely which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: type II pneumocytes. Why: your El-Husseiny respiratory notes (p. 9) describe two alveolar lining cells. Type I cells are thin and squamous, cover about 97% of the alveolar surface, and are built for gas diffusion. Type II cells are cuboidal, sit in clusters, and secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension and keeps alveoli from collapsing at the end of expiration. Your notes add that type II cells multiply when the lung is damaged and act as the precursors of both new type I cells and more type II cells. So after an injury that strips the thin type I lining, the alveoli are relined first by dividing cuboidal type II cells, which later give rise to new type I cells. A 2023 review in the Journal of Clinical Investigation agrees that type II cells are small cuboidal cells that secrete surfactant, renew themselves, and give rise to type I cells, making them the main progenitor cells of the alveolus. After injury they divide, with one daughter cell becoming a new type I cell. Other source: the same review says type I cells cover about 95% of the alveolar surface, close to the 97% in your notes.

whyWrong.b: Type I pneumocytes are the thin, flat cells that are lost in the injury; they do not divide to repair the lining (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 9).
whyWrong.c: Club cells are nonciliated cells of the bronchioles that secrete part of surfactant, break down toxins, and act as reserve cells for the airway, not the alveolar wall (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 9).
whyWrong.d: Alveolar macrophages float in the air spaces and eat debris and microbes; they are not epithelial cells and do not form the alveolar lining (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Ciliated columnar cells line the larger airways, not the alveoli (standard teaching).

questions.topic: Liver lobule zones: centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis in Budd-Chiari syndrome
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with polycythemia vera has had 3 weeks of pain in the right upper abdomen and a growing belly. Her liver is enlarged and tender, and she has ascites. Doppler ultrasonography shows clots blocking her hepatic veins. A liver biopsy is done.
questions.leadIn: Damage would be most marked in which part of the liver lobule?

options.text: Midway between portal triads and central veins (zone 2)
In the lining of the small bile ducts

questions.explanation: Answer: around the central veins (zone 3). Why: this is Budd-Chiari syndrome. Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 101) describe it as congestive liver disease caused by blocked hepatic venous outflow, most often from a clot, with myeloproliferative disorders such as polycythemia vera as a risk factor. The classic triad is an enlarged liver, abdominal pain, and ascites. Your notes explain that the venous congestion causes ischemia and centrilobular necrosis, along with portal hypertension. Blood enters the lobule at the portal triads (zone 1) and drains out through the central vein (zone 3). When outflow is blocked, blood backs up into the sinusoids around the central veins first, and those hepatocytes also get the least oxygen, so they die first (standard teaching). The MSD Manual agrees that Budd-Chiari syndrome is obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, that in Western countries the most common cause is a clot blocking the hepatic veins and the nearby inferior vena cava, and that myeloproliferative disorders such as polycythemia are among the causes. It describes right upper quadrant pain, a tender enlarged liver, and ascites, and recommends Doppler ultrasonography as the first test.

whyWrong.b: Zone 1 hepatocytes sit next to the portal triads, where blood arrives with the most oxygen, so they are the last to suffer from blocked outflow (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Zone 2 lies between the other two zones; congestion from the hepatic veins hits zone 3 first (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Bile duct injury is the main problem in biliary diseases such as primary biliary cholangitis, not in blocked venous outflow (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Venous congestion is not even across the lobule; your notes specifically describe centrilobular necrosis (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 101).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal (Emily's file), Budd-Chiari syndrome, p. 101
MSD Manual Professional: Budd-Chiari Syndrome

questions.topic: Cytoskeleton: microtubules and colchicine in gout
questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a hot, swollen, very painful big toe that started overnight. Joint fluid shows needle-shaped crystals inside neutrophils. He had a bleeding peptic ulcer last year and cannot take NSAIDs, so he is given colchicine, and the pain eases over the next day.
questions.leadIn: Colchicine most likely helps by blocking which of the following?

options.text: Xanthine oxidase conversion of xanthine to urate
Reabsorption of urate by the renal tubules
Conversion of uric acid to allantoin

questions.explanation: Answer: polymerization of tubulin into microtubules. Why: StatPearls' Colchicine article explains that the drug disrupts the cytoskeleton by inhibiting the polymerization of beta-tubulin into microtubules. Without working microtubules, neutrophils cannot be activated, release their granules, or migrate into the joint, which damps the inflammation that urate crystals set off. StatPearls adds that the same microtubule block stops dividing cells at metaphase. Your el-husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 217) say the same: colchicine binds and stabilizes tubulin so microtubules cannot form, which disrupts cell functions that need the cytoskeleton, such as chemotaxis and phagocytosis, and it does not change how uric acid is made or excreted. Your notes (pp. 216-217) make NSAIDs the first choice for an acute attack, use colchicine for patients who cannot take NSAIDs, such as those with peptic ulcer disease, and say to avoid colchicine in older patients and those with kidney problems; glucocorticoids are for patients who can take neither, such as those with renal failure. Your el-husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 52) list colchicine with mebendazole, griseofulvin, vincristine, vinblastine, and paclitaxel as drugs that act on microtubules.

whyWrong.b: Blocking xanthine oxidase is how allopurinol and febuxostat lower urate production; your notes list them for long-term prevention, not for the acute attack (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 145, 217).
whyWrong.c: Blocking cyclooxygenase is how NSAIDs such as indomethacin work, and he cannot take them (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Blocking urate reabsorption in the kidney is how uricosuric drugs such as probenecid work (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Turning uric acid into allantoin is what the enzyme drugs rasburicase and pegloticase do (standard teaching); colchicine does not affect how uric acid is made or excreted (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 217).

questions.topic: Gastric cells: parietal cell loss in autoimmune gastritis
questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has had tiredness and tingling in her feet for 6 months. She has a macrocytic anemia and antibodies against intrinsic factor. Her fasting serum gastrin is markedly increased. Endoscopy shows a thin, flat mucosa without folds in the body and fundus of the stomach, while the antrum looks normal.
questions.leadIn: Loss of which of the following cells best explains her high serum gastrin?

options.text: Parietal cells of the gastric body
G cells of the gastric antrum
Chief cells of the gastric body
D cells of the gastric antrum
Mucous cells of the gastric cardia

questions.explanation: Answer: parietal cells of the gastric body. Why: this is autoimmune atrophic gastritis. Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 39) explain that the damage is limited to the fundus and body, where the acid-making parietal cells live, and that patients have antibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor. Losing parietal cells means little or no acid (achlorhydria). With no acid to switch it off, gastrin release from the antrum goes unchecked, so serum gastrin rises. Your notes add that loss of intrinsic factor causes vitamin B12 malabsorption and pernicious anemia, which explains her macrocytic anemia and tingling feet. The MSD Manual agrees that patients have antibodies to parietal cells and their components, including intrinsic factor and the proton pump, and that the resulting low acid (hypochlorhydria) leads to G-cell hyperplasia and high serum gastrin. It notes that up to one-third of people with autoimmune thyroid disease also have autoimmune gastritis. Normally, acid in the antrum stimulates D cells to release somatostatin, which turns down G cells (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: G cells make gastrin and sit in the antrum, which is spared here; losing them would lower gastrin, not raise it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Chief cells are also lost in the body, which lowers serum pepsinogen, but chief cells do not make acid, so their loss does not explain the high gastrin (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 39).
whyWrong.d: Fewer active antral D cells would raise gastrin, but the antrum is normal here; the D cells are quiet because no acid reaches them after the parietal cells are lost (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Mucous cells protect the lining and do not control gastrin release (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal (Emily's file), Gastritis (autoimmune atrophic gastritis), p. 39
MSD Manual Professional: Autoimmune Metaplastic Atrophic Gastritis

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a mass behind his left eye that has pushed the eye forward over 3 weeks. A biopsy shows sheets of small, round, blue-staining cells. A few larger cells have pink cytoplasm with faint cross-striations.
questions.leadIn: A positive stain for which of the following proteins would best support the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: desmin. Why: a fast-growing orbital mass in a young child, with small round blue cells and some cells showing striations, points to rhabdomyosarcoma. StatPearls' Rhabdomyosarcoma article calls it the most common soft tissue sarcoma diagnosed in children and lists the head, neck, and genitourinary areas as the most common sites. It explains that the tumor is believed to come from primitive mesenchymal cells that usually develop into skeletal tissue, and that the diagnosis is supported by staining for skeletal muscle markers such as myogenin, desmin, and MyoD1. Desmin is an intermediate filament of muscle. Your el-husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 85) note that the Z line of the sarcomere contains vimentin and desmin, which are used as tumor markers for muscle tumors.

whyWrong.b: Cytokeratin is the intermediate filament of epithelial cells and marks carcinomas, not muscle tumors (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Glial fibrillary acidic protein is the intermediate filament of astrocytes and marks glial tumors (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: S-100 marks cells derived from the neural crest, such as melanoma and Schwann cell tumors (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: CD99 is the classic marker of Ewing sarcoma, another small round blue cell tumor, but it is not a muscle marker (standard teaching).

sources.title: StatPearls: Rhabdomyosarcoma
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Sarcomere (Z line), p. 85

questions.topic: Parkinson disease: substantia nigra pars compacta
questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has had 2 years of a shaking right hand that is worse when the hand is resting in his lap. He moves slowly, takes small shuffling steps, and his arms feel stiff when moved passively. His wife says he lost his sense of smell and has had constipation for years before the shaking began.
questions.leadIn: Loss of which of the following neurons best explains his movement problems?

options.text: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra
GABAergic neurons of the caudate nucleus
Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis
Noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus
Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex

questions.explanation: Answer: dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra. Why: resting tremor, slow movement, rigidity, and a shuffling gait are classic Parkinson disease. Your Osmosis neurology notes (pp. 162-163) explain that dopamine-making neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta degenerate, which depletes dopamine in the basal ganglia (the striatum) and disrupts their connections to the thalamus and motor cortex. Abnormal protein such as alpha-synuclein builds up in neurons as Lewy bodies, and autopsy shows loss of the pigmented dopaminergic neurons of the pars compacta. Your notes also list loss of smell as a common first symptom, often years before the movement problems, and autonomic problems such as constipation. The MSD Manual agrees that pigmented dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra and other brain stem cell groups degenerate, with Lewy bodies filled with synuclein in the nigrostriatal system. It describes a resting tremor of one hand as often the first symptom, with rigidity, slow movement, and a shuffling gait, and notes that loss of smell and constipation can come before the movement symptoms.

whyWrong.b: Loss of GABAergic neurons in the caudate is the lesion of Huntington disease, which causes chorea rather than tremor and slowness (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert is linked to Alzheimer disease and memory loss (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Your notes say the locus coeruleus does degenerate in Parkinson disease, but early and without symptoms; the movement problems come from the substantia nigra (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 162).
whyWrong.e: Purkinje cell loss causes cerebellar signs such as ataxia and an intention tremor, not a resting tremor with rigidity (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Parkinson's disease, pp. 162-163
MSD Manual Professional: Parkinson Disease

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man is brought to the physician by his wife because of 2 years of fidgety, jerky movements of his face and arms. He has also become irritable and has trouble planning his work. His father had similar problems and died at age 52. Genetic testing shows an expanded CAG repeat.
questions.leadIn: Brain MRI would most likely show atrophy of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: caudate nucleus. Why: middle-age onset of chorea, mood change, and thinking problems, with an affected father and a CAG repeat expansion, is Huntington disease. The MSD Manual explains that it is autosomal dominant and results from a mutation in the huntingtin (HTT) gene on chromosome 4, and that more CAG repeats bring earlier onset and more severe disease. The number of repeats can increase from one generation to the next. Levels of the neurotransmitters GABA and substance P decrease. Symptoms start insidiously at about age 35 to 40, and abnormal movements include chorea, athetosis, and myoclonic jerks. MSD notes that neuroimaging helps identify caudate atrophy, often with some cortical atrophy that is worse in the frontal lobes. Your El-Husseiny neurology notes (pp. 101-102) agree: the CAG repeat on chromosome 4 leads to loss of GABA-making neurons in the striatum, mainly the caudate, so the caudate shrinks and the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles enlarge. Your notes add that the disease shows anticipation, that GABA and acetylcholine fall while dopamine is relatively high, and that onset is usually between ages 20 and 50.

whyWrong.b: Substantia nigra loss causes Parkinson disease, with slowness, rigidity, and resting tremor rather than chorea (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Atrophy of the cerebellar vermis, typically from long-term alcohol use, causes an unsteady, wide-based gait (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Shrunken mammillary bodies point to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Damage to the subthalamic nucleus, most often from a small (lacunar) stroke in someone with long-standing high blood pressure, causes hemiballismus: wild flinging of the limbs on the opposite side (your El-Husseiny neurology notes, p. 102).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Huntington Disease
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Neurology (Emily's file), Huntington disease and hemiballismus, pp. 101-102

questions.topic: Oculomotor nerve palsy: posterior communicating artery aneurysm
questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has had 2 days of pain behind her right eye and double vision. Her right upper eyelid droops. When she looks straight ahead, her right eye points down and out. The right pupil is 7 mm and does not react to light; the left pupil is 3 mm and reacts normally. She has no history of diabetes.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.text: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery
Ischemia of the nerve from small-vessel disease
Demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus
Injury to the sympathetic chain in the neck

questions.explanation: Answer: aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery. Why: ptosis, an eye that rests down and out, and a large pupil that does not react to light mean a complete third (oculomotor) nerve palsy with pupil involvement. The MSD Manual explains that third nerve palsies that affect the pupil commonly result from aneurysms, especially of the posterior communicating artery, and from transtentorial herniation. Palsies that spare the pupil are most commonly caused by ischemia, usually from diabetes or hypertension. MSD describes the affected eye as deviating slightly out and down, with diplopia and ptosis, and a dilated pupil with impaired light reflexes. Your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 22) also list posterior communicating artery aneurysm as a cause of oculomotor palsy with ipsilateral ptosis, an eye pointing down and out, a dilated pupil, and loss of the pupillary light reflex. Your El-Husseiny neurology notes (p. 53) list the same causes (ischemia, uncal herniation, posterior communicating artery aneurysm, cavernous sinus thrombosis, midbrain stroke) and explain that the nerve's parasympathetic fibers, which constrict the pupil, run on its outside, while the motor fibers run in the middle. That is why ischemia usually spares the pupil, while pressure from an aneurysm outside the nerve affects it early.

whyWrong.b: Ischemic third nerve palsy, usually from diabetes or hypertension, is the most common cause of palsies that spare the pupil; this pupil is dilated and fixed (MSD Manual, Third Cranial Nerve Disorders).
whyWrong.c: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, with poor adduction on side gaze but no ptosis or pupil changes (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Myasthenia gravis can cause ptosis and double vision, but it never affects the pupil (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Sympathetic injury causes Horner syndrome, with mild ptosis and a small pupil, not a large one (standard teaching).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Third Cranial Nerve (Oculomotor) Disorders
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Subarachnoid hemorrhage, p. 22
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Neurology (Emily's file), CN III damage, p. 53

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has had headaches for a year. He keeps bumping into door frames on both sides. His ring and shoe sizes have gone up over the past few years. Visual field testing shows loss of the outer (temporal) half of the field in each eye.
questions.leadIn: A lesion at which of the following sites best explains his visual loss?

options.text: Meyer loop of the temporal lobe

questions.explanation: Answer: optic chiasm. Why: growing hands and feet suggest a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma. Your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 202) explain that bitemporal hemianopsia, loss of the lateral half of the visual field in both eyes, usually comes from a lesion at the optic chiasm. As a mass in the sella grows, it presses on the chiasm from below and damages the crossing fibers, which carry vision from the temporal fields of both eyes. Your notes list pituitary enlargement (adenoma or hyperplasia), craniopharyngioma, meningioma, and anterior communicating artery aneurysm as causes. They add that the vision loss can go unnoticed because it is slow, and that a hormone-secreting adenoma can cause hormone excess. The MSD Manual's table of field defects agrees that bitemporal hemianopia, loss of the lateral half of both visual fields, comes from a lesion of the chiasm, such as a pituitary adenoma, meningioma, craniopharyngioma, aneurysm, or glioma. It lists lesions behind the chiasm, in the optic tract or lateral geniculate body, as causes of a homonymous hemianopia.

whyWrong.b: A lesion of one optic nerve causes blindness in that eye only (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A lesion of one optic tract causes a homonymous hemianopia: loss of the same half of the field (here the right half) in both eyes (MSD Manual, The Optic Pathway).
whyWrong.d: Damage to Meyer loop causes loss of the upper quarter of the field on the opposite side in both eyes, the 'pie in the sky' defect (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Damage to one visual cortex causes a homonymous hemianopia, often with the center of vision spared (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Neurology (Emily's file), Bitemporal hemianopsia, p. 202
MSD Manual Professional: The Optic Pathway

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had double vision for 3 days. A year ago she had an episode of blurred vision with pain on moving her right eye that went away on its own. When she looks to the right, her left eye does not move past the midline toward her nose, and her right eye moves fully but jerks repeatedly. When she focuses on a near object, both eyes turn inward normally.
questions.leadIn: A lesion in which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). Why: this is internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and with her earlier episode of optic neuritis, multiple sclerosis is the likely cause. The MSD Manual describes the condition as weak adduction of the eye on the same side as the lesion during side gaze. It results from a lesion in the MLF, the pathway that links the abducens nucleus on one side to the oculomotor nucleus on the other so the eyes move together. The eye on the affected side cannot adduct, or adducts weakly, past the midline, and nystagmus often appears in the eye that abducts. That eye still adducts normally during convergence, because convergence does not use the MLF. MSD notes that in young people the cause is commonly multiple sclerosis and is often bilateral, while in older adults it is typically a stroke and is on one side. Here the left eye fails to adduct, so the lesion is in the left MLF. Your El-Husseiny neurology notes (pp. 73, 75, 157-158) agree: the MLF connects the abducens and oculomotor nuclei so one eye adducts as the other abducts. Because it is heavily myelinated, it is a common target in multiple sclerosis. Their table lists a left MLF lesion as making the left eye unable to look right while convergence stays intact.

whyWrong.b: A right MLF lesion would stop the right eye from adducting when she looks to the left (MSD Manual, Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia).
whyWrong.c: A left third nerve lesion would also weaken adduction during convergence and would cause ptosis, a dilated pupil, and loss of accommodation (your El-Husseiny neurology notes, p. 73).
whyWrong.d: A right abducens nucleus lesion causes a gaze palsy: neither eye can look to the right, often with a right facial palsy (your El-Husseiny neurology notes, p. 75).
whyWrong.e: A right PPRF lesion also causes a gaze palsy to the right, with neither eye moving that way (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has had sudden, stabbing pains in his legs for a year and keeps losing his balance in the dark. He stands steadily with his eyes open but sways and nearly falls when he closes them. Vibration and joint position sense are lost in both feet, and ankle reflexes are absent. Strength is normal. His pupils are small and irregular; they constrict when he looks at a near object but not to light.
questions.leadIn: Damage to which of the following best explains his sensory findings?

options.text: Spinothalamic fibers crossing in the anterior commissure

questions.explanation: Answer: dorsal columns and dorsal roots. Why: this is tabes dorsalis, a late form of neurosyphilis. StatPearls' Tabes Dorsalis article describes it as a slowly progressive degenerative disease of the dorsal columns and dorsal roots of the spinal cord, from loss of myelin on the sensory fibers there. It has the longest latent period of any form of neurosyphilis, about 20 years on average after the original infection. Features include brief, sudden, severe stabbing pains in the back, limbs, or face; loss of vibration and position sense with sensory ataxia and trouble walking; and small, irregular Argyll Robertson pupils that constrict to a near target but not to light. Charcot (neuropathic) joints, most often of the knees and hips, may also be present. Your El-Husseiny neurology notes (p. 31) agree that tabes is a late form of neurosyphilis with degeneration of the dorsal roots and dorsal columns on both sides, usually at the lumbar level. Loss of position sense from the legs causes a wide-based sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg sign: balance holds with the eyes open because vision makes up for it, but fails when the eyes close. The ankle reflexes disappear because the dorsal roots carry the sensory side of the stretch reflex. Your notes (pp. 31, 53) explain that the Argyll Robertson pupil comes from damage to the pretectal area of the midbrain, which starts the light reflex, while the near response still works.

whyWrong.b: Damage to the lateral corticospinal tracts causes weakness with brisk reflexes; his strength is normal and his reflexes are absent (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Loss of anterior horn cells causes weakness, wasting, and fasciculations, not sensory loss (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers, as in syringomyelia, causes loss of pain and temperature sense in a cape pattern, with vibration and position sense spared (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A patient with cerebellar ataxia sways even with the eyes open, and cerebellar damage does not cause loss of vibration sense (your El-Husseiny neurology notes, p. 31).

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman had 3 years of worsening memory loss before her death. Toward the end she got lost in her own neighborhood and could not manage her bills. At autopsy, the brain shows widespread cortical atrophy. Microscopy shows many extracellular plaques and flame-shaped inclusions inside the cell bodies of cortical and hippocampal neurons.
questions.leadIn: The inclusions inside the neurons are made mainly of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: hyperphosphorylated tau. Why: slowly progressive memory loss with plaques and tangles is Alzheimer disease. Your Osmosis neurology notes (p. 74) explain that tau is a protein that normally helps hold microtubules together inside neurons. In Alzheimer disease, tau becomes excessively phosphorylated, clumps together, and stops supporting the microtubules. The clumps form neurofibrillary tangles inside neurons, which block signaling and lead to neuron death. The plaques are different: they form outside cells when amyloid precursor protein is cut by beta secretase into insoluble beta-amyloid fragments. Your notes list sporadic disease in people over 60 as about 95% of cases, and diffuse cortical atrophy, reduced acetylcholine, and neurofibrillary tangles as key features. The MSD Manual agrees that the tangles lie inside neurons and come from hyperphosphorylation of tau, a protein that stabilizes microtubules, while beta-amyloid is the main component of the plaques outside the cells. Other source: MSD says about 5 to 15% of cases are familial, a little higher than the roughly 5% implied by your notes, and that most cases are sporadic with onset at 65 or older.

whyWrong.b: Alpha-synuclein builds up as Lewy bodies, the inclusions of Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 162).
whyWrong.c: Beta-amyloid forms the plaques outside the neurons, not the inclusions inside them (your Osmosis neurology notes, p. 74).
whyWrong.d: Misfolded prion protein causes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, with spongy vacuoles and a much faster decline over months (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Huntingtin aggregates are seen in Huntington disease, which causes chorea and mainly affects the caudate (standard teaching).

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has trouble reaching for things on a high shelf since she had a mastectomy with removal of axillary lymph nodes 6 weeks ago. When she pushes against a wall with both hands, the inner (medial) border and lower tip of her right scapula stick out from her back.
questions.leadIn: Injury to which of the following nerves is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: long thoracic nerve. Why: Your el-husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 27) explain that the long thoracic nerve (roots C5-C7) supplies serratus anterior. The muscle arises from the first 8 ribs and inserts on the medial border of the scapula, holding the scapula against the chest wall and rotating it upward. The deltoid and supraspinatus raise the arm to horizontal, and the serratus anterior and trapezius then rotate the glenoid upward so the arm can go fully overhead. When the nerve is injured, the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula wing out when the patient pushes against a wall, and the arm cannot be raised above horizontal. Your notes list axillary lymph node dissection during mastectomy, chest tube placement, and penetrating injury to the side of the chest as causes. StatPearls' article on scapular winging agrees that the most common cause of winging is paralysis of serratus anterior after injury to the long thoracic nerve, which causes medial winging. It lists chest tube placement, axillary lymph node dissection, and blunt trauma among the causes, and notes weakness when lifting the arm above shoulder level.

whyWrong.b: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor; injury weakens abduction and causes numbness over the lateral shoulder, but not winging (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi, which extends and adducts the arm; its injury does not cause winging of the medial border (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus, so its injury weakens starting abduction and external rotation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids; StatPearls notes that rhomboid weakness causes lateral winging, not the medial winging seen here (StatPearls, Winging of the Scapula).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Winged scapula, p. 27
StatPearls: Winging of the Scapula

questions.topic: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after thyroidectomy
questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a hoarse, breathy voice the morning after a total thyroidectomy. She has no stridor and breathes comfortably. Laryngoscopy shows that her left vocal fold does not move and rests slightly to the side of the midline, while the right fold moves normally.
questions.leadIn: Injury to which of the following nerves is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: left recurrent laryngeal nerve. Why: the MSD Manual lists thyroidectomy among the causes of recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis. With one side paralyzed, the voice may be hoarse and breathy, but the airway is usually open because the normal fold opens enough. The paralyzed fold generally rests 2 to 3 mm to the side of the midline. When both sides are paralyzed, as after some thyroid surgery, the airway is too narrow and causes stridor and shortness of breath on moderate exertion. MSD adds that the left recurrent nerve takes a longer path from the brain stem to the larynx, which gives more chances for compression, stretching, or surgical injury. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid (standard teaching). Your el-husseiny respiratory notes (p. 117) also list compression of this nerve, causing hoarseness, as a complication of lung cancer.

whyWrong.b: The superior laryngeal nerve's external branch supplies the cricothyroid, which tenses the fold; injury makes it hard to reach high notes, but the fold still moves (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue; injury makes the tongue point toward the weak side when stuck out (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; injury raises the diaphragm on that side but does not change the voice (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensation from the back of the tongue and throat and the gag reflex; it does not move the vocal folds (standard teaching).
