questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has a painless lump in the middle of the front of his neck, just below the hyoid bone. It has been there for several months. The lump moves up when he swallows. It is round, soft, and does not glow when a light is shone through it.
questions.leadIn: This mass most likely comes from which of the following?

options.text: A remnant of the thyroglossal duct
A remnant of the second pharyngeal cleft
Persistent cervical sinus of the third pouch
Blocked lymphatic sacs of the neck
Skin ectoderm trapped at a fusion line

questions.explanation: Answer: a remnant of the thyroglossal duct. Why: your Osmosis GI notes (p. 172) explain that the thyroid starts at the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue and moves down the neck, leaving a track called the thyroglossal duct. If the duct stays open, it fills with mucus and forms a benign cyst. It shows up as a painless lump at or near the front midline of the neck that moves when the patient swallows, and it can become infected. Your notes add that thyroid cells left in the cyst can rarely give rise to thyroid cancer, and that treatment is surgical removal (the Sistrunk procedure). StatPearls' Thyroglossal Duct Cyst article agrees that the cyst forms when the duct fails to close, that it is the most common congenital neck anomaly, and that it sits in the midline near the hyoid bone and moves upward when the tongue sticks out or the patient swallows. It puts the cancer risk at less than 1%.

whyWrong.b: StatPearls notes that second branchial cleft cysts sit to the side of the neck, not in the midline; they lie along the front edge of the sternocleidomastoid (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Third pouch remnants are rare and lie on the side of the neck, not in the midline (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: A cystic hygroma comes from blocked lymphatics, is usually on the side of the neck, and glows when a light is shone through it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A dermoid cyst can sit in the midline, but it does not move with swallowing because it is not attached to the hyoid and the thyroid's path (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal (Emily's file), Thyroglossal duct cyst, p. 172
StatPearls: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst

questions.stem: A term newborn boy develops increasing breathing difficulty in his first few hours of life. His abdomen looks flat and sunken. Breath sounds are absent over the left chest, where bowel sounds can be heard, and his heart sounds are loudest on the right.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the main cause of his breathing difficulty?

options.text: Underdeveloped lung on the affected side
Air leaking into the left pleural space
A fluid-filled cyst budding off the foregut

questions.explanation: Answer: underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of the lung on the affected side. Why: this is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, with abdominal organs pushed into the chest through a hole in the diaphragm. The MSD Manual explains that the hole is in the back and side of the diaphragm (a Bochdalek hernia) in 95% of cases and on the left in 85%. Breathing difficulty usually starts within the first several hours after birth. The abdomen looks sunken (scaphoid) because the organs have moved into the chest, and bowel sounds may be heard over that side while breath sounds are absent. With a large defect, the lung on that side is underdeveloped, and the small lungs can cause pulmonary hypertension. Your el-husseiny respiratory notes (p. 11) also list congenital diaphragmatic hernia as a cause of pulmonary hypoplasia, along with bilateral renal agenesis. The hole usually comes from incomplete closure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Surfactant deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in premature babies; this baby is term and has bowel in the chest (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Meconium aspiration happens in babies born through meconium-stained fluid and does not move bowel sounds into the chest (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: A pneumothorax also removes breath sounds, but it would not make the abdomen sunken or bring bowel sounds into the chest (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A bronchogenic cyst comes from abnormal budding of the foregut and shows as a round, sharply outlined density on x-ray (your El-Husseiny respiratory notes, p. 11).

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Diaphragmatic Hernia
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Respiratory System (Emily's file), Congenital lung malformations (pulmonary hypoplasia), p. 11

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl with Turner syndrome has an abdominal ultrasound. It shows that the lower poles of her two kidneys are joined across the midline in front of the aorta, and that both kidneys sit lower than usual.
questions.leadIn: The rise of her kidneys toward their normal position was most likely blocked by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: inferior mesenteric artery. Why: this is a horseshoe kidney. Your el-husseiny nephrology notes (p. 9) explain that the kidneys start out in the sacral region and seem to rise to their adult position at about T12-L3 as the lower part of the embryo grows quickly. In a horseshoe kidney, the two kidneys fuse at their poles early in development, at the lower poles in about 90% of cases. The joined middle part (the isthmus) lies across the midline in front of the aorta and inferior vena cava. As the kidneys rise, the isthmus gets caught under the inferior mesenteric artery, so the kidneys stay low. Your notes add that horseshoe kidney is linked with blockage at the ureteropelvic junction, kidney stones, infection, and a higher risk of kidney cancer. It is more common in chromosome disorders such as Turner syndrome and trisomies 13, 18, and 21. StatPearls' Horseshoe Kidney article agrees that the isthmus joins the lower poles in over 90% of cases and that the inferior mesenteric artery stops the kidneys' rise. It links horseshoe kidney with trisomy 18 and Turner syndrome, and lists ureteropelvic junction obstruction as the most common complication, along with stones and renal cell cancer.

whyWrong.b: The superior mesenteric artery arises higher on the aorta; your notes describe the isthmus trapped below the inferior mesenteric artery (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 9).
whyWrong.c: The celiac trunk arises even higher, near the diaphragm, far above where a fused kidney gets stuck (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta below the superior mesenteric artery, but it is not what traps a horseshoe kidney (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The common iliac arteries sit below the starting point of the rise; the fused kidney gets caught higher, under the inferior mesenteric artery (your El-Husseiny nephrology notes, p. 9).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Horseshoe kidney, p. 9
StatPearls: Horseshoe Kidney

questions.topic: Urinary tract development: posterior urethral valves
questions.stem: A prenatal ultrasound at 24 weeks' gestation shows a male fetus with very little amniotic fluid. The fetal bladder is large and thick-walled, and both ureters and both kidney collecting systems are dilated.
questions.leadIn: Blockage at which of the following sites best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: prostatic urethra. Why: a large bladder with dilation of both ureters and both kidneys in a boy points to posterior urethral valves. Your el-husseiny nephrology notes (p. 5) explain that these valves are the leading cause of blocked urine flow in baby boys. Extra flaps of tissue at the lower end of the prostatic urethra hold back urine, so the bladder, then the ureters, then the kidneys swell. A big bladder with dilated ureters and collecting systems on both sides on prenatal ultrasound strongly suggests the diagnosis. Much of the amniotic fluid is fetal urine, so when little urine gets out, the fluid runs low (oligohydramnios). Your notes stress that low fluid in the second trimester is a bad sign with high perinatal mortality, because the lungs need normal amniotic fluid to develop. Low fluid also limits fetal movement and leads to flat facies and limb deformities (Potter sequence). StatPearls' Posterior Urethral Valves article agrees that the valves are folds in the posterior urethra, found only in males, and are the most common cause of lower urinary tract blockage in male newborns. A distended, thick-walled bladder with hydronephrosis on both sides suggests the diagnosis, and severe cases cause oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia.

whyWrong.b: A ureteropelvic junction blockage dilates the kidney above it but leaves the ureter and bladder normal, and it is usually on one side (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: A ureterovesical junction blockage dilates the ureter and kidney above it but not the bladder (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: A narrowed urethral meatus is rarely severe enough to cause oligohydramnios before birth (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: A patent urachus leaks urine from the bladder to the umbilicus; it does not block outflow (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Nephrology (Emily's file), Posterior urethral valves, p. 5
StatPearls: Posterior Urethral Valves

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man has a bulge in his right groin that gets bigger when he coughs and reaches into the top of his scrotum. At surgery, the hernia sac is found entering the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring and leaving through the superficial ring.
questions.leadIn: Compared with the inferior epigastric vessels, where does this hernia sac begin?
questions.explanation: Answer: lateral to them. Why: a hernia that enters the canal through the deep ring and follows the cord into the scrotum is an indirect inguinal hernia. StatPearls' article on the inguinal region explains that an indirect hernia occurs when the peritoneal sac enters the canal through the deep (internal) inguinal ring and pushes out through the external ring. The deep ring sits just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament and lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. A direct hernia, by contrast, pushes straight through a weak spot in the posterior wall of the canal. StatPearls adds that a processus vaginalis that stays open may raise the risk of inguinal hernia, and that peritoneal fluid running down an open processus causes a hydrocele. Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 78-79) agree: the indirect hernia is the most common type, comes from failure of the processus vaginalis to close, passes through the internal inguinal ring with the spermatic cord, and on imaging its neck lies above and lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle, medial to those vessels, and is acquired, usually in older men.

whyWrong.b: A sac that starts medial to the inferior epigastric vessels is a direct hernia, which pushes through Hesselbach triangle in the weak posterior wall rather than through the deep ring (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 78).
whyWrong.c: Hernias are described as lateral (indirect) or medial (direct) to these vessels; the deep ring sits lateral to them (StatPearls, Inguinal Region).
whyWrong.d: A sac below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, is a femoral hernia, which does not travel through the inguinal canal (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The arcuate line is a landmark on the back of the rectus sheath higher on the abdomen; it has nothing to do with groin hernias (standard teaching).

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Inguinal Region (Inguinal Canal)
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal (Emily's file), Inguinal hernias, pp. 78-79

questions.topic: Frank-Starling relationship: preload and stroke volume
questions.stem: A healthy 24-year-old man takes part in a research study. While he lies still, he receives 1 L of normal saline IV over 15 minutes. Echocardiography shows that his left ventricular end-diastolic volume has risen and his stroke volume has gone up. His heart rate, blood pressure, and plasma catecholamine levels have not changed.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the increase in stroke volume?

options.text: Greater sarcomere stretch improving actin-myosin overlap
More beta-1 adrenergic stimulation of the heart muscle cells
Lower afterload from widening of the aorta
Faster heart rate giving more ejections per minute overall
Lower calcium sensitivity of troponin C

questions.explanation: Answer: greater sarcomere stretch that improves actin-myosin overlap. Why: this is the Frank-Starling relationship. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 119) explain that the force of contraction depends on the resting length of the sarcomere, which depends on how much blood fills the ventricle in diastole (the EDV). More filling stretches the sarcomere toward the length where actin and myosin overlap best, so more myosin heads bind and the stroke volume rises. Your notes add that this lets the heart match its stroke volume to venous return on its own (intrinsic control), while nerves, hormones, and drugs change contractility from outside (extrinsic control). Overstretching moves the sarcomere past its best overlap and weakens the contraction. CV Physiology (Klabunde) agrees that more venous return stretches the ventricle and lets it eject the extra blood, and it gives one cellular reason: a longer sarcomere makes troponin C more sensitive to calcium. It adds that other mechanisms are surely involved too. Here nothing changed except the filling volume, so the extra stroke volume came from stretch.

whyWrong.b: Beta-1 stimulation raises contractility (positive inotropy), but his catecholamines did not change; your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 119) list sympathetic stimulation as extrinsic control, separate from the Frank-Starling effect.
whyWrong.c: Nothing in the stem lowers afterload; his blood pressure is unchanged, and a saline bolus does not widen the aorta (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: His heart rate did not change, and the question asks about stroke volume (blood per beat), not beats per minute (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Stretch makes troponin C more sensitive to calcium, not less; CV Physiology names this as one reason stretch strengthens contraction.

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Frank-Starling relationship, p. 119
CV Physiology (Klabunde): Frank-Starling Mechanism

questions.topic: Cardiac cycle: isovolumic contraction on the pressure-volume loop
questions.stem: A physiology class studies a normal left ventricular pressure-volume loop. At one point the ventricle holds 140 mL of blood. Over the next part of the loop, the ventricular pressure climbs from about 10 mm Hg to about 80 mm Hg while the volume stays at 140 mL. The first heart sound has just been heard.
questions.leadIn: This part of the loop is which phase of the cardiac cycle?
questions.explanation: Answer: isovolumic contraction. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 113) describe the pressure-volume loop in four phases. Filling ends with the mitral valve closed and the ventricle full (EDV about 140 mL). Systole then begins with isovolumic contraction: the mitral and aortic valves are both closed, so the volume cannot change, and pressure builds. Ejection starts only when left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens. CV Physiology (Klabunde) adds that all valves are closed in this phase, that ventricular pressure rises fast with no change in volume, and that the phase lasts from closure of the AV valves to opening of the aortic and pulmonic valves. AV valve closure makes the first heart sound (S1), which is why S1 marks the start of this phase.

whyWrong.b: During ejection the aortic valve is open and the volume falls; your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 113) say ejection starts when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure.
whyWrong.c: Isovolumic relaxation is also a fixed-volume phase, but pressure falls, not rises, and it happens at the end-systolic volume (about 70 mL in your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 113) after the aortic valve closes.
whyWrong.d: During rapid filling the mitral valve is open, the volume rises, and the pressure stays low (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Atrial systole tops off filling at the end of diastole while the mitral valve is still open, so the volume rises (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Pressure-volume loops, p. 113
CV Physiology (Klabunde): Cardiac Cycle - Isovolumetric Contraction (Phase 2)

questions.topic: Hemodynamics: Poiseuille equation and vessel radius
questions.stem: In a laboratory experiment, a segment of a small artery is perfused with blood. The vessel's smooth muscle is then made to contract until the inner radius of the segment is half of its starting value. The length of the segment and the viscosity of the blood do not change.
questions.leadIn: Compared with baseline, the resistance to flow through this segment has changed by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: increased 16-fold. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 141) give the Poiseuille equation, R = 8ηl / πr⁴. Resistance rises in direct proportion to viscosity and vessel length, and in inverse proportion to the radius raised to the fourth power. Your notes use this exact example: when the radius falls by half, resistance goes up 16-fold, because 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. CV Physiology (Klabunde) states the same fourth-power rule from the other direction: doubling the diameter cuts resistance 16-fold. It also points out that vessel diameter, which changes with smooth muscle tone, is the most important factor in resistance. This is why small changes in arteriolar tone change blood flow so much (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: A 2-fold rise would mean resistance depends on radius to the first power; the Poiseuille equation uses the fourth power (r⁴).
whyWrong.c: A 4-fold rise would mean resistance depends on radius squared; the equation uses r⁴, which gives 16-fold.
whyWrong.d: An 8-fold rise would mean radius cubed; the equation uses r⁴, which gives 16-fold.
whyWrong.e: Narrowing raises resistance; a 16-fold decrease would happen if the radius doubled, as CV Physiology describes for a doubled diameter.

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Resistance to blood flow (Poiseuille equation), p. 141
CV Physiology (Klabunde): Determinants of Resistance to Flow (Poiseuille's Equation)

questions.topic: Cardiac myocyte action potential: phase 2 plateau
questions.stem: Researchers record action potentials from isolated human ventricular muscle cells. They add a drug that shortens the plateau of the action potential and makes each contraction weaker. The resting membrane potential and the rapid upstroke of the action potential do not change.
questions.leadIn: The drug most likely blocks which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: L-type calcium channels. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 122) list the phases of the myocyte action potential. Phase 0 is a fast inward sodium current. In phase 1 the sodium current stops and potassium starts to leave. In phase 2, calcium flows into the cell and balances the potassium flowing out, and this balance makes the plateau. In phase 3 the calcium current stops while potassium keeps leaving, so the cell repolarizes. CV Physiology (Klabunde) agrees and names the channel: the plateau comes mainly from a slow inward calcium current through L-type calcium channels. The calcium that enters during the plateau also triggers the release of more calcium inside the cell, which drives contraction (standard teaching). So blocking these channels shortens the plateau and weakens contraction. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as verapamil act on these channels (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Blocking fast sodium channels would slow the phase 0 upstroke, which did not change; your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 122) tie phase 0 to sodium entry.
whyWrong.c: Blocking delayed rectifier potassium channels would slow repolarization and lengthen the action potential, not shorten the plateau (CV Physiology ties phase 3 to rising potassium conductance).
whyWrong.d: HCN channels carry the funny current that drives phase 4 depolarization in pacemaker cells, not the plateau of ventricular muscle cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Blocking the Na-K ATPase (as digoxin does) raises intracellular calcium and strengthens contraction; it does not shorten the plateau (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Action potentials in myocytes, p. 122
CV Physiology (Klabunde): Non-Pacemaker Action Potentials

questions.topic: Ventilation-perfusion: dead space in pulmonary embolism
questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman suddenly becomes short of breath 4 days after hip replacement surgery. CT angiography shows a large clot that completely blocks blood flow to the right lower lobe. The airways to that lobe are open, and the lobe is still being ventilated normally.
questions.leadIn: The gas in the alveoli of the right lower lobe will most closely match which of the following?

options.text: PO2 about 150 mm Hg, PCO2 about 0 mm Hg
PO2 about 40 mm Hg, PCO2 about 46 mm Hg
PO2 about 100 mm Hg, PCO2 about 40 mm Hg
PO2 about 60 mm Hg, PCO2 about 50 mm Hg
PO2 about 120 mm Hg, PCO2 about 20 mm Hg

questions.explanation: Answer: PO2 about 150 mm Hg and PCO2 about 0 mm Hg. Why: the lobe is ventilated but not perfused, so it is dead space and its V/Q ratio approaches infinity (standard teaching). Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 621) explain that in dead space no gas exchange happens because there is no blood. The alveolar gas therefore stays the same as humidified inspired air, with a PAO2 of about 150 mm Hg and a PACO2 of 0. Your notes list pulmonary embolism as the example. StatPearls agrees that pulmonary embolism is one of the conditions that suddenly cuts perfusion and raises dead space, and that dead-space air is assumed to hold almost no carbon dioxide.

whyWrong.b: These are mixed venous values. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 621) give them for the opposite problem, a shunt (perfused but not ventilated, V/Q of 0).
whyWrong.c: These are normal alveolar values, where ventilation and perfusion are matched (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: A low PO2 with a high PCO2 fits a region with low V/Q (more blood than air), such as asthma or chronic bronchitis (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 621), not a region with no blood.
whyWrong.e: A raised PO2 with a lowered PCO2 fits a high but finite V/Q, where some blood still flows (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 621); with no blood flow at all, the gas matches inspired air.

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Ventilation-perfusion ratios and V/Q mismatch, p. 621
StatPearls: Physiology, Lung Dead Space

questions.topic: Pulmonary circulation: hypoxic vasoconstriction at high altitude
questions.stem: A 34-year-old man moved from a coastal city to a mining town at 4,300 m (14,000 ft) 6 years ago. He now has mild shortness of breath when he climbs stairs. His lungs are clear, and spirometry is normal. Echocardiography shows a thick right ventricular wall and a high pulmonary artery pressure. The left ventricle is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following most directly explains his heart finding?

options.text: Low alveolar PO2 narrowing the pulmonary arterioles
Low arterial PO2 widening the systemic arterioles
Thinner blood lowering pulmonary vascular resistance
Fluid backing up from a failing left ventricle
Carotid body firing that slows the heart rate

questions.explanation: Answer: low alveolar PO2 narrowing the pulmonary arterioles. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (pp. 623-624) explain that alveolar PO2 is a major control of pulmonary blood flow. When alveolar PO2 falls, pulmonary arterioles constrict. This is the opposite of systemic vessels, which widen when oxygen is low. In one diseased region, this steers blood toward better-ventilated lung. At high altitude, though, the whole lung has a low alveolar PO2, so arteriolar resistance rises everywhere. The chronic rise in pulmonary vascular resistance increases right heart afterload and leads to right heart hypertrophy. Your notes add the likely mechanism: hypoxia depolarizes the smooth muscle, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and calcium entry causes contraction. StatPearls (Altitude-Induced Pulmonary Hypertension) agrees that hypoxia triggers pulmonary vasoconstriction and raises pulmonary artery pressure, that long-term exposure can remodel the pulmonary vessels, and that these patients can develop right ventricular hypertrophy and right heart failure.

whyWrong.b: Systemic arterioles do widen with low oxygen (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 623), but that lowers systemic afterload and does not thicken the right ventricle.
whyWrong.c: Living at high altitude raises the red cell count, which makes blood thicker, not thinner; by the Poiseuille equation, higher viscosity raises resistance (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: His left ventricle is normal, so this is not right heart strain from left heart failure (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Hypoxia stimulates the carotid bodies to increase breathing; slowing of the heart rate would not thicken the right ventricle (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Hypoxic vasoconstriction; high altitude and hypoxic vasoconstriction, pp. 623-624
StatPearls: Altitude-Induced Pulmonary Hypertension

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has had severe left flank pain for 2 days. CT shows a 7-mm stone stuck in the left ureter, with a swollen, urine-filled left renal pelvis above it. The right kidney is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which change in the left kidney's glomerular forces most directly lowers its GFR?

options.text: Higher hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space
Higher hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries
Lower oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillaries
Larger filtration coefficient (Kf) of the glomerulus

questions.explanation: Answer: higher hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space. Why: your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 534) list three Starling forces across the glomerulus: hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillary pushes fluid out, while hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space and oncotic pressure in the capillary push back. Net filtration pressure is Pgc minus (Pbs plus πgc), and GFR equals that pressure times Kf. Your notes say Bowman space pressure has a negative relationship with GFR and does not normally change. It rises when urine flow is blocked, and they give a stone stuck in the ureter as the example. Urine backs up, Bowman space pressure rises, and GFR falls. The MSD Manual (Obstructive Uropathy) agrees that pressure rises inside the urinary tract above a blockage and lists stones as a common cause in young adults.

whyWrong.b: Higher glomerular capillary pressure would raise GFR, not lower it (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 534).
whyWrong.c: Lower capillary oncotic pressure would also raise GFR (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 534); a stone does not change plasma proteins.
whyWrong.d: Efferent arteriole constriction raises glomerular capillary pressure and raises GFR (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 534).
whyWrong.e: A larger Kf would raise GFR, since GFR equals net filtration pressure times Kf (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 534).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Starling forces and GFR, p. 534
MSD Manual Professional: Obstructive Uropathy

questions.stem: In an animal study, researchers perfuse a single nephron so that more sodium chloride reaches the macula densa. Soon afterward, blood flow into that nephron's glomerulus falls, and its single-nephron GFR goes down.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains this response?

options.text: Angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole
Prostaglandin E2 dilating the afferent arteriole
Nitric oxide dilating the efferent arteriole
Natriuretic peptide dilating the afferent arteriole

questions.explanation: Answer: adenosine constricting the afferent arteriole. Why: this is tubuloglomerular feedback. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 531) explain that the kidney keeps renal blood flow and GFR fairly constant over a wide range of blood pressures. One way it does this is the tubuloglomerular mechanism: when macula densa cells sense more sodium and chloride reaching the distal tubule (a sign that GFR is too high), they release adenosine. Adenosine raises resistance in the afferent arteriole, which lowers glomerular pressure and brings GFR back down. Your notes name the myogenic response as the other mechanism. Carlström and colleagues' review in Physiological Reviews agrees that the feedback is set off by salt delivery to the macula densa and that the vasoconstriction comes mainly from adenosine A1 receptors on the afferent arteriole.

whyWrong.b: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, which raises GFR, not lowers it; and it acts through the renin system rather than this fast feedback from the macula densa (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Prostaglandin E2 dilates the afferent arteriole, which would raise glomerular blood flow, the opposite of what happened (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Dilating the efferent arteriole lowers glomerular pressure (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 534), but tubuloglomerular feedback acts on the afferent arteriole through adenosine (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 531).
whyWrong.e: Natriuretic peptides dilate the afferent arteriole and raise GFR, the opposite of the response seen (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Autoregulation of renal blood flow, p. 531
Carlström M, Wilcox CS, Arendshorst WJ. Renal autoregulation in health and disease. Physiol Rev 2015;95(2):405-511

questions.topic: Phosphate handling: PTH and the proximal tubule
questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has kidney stones and aching bones. Her serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, her serum phosphate is 2.0 mg/dL (low), and her PTH is high. Her urine phosphate is high. Imaging shows a single enlarged parathyroid gland.
questions.leadIn: Her low serum phosphate is best explained by which of the following?

options.text: Less Na-phosphate cotransport in the proximal tubule
More phosphate absorption by the small intestine
More phosphate release from bone resorption
Less phosphate filtration at the glomerulus
More active phosphate secretion into the collecting duct

questions.explanation: Answer: less Na-phosphate (sodium-phosphate) cotransport in the proximal tubule. Why: she has primary hyperparathyroidism. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 540) explain that phosphate is freely filtered and that most of it is taken back in the proximal tubule by a sodium-phosphate cotransporter in the luminal membrane. When this transport reaches its maximum (Tm), the extra phosphate is lost in the urine. PTH blocks the sodium-phosphate cotransporter, which lowers the Tm and causes phosphaturia (phosphate in the urine). StatPearls (Hypophosphatemia) agrees that PTH increases phosphate excretion and that PTH causes renal phosphate loss through the NaPi-IIa cotransporter in the proximal tubule.

whyWrong.b: Taking in more phosphate from the gut would raise serum phosphate, not lower it (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Bone resorption releases phosphate along with calcium, which would push serum phosphate up; the kidney losing phosphate is what makes it low (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Phosphate is freely filtered (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 540); less filtration would keep phosphate in the blood and raise it, and her urine phosphate is high.
whyWrong.e: Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 540) describe phosphate handling as filtration and proximal reabsorption; PTH acts by blocking proximal reabsorption, not by causing collecting duct secretion.

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Phosphate homeostasis, p. 540
StatPearls: Hypophosphatemia

questions.topic: Menstrual cycle: the LH surge and ovulation
questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles is trying to get pregnant. She uses home urine ovulation tests, and on day 13 of her cycle the test turns positive. Her doctor explains that the test detects a sudden rise of a pituitary hormone that comes just before ovulation.
questions.leadIn: This hormone surge is triggered mainly by which of the following?

options.text: hCG released by the corpus luteum
A fall in prolactin from the pituitary
Inhibin released by the theca cells

questions.explanation: Answer: positive feedback from high estradiol levels. Why: the test detects the LH surge. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 561) explain that during days 1 to 13 the follicle grows and makes estrogen, and that estrogen feeds back to the hypothalamus and pituitary to turn off GnRH, FSH, and LH. On day 14, a brief LH surge makes the follicle rupture and release the oocyte. The MSD Manual (Female Reproductive Endocrinology) explains what flips this switch: estradiol peaks as the ovulatory phase begins, and at this point the high estradiol makes the pituitary release LH (positive feedback). It adds that the surge usually lasts 36 to 48 hours and that the oocyte is released within about 16 to 32 hours after the surge begins. Other source: your notes describe only the negative feedback of estrogen; MSD adds that very high estradiol just before ovulation switches to positive feedback.

whyWrong.b: Negative feedback lowers LH rather than causing a surge. Most progesterone comes from the corpus luteum after ovulation (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 562). MSD notes that progesterone starts to rise just before ovulation and helps stimulate the surge, but the main trigger is high estradiol switching to positive feedback.
whyWrong.c: hCG comes from embryonic tissue after fertilization and keeps the corpus luteum going (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 562); the corpus luteum itself makes progesterone, not hCG.
whyWrong.d: Prolactin does not trigger the LH surge; high prolactin actually suppresses GnRH and ovulation (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Inhibin comes from granulosa cells and lowers FSH, not LH (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Menstrual cycle, pp. 561-562
MSD Manual Professional: Female Reproductive Endocrinology

questions.topic: Innate immunity: NK cells and missing MHC class I
questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has metastatic melanoma. Testing shows that his tumor cells have stopped putting MHC class I molecules on their surface. Because of this, his tumor-specific CD8+ T cells can no longer recognize the tumor cells.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following cells is best suited to recognize and kill these tumor cells?
questions.explanation: Answer: natural killer (NK) cells. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes (p. 380) explain that NK cells recognize and kill cells that have lost or lowered their surface MHC class I, for example tumor cells and cells infected by viruses. NK cells belong to innate immunity. They do not need earlier exposure to the antigen, do not need the thymus to mature, and carry CD16 or CD56 rather than CD3, CD4, or CD8. They kill with granules of perforin, which punches holes in the target cell membrane, and granzymes, which push the target cell into apoptosis. Raulet's review in Seminars in Immunology calls this missing self recognition: NK cells attack cells that do not show enough MHC class I. This covers the gap left when tumors hide from CD8+ T cells by dropping MHC class I.

whyWrong.b: CD8+ T cells need MHC class I to see their antigen (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 408), so tumor cells without it escape them, as the stem says.
whyWrong.c: CD4+ helper T cells recognize antigen on MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 412) and do not directly kill tumor cells that lack MHC class I.
whyWrong.d: Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses rather than kill tumor cells (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Plasma cells are the end stage of B cells and make antibody (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 380); they do not kill cells directly.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Natural killer cells, p. 380
Raulet DH. Missing self recognition and self tolerance of natural killer (NK) cells. Semin Immunol 2006;18:145-150

questions.topic: Antigen processing: the MHC class I pathway
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has chronic hepatitis B. Inside his infected liver cells, viral proteins are made in the cytoplasm. Some of these proteins are cut into short peptides by proteasomes. The peptides are later shown on the liver cell surface, where his CD8+ T cells recognize them and kill the infected cells.
questions.leadIn: The viral peptides are moved from the cytoplasm into the endoplasmic reticulum by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer: the TAP peptide transporter. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes (p. 408) explain the MHC class I (endogenous) pathway. MHC class I is made in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Proteins made in the cytosol, including viral proteins, are broken down in proteasomes. The resulting peptides are carried into the ER by the TAP transporter, where they load onto new MHC class I molecules. The loaded molecules then go to the cell surface and are presented to CD8+ T cells. StatPearls (Genetics, Human MHC) agrees that class I molecules show peptides from broken-down cytosolic proteins to CD8+ T cells, and that class II molecules show peptides from endocytosed proteins to CD4+ T cells.

whyWrong.b: The invariant chain belongs to the MHC class II pathway; it blocks the class II groove until the molecule reaches an endosome (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Clathrin-coated vesicles carry cargo taken in at the cell surface or sorted from the Golgi; they do not move cytosolic peptides into the ER (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: The mannose-6-phosphate receptor sends lysosomal enzymes from the Golgi to lysosomes; it does not carry peptides into the ER (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The signal recognition particle guides newly made secretory and membrane proteins to the ER while they are being made; it does not carry proteasome-made peptides (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), MHC class I, p. 408
StatPearls: Genetics, Human Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department on day 3 of her menstrual period with fever, vomiting, and confusion. She has been using high-absorbency tampons. Her temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F) and blood pressure is 78/40 mm Hg. She has a diffuse red rash like a sunburn. Blood cultures are negative. A vaginal swab grows Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.leadIn: The toxin behind her illness acts mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Linking MHC II to T-cell receptors outside the peptide groove
ADP-ribosylating elongation factor 2 and stopping protein synthesis
Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Forming pores that lyse red blood cells
Raising cAMP by ADP-ribosylating the Gs protein

questions.explanation: Answer: linking MHC class II to T-cell receptors outside the peptide groove. Why: this is staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, caused by toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1). Your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes (p. 413) explain that superantigens cross-link the variable beta part of the T-cell receptor to the alpha chain of an MHC class II molecule, outside the groove where peptides normally sit. Because they skip normal antigen recognition, they turn on every T-cell clone that carries a certain V-beta region (polyclonal activation). The flood of IFN-gamma activates macrophages, which pour out IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, and these cytokines cause the whole-body illness. Your notes (p. 41) list TSST-1 among the superantigen toxins and link the cytokines to capillary leak, low blood pressure, shock, fever, rash, and organ failure. StatPearls (Toxic Shock Syndrome) agrees that superantigens bypass the normal pathway for T-cell activation, that TSS was classically tied to high-absorbency tampons, and that the clinical criteria are fever, rash, low blood pressure, and multiorgan involvement. It adds that the rash peels 1 to 2 weeks later.

whyWrong.b: Stopping protein synthesis through elongation factor 2 is how diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A work (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Blocking acetylcholine release is how botulinum toxin works, causing flaccid paralysis (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Pore-forming toxins such as staphylococcal alpha toxin lyse cell membranes (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 40), but they do not cause this cytokine-driven shock.
whyWrong.e: Raising cAMP through Gs is how cholera toxin and heat-labile E. coli toxin cause watery diarrhea (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Superantigens, p. 413; staphylococcal exotoxins, pp. 40-41
StatPearls: Toxic Shock Syndrome

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had pneumonia 4 times, ear infections many times, and one episode of bloodstream infection since infancy. Cultures have grown Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. His IgG, IgA, and IgM levels are normal, and his T-cell counts are normal. His total complement activity (CH50) is undetectable, and serum C3 is absent.
questions.leadIn: Loss of which complement product, which normally coats bacteria so phagocytes can take them in, best explains his infections?
questions.explanation: Answer: C3b. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes (p. 432) explain that complement drives inflammation, helps phagocytosis by opsonization, and lyses cells by forming membrane pores. C3b does the opsonizing, C3a, C4a, and C5a cause anaphylaxis-like effects, C5a draws in neutrophils, and C5b-9 forms the membrane attack complex. Your notes add that C3b and IgG are the two main opsonins in defense against bacteria, and that C3b also helps clear immune complexes. StatPearls (Complement Deficiency) agrees that C3b defects lead to poor opsonization, and that C3 deficiency causes severe, recurring pyogenic infections early in life. It names encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae among the infections that should prompt testing for a complement deficiency.

whyWrong.b: C3a is an anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 432); it does not coat bacteria.
whyWrong.c: C5a draws neutrophils in and is an anaphylatoxin (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 432), but it does not coat bacteria for phagocytosis.
whyWrong.d: C5b-9 forms the membrane attack complex that lyses cells (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 432). Lack of the terminal components mainly causes repeated Neisseria infections (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: C1 esterase inhibitor keeps complement from being activated on the body's own cells (your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes, p. 432); its lack causes hereditary angioedema, not pyogenic infections (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Complement functions, p. 432
StatPearls: Complement Deficiency

questions.stem: In an experiment, naive CD4+ T cells are mixed with antigen-presenting cells that display the matching peptide on MHC class II. An antibody is added that blocks CD28 on the T cells. The T cells bind the peptide-MHC complex but do not make IL-2 or multiply. A week later, the same T cells are given the same peptide on fully working antigen-presenting cells, and they still do not respond.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes what happened to these T cells?

options.text: Change into CD8+ cytotoxic T cells

questions.explanation: Answer: anergy. Why: your El-Husseiny microbiology and immunology notes (p. 412) explain that a naive T cell needs two signals. The first is the T-cell receptor binding the peptide-MHC complex, steadied by CD4 or CD8, which gives the response its specificity. The second is costimulation: B7 (CD80/86) on the antigen-presenting cell binds CD28 on the T cell. IL-2 is then the main growth signal that makes the T-cell clone multiply. StatPearls (Biochemistry, Autoimmunity) agrees that CD28 on the T cell binds B7 on the antigen-presenting cell, that anergy is a lack of response caused by missing costimulation, and that the response goes no further without the second signal. It adds that CTLA-4 binds B7 more tightly than CD28 does and blocks costimulation. Here, signal 1 came without signal 2, so the cells became anergic and stayed unresponsive even when offered both signals later.

whyWrong.b: Full activation needs both signals; with CD28 blocked, the cells made no IL-2 (StatPearls, Biochemistry, Autoimmunity).
whyWrong.c: Memory cells form only after a successful activation, which did not happen here (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Deletion of strongly self-reactive T cells happens while they develop in the thymus (central tolerance), not to mature T cells in a dish (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: CD4+ T cells do not turn into CD8+ cells; the CD4 or CD8 choice is made in the thymus (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Microbiology & Immunology (Emily's file), Activation of T lymphocytes, p. 412
StatPearls: Biochemistry, Autoimmunity

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had 4 sudden episodes over the past 2 months. Each starts with a pounding heart, sweating, shaking, chest tightness, tingling hands, and a fear that she is dying. Symptoms peak within about 10 minutes and are gone within half an hour. The episodes come without warning, once while she was relaxing at home. For the past 6 weeks she has worried constantly about the next one and has stopped going to the gym. ECG, TSH, and a urine drug screen are normal. She drinks one cup of coffee a day.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: panic disorder. Why: DSM-5-TR (pp. 235-236) defines a panic attack as a sudden wave of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 listed symptoms, such as a pounding heart, sweating, shaking, chest pain, tingling, and fear of dying. Panic disorder needs repeated attacks that come unexpectedly. At least one attack must be followed by 1 month or more of ongoing worry about more attacks or a harmful change in behavior to avoid them. The symptoms must not be due to a substance or a medical condition such as hyperthyroidism or heart or lung disease, and must not be better explained by another mental disorder. She has all of these. The MSD Manual (Panic Attacks and Panic Disorder) agrees that panic disorder needs recurrent, unexpected attacks plus at least 1 month of worry or behavior change, and that it is diagnosed only after medical causes are ruled out. MSD adds that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works, and that SSRIs and SNRIs have fewer adverse effects than older antidepressants.

whyWrong.b: In generalized anxiety disorder the worry is about many everyday things for at least 6 months, not about sudden attacks (DSM-5-TR, pp. 250-251).
whyWrong.c: Illness anxiety disorder is a lasting worry about having or getting a serious illness (standard teaching); her worry is about the attacks themselves, which is part of panic disorder (DSM-5-TR, p. 236).
whyWrong.d: In specific phobia, fear comes only in response to one feared object or situation; her attacks are unexpected (DSM-5-TR, p. 236).
whyWrong.e: In social anxiety disorder, panic comes only in feared social situations; her attacks come without warning, even at home alone (DSM-5-TR, p. 236).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Panic disorder, pp. 235-236; generalized anxiety disorder, pp. 250-251
MSD Manual Professional: Panic Attacks and Panic Disorder

questions.topic: Anxiety disorders: generalized anxiety disorder treatment
questions.stem: A 38-year-old teacher has worried most days for the past 8 months about her job, her children's safety, money, and her parents' health. She knows the worry is out of proportion but cannot turn it off. She feels keyed up, has tense shoulders, tires easily, has trouble concentrating, and sleeps poorly. She has never had a panic attack. Physical exam, TSH, and a urine drug screen are normal. She asks for a medicine she can take every day.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line medication?
questions.explanation: Answer: escitalopram. Why: she has generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). DSM-5-TR (pp. 250-251) requires too much worry about many events or activities on most days for 6 months or longer, worry that is hard to control, and at least 3 of 6 symptoms in adults: restlessness or feeling on edge, tiring easily, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and poor sleep. It must cause distress or trouble functioning and not be due to a substance, a medical condition such as hyperthyroidism, or another mental disorder. The MSD Manual (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) says SSRIs and SNRIs are the preferred medications for GAD and names escitalopram and venlafaxine as examples. It adds that buspirone may also work, that cognitive behavioral therapy is the most effective form of psychotherapy, and that GAD is twice as common in women as in men.

whyWrong.b: Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam relieve anxiety quickly but carry risks of dependence and withdrawal, so they are not first-line daily treatment for GAD (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Haloperidol is an antipsychotic; she has no psychotic symptoms (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, not a treatment for GAD (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Propranolol can blunt physical symptoms such as tremor in performance anxiety, but it does not treat the ongoing worry of GAD (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Generalized anxiety disorder, pp. 250-251
MSD Manual Professional: Generalized Anxiety Disorder

questions.stem: A 21-year-old college student has intrusive thoughts that she will spread germs and make other people sick. She washes her hands about 40 times a day, for about 3 hours in total, until the skin cracks and bleeds. She knows the washing is excessive but feels intense anxiety if she tries to stop. She is starting an SSRI.
questions.leadIn: Which form of psychotherapy is most likely to help her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Answer: exposure and response prevention (ERP). Why: she has obsessive-compulsive disorder. DSM-5-TR (pp. 265-266) describes obsessions as repeated, unwanted thoughts, urges, or images that cause marked anxiety and that the person tries to ignore, push away, or cancel out. Compulsions are repeated actions (such as hand washing) or mental acts that the person feels driven to do in response to an obsession, to reduce distress or prevent a feared event, even though they are not realistically connected to it or are clearly excessive. The symptoms must take a lot of time (for example, more than 1 hour a day) or cause distress or trouble functioning. The MSD Manual (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder) says the key part of exposure and ritual prevention therapy is gradual exposure to the feared situations while the patient holds back from doing the rituals. It adds that SSRIs and clomipramine are often very effective, and that an SSRI is usually tried first. MSD also notes that most people with OCD recognize, at least partly, that their obsessive beliefs are not realistic.

whyWrong.b: Psychodynamic therapy explores past conflicts; it is not the evidence-based therapy for OCD (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Dialectical behavior therapy was built for borderline personality disorder and self-harm, not OCD (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Interpersonal psychotherapy targets relationship problems and is used mainly for depression (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing is a therapy for trauma-related symptoms, not OCD; for OCD, MSD names exposure with ritual prevention (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Obsessive-compulsive disorder, pp. 265-266
MSD Manual Professional: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after shouting at strangers that he has been chosen to fix the world's economy. For the past 4 days he has slept about 2 hours a night but says he feels full of energy. He has spent his savings on business supplies, talks so fast that he is hard to interrupt, and jumps from topic to topic. He is admitted to the hospital for his safety. He has never had a depressive episode. A urine drug screen is negative.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: bipolar I disorder. Why: DSM-5-TR (pp. 139-140) needs only one lifetime manic episode for bipolar I disorder; depressive or hypomanic episodes may come before or after it but are not required. A manic episode is a distinct period of abnormally high, expansive, or irritable mood with a rise in energy or activity, for 1 week or longer, or any length of time if hospitalization is needed. During it, at least 3 symptoms are present (4 if the mood is only irritable), such as grandiosity, less need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, more goal-directed activity, and risky spending. The episode must cause marked impairment, need hospitalization, or include psychotic features, and must not be due to a substance. His episode lasted only 4 days, but he needed hospitalization, so it counts as mania. The MSD Manual (Bipolar Disorders) agrees that bipolar I requires at least one manic episode, that mania lasts 1 week or more (or less if hospitalization is needed), and that most patients also have depressive episodes.

whyWrong.c: Bipolar II needs at least one major depressive episode plus hypomania and no mania ever (MSD Manual); he has had mania and no depression.
whyWrong.b: Cyclothymic disorder involves more than 2 years of milder hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet full episode criteria (MSD Manual).
whyWrong.d: Brief psychotic disorder involves psychotic symptoms without a full manic syndrome; his decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and spending spree make this a manic episode (DSM-5-TR, p. 140).
whyWrong.e: Major depressive disorder requires depressive episodes and no history of mania; he has had no depression (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Bipolar I disorder: manic episode, pp. 139-140
MSD Manual Professional: Bipolar Disorders

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is in the hospital 2 days after a knee replacement. He is now anxious, sweaty, and shaky, and he cannot sleep. His pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 164/96 mm Hg. He has a coarse tremor of both hands and says he saw bugs crawling on the wall, although he knows where he is and the date. His wife says he drinks 8 to 10 beers every day. Blood glucose is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug treatment now?
questions.explanation: Answer: lorazepam. Why: he has alcohol withdrawal. DSM-5-TR (pp. 564-565) requires stopping or cutting down heavy, long-term drinking and, within several hours to a few days, at least 2 of these: autonomic hyperactivity (such as sweating or a pulse over 100/min), more hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, brief hallucinations or illusions, agitation, anxiety, or generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Hallucinations with intact reality testing and no delirium count as withdrawal with perceptual disturbances. He has stopped drinking because he is in the hospital. The MSD Manual (Alcohol Toxicity and Withdrawal) says benzodiazepines are the mainstay of treatment, with diazepam, lorazepam, or chlordiazepoxide as options. It adds that symptoms usually start within about 6 hours of stopping, seizures generally come 6 to 48 hours after the last drink, and delirium tremens usually starts 48 to 72 hours after. MSD also gives thiamine 100 mg IV with IV fluids to treat or prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

whyWrong.b: Haloperidol may calm hallucinations but does not treat the withdrawal itself and can lower the seizure threshold (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Naltrexone lowers craving to help maintain sobriety in alcohol use disorder; it does not treat acute withdrawal (standard teaching).
whyWrong.d: Disulfiram makes drinking unpleasant to discourage relapse; it has no role in treating acute withdrawal (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures; benzodiazepines do (standard teaching).

sources.title: DSM-5-TR (Emily's file), Alcohol withdrawal, pp. 564-565
MSD Manual Professional: Alcohol Toxicity and Withdrawal

questions.topic: GI histology: Brunner glands identify the duodenum
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has upper endoscopy for indigestion. A biopsy is taken from the small intestine. Under the microscope, the mucosa has finger-like villi and crypts. Beneath the mucosa, in the submucosa, are clusters of branched glands made of pale, mucus-filled cells. Their ducts empty into the crypts.
questions.leadIn: This biopsy most likely came from which part of the GI tract?
questions.explanation: Answer: the duodenum. Why: glands in the submucosa are the key clue. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 297) explain that the duodenal (Brunner) glands sit in the submucosa of the duodenum and release alkaline mucus that neutralizes the acidic chyme coming from the stomach. StatPearls (Anatomy, Small Intestine) agrees that the duodenum is the only part of the gut with submucosal Brunner glands, and that they secrete bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid before the chyme reaches the jejunum. The villi show this is small intestine, and the submucosal glands narrow it to the duodenum.

whyWrong.b: The jejunum has villi and crypts but no submucosal Brunner glands; StatPearls says the duodenum is the only part of the gut that has them.
whyWrong.c: The ileum has villi but no Brunner glands; its clue is many lymphoid nodules (Peyer patches), per StatPearls (Anatomy, Small Intestine).
whyWrong.d: The gastric antrum has pits and glands but no villi (standard teaching); its glands lie in the mucosa, not the submucosa.
whyWrong.e: The colon has crypts full of goblet cells but no villi (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Small intestine histology (duodenal glands), p. 297
StatPearls: Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis, Small Intestine

questions.topic: GI histology: Paneth cells in the crypts
questions.stem: A pathologist examines a normal biopsy from the terminal ileum. At the very bottom of the crypts are clusters of cells packed with large, bright red (eosinophilic) granules in the part of the cell facing the crypt lumen.
questions.leadIn: The main job of these cells is to do which of the following?

options.text: Secrete alkaline mucus to neutralize acid
Release secretin when acid enters the gut
Carry antigens to the lymphoid tissue below
Absorb nutrients across a brush border

questions.explanation: Answer: release defensins and lysozyme, which act against microbes. Why: these are Paneth cells. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 297) place Paneth cells deep in the intestinal crypts and say they release defensins and lysozyme to protect against pathogens. StatPearls (Anatomy, Small Intestine) agrees that Paneth cells are found in the crypts of Lieberkühn and secrete antimicrobial peptides such as defensins and lysozyme. Their large red-staining granules hold these proteins (standard teaching).

whyWrong.b: Alkaline mucus comes from the Brunner glands in the duodenal submucosa (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 297), not from cells at the base of ileal crypts.
whyWrong.c: Secretin comes from enteroendocrine S cells in the proximal small intestine (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 306).
whyWrong.d: Carrying antigens to the lymphoid tissue is the job of M cells over Peyer patches, which take up antigens and pass them to antigen-presenting cells (StatPearls, Peyer Patches).
whyWrong.e: Absorptive cells with microvilli line the villi, not the crypt bases (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 297).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Small intestine histology (Paneth cells), p. 297
StatPearls: Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis, Small Intestine

questions.topic: Mucosal immunity: Peyer patches and M cells
questions.stem: A 22-year-old man develops fever and abdominal pain 2 weeks after returning from travel. Blood cultures grow Salmonella Typhi. He later needs surgery for a perforation of the terminal ileum. The pathologist finds ulcers over oval clusters of lymphoid tissue in the wall of the ileum.
questions.leadIn: In a healthy ileum, these lymphoid clusters mainly do which of the following?

options.text: Make IgA plasma cells from M-cell antigens
Release defensins and lysozyme from crypt bases
Secrete bicarbonate-rich mucus into the lumen
Filter old red blood cells from the circulation
Produce IgE that protects against parasites

questions.explanation: Answer: they make IgA plasma cells after M cells sample antigen. Why: the lymphoid clusters are Peyer patches. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 297) describe Peyer patches as lymphatic tissue in the lamina propria, mostly in the ileum, made mainly of dividing B cells that release IgA to protect against harmful bacteria. StatPearls (Peyer Patches) agrees that they sit in the lamina propria and submucosa of the distal small intestine, with almost half in the distal ileum. It explains that M cells take in antigens and bring them to antigen-presenting cells, and that B cells in the germinal centers become IgA-secreting plasma cells. It also notes that in Salmonella Typhi infection, the intestinal necrosis happens at the Peyer patches, which explains his ileal perforation.

whyWrong.b: Defensins and lysozyme come from Paneth cells at the base of the crypts (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 297).
whyWrong.c: Bicarbonate-rich mucus comes from Brunner glands in the duodenum (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 297).
whyWrong.d: Removing old red blood cells is a job of the spleen's red pulp, not of gut lymphoid tissue (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Peyer patches are known for IgA, the main antibody at mucosal surfaces (StatPearls, Peyer Patches); IgE against parasites is not their main product (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Small intestine histology (Peyer patches), p. 297
StatPearls: Peyer Patches

questions.topic: Liver histology: stellate (Ito) cells and fibrosis
questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has had chronic hepatitis C for 25 years. A liver biopsy shows thick bands of collagen dividing the liver into nodules of regenerating hepatocytes. The pathologist explains that one type of cell, which normally stores fat in the space between the hepatocytes and the sinusoids, changed into a collagen-making cell.
questions.leadIn: Which cell type is the main source of this scar tissue?
questions.explanation: Answer: hepatic stellate (Ito) cells. Why: your Osmosis GI notes (p. 104) explain that in cirrhosis, damage to the liver activates stellate cells, which sit between the sinusoids and the hepatocytes in the perisinusoidal space. They release TGF-beta 1, which turns them into myofibroblasts that lay down scar, and they release TIMP 1 and 2, which block the enzymes that would break the scar down. Bands of fibrous tissue then cut the liver into regenerating nodules. Your Osmosis physiology notes (p. 334) add that stellate (Ito) cells are scattered among the hepatocytes, are the main storage site for vitamin A, control the turnover of the liver's extracellular matrix, and are responsible for cirrhosis. StatPearls (Physiology, Liver) agrees that Ito cells sit in the space of Disse and store fat such as vitamin A, and that the fibrosis in cirrhosis comes from TGF-beta released by Ito cells. The MSD Manual (Hepatic Fibrosis) adds that activation of these fat-storing Ito cells starts fibrosis, and that they become contractile myofibroblasts that make too much collagen and other matrix.

whyWrong.b: Kupffer cells are the liver's own macrophages and line the sinusoids (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 334); they protect against gut germs and release inflammatory signals, but stellate cells make the collagen (your Osmosis physiology notes, p. 334).
whyWrong.c: Injured hepatocytes form regenerative nodules between the fibrous bands (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 104); they are not the cells that make the scar.
whyWrong.d: Bile duct cells line the bile ducts and do not normally store fat in the space of Disse (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: Sinusoidal endothelial cells line the sinusoids; the fat-storing cell in the space of Disse is the stellate cell (StatPearls, Physiology, Liver).

Osmosis High-Yield Physiology notes (Emily's file), Liver cells, p. 334

questions.stem: A 3-week-old girl is evaluated for being very floppy and having seizures. She has a high forehead, a large anterior fontanelle, wide skull sutures, and an enlarged liver. Her parents are healthy first cousins. Blood tests show high levels of very-long-chain fatty acids and low levels of plasmalogens.
questions.leadIn: A defect in which organelle best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: the peroxisome. Why: this is Zellweger syndrome. Your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes (p. 195) list the jobs of peroxisomes: beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, alpha-oxidation, breakdown of branched-chain fatty acids, and making cholesterol, bile acids, and plasmalogens (membrane lipids that matter most in the brain's white matter). Zellweger syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder of peroxisome formation caused by mutated PEX genes. Infants cannot form myelin properly in the brain. Your notes list wide sutures, a large anterior fontanelle, low muscle tone, seizures, an enlarged liver, and death within months. The MSD Manual (Peroxisomal Disorders) agrees that the defect is in 1 of at least 12 genes for forming peroxisomes or importing proteins into them. It lists high very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid, and pipecolate with low plasmalogens, and says peroxisomal disorders other than X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy are autosomal recessive and have no specific treatment.

whyWrong.b: Lysosomal storage diseases trap undigested material inside lysosomes; they do not raise very-long-chain fatty acids or lower plasmalogens (standard teaching).
whyWrong.c: Mitochondria break down shorter fatty acids, but very-long-chain fatty acids must first be shortened in peroxisomes (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 195).
whyWrong.d: The Golgi tags proteins with mannose-6-phosphate to send them to lysosomes, the step that fails in I-cell disease (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, pp. 43-44); it does not break down very-long-chain fatty acids.
whyWrong.e: The smooth ER makes lipids and steroids and detoxifies drugs (standard teaching), but plasmalogen synthesis and very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation are peroxisomal jobs (your El-Husseiny biochemistry notes, p. 195).
