MSD Manual Professional: Peroxisomal Disorders

questions.topic: Lower limb nerves: superior gluteal nerve and Trendelenburg sign
questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has trouble walking 6 weeks after surgery on her right hip. When she stands on her right leg alone, her left hip drops. When she walks, she leans her trunk toward the right with each step. Hip extension and knee extension are strong, and sensation is normal.
questions.leadIn: Injury to which nerve best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: the right superior gluteal nerve. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 53-54) explain that the superior gluteal nerve (L4 to S1) supplies the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae, which abduct the thigh and keep the pelvis level. When these muscles are weak, standing on the affected leg lets the pelvis sag toward the opposite, unsupported side (a positive Trendelenburg sign). When walking, the patient leans toward the affected side to make up for the hip drop. Your notes add that the nerve can be hurt by injections into the upper inner part of the buttock, and that the upper outer quadrant is the safer site. StatPearls (Trendelenburg Sign) agrees that the gluteus medius and minimus are the main hip abductors, that the superior gluteal nerve supplies them, and that in a positive test the pelvis drops on the unaffected side. It lists nerve damage after surgery among the causes. Her left hip drops when she stands on her right leg, so the weak side is the right.

whyWrong.b: If the left superior gluteal nerve were injured, her right hip would drop when she stood on her left leg; the weak side is the stance side (StatPearls, Trendelenburg Sign).
whyWrong.c: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus maximus; injury weakens hip extension and makes climbing stairs and rising from a chair hard (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 54). Her hip extension is strong.
whyWrong.d: The femoral nerve supplies the front of the thigh for hip flexion and knee extension (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 45-46); her knee extension is strong.
whyWrong.e: The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh muscles for adduction (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 44), not the abductors that keep the pelvis level.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Superior and inferior gluteal nerves, pp. 53-54
El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Obturator and femoral nerves, pp. 44-46
StatPearls: Trendelenburg Sign

questions.topic: Knee injuries: anterior cruciate ligament tear
questions.stem: A 19-year-old soccer player felt a pop in her right knee when she planted her foot and quickly changed direction. Her knee swelled up within 2 hours. On exam, with the knee bent about 20 degrees, the examiner can pull her tibia forward relative to the femur much more than on the other side.
questions.leadIn: Which structure is most likely torn?
questions.explanation: Answer: the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 60, 62) explain that the ACL runs from the lateral femoral condyle to the front of the tibia and stops the tibia from sliding forward. ACL tears are common in young athletes in sports with quick changes of direction, such as soccer and basketball. Patients feel a pop, the knee fills with blood within a short time (hemarthrosis), and it feels unstable. The tibia can be pulled forward on the femur: with the knee bent 20 degrees this is the Lachman test, and with it bent 90 degrees it is the anterior drawer test. MRI confirms the diagnosis. The MSD Manual (Knee Sprains and Meniscal Injuries) agrees that some patients hear or feel a pop and that the Lachman test is the most sensitive physical test for an acute ACL tear. Other source: your notes call both the Lachman test and the anterior drawer test highly sensitive and specific; MSD says the anterior drawer test is less sensitive and specific than the Lachman test.

whyWrong.b: The PCL runs from the medial femoral condyle to the back of the tibia and stops the tibia from sliding backward; it is tested with the posterior drawer test (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, pp. 60, 62).
whyWrong.c: The MCL resists valgus stress, so an MCL tear causes laxity when the knee is pushed inward, not forward tibial movement (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 60).
whyWrong.d: The LCL resists varus stress; it does not stop forward sliding of the tibia (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 60).
whyWrong.e: A meniscal tear causes catching, locking, and joint-line pain, with swelling that comes on slowly (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 63); it does not let the tibia slide forward.

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Knee injury and ACL injury, pp. 60, 62
MSD Manual Professional: Knee Sprains and Meniscal Injuries

questions.stem: A 24-year-old basketball player twisted his left knee while his foot was planted. He felt a pop and pain, but the knee did not swell until the next morning. Since then the knee sometimes catches and locks when he straightens it. There is tenderness along the inner (medial) joint line. A Lachman test is normal. Rotating the bent knee while straightening it causes a painful click.
questions.leadIn: Which structure is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: Answer: the medial meniscus. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 63) explain that medial meniscus tears in young people often happen when the knee twists while the foot stays planted, and that the medial meniscus is injured more often than the lateral. Patients report a pop and then pain, with catching, locking, and less range of motion when a torn piece gets stuck between the femur and tibia. Because the meniscus does not have a direct blood supply, the swelling usually takes many hours to show up. The exam shows tenderness along the joint line on the injured side, and tests such as McMurray and Thessaly can cause locking or catching. The MSD Manual (Knee Sprains and Meniscal Injuries) agrees that weight bearing with rotation usually injures the menisci, that medial meniscal injuries cause medial joint line tenderness and locking, and that the McMurray test is positive when it causes a painful click or locking.

whyWrong.b: An ACL tear causes rapid swelling from bleeding into the joint and a positive Lachman test (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 62); his swelling was slow and his Lachman test is normal.
whyWrong.c: A PCL tear lets the tibia slide backward (positive posterior drawer test) and does not cause catching or locking (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 62).
whyWrong.d: The LCL is on the outer side of the knee and resists varus stress (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 60); his tenderness is on the inner side.
whyWrong.e: A patellar tendon tear causes loss of active knee extension, not locking with medial joint line pain (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Meniscal tear, p. 63
MSD Manual Professional: Knee Sprains and Meniscal Injuries

questions.stem: A 50-year-old house painter has had right shoulder pain for 4 months. It is worst when he reaches overhead and when he raises his arm out to the side between about 60 and 120 degrees. When he holds his arms out at shoulder height, angled slightly forward, with his thumbs pointing down, pushing down on the right arm causes pain and weakness.
questions.leadIn: The tendon of which muscle is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Answer: the supraspinatus. Why: your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (pp. 29, 31) explain that the supraspinatus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve, starts arm abduction before the deltoid takes over, and is the most common rotator cuff injury. Because it sits on top of the humeral head, its tendon gets pinched between the humeral head and the acromion with repeated overhead movement, such as painting ceilings. The empty-can test, done with the arm abducted, angled forward, and thumbs down, causes pain and weakness on the injured side. The MSD Manual (Rotator Cuff Injury/Subacromial Bursitis) agrees that the supraspinatus tendon is especially prone to injury from chronic impingement under the coracoacromial arch, especially with repeated overhead activity. It adds that pain is usually worst between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction (the painful arc), and that the supraspinatus is tested by having the patient resist downward pressure on the arms with the thumbs pointing down.

whyWrong.b: The infraspinatus rotates the arm outward and is linked to pitching injuries (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 29); the empty-can test targets the supraspinatus.
whyWrong.c: The teres minor (axillary nerve) helps with adduction and outward rotation (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 29), not the first part of abduction.
whyWrong.d: The subscapularis rotates the arm inward and adducts it (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 29); it sits in front of the joint, not under the acromion.
whyWrong.e: The deltoid is not a rotator cuff muscle, and its tendon is not pinched under the acromion (standard teaching).

sources.title: El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Rotator cuff muscles and rotator cuff syndrome, pp. 29, 31
MSD Manual Professional: Rotator Cuff Injury/Subacromial Bursitis

questions.stem: A 68-year-old thin woman has had nausea, vomiting, and a swollen belly for 1 day. She has a firm, tender lump in her right groin that she cannot push back in. The lump lies below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Imaging shows a loop of small bowel trapped in the hernia.
questions.leadIn: The hernia most likely passes through which of the following?

options.text: The femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein
The deep inguinal ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
Hesselbach triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
The obturator canal in the pelvic wall
A defect at the base of the umbilical ring

questions.explanation: Answer: the femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein. Why: this is a femoral hernia. Your Osmosis GI notes (p. 75) describe intestine pushing through the femoral canal next to the femoral artery and vein, below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Your notes list female sex, obesity, pregnancy, and frequent heavy lifting as risk factors, and explain that the narrow femoral canal raises the risk of incarceration and strangulation, which can cause bowel obstruction. A review by Akrami and colleagues agrees that femoral hernias lie medial to the femoral vessels and below the inguinal ligament, that the lacunar ligament forms the inner edge of the femoral ring, that they are more common in women, and that the narrow femoral canal gives them a high risk of strangulation.

whyWrong.b: An indirect inguinal hernia enters through the deep (internal) inguinal ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels (your Osmosis GI notes, pp. 78-79); inguinal hernias lie above the inguinal ligament.
whyWrong.c: A direct inguinal hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, with the inguinal ligament as its lower border (your Osmosis GI notes, pp. 78-79).
whyWrong.d: An obturator hernia passes through the obturator canal deep in the pelvis and does not cause a lump below the inguinal ligament lateral to the pubic tubercle (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: An umbilical hernia comes through the navel, not the groin (standard teaching).

sources.title: Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal (Emily's file), Femoral hernia, p. 75
Osmosis High-Yield Pathology Notes: Gastrointestinal (Emily's file), Inguinal hernias, pp. 78-79

questions.stem: A newborn boy has a gap in the left side of his upper lip that runs up into the nostril. His hard and soft palate are intact. His mother took phenytoin for epilepsy throughout the pregnancy.
questions.leadIn: Failure of which embryonic structures to fuse best explains this finding?
questions.explanation: Answer: the maxillary and medial nasal prominences. Why: Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 167-168) explain that cleft lip and palate come from improper fusion of the facial bones and nearby tissues. A cleft can be only in the lip, only in the palate, or both. Your notes list Patau syndrome, anticonvulsant drugs, folate deficiency, and low oxygen in the womb as risk factors. Complications include speech problems, ear infections, and trouble feeding, and folate in pregnancy lowers the risk. StatPearls (Embryology, Face) explains that the medial nasal processes fuse with the maxillary processes around the 6th week to form the middle part of the upper lip and jaw, and that an orofacial cleft forms when these processes fail to fuse. Your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes (p. 2) explain that the lip and palate form in weeks 5 to 6. First the two medial nasal prominences fuse into the midline intermaxillary segment, and then each maxillary prominence fuses with that segment to form the upper lip. If one maxillary prominence fails to fuse with it, a cleft lip forms on that side, and your notes say this happens more often on the left. The MSD Manual (Cleft Lip and Cleft Palate) adds that oral clefts are the most common birth defects of the head and neck, at about 1 in 600 to 1000 live births. It also notes that antiseizure drugs that act against folate, such as phenytoin, valproate, and carbamazepine, may call for higher folate doses. Other source: your notes say the lip is closed by about 3 months of age; MSD says repair has traditionally been done at 3 to 6 months.

whyWrong.b: Cleft palate comes from palatine shelves that fail to fuse with each other or with the primary palate (your El-Husseiny musculoskeletal notes, p. 2); StatPearls (Embryology, Face) says these shelves fuse by the end of the 8th week. His palate is intact.
whyWrong.c: The mandibular prominences form the lower jaw and lower lip (standard teaching), not the upper lip.
whyWrong.d: Problems with the first and second pharyngeal arches affect the jaw, ear, and face more widely (for example, Treacher Collins syndrome), not an isolated upper lip cleft (standard teaching).
whyWrong.e: The upper lip forms where the medial nasal processes meet the maxillary processes (StatPearls, Embryology, Face); the mandibular prominences form the lower jaw and do not take part (standard teaching).

El-Husseiny's Essentials for USMLE Step 1: Musculoskeletal System (Emily's file), Cleft lip and cleft palate (embryology), p. 2
StatPearls: Embryology, Face
MSD Manual Professional: Cleft Lip and Cleft Palate

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman who smokes has a routine ultrasound at 20 weeks of pregnancy. Her serum alpha-fetoprotein is high. The ultrasound shows loops of fetal bowel floating freely in the amniotic fluid, with no covering membrane. The defect is just to the right of a normally placed umbilical cord.
questions.leadIn: This defect most likely results from which of the following?

options.text: Failure of the lateral body folds to fuse
Failure of the midgut to return from the cord
Failed neural crest migration into the bowel
Failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to close

questions.explanation: Answer: failure of the lateral body folds to fuse. Why: this is gastroschisis. Your Osmosis GI notes (pp. 123-124) explain that around week 4 the lateral folds fail to fuse, leaving a hole in the abdominal wall near the umbilicus through which organs push out, most often on the right side and usually small intestine. Risk factors include a young mother and exposure to alcohol or tobacco. The exposed bowel can become inflamed from the amniotic fluid. Maternal serum AFP is high, and surgery returns the organs and closes the wall. The MSD Manual (Gastroschisis) agrees that it is a full-thickness defect beside the umbilicus, usually to the right of where the cord inserts, with no membrane over the bowel. It adds that other birth defects are uncommon (10 to 15%), though GI problems such as malrotation and atresia occur in about 25%, and that gastroschisis is more common than omphalocele.

whyWrong.b: Failure of the midgut to return from the umbilical cord gives an omphalocele, which MSD describes as a midline defect at the base of the umbilicus, covered by a membrane; your notes put it as 'midgut doesn't return' (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 132).
whyWrong.c: A vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct that does not close properly causes a Meckel diverticulum (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 130), not an open abdominal wall.
whyWrong.d: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the bowel causes Hirschsprung disease (your Osmosis GI notes, p. 125).
whyWrong.e: Failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to close causes a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, with bowel in the chest (standard teaching).
